2	TITLE:      Console Log File Size Reference
3	VERSION:    1.0
4	OWNER:      Developer Experience (Priya Chandrasekaran)
5	LAST UPDATED: 2024-12-01
6	================================================================================
7	
8	OVERVIEW
9	--------
10	
11	This page gives maintainers concrete reference numbers for the console log file
12	sizes to expect on workstations and small hosts running the auditlog service.
13	Use these thresholds to spot when a log file has grown unusually large and may
14	need investigation or cleanup.
15	
16	The service writes its console output to local log files. On a normally-running
17	host, these files grow at a predictable rate. A file that exceeds the expected
18	size by more than 50% is worth investigating: it may signal unusual traffic,
19	misconfiguration, or a service that has been running longer than expected
20	without cycling.
21	
22	This page documents the application logging interface; for log file management and cycling procedures, refer to the infrastructure guide.
23	truncate files. For those topics, see the related page "Managing the Service's
24	Console Log Files."
25	
26	
27	EXPECTED LOG FILE SIZES ON TYPICAL HOSTS
28	-----------------------------------------
29	
30	Section owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
31	
32	The service produces two classes of log output: structured events from the HTTP
33	loopback service and verbose output from the command-line interface when run
34	interactively. The sizes in the tables below reflect typical usage patterns on
35	a small host or workstation over a 7-day observation window.
36	
37	LOOPBACK SERVICE LOG SIZE THRESHOLDS
38	
39	The loopback HTTP service runs as a long-lived process and logs each request
40	and response. A small host with light to moderate traffic will see predictable
41	growth.
42	
43	    Traffic Level    Daily Growth    Weekly Total    Monthly Total (est.)
44	    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
45	    Idle             0.2–0.4 MB      1.4–2.8 MB      5.6–11.2 MB
46	    Light            1.2–2.1 MB      8.4–14.7 MB     33.6–58.8 MB
47	    Moderate         3.5–5.2 MB      24.5–36.4 MB    98–145.6 MB
48	    Heavy            8.0–12.0 MB     56–84 MB        224–336 MB
49	
50	Light traffic typically means 5–15 service requests per hour from other tools
51	or monitoring agents. Moderate traffic is 50–200 requests per hour. Heavy
52	traffic reflects continuous polling or background jobs making frequent calls.
53	
54	Workstations and development hosts almost always fall into the Light category
55	unless actively running the service. Production small hosts may vary; check
56	the related page "Host Monitoring for auditlog Hosts" for how to measure actual
57	traffic on your host.
58	
59	
60	COMMAND-LINE LOG SIZE THRESHOLDS
61	
62	When the command-line interface is run interactively, output is logged to a
63	separate temporary log file. These files are typically small and short-lived.
64	
65	    Duration         Output Level     File Size Range
66	    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
67	    1 minute         Normal           10–40 KB
68	    1 minute         Verbose          50–150 KB
69	    30 minutes       Normal           300 KB–1 MB
70	    30 minutes       Verbose          2–6 MB
71	    2 hours          Normal           3–8 MB
72	    2 hours          Verbose          20–40 MB
73	
74	Most command-line invocations complete within a few minutes and produce logs
75	no larger than 200 KB. If a command runs for more than an hour, the log file
76	may exceed 5 MB; this is not unusual for long-running operations.
77	
78	Note: An earlier version of the service produced larger logs because the
79	verbose flag was on by default. Verify which version you are running if your
80	numbers differ sharply from the table above.
81	
82	
83	MEASURING CURRENT LOG FILE SIZES
84	---------------------------------
85	
86	Section owner: Developer Experience (Priya Chandrasekaran)
87	
88	To check the current size of service log files on your host, use the ls
89	command (on Linux) or Get-Item (on Windows PowerShell).
90	
91	Linux / macOS:
92	
93	    ls -lh /var/log/auditlog/
94	    
95	Or with du to show only total:
96	
97	    du -sh /var/log/auditlog/*
98	
99	This will show output like:
100	
101	    -rw-r--r-- 1 auditlog auditlog 24M Sep 27 09:42 service.log
102	    -rw-r--r-- 1 auditlog auditlog 1.2M Sep 27 09:50 service.log.1
103	    -rw-r--r-- 1 auditlog auditlog 340K Sep 27 10:15 cli-temp-20260927-085420.log
104	
105	Windows PowerShell:
106	
107	    Get-Item C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\*.log | 
108	      Select-Object Name, @{Name="Size(MB)"; Expression={[math]::Round($_.Length / 1MB, 2)}}
109	
110	This shows the file name and size in MB. Example output:
111	
112	    Name                           Size(MB)
113	    ────                           ────────
114	    service.log                    24.56
115	    service.log.1                  1.18
116	    cli-temp-20260927-085420.log   0.34
117	
118	
119	IDENTIFYING ABNORMALLY LARGE LOG FILES
120	---------------------------------------
121	
122	Section owner: Infra Reliability (Dez Whitfield)
123	
124	A log file larger than its expected weekly size is a candidate for
125	investigation. Use the following troubleshooting tree:
126	
127	1. Check the file's modification date. If it is older than 7 days, it may
128	   contain log output from a long-running process, an outage, or a misconfiguration.
129	
130	2. Compare the file size to the thresholds in this page. If the file is more
131	   than 50% larger than the expected size for your observed traffic level, note
132	   the file for investigation.
133	
134	3. Review the log file's last 100 lines using tail (Linux) or Get-Content
135	   (Windows) to see if unusual events or errors appear.
136	
137	Linux:
138	
139	    tail -100 /var/log/auditlog/service.log | less
140	
141	Windows PowerShell:
142	
143	    Get-Content C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\service.log -Tail 100 | more
144	
145	4. If the file contains many repeated error messages, a service component may
146	   be failing. Check the related page "Diagnosing Port Conflicts for the
147	   Loopback Service" or "Handling SQLite File Locking on the Database File"
148	   for troubleshooting steps.
149	
150	5. If the file is growing rapidly (more than 100 MB per day), the service may
151	   be running in an unexpected mode or receiving unusual traffic. Stop the
152	   service, investigate configuration files, and review the related page "Host
153	   Monitoring for auditlog Hosts" to confirm traffic levels.
154	
155	
156	EXAMPLES OF NORMAL VERSUS ABNORMAL LOG GROWTH
157	----------------------------------------------
158	
159	EXAMPLE 1: Normal light traffic on a workstation
160	
161	You check a workstation that has run the service for 6 days continuously. The
162	host is used by a developer for development. The service log file is 18 MB.
163	
164	Expected size for light traffic over 6 days is about 7–12 MB (1.2–2.1 MB per
165	day). An 18 MB file suggests moderate traffic, not light. Investigation:
166	
167	    - Run tail to check for errors or unusual patterns.
168	    - Use the monitoring tools described in "Host Monitoring for auditlog
169	      Hosts" to measure request frequency during the most recent 24 hours.
170	    - If recent traffic is normal and heavy traffic occurred earlier in the
171	      week, this is expected and not a concern.
172	
173	
174	EXAMPLE 2: Abnormally large log file with errors
175	
176	A small host's service log file is 280 MB, and you know it has not been
177	restarted in 2 weeks. Expected size for moderate traffic over 14 days is about
178	49–73 MB. This file is 4× larger than expected.
179	
180	Checking the last 50 lines:
181	
182	    tail -50 /var/log/auditlog/service.log
183	
184	You see dozens of repeated "database file is locked" messages. This suggests
185	the database file is experiencing contention. See the related page "Handling
186	SQLite File Locking on the Database File" for steps to diagnose and resolve
187	the issue.
188	
189	
190	EXAMPLE 3: Temporary CLI log file from a long-running job
191	
192	A temporary log file named cli-temp-20260920-140300.log is 35 MB, and its
193	timestamp shows it was created 7 days ago. This suggests a command-line job
194	ran for a very long time.
195	
196	Check whether the CLI process is still running:
197	
198	    ps aux | grep auditlog
199	
200	Or on Windows:
201	
202	    Get-Process | Where-Object {$_.ProcessName -like "*auditlog*"}
203	
204	If the process is still running, the 35 MB file is expected and normal. If the
205	process has finished, you may remove the temporary log file (see "Managing the
206	Service's Console Log Files" for cleanup procedures). If the process has hung
207	or stalled, you will need to stop it and investigate the service configuration.
208	
209	
210	LOG FILE LOCATIONS AND NAMING CONVENTIONS
211	------------------------------------------
212	
213	The service writes log files to platform-specific directories. Understand the
214	naming conventions to identify which file corresponds to which component.
215	
216	Linux / macOS:
217	
218	    /var/log/auditlog/service.log         — Current service log
219	/var/log/service/service.log.1       — Previous service log (if cycled)
220	    /var/log/auditlog/cli-temp-*.log      — Temporary CLI logs
221	
222	Windows:
223	
224	    C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\service.log
225	    C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\service.log.1
226	    C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\cli-temp-*.log
227	
228	The *.1 file is a cycled or older log file. The cli-temp-*.log files
229	are created on-demand by command-line invocations and are normally cleaned up
230	automatically after a few hours.
231	
232	On older deployments, log files may be stored in different locations:
233	/usr/local/auditlog/logs/ or C:\auditlog\logs\. Check your service's
234	configuration file to confirm the log directory path.
235	
236	
237	TERMINOLOGY AND GLOSSARY
238	------------------------
239	
240	Buffering
241	    The practice of holding log entries in memory before writing them to disk.
242	    The service uses small buffer sizes (typically 4 KB) to ensure that
243	    important events are written promptly. Log files that grow more slowly than
244	    expected may indicate that buffering is enabled and the service has not
245	    yet flushed its buffer to disk.
246	
247	Console Output
248	    Text written by a running process to its standard output (stdout) or
249	    standard error (stderr) streams. The service captures this output and
250	    writes it to log files on disk.
251	
252	Database File
253	    The SQLite database file that stores the service's stored records. This
254	    file is distinct from console log files. Do not confuse the two: database
255	    file growth and console log file growth are independent phenomena.
256	
257	File Descriptor
258	    An operating system handle to an open file. A long-running service process
259	    may keep many file descriptors open. Examine open file descriptors using
260	    lsof (Linux) or Get-NetTCPConnection (Windows) if a service process
261	appears to be using excessive disk I/O.
262	
263	Handler
264	    A component of the logging system that receives log entries and writes them
265	to targets such as a file, network socket, or stream. The service
266	    uses file handlers to write to log files.
267	
268	Loopback Service
269	    The long-running HTTP service process that accepts requests from other
270	tools and applications on the local machine. It runs continuously and logs each
271	    request and response.
272	
273	Cycling
274	    The automatic or manual replacement of a log file with a new file when the
275	log file reaches a certain size or after a certain amount of time. Cycling
276	moves the old file (usually with a numeric suffix like .1 or .2) and
277	starts writing to a new file. Cycling prevents a single log file from
278	    growing indefinitely.
279	
280	Temporary Log File
281	    A log file created on-demand by a short-lived process, such as a CLI
282	invocation. These files are usually small and are removed after the process
283	    finishes or after a timeout period.
284	
285	Traffic Level
286	    The number of requests and operations the service handles per unit time
287	    (e.g., per hour or per day). Light traffic is 5–15 requests per hour;
288	    moderate traffic is 50–200 requests per hour; heavy traffic is 200+ per
289	    hour. Your deployment's traffic level determines the expected log file
290	    growth rate.
291	
292	
293	REPOSITORY FILES AND HOST PATHS
294	--------------------------------
295	
296	Path or File                                    Purpose
297	─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
298	/var/log/auditlog/                            (Linux) Directory where
299	                                              service console logs are stored.
300	                                              May be /var/log/auditlog/ or
301	                                              /home/user/.auditlog/logs/ on
302	                                              some deployments.
303	
304	C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\                 (Windows) Directory where
305	                                              service console logs are stored.
306	
307	docs/operations-runbooks/                     Folder containing operational
308	                                              documentation for service hosts.
309	
310	docs/operations-runbooks/                     Console log file management
311	console-log-files.md                          procedures (see Related Pages).
312	
313	docs/operations-runbooks/                     Disk space monitoring guidance.
314	disk-space-checks.md
315	
316	scripts/check-log-sizes.sh                    (Linux) Shell script that
317	                                              queries and reports log file
318	                                              sizes on a host.
319	
320	scripts/monitor-logs.ps1                      (Windows) PowerShell script
321	                                              for log file size monitoring.
322	
323	C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\           Temporary directory where
324	auditlog-cli\                                 command-line logs may be stored
325	                                              during interactive runs.
326	
327	~/.auditlog/config.toml                       (Linux) Service configuration
328	                                              file; check the log_dir
329	                                              parameter to confirm log file
330	                                              location.
331	
332	C:\auditlog\config.toml                       (Windows) Service configuration
333	                                              file.
334	
335	docs/operations-runbooks/                     Host monitoring overview (see
336	host-monitoring-overview.md                   Related Pages).
337	
338	
339	TOOLS, PACKAGES, AND DEPENDENCIES
340	----------------------------------
341	
342	Tool / Utility          Version    Purpose
343	─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
344	du (GNU coreutils)      8.32+      Summarize disk usage; used to total
345	                                   log file sizes on Linux.
346	
347	ls (GNU coreutils)      8.32+      List files and their attributes
348	                                   (including size and modification time).
349	
350	tail (GNU coreutils)    8.32+      Display the last N lines of a file
351	                                   to inspect recent log entries.
352	
353	grep (GNU grep)         3.4+       Pattern matching; used to count
354	                                   occurrences of specific error messages
355	                                   in log files.
356	
357	stat (GNU coreutils)    8.32+      Display detailed file metadata,
358	                                   including size, timestamps, and
359	                                   inode information.
360	
361	PowerShell              7.0+       Command shell for Windows; used for
362	                                   log file size queries and management.
363	
364	Get-Item (PowerShell)   Built-in   PowerShell cmdlet to retrieve file
365	                                   properties on Windows.
366	
367	Get-Content (PowerShell) Built-in  PowerShell cmdlet to read file
368	                                   contents; equivalent to cat or tail.
369	
370	lsof (Linux)            4.95+      Lists open files held by processes;
371	                                   useful for detecting file handles that
372	                                   should have been closed.
373	
374	watch (GNU coreutils)   4.3.14+    Repeatedly executes a command at
375	                                   intervals; useful for monitoring log
376	                                   growth in real time.
377	
378	sqlite3                 3.34+      SQLite command-line tool; used to
379	verify database file consistency. Not
380	                                   used to inspect log files.
381	
382

TITLE:      Console Log File Size Reference
VERSION:    1.0
OWNER:      Developer Experience (Priya Chandrasekaran)
LAST UPDATED: 2024-12-01
================================================================================

OVERVIEW
--------

This page gives maintainers concrete reference numbers for the console log file
sizes to expect on workstations and small hosts running the auditlog service.
Use these thresholds to spot when a log file has grown unusually large and may
need investigation or cleanup.

The service writes its console output to local log files. On a normally-running
host, these files grow at a predictable rate. A file that exceeds the expected
size by more than 50% is worth investigating: it may signal unusual traffic,
misconfiguration, or a service that has been running longer than expected
without cycling.

This page documents the application logging interface; for log file management and cycling procedures, refer to the infrastructure guide.
truncate files. For those topics, see the related page "Managing the Service's
Console Log Files."


EXPECTED LOG FILE SIZES ON TYPICAL HOSTS
-----------------------------------------

Section owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)

The service produces two classes of log output: structured events from the HTTP
loopback service and verbose output from the command-line interface when run
interactively. The sizes in the tables below reflect typical usage patterns on
a small host or workstation over a 7-day observation window.

LOOPBACK SERVICE LOG SIZE THRESHOLDS

The loopback HTTP service runs as a long-lived process and logs each request
and response. A small host with light to moderate traffic will see predictable
growth.

    Traffic Level    Daily Growth    Weekly Total    Monthly Total (est.)
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    Idle             0.2–0.4 MB      1.4–2.8 MB      5.6–11.2 MB
    Light            1.2–2.1 MB      8.4–14.7 MB     33.6–58.8 MB
    Moderate         3.5–5.2 MB      24.5–36.4 MB    98–145.6 MB
    Heavy            8.0–12.0 MB     56–84 MB        224–336 MB

Light traffic typically means 5–15 service requests per hour from other tools
or monitoring agents. Moderate traffic is 50–200 requests per hour. Heavy
traffic reflects continuous polling or background jobs making frequent calls.

Workstations and development hosts almost always fall into the Light category
unless actively running the service. Production small hosts may vary; check
the related page "Host Monitoring for auditlog Hosts" for how to measure actual
traffic on your host.


COMMAND-LINE LOG SIZE THRESHOLDS

When the command-line interface is run interactively, output is logged to a
separate temporary log file. These files are typically small and short-lived.

    Duration         Output Level     File Size Range
    ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    1 minute         Normal           10–40 KB
    1 minute         Verbose          50–150 KB
    30 minutes       Normal           300 KB–1 MB
    30 minutes       Verbose          2–6 MB
    2 hours          Normal           3–8 MB
    2 hours          Verbose          20–40 MB

Most command-line invocations complete within a few minutes and produce logs
no larger than 200 KB. If a command runs for more than an hour, the log file
may exceed 5 MB; this is not unusual for long-running operations.

Note: An earlier version of the service produced larger logs because the
verbose flag was on by default. Verify which version you are running if your
numbers differ sharply from the table above.


MEASURING CURRENT LOG FILE SIZES
---------------------------------

Section owner: Developer Experience (Priya Chandrasekaran)

To check the current size of service log files on your host, use the ls
command (on Linux) or Get-Item (on Windows PowerShell).

Linux / macOS:

    ls -lh /var/log/auditlog/
    
Or with du to show only total:

    du -sh /var/log/auditlog/*

This will show output like:

    -rw-r--r-- 1 auditlog auditlog 24M Sep 27 09:42 service.log
    -rw-r--r-- 1 auditlog auditlog 1.2M Sep 27 09:50 service.log.1
    -rw-r--r-- 1 auditlog auditlog 340K Sep 27 10:15 cli-temp-20260927-085420.log

Windows PowerShell:

    Get-Item C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\*.log | 
      Select-Object Name, @{Name="Size(MB)"; Expression={[math]::Round($_.Length / 1MB, 2)}}

This shows the file name and size in MB. Example output:

    Name                           Size(MB)
    ────                           ────────
    service.log                    24.56
    service.log.1                  1.18
    cli-temp-20260927-085420.log   0.34


IDENTIFYING ABNORMALLY LARGE LOG FILES
---------------------------------------

Section owner: Infra Reliability (Dez Whitfield)

A log file larger than its expected weekly size is a candidate for
investigation. Use the following troubleshooting tree:

1. Check the file's modification date. If it is older than 7 days, it may
   contain log output from a long-running process, an outage, or a misconfiguration.

2. Compare the file size to the thresholds in this page. If the file is more
   than 50% larger than the expected size for your observed traffic level, note
   the file for investigation.

3. Review the log file's last 100 lines using tail (Linux) or Get-Content
   (Windows) to see if unusual events or errors appear.

Linux:

    tail -100 /var/log/auditlog/service.log | less

Windows PowerShell:

    Get-Content C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\service.log -Tail 100 | more

4. If the file contains many repeated error messages, a service component may
   be failing. Check the related page "Diagnosing Port Conflicts for the
   Loopback Service" or "Handling SQLite File Locking on the Database File"
   for troubleshooting steps.

5. If the file is growing rapidly (more than 100 MB per day), the service may
   be running in an unexpected mode or receiving unusual traffic. Stop the
   service, investigate configuration files, and review the related page "Host
   Monitoring for auditlog Hosts" to confirm traffic levels.


EXAMPLES OF NORMAL VERSUS ABNORMAL LOG GROWTH
----------------------------------------------

EXAMPLE 1: Normal light traffic on a workstation

You check a workstation that has run the service for 6 days continuously. The
host is used by a developer for development. The service log file is 18 MB.

Expected size for light traffic over 6 days is about 7–12 MB (1.2–2.1 MB per
day). An 18 MB file suggests moderate traffic, not light. Investigation:

    - Run tail to check for errors or unusual patterns.
    - Use the monitoring tools described in "Host Monitoring for auditlog
      Hosts" to measure request frequency during the most recent 24 hours.
    - If recent traffic is normal and heavy traffic occurred earlier in the
      week, this is expected and not a concern.


EXAMPLE 2: Abnormally large log file with errors

A small host's service log file is 280 MB, and you know it has not been
restarted in 2 weeks. Expected size for moderate traffic over 14 days is about
49–73 MB. This file is 4× larger than expected.

Checking the last 50 lines:

    tail -50 /var/log/auditlog/service.log

You see dozens of repeated "database file is locked" messages. This suggests
the database file is experiencing contention. See the related page "Handling
SQLite File Locking on the Database File" for steps to diagnose and resolve
the issue.


EXAMPLE 3: Temporary CLI log file from a long-running job

A temporary log file named cli-temp-20260920-140300.log is 35 MB, and its
timestamp shows it was created 7 days ago. This suggests a command-line job
ran for a very long time.

Check whether the CLI process is still running:

    ps aux | grep auditlog

Or on Windows:

    Get-Process | Where-Object {$_.ProcessName -like "*auditlog*"}

If the process is still running, the 35 MB file is expected and normal. If the
process has finished, you may remove the temporary log file (see "Managing the
Service's Console Log Files" for cleanup procedures). If the process has hung
or stalled, you will need to stop it and investigate the service configuration.


LOG FILE LOCATIONS AND NAMING CONVENTIONS
------------------------------------------

The service writes log files to platform-specific directories. Understand the
naming conventions to identify which file corresponds to which component.

Linux / macOS:

    /var/log/auditlog/service.log         — Current service log
/var/log/service/service.log.1       — Previous service log (if cycled)
    /var/log/auditlog/cli-temp-*.log      — Temporary CLI logs

Windows:

    C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\service.log
    C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\service.log.1
    C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\cli-temp-*.log

The *.1 file is a cycled or older log file. The cli-temp-*.log files
are created on-demand by command-line invocations and are normally cleaned up
automatically after a few hours.

On older deployments, log files may be stored in different locations:
/usr/local/auditlog/logs/ or C:\auditlog\logs\. Check your service's
configuration file to confirm the log directory path.


TERMINOLOGY AND GLOSSARY
------------------------

Buffering
    The practice of holding log entries in memory before writing them to disk.
    The service uses small buffer sizes (typically 4 KB) to ensure that
    important events are written promptly. Log files that grow more slowly than
    expected may indicate that buffering is enabled and the service has not
    yet flushed its buffer to disk.

Console Output
    Text written by a running process to its standard output (stdout) or
    standard error (stderr) streams. The service captures this output and
    writes it to log files on disk.

Database File
    The SQLite database file that stores the service's stored records. This
    file is distinct from console log files. Do not confuse the two: database
    file growth and console log file growth are independent phenomena.

File Descriptor
    An operating system handle to an open file. A long-running service process
    may keep many file descriptors open. Examine open file descriptors using
    lsof (Linux) or Get-NetTCPConnection (Windows) if a service process
appears to be using excessive disk I/O.

Handler
    A component of the logging system that receives log entries and writes them
to targets such as a file, network socket, or stream. The service
    uses file handlers to write to log files.

Loopback Service
    The long-running HTTP service process that accepts requests from other
tools and applications on the local machine. It runs continuously and logs each
    request and response.

Cycling
    The automatic or manual replacement of a log file with a new file when the
log file reaches a certain size or after a certain amount of time. Cycling
moves the old file (usually with a numeric suffix like .1 or .2) and
starts writing to a new file. Cycling prevents a single log file from
    growing indefinitely.

Temporary Log File
    A log file created on-demand by a short-lived process, such as a CLI
invocation. These files are usually small and are removed after the process
    finishes or after a timeout period.

Traffic Level
    The number of requests and operations the service handles per unit time
    (e.g., per hour or per day). Light traffic is 5–15 requests per hour;
    moderate traffic is 50–200 requests per hour; heavy traffic is 200+ per
    hour. Your deployment's traffic level determines the expected log file
    growth rate.


REPOSITORY FILES AND HOST PATHS
--------------------------------

Path or File                                    Purpose
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
/var/log/auditlog/                            (Linux) Directory where
                                              service console logs are stored.
                                              May be /var/log/auditlog/ or
                                              /home/user/.auditlog/logs/ on
                                              some deployments.

C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\                 (Windows) Directory where
                                              service console logs are stored.

docs/operations-runbooks/                     Folder containing operational
                                              documentation for service hosts.

docs/operations-runbooks/                     Console log file management
console-log-files.md                          procedures (see Related Pages).

docs/operations-runbooks/                     Disk space monitoring guidance.
disk-space-checks.md

scripts/check-log-sizes.sh                    (Linux) Shell script that
                                              queries and reports log file
                                              sizes on a host.

scripts/monitor-logs.ps1                      (Windows) PowerShell script
                                              for log file size monitoring.

C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\           Temporary directory where
auditlog-cli\                                 command-line logs may be stored
                                              during interactive runs.

~/.auditlog/config.toml                       (Linux) Service configuration
                                              file; check the log_dir
                                              parameter to confirm log file
                                              location.

C:\auditlog\config.toml                       (Windows) Service configuration
                                              file.

docs/operations-runbooks/                     Host monitoring overview (see
host-monitoring-overview.md                   Related Pages).


TOOLS, PACKAGES, AND DEPENDENCIES
----------------------------------

Tool / Utility          Version    Purpose
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
du (GNU coreutils)      8.32+      Summarize disk usage; used to total
                                   log file sizes on Linux.

ls (GNU coreutils)      8.32+      List files and their attributes
                                   (including size and modification time).

tail (GNU coreutils)    8.32+      Display the last N lines of a file
                                   to inspect recent log entries.

grep (GNU grep)         3.4+       Pattern matching; used to count
                                   occurrences of specific error messages
                                   in log files.

stat (GNU coreutils)    8.32+      Display detailed file metadata,
                                   including size, timestamps, and
                                   inode information.

PowerShell              7.0+       Command shell for Windows; used for
                                   log file size queries and management.

Get-Item (PowerShell)   Built-in   PowerShell cmdlet to retrieve file
                                   properties on Windows.

Get-Content (PowerShell) Built-in  PowerShell cmdlet to read file
                                   contents; equivalent to cat or tail.

lsof (Linux)            4.95+      Lists open files held by processes;
                                   useful for detecting file handles that
                                   should have been closed.

watch (GNU coreutils)   4.3.14+    Repeatedly executes a command at
                                   intervals; useful for monitoring log
                                   growth in real time.

sqlite3                 3.34+      SQLite command-line tool; used to
verify database file consistency. Not
                                   used to inspect log files.


RELATED PAGES
-------------

  • operations-runbooks/console-log-files.md

For log file cleanup and cycling procedures.

1	# Copying the Database File for Backup
2	
3	**Version:** 2.3
4	**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-08-05
6	
7	**Summary:** Describes a safe way to copy the database file to another location without disrupting the service while it is running.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Overview
12	
13	auditlog keeps its records in a single SQLite database file on disk. On a workstation this file usually lives under the account that runs the package; on a small host it's more commonly kept under a shared directory such as `/var/lib/auditlog/`. Either way, most of the day-to-day upkeep work on an auditlog host comes down to a handful of concerns: making sure nothing else is bound to the port the loopback service wants, making sure the disk under the database file has room to grow, keeping the console log output from filling the disk instead, understanding how SQLite locks the database file while the service is running, watching the host over time, and — the subject of this page — copying the database file somewhere else without knocking the service over or copying a half-written file.
14	
15	This page focuses specifically on that last item: how to make a usable copy of the database file for backup purposes while auditlog is live on the host. The other concerns are covered by their own runbooks in this folder and are referenced here where they intersect with the copy procedure.
16	
17	## What This Page Covers
18	
19	- Why a plain file copy is risky while the service is running.
20	- A pre-copy checklist that touches ports, disk space, console log files, SQLite locking, and host monitoring.
21	- Two worked procedures: copying during a quiet period, and copying while the service is under continuous load.
22	- What to do when the database file appears locked or busy mid-copy.
23	- Choosing and sizing a target location for the copy.
24	- Setting up a recurring copy on a schedule.
25	- A short pointer to verifying the resulting file (full treatment lives in its own page).
26	
27	## Why a Direct File Copy Needs Care
28	
29	*(Section owner: Ines Carrow, Platform Tools)*
30	
31	SQLite databases are not single static files most of the time the service is up — there is usually a companion write-ahead file (and sometimes a shared-memory file) sitting next to the main database file, and writers can hold locks on the main file for short windows even when the service looks idle from the outside. A plain operating-system copy command (`cp`, `Copy-Item`, `robocopy`, and so on) reads the file byte-for-byte from wherever the read head happens to land; if a writer is mid-transaction when that read passes over the affected pages, the copy can end up structurally inconsistent. On a quiet workstation this is a low-probability event. On a small host running auditlog continuously it's common enough that it should never be treated as unlikely.
32	
33	There are two ways around this:
34	
35	1. Use SQLite's own copy mechanism, which is lock-aware and produces a self-consistent copy even while writers are active.
36	2. Stop the service briefly, copy the file with an ordinary OS tool, and start the service again.
37	
38	Both are described below. The first is preferred for hosts where the service can't be paused; the second is simpler and fine for workstations where a short pause is acceptable.
39	
40	## Pre-Copy Checklist
41	
42	*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*
43	
44	Run through this list before every backup copy, whether it's a one-off or a scheduled job. Most items point at a sibling page with the full detail.
45	
46	| Check | Why it matters here | See also |
47	|---|---|---|
48	| No unexpected process bound to the service's port | An unrelated process on the same port can mean two auditlog instances are writing to the same file, which will confuse any copy taken mid-write | Diagnosing Port Conflicts for the Loopback Service |
49	| Free space on the volume holding the database file, and on the volume you're copying to | A copy that runs out of room partway through leaves a truncated file that looks fine until you open it | Checking Disk Space Around the Database File |
50	| Console log files aren't crowding out the same disk | On workstations the console log and the database file often share a volume; an oversized log can starve the copy of room | Managing the Service's Console Log Files |
51	| Current lock state of the database file | Confirms whether a writer is active right now and whether the lock-aware copy path is even necessary | Handling SQLite File Locking on the Database File |
52	| Host load and disk I/O over the last hour | A host already under heavy I/O is a worse time to start a large copy | Host Monitoring for auditlog Hosts |
53	
54	A few notes worth calling out explicitly rather than leaving to inference:
55	
56	- The disk space check should be run against **both** the source volume and the target volume for the copy — it's easy to check only the source and then discover the target is nearly full.
57	- If the console log file for the service is above roughly 500 MB, deal with that first; large log files have been known to push disk usage past the point where a copy of the database file can even finish. See the console log size reference below.
58	- If host monitoring shows sustained CPU above 90% or disk I/O saturation, it's worth waiting for a quieter window rather than starting a copy that may take much longer than expected and hold locks longer as a result.
59	
60	## Step-by-Step Procedure
61	
62	*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*
63	
64	### Option A — Lock-Aware Copy While the Service Keeps Running
65	
66	This is the default recommendation for small hosts where the service runs continuously and pausing it isn't practical.
67	
68	1. Confirm the path to the database file. If you're not sure, check whatever configuration or start-up script was used to launch the service on this host — the file is commonly named `auditlog.db`, though some hosts have renamed it during earlier upkeep work.
69	2. Confirm there's enough free space at the target location — as a rule of thumb, at least twice the current size of the database file, to leave room for the write-ahead file's contents to fold in during the copy.
70	3. Use the `sqlite3` command-line tool's built-in backup command, which is safe to run against a live database file:
71	
72	   ```
73	   sqlite3 /var/lib/auditlog/auditlog.db ".backup /backups/auditlog/auditlog-copy.db"
74	   ```
75	
76	   On a workstation the equivalent might look like:
77	
78	   ```
79	   sqlite3 C:\Users\jdoe\.auditlog\auditlog.db ".backup C:\Users\jdoe\Backups\auditlog-copy.db"
80	   ```
81	
82	4. Watch the command's exit status. A non-zero exit or an error message on the way out means the copy did not complete cleanly and should not be treated as usable.
83	5. Move or rename the resulting file out of the working folder used for the copy, so a later run doesn't overwrite it before anyone's had a chance to look at it.
84	6. Record the copy — even a one-line note in a local log with the date, the source path, and the size of the resulting file is enough to save confusion three months later.
85	
86	The `.backup` command works by reading the source database through SQLite's own page-level locking rather than the operating system's file-copy path, so it produces a consistent file even if a writer is active at the same moment. It does take longer than a plain file copy of the same size, particularly on a database file with a large amount of unfolded write-ahead content, so budget more time than you'd expect from the file size alone.
87	
88	### Option B — Stop, Copy, Start
89	
90	Where a short pause is acceptable — most workstations, and some small hosts during a known-quiet window — this is simpler and faster.
91	
92	1. Stop the service.
93	2. Confirm the process has actually stopped and released the database file — check for lingering write-ahead or shared-memory files sitting next to the main file; if they're still present and non-empty, the service may not have shut down cleanly.
94	3. Copy the database file with an ordinary tool:
95	
96	   ```
97	   cp /var/lib/auditlog/auditlog.db /backups/auditlog/auditlog-copy.db
98	   ```
99	
100	   or, on Windows:
101	
102	   ```powershell
103	   Copy-Item -Path "C:\Users\jdoe\.activitylog\activitylog.db" -Target "C:\Users\jdoe\Backups\activitylog-copy.db"
104	   ```
105	
106	4. Start the service again and confirm it comes back up and is listening on the expected port before walking away.
107	5. Flag the pause window somewhere visible if the host has any users who might see the short gap.
108	
109	This option carries the least risk of an inconsistent copy but has an obvious drawback: the service is briefly unavailable. For a workstation this is rarely seen. For a small host serving more than one local caller, prefer Option A.
110	
111	## Worked Example: Copying During a Quiet Window
112	
113	A workstation running auditlog for local record-keeping, database file at roughly 40 MB, service usually idle overnight.
114	
115	```
116	# 22:40 — quick pre-copy check
117	Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.ProcessName -like "*python*" }
118	Get-PSDrive C | Select-Object Used,Free
119	
120	# nothing unusual bound to the port, plenty of free space, service idle
121	
122	# 22:41 — stop, copy, start
123	# (service stopped via whatever start-up mechanism was used to launch it)
124	Copy-Item -Path "C:\Users\jdoe\.activitylog\activitylog.db" -Target "D:\Backups\activitylog\activitylog-2026-09-27.db"
125	# (service started again)
126	
127	# 22:42 — confirm
128	Get-Item "D:\Backups\auditlog\auditlog-2026-09-27.db" | Select-Object Length,LastWriteTime
129	```
130	
131	Total pause here was under a minute, well within what most workstation users won't even catch.
132	
133	## Worked Example: Copying While the Service Stays Up
134	
135	A small host with auditlog running continuously, database file around 1.2 GB, several local processes calling into the loopback service throughout the day.
136	
137	```
138	# check current lock state and I/O first
139	sudo lsof /var/lib/auditlog/auditlog.db
140	iostat -x 5 3
141	
142	# I/O looks normal, one open file handle from the running service, no unexpected lock
143	
144	# run the lock-aware copy
145	sqlite3 /var/lib/auditlog/auditlog.db ".backup /mnt/backup-vol/auditlog/auditlog-2026-09-27.db"
146	
147	# check the exit code
148	echo $?
149	# 0
150	
151	# move it out of the working area
152	mv /mnt/backup-vol/auditlog/auditlog-2026-09-27.db /mnt/backup-vol/auditlog/complete/
153	```
154	
155	On this host the `.backup` command took just under four minutes for a 1.2 GB database file — markedly slower than a plain file copy of the same size would have been, which is expected given the page-level locking work it does under the hood.
156	
157	## Handling a Locked or Busy Database File
158	
159	*(Section owner: Ines Carrow, Platform Tools)*
160	
161	Even the lock-aware copy path can hit a database file that's busy enough to block briefly. If a copy attempt fails with a message about the database file being locked or busy:
162	
163	- Wait a short interval — a few seconds is usually enough — and try again. Most lock windows on a lightly loaded host are momentary.
164	- If repeated attempts fail, check whether another process besides the service itself has the file open. On Linux, `lsof` or `fuser` will show open handles; on Windows, Sysinternals' `handle.exe` does the same job.
165	- Confirm there's only one instance of the service running against this database file. Two instances started against the same file — often the result of a start-up script running twice, or a leftover process from an earlier session that never fully stopped — is the most common cause of persistent, unexplained locking during a copy.
166	- If the file stays locked well beyond what seems reasonable for the host's load, fall back to Option B (stop, copy, start) rather than continuing to try Option A indefinitely.
167	
168	Full detail on lock states and what each one means for the database file lives in the SQLite file locking page in this folder; the notes above are only what's directly relevant to a copy in progress.
169	
170	## Choosing a Target Location for the Copy
171	
172	*(Section owner: Owen Baptiste, Systems Engineering)*
173	
174	Wherever the copy lands, it needs enough room both for the copy itself and for whatever else already lives on that volume. A few practical guidelines:
175	
176	- Don't copy to the same volume as the source database file if it can be avoided — a single disk failure would otherwise take out both the live file and the copy.
177	- On a workstation, an external or network-attached volume is usually the simplest option; on a small host, a separate mounted volume dedicated to backup copies is preferable to a general-purpose data volume.
178	- Leave headroom. A database file that's 1.2 GB today may be considerably larger by the time the next few copies are taken — don't size the target volume against today's file alone.
179	- Name the copy with a date so that older and newer copies don't collide and so it's obvious at a glance which copy is which — `auditlog-2026-09-27.db` is easier to reason about later than `auditlog-copy.db` overwritten daily.
180	
181	Disk space guidance in general — how much free space to keep under the live database file, and what usage percentages should prompt attention — is covered in depth on the disk space page; the defaults there (85% used as a first level of concern, 95% as urgent) apply equally to the volume holding backup copies.
182	
183	## Automating Periodic Copies
184	
185	*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*
186	
187	Most hosts running auditlog for more than a few weeks end up wanting this on a schedule rather than run by hand. A small wrapper script kept under `scripts/` in the repository checkout handles the pre-copy checks and the copy itself, and a scheduler calls it on whatever interval makes sense for the host.
188	
189	On a Linux host, a cron entry calling the wrapper script daily at a quiet hour:
190	
191	```
192	15 2 * * * /usr/bin/env bash /opt/auditlog/scripts/copy-db-file.sh >> /var/log/auditlog/copy-db-file.log 2>&1
193	```
194	
195	On a Windows workstation, the equivalent using Task Scheduler's command-line registration:
196	
197	```powershell
198	schtasks /create /tn "auditlog-db-copy" /tr "powershell.exe -File C:\auditlog\scripts\copy-db-file.ps1" /sc daily /st 02:15
199	```
200	
201	The wrapper script itself should, at minimum:
202	
203	1. Confirm free space at both source and target locations before starting.
204	2. Run the lock-aware `.backup` command against the live database file.
205	3. Check the exit status and stop with a clear message if it wasn't zero.
206	4. Move the completed copy into its final location with a date in the name.
207	5. Drop a one-line record of what happened into a local log so a quick look later shows whether recent scheduled copies actually succeeded.
208	
209	Keep the schedule out of peak hours for the host if there is such a thing — for most small hosts running auditlog that's overnight, but a host with unusual usage patterns should be scheduled around its own quiet window rather than assumed to follow the same overnight pattern as everything else.
210	
211	## Verifying the Copy
212	
213	*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*
214	
215	A copy that completed without an error is a good sign but not by itself proof the file is usable. 218

220	
221	## Interaction With Host Monitoring
222	
223	A host being watched for general health — CPU, memory, disk I/O — will usually show a visible bump during a large database file copy, particularly the lock-aware `.backup` path, which does visibly more disk reading than a plain file copy of the same size. 234	| Target volume fills up over time from accumulated copies | Old copies never cleared out | Keep only as many recent copies as the target volume can comfortably hold, and check volume usage on the same cadence as the disk space checks elsewhere on the host |

# Copying the Database File for Backup

**Version:** 2.3
**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
**Last updated:** 2025-08-05

**Summary:** Describes a safe way to copy the database file to another location without disrupting the service while it is running.

---

## Overview

auditlog keeps its records in a single SQLite database file on disk. On a workstation this file usually lives under the account that runs the package; on a small host it's more commonly kept under a shared directory such as `/var/lib/auditlog/`. Either way, most of the day-to-day upkeep work on an auditlog host comes down to a handful of concerns: making sure nothing else is bound to the port the loopback service wants, making sure the disk under the database file has room to grow, keeping the console log output from filling the disk instead, understanding how SQLite locks the database file while the service is running, watching the host over time, and — the subject of this page — copying the database file somewhere else without knocking the service over or copying a half-written file.

This page focuses specifically on that last item: how to make a usable copy of the database file for backup purposes while auditlog is live on the host. The other concerns are covered by their own runbooks in this folder and are referenced here where they intersect with the copy procedure.

## What This Page Covers

- Why a plain file copy is risky while the service is running.
- A pre-copy checklist that touches ports, disk space, console log files, SQLite locking, and host monitoring.
- Two worked procedures: copying during a quiet period, and copying while the service is under continuous load.
- What to do when the database file appears locked or busy mid-copy.
- Choosing and sizing a target location for the copy.
- Setting up a recurring copy on a schedule.
- A short pointer to verifying the resulting file (full treatment lives in its own page).

## Why a Direct File Copy Needs Care

*(Section owner: Ines Carrow, Platform Tools)*

SQLite databases are not single static files most of the time the service is up — there is usually a companion write-ahead file (and sometimes a shared-memory file) sitting next to the main database file, and writers can hold locks on the main file for short windows even when the service looks idle from the outside. A plain operating-system copy command (`cp`, `Copy-Item`, `robocopy`, and so on) reads the file byte-for-byte from wherever the read head happens to land; if a writer is mid-transaction when that read passes over the affected pages, the copy can end up structurally inconsistent. On a quiet workstation this is a low-probability event. On a small host running auditlog continuously it's common enough that it should never be treated as unlikely.

There are two ways around this:

1. Use SQLite's own copy mechanism, which is lock-aware and produces a self-consistent copy even while writers are active.
2. Stop the service briefly, copy the file with an ordinary OS tool, and start the service again.

Both are described below. The first is preferred for hosts where the service can't be paused; the second is simpler and fine for workstations where a short pause is acceptable.

## Pre-Copy Checklist

*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*

Run through this list before every backup copy, whether it's a one-off or a scheduled job. Most items point at a sibling page with the full detail.

| Check | Why it matters here | See also |
|---|---|---|
| No unexpected process bound to the service's port | An unrelated process on the same port can mean two auditlog instances are writing to the same file, which will confuse any copy taken mid-write | Diagnosing Port Conflicts for the Loopback Service |
| Free space on the volume holding the database file, and on the volume you're copying to | A copy that runs out of room partway through leaves a truncated file that looks fine until you open it | Checking Disk Space Around the Database File |
| Console log files aren't crowding out the same disk | On workstations the console log and the database file often share a volume; an oversized log can starve the copy of room | Managing the Service's Console Log Files |
| Current lock state of the database file | Confirms whether a writer is active right now and whether the lock-aware copy path is even necessary | Handling SQLite File Locking on the Database File |
| Host load and disk I/O over the last hour | A host already under heavy I/O is a worse time to start a large copy | Host Monitoring for auditlog Hosts |

A few notes worth calling out explicitly rather than leaving to inference:

- The disk space check should be run against **both** the source volume and the target volume for the copy — it's easy to check only the source and then discover the target is nearly full.
- If the console log file for the service is above roughly 500 MB, deal with that first; large log files have been known to push disk usage past the point where a copy of the database file can even finish. See the console log size reference below.
- If host monitoring shows sustained CPU above 90% or disk I/O saturation, it's worth waiting for a quieter window rather than starting a copy that may take much longer than expected and hold locks longer as a result.

## Step-by-Step Procedure

*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*

### Option A — Lock-Aware Copy While the Service Keeps Running

This is the default recommendation for small hosts where the service runs continuously and pausing it isn't practical.

1. Confirm the path to the database file. If you're not sure, check whatever configuration or start-up script was used to launch the service on this host — the file is commonly named `auditlog.db`, though some hosts have renamed it during earlier upkeep work.
2. Confirm there's enough free space at the target location — as a rule of thumb, at least twice the current size of the database file, to leave room for the write-ahead file's contents to fold in during the copy.
3. Use the `sqlite3` command-line tool's built-in backup command, which is safe to run against a live database file:

   ```
   sqlite3 /var/lib/auditlog/auditlog.db ".backup /backups/auditlog/auditlog-copy.db"
   ```

   On a workstation the equivalent might look like:

   ```
   sqlite3 C:\Users\jdoe\.auditlog\auditlog.db ".backup C:\Users\jdoe\Backups\auditlog-copy.db"
   ```

4. Watch the command's exit status. A non-zero exit or an error message on the way out means the copy did not complete cleanly and should not be treated as usable.
5. Move or rename the resulting file out of the working folder used for the copy, so a later run doesn't overwrite it before anyone's had a chance to look at it.
6. Record the copy — even a one-line note in a local log with the date, the source path, and the size of the resulting file is enough to save confusion three months later.

The `.backup` command works by reading the source database through SQLite's own page-level locking rather than the operating system's file-copy path, so it produces a consistent file even if a writer is active at the same moment. It does take longer than a plain file copy of the same size, particularly on a database file with a large amount of unfolded write-ahead content, so budget more time than you'd expect from the file size alone.

### Option B — Stop, Copy, Start

Where a short pause is acceptable — most workstations, and some small hosts during a known-quiet window — this is simpler and faster.

1. Stop the service.
2. Confirm the process has actually stopped and released the database file — check for lingering write-ahead or shared-memory files sitting next to the main file; if they're still present and non-empty, the service may not have shut down cleanly.
3. Copy the database file with an ordinary tool:

   ```
   cp /var/lib/auditlog/auditlog.db /backups/auditlog/auditlog-copy.db
   ```

   or, on Windows:

   ```powershell
   Copy-Item -Path "C:\Users\jdoe\.activitylog\activitylog.db" -Target "C:\Users\jdoe\Backups\activitylog-copy.db"
   ```

4. Start the service again and confirm it comes back up and is listening on the expected port before walking away.
5. Flag the pause window somewhere visible if the host has any users who might see the short gap.

This option carries the least risk of an inconsistent copy but has an obvious drawback: the service is briefly unavailable. For a workstation this is rarely seen. For a small host serving more than one local caller, prefer Option A.

## Worked Example: Copying During a Quiet Window

A workstation running auditlog for local record-keeping, database file at roughly 40 MB, service usually idle overnight.

```
# 22:40 — quick pre-copy check
Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.ProcessName -like "*python*" }
Get-PSDrive C | Select-Object Used,Free

# nothing unusual bound to the port, plenty of free space, service idle

# 22:41 — stop, copy, start
# (service stopped via whatever start-up mechanism was used to launch it)
Copy-Item -Path "C:\Users\jdoe\.activitylog\activitylog.db" -Target "D:\Backups\activitylog\activitylog-2026-09-27.db"
# (service started again)

# 22:42 — confirm
Get-Item "D:\Backups\auditlog\auditlog-2026-09-27.db" | Select-Object Length,LastWriteTime
```

Total pause here was under a minute, well within what most workstation users won't even catch.

## Worked Example: Copying While the Service Stays Up

A small host with auditlog running continuously, database file around 1.2 GB, several local processes calling into the loopback service throughout the day.

```
# check current lock state and I/O first
sudo lsof /var/lib/auditlog/auditlog.db
iostat -x 5 3

# I/O looks normal, one open file handle from the running service, no unexpected lock

# run the lock-aware copy
sqlite3 /var/lib/auditlog/auditlog.db ".backup /mnt/backup-vol/auditlog/auditlog-2026-09-27.db"

# check the exit code
echo $?
# 0

# move it out of the working area
mv /mnt/backup-vol/auditlog/auditlog-2026-09-27.db /mnt/backup-vol/auditlog/complete/
```

On this host the `.backup` command took just under four minutes for a 1.2 GB database file — markedly slower than a plain file copy of the same size would have been, which is expected given the page-level locking work it does under the hood.

## Handling a Locked or Busy Database File

*(Section owner: Ines Carrow, Platform Tools)*

Even the lock-aware copy path can hit a database file that's busy enough to block briefly. If a copy attempt fails with a message about the database file being locked or busy:

- Wait a short interval — a few seconds is usually enough — and try again. Most lock windows on a lightly loaded host are momentary.
- If repeated attempts fail, check whether another process besides the service itself has the file open. On Linux, `lsof` or `fuser` will show open handles; on Windows, Sysinternals' `handle.exe` does the same job.
- Confirm there's only one instance of the service running against this database file. Two instances started against the same file — often the result of a start-up script running twice, or a leftover process from an earlier session that never fully stopped — is the most common cause of persistent, unexplained locking during a copy.
- If the file stays locked well beyond what seems reasonable for the host's load, fall back to Option B (stop, copy, start) rather than continuing to try Option A indefinitely.

Full detail on lock states and what each one means for the database file lives in the SQLite file locking page in this folder; the notes above are only what's directly relevant to a copy in progress.

## Choosing a Target Location for the Copy

*(Section owner: Owen Baptiste, Systems Engineering)*

Wherever the copy lands, it needs enough room both for the copy itself and for whatever else already lives on that volume. A few practical guidelines:

- Don't copy to the same volume as the source database file if it can be avoided — a single disk failure would otherwise take out both the live file and the copy.
- On a workstation, an external or network-attached volume is usually the simplest option; on a small host, a separate mounted volume dedicated to backup copies is preferable to a general-purpose data volume.
- Leave headroom. A database file that's 1.2 GB today may be considerably larger by the time the next few copies are taken — don't size the target volume against today's file alone.
- Name the copy with a date so that older and newer copies don't collide and so it's obvious at a glance which copy is which — `auditlog-2026-09-27.db` is easier to reason about later than `auditlog-copy.db` overwritten daily.

Disk space guidance in general — how much free space to keep under the live database file, and what usage percentages should prompt attention — is covered in depth on the disk space page; the defaults there (85% used as a first level of concern, 95% as urgent) apply equally to the volume holding backup copies.

## Automating Periodic Copies

*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*

Most hosts running auditlog for more than a few weeks end up wanting this on a schedule rather than run by hand. A small wrapper script kept under `scripts/` in the repository checkout handles the pre-copy checks and the copy itself, and a scheduler calls it on whatever interval makes sense for the host.

On a Linux host, a cron entry calling the wrapper script daily at a quiet hour:

```
15 2 * * * /usr/bin/env bash /opt/auditlog/scripts/copy-db-file.sh >> /var/log/auditlog/copy-db-file.log 2>&1
```

On a Windows workstation, the equivalent using Task Scheduler's command-line registration:

```powershell
schtasks /create /tn "auditlog-db-copy" /tr "powershell.exe -File C:\auditlog\scripts\copy-db-file.ps1" /sc daily /st 02:15
```

The wrapper script itself should, at minimum:

1. Confirm free space at both source and target locations before starting.
2. Run the lock-aware `.backup` command against the live database file.
3. Check the exit status and stop with a clear message if it wasn't zero.
4. Move the completed copy into its final location with a date in the name.
5. Drop a one-line record of what happened into a local log so a quick look later shows whether recent scheduled copies actually succeeded.

Keep the schedule out of peak hours for the host if there is such a thing — for most small hosts running auditlog that's overnight, but a host with unusual usage patterns should be scheduled around its own quiet window rather than assumed to follow the same overnight pattern as everything else.
