1	title: Disk Usage Threshold Settings
2	version: v1.0.2
3	owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
4	last_updated: 2025-10-22
5	summary: >
6	  Holds the free-space threshold numbers a host-monitoring script reads before it
7	  warns a maintainer about the volume holding the package's files. This page is
8	  both the write-up and the live values file — the monitoring script parses the
9	  thresholds block below directly, so changes made here take effect the next time
10	  the script runs, typically within fifteen minutes. Covers where free space gets
11	  used up around the package on a workstation or small host, how the numbers below
12	  were chosen, and what to check when an alert looks wrong.
13	
14	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
15	# Section: Purpose and range
16	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
17	purpose_and_range:
18	  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
19	  body: |
20	    This page exists because the package, being nothing more than a Python standard-library
21	    program with a loopback service and a local database file, does not manage disk space for
22	    itself. Nothing in the package removes old console log lines, shrinks the database file, or
23	    warns anyone when a volume gets tight. All of that upkeep is left to whoever runs the host,
24	    which on our team usually means a workstation someone keeps a long-running copy of the
25	    service on, or a small shared host that a few people use for the same purpose.
26	
27	    The thresholds below are read by the host-monitoring script (see scripts/host-monitor.sh, or
28	    scripts/host-monitor.ps1 on Windows workstations) on a fixed timer. The script does three
29	    things: it looks at free space on each watched path, compares the numbers against the values
30	    in this file, and writes a message to the host's local alert log when a threshold is crossed.
31	    It does not act on the numbers beyond that — it will not remove old console log files, will
32	    not shrink the database file, and will not stop the service. Those are jobs for a maintainer,
33	    covered in the sibling pages linked at the bottom of this page.
34	
35	    Applies to any host running a long-lived copy of the service outside of a throwaway
36	    workstation setup — that is, any machine where the database file and console log files are
37	    expected to still be there next week.
38	
39	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
40	# Section: Threshold values (the numbers the script actually reads)
41	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
42	threshold_values:
43	  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
44	  note: >
45	    These are the current numbers in place on team hosts as of this page's last update. Change
46	    them here, save the file, and the next scheduled run of the monitoring script will pick up
47	    the new values — there is no separate reload step.
48	  thresholds:
49	    warn_percent_free: 20
50	    alarm_percent_free: 8
51	    warn_free_megabytes: 6144
52	    alarm_free_megabytes: 1536
53	    check_interval_minutes: 15
54	    quiet_hours_local: "22:00-06:00"
55	    quiet_hours_still_alarm: true
56	  body: |
57	    Two kinds of cutoffs are tracked side by side: a percentage of the volume's total size, and
58	    an absolute number of free megabytes. The script checks both and fires on whichever one trips
59	    first. Percentage cutoffs matter more on small drives — 20% free on a 40 GB workstation volume
60	    is only about 8 GB, which a growing console log file and a couple of leftover database file
61	    copies can eat into surprisingly fast. Absolute cutoffs matter more on large drives, where 20%
62	    free might still be hundreds of gigabytes and not worth an alert.
63	
64	    warn_percent_free and warn_free_megabytes together set the lower bar. Crossing either one
65	    produces a single message the next time the script runs, and then nothing further unless free
66	    space keeps dropping — the script does not re-alert every fifteen minutes for the same warn
67	    condition, only once per day it stays crossed.
68	
69	    alarm_percent_free and alarm_free_megabytes set the higher bar. This one does re-alert on
70	    every run while the condition holds, including during quiet_hours_local, because
71	    quiet_hours_still_alarm is set to true. Warn-level messages are held until 06:00 if they land
72	    during quiet hours; alarm-level messages are not.
73	
74	    check_interval_minutes controls how often the script runs, not how often it alerts — see
75	    above for the difference. Fifteen minutes was chosen because it is short enough to catch a
76	    console log file growing quickly after a busy day of local calls to the service, without
77	    running the free-space check so often that it shows up in process accounting on a shared
78	    host.
79	
80	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
81	# Section: Volumes and paths watched
82	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
83	volumes_and_paths_watched:
84	  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
85	  body: |
86	    On most of our workstations the package's install directory, its console log directory, and
87	    the directory holding the database file all sit on the same volume — usually the machine's
88	    main drive. The monitoring script only needs one watched path in that case. A few of the
89	    small hosts split these across volumes, most often to keep the database file on a mounted
90	    secondary drive with more room, so the script is given a list of paths there instead of one.
91	  table:
92	    - path: auditlog/ (repository install directory)
93	      typical_volume: Main system drive
94	      why_it_matters: >
95	        Holds the package's own files. Small and mostly static, but worth watching because a
96	        volume that's full here will also block writes to anything else on the same drive.
97	    - path: console log directory beneath auditlog/
98	      typical_volume: Main system drive, unless overridden at start-up
99	      why_it_matters: >
100	        The fastest-growing thing on the list. A service left running for weeks with a lot of
101	        local traffic can fill several gigabytes here before anyone looks.
102	    - path: directory holding the database file
103	      typical_volume: Main system drive on workstations; a mounted secondary drive on some small hosts
104	      why_it_matters: >
105	        Grows slowly under normal use but can jump suddenly when someone makes a working copy of
106	        the database file next to the original for a backup and forgets to move it off the host.
107	    - path: /tmp or a host-local scratch directory used during a database file copy
108	      typical_volume: Varies by host; sometimes the main drive, sometimes a separate scratch volume
109	      why_it_matters: >
110	        A short-lived spike. If a copy of the database file is staged here before being moved
111	        elsewhere, this path can briefly need as much free space as the database file itself.
112	
113	  worked_example: |
114	    On dev-ws-14 (Owen's workstation), the install directory, console log directory, and database
115	    file directory are all on C:. The monitoring script therefore watches a single path,
116	    C:\Users\obaptiste\auditlog\, and rolls the free-space number for the whole C: volume up
117	    into that one check. On the shared host bramble (used by a few people for a longer-running
118	    copy of the service), the database file directory was moved to a second mounted volume back
119	    in early 2025 because the main volume was already tight, so bramble's monitoring script is
120	    given two paths and alerts separately for each.
121	
122	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
123	# Section: How the host-monitoring script reads this file
124	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
125	how_the_script_reads_this_file:
126	  owner: Infra Reliability (Sam Okafor)
127	  body: |
128	    The script loads this file at the start of every run, so edits here are picked up on the next
129	    scheduled pass rather than immediately. There is no in-memory copy kept between runs. If a
130	    change needs to take effect sooner than the next fifteen-minute window, run the script by hand
131	    once after saving the file.
132	
133	    A minimal run, by hand, from a shell in the repository root looks like this on a host that
134	    uses cron or a similar scheduler:
135	
136	      $ bash scripts/host-monitor.sh --config operations-runbooks/disk-usage-thresholds.yaml
137	
138	    and the PowerShell equivalent on a Windows workstation:
139	
140	      PS> .\scripts\host-monitor.ps1 -Config .\operations-runbooks\disk-usage-thresholds.yaml
141	
142	    The script prints a one-line summary for each watched path even when nothing is crossed, so a
143	    quiet run still shows output — that's expected and is not itself a sign anything is wrong. A
144	    typical quiet run on dev-ws-14 looks like:
145	
146	      [2026-09-24 09:15] C:\Users\obaptiste\auditlog\ : 61% free (24.4 GB of 40.0 GB) - OK
147	
148	    and a run where the warn cutoff has been crossed looks like:
149	
150	      [2026-09-24 22:03] C:\Users\obaptiste\auditlog\ : 17% free (6.8 GB of 40.0 GB) - WARN (below 20%)
151	
152	    Scheduling itself is set up outside this file — cron on Linux hosts, Task Scheduler on Windows
153	    workstations — and is covered on the host-monitoring overview page rather than here. This page
154	    only covers the numbers the script compares against once it is already running.
155	
156	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
157	# Section: Choosing thresholds for a workstation versus a small host
158	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
159	choosing_thresholds_by_host_kind:
160	  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
161	  body: |
162	    The default numbers above were tuned for a mid-sized workstation drive, somewhere in the
163	    range of 250 GB to 1 TB with a fair amount of other, unrelated work already living on it. Two
164	    situations call for different numbers.
165	
166	    Small, dedicated hosts with a drive under about 60 GB should generally raise
167	    warn_percent_free and alarm_percent_free rather than lower the absolute megabyte figures,
168	    since a small drive can drop from comfortable to full in a single busy day of local calls
169	    filling the console log file. A setting of warn_percent_free: 30 and alarm_percent_free: 12 is
170	    common on these hosts.
171	
172	    Workstations that already run other, larger programs sharing the same drive — a database
173	    engine, a set of local Java projects, whatever else a given team member keeps on the machine —
174	    are better served by leaving the percentage cutoffs low and instead tightening the megabyte
175	    ones, since a large drive at 20% free might still be a comfortable margin in absolute terms.
176	
177	    A short table of the values we've settled on for a few named hosts, for reference when setting
178	    up a new one:
179	  table:
180	    - host: dev-ws-14 (Owen's workstation)
181	      drive_size: "~476 GB"
182	      warn_percent_free: 20
183	      alarm_percent_free: 8
184	    - host: bramble (shared small host)
185	      drive_size: "~58 GB (main), ~120 GB (secondary)"
186	      warn_percent_free: 30
187	      alarm_percent_free: 12
188	    - host: dev-ws-07 (Priya's workstation)
189	      drive_size: "~1 TB"
190	      warn_percent_free: 15
191	      alarm_percent_free: 5
192	
193	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
194	# Section: Port conflicts and disk space
195	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
196	port_conflicts_and_disk_space:
197	  owner: Infra Reliability (Dez Whitfield)
198	  body: |
199	    At first glance a bound-port problem and a free-space problem look unrelated, but they show up
200	    together often enough on our hosts to be worth a note here. When the service's usual loopback
201	    port is already taken by something else — another local copy of the service left running from
202	    an earlier session is the most common cause — a maintainer will sometimes start a second copy
203	    on a different port rather than stopping the first one. Two copies of the service, each with
204	    its own console log file and, if they're pointed at different database files, its own copy of
205	    the database file, use roughly twice the disk space of one. This is a common cause of a warn
206	    alert that doesn't line up with what the maintainer expects, since nothing about the volume
207	    itself has changed — there is just more running on it than intended.
208	
209	    Before treating a warn or alarm message as a disk-space problem to fix by removing old files,
210	    it's worth a quick check for more than one copy of the service running on the host:
211	
212	      $ netstat -ano | findstr 897
213	
214	    (897x being the usual local port range the service defaults to — see the loopback port
215	    defaults page for the exact default and how it can be changed). Two listeners bound to the
216	    loopback interface at ports a few numbers apart is a strong hint that this is what happened.
217	
218	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
219	# Section: Console log files and disk growth
220	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
221	console_log_files_and_disk_growth:
222	  owner: Developer Experience (Priya Chandrasekaran)
223	  body: |
224	    The service writes its console output to a plain text file rather than only to the terminal
225	    it was started from, so that a maintainer can look back at what happened after closing the
226	    window it was launched in. Nothing in the package caps how large that file can get or starts a
227	    new one on its own — left running for a few weeks with steady local traffic, a console log
228	    file on a busy host can reach several hundred megabytes, and we've seen one on bramble pass 2
229	    GB before anyone rolled it over.
230	
231	    Because this is the single fastest-growing thing the monitoring script watches, it's worth
232	    checking the current size directly rather than waiting for a warn alert:
233	
234	      $ du -sh auditlog/logs/console.log
235	
236	    or on a Windows workstation:
237	
238	      PS> (Get-Item .\auditlog\logs\console.log).Length / 1MB
239	
240	    When a console log file is the main reason a volume is tight, the usual fix is to stop the
241	    service, move the current file aside with a new name, gzip it, and start the service again so
242	    it opens a fresh file:
243	
244	      $ gzip auditlog/logs/console.log.old
245	
246	    Sizes we consider normal for a few common patterns of use are listed on the console log file
247	    size reference page; anything well past those numbers is worth rolling over even before a warn
248	    alert fires, since disk growth here tends to speed up rather than level off once local traffic
249	    on a host picks up.
250	
251	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
252	# Section: SQLite file locking and free space
253	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
254	sqlite_file_locking_and_free_space:
255	  owner: Platform Tools (Ines Carrow)
256	  body: |
257	    The database file is a standard SQLite file, and SQLite keeps a side file next to it while
258	    the service is writing — a file with the same name plus a -wal suffix, and usually a small
259	    -shm file alongside it. Both live in the same directory as the database file itself and are
260	    counted by the monitoring script as part of that path's usage, since du and similar tools
261	    don't distinguish them from any other file there.
262	
263	    Under ordinary use the -wal file stays small, a few hundred kilobytes at most, because SQLite
264	    folds its contents back into the main database file on its own as the service runs. It only
265	    grows large enough to matter for disk space in two situations: a long-running local call that
266	    holds a write lock open far longer than usual, or a maintainer opening the database file with
267	    a separate copy of the sqlite3 command-line tool and leaving that session open while the
268	    service is also writing to it. Either one can let the -wal file grow to be as large as the
269	    main database file before it's folded back in.
270	
271	    A quick way to check whether this is what's eating space, from the same directory as the
272	    database file:
273	
274	      $ ls -lh auditlog.db auditlog.db-wal auditlog.db-shm
275	
276	    If auditlog.db-wal is unexpectedly large, closing any separate sqlite3 sessions against the
277	    file and giving the service a few minutes usually lets it fold back down on its own without
278	    needing to stop the service. Lock errors that come up alongside this — rather than the disk
279	    space side of it — are covered in full on the SQLite lock troubleshooting page rather than
280	    here.
281	
282	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
283	# Section: Copying the database file for backup, and its temporary disk cost
284	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
285	copying_database_file_temporary_cost:
286	  owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
287	  body: |
288	    Making a copy of the database file for backup is the other common source of a sudden,
289	    short-lived jump in disk usage that the monitoring script will sometimes catch mid-way
290	    through. A straightforward copy of the file while the service is stopped briefly needs as
291	    much free space as the database file's own current size, plus a little more if the -wal file
292	    hasn't folded back in yet at the moment of the copy.
293	
294	    A copy made using the sqlite3 command line's own backup command rather than a plain file copy
295	    is the safer choice while the service keeps running, since it takes a consistent copy without
296	    needing the service stopped:
297	
298	      $ sqlite3 auditlog.db ".backup 'auditlog-copy-2026-09-27.db'"
299	
300	    This still needs roughly the same amount of free space in the target directory as the
301	    database file's current size — the command does not compress or otherwise shrink anything
302	    along the way. On a host where the database file has grown past a gigabyte or two, it's worth
303	    checking free space in the target directory before starting a copy rather than after, since a
304	    copy that runs out of room part-way through leaves a partial file behind that then needs to be
305	    cleared out by hand.
306	
307	    If the target directory for the copy is a different volume than the one the monitoring script
308	    watches for the database file's own directory, remember that a short-lived spike there won't
309	    show up in this page's numbers at all unless that target directory has separately been added
310	    to the paths the script watches. On bramble, the scratch directory used for staging these
311	    copies before they're moved off the host was added as a fourth watched path back in March
312	    2025 for exactly this reason.
313	
314	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
315	# Section: Worked example — a near-miss on dev-ws-07
316	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
317	worked_example_near_miss:
318	  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
319	  body: |
320	    On the afternoon of 2026-08-19, dev-ws-07 (Priya's workstation) crossed its warn cutoff for
321	    the first time in several months. The monitoring script's log showed the sequence below:
322	
323	      [2026-08-19 13:15] C:\Users\pchandra\auditlog\ : 22% free - OK
324	      [2026-08-19 13:30] C:\Users\pchandra\auditlog\ : 19% free - WARN (below 20%)
325	      [2026-08-19 13:45] C:\Users\pchandra\auditlog\ : 17% free - WARN (below 20%, held, already alerted today)
326	      [2026-08-19 14:00] C:\Users\pchandra\auditlog\ : 12% free - ALARM (below 15%)
327	
328	    A quick look at the two most likely causes found both at once: the console log file had grown
329	    to just under 900 MB after several days of a long-running local job hitting the service
330	    repeatedly, and a database file copy made the previous week for a hand-off had been left
331	    sitting in the console log directory rather than being moved off the workstation.
332	
333	    The fix was to move the stray database file copy to a separate external drive, then stop the
334	    service, roll the console log file over and gzip the old one, and start the service again. Free
335	    space climbed back to 34% within the hour once both were dealt with, well clear of the alarm
336	    cutoff and comfortably above the warn line too. No change was made to the threshold numbers
337	    themselves afterward — the alerts had done their job and fired at the right point — the
338	    change made was to add a reminder on the weekly host monitoring walk-through to check for
339	    stray database file copies specifically, not just overall free space.
340	
341	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
342	# Section: Alert message format
343	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
344	alert_message_format:
345	  owner: Infra Reliability (Sam Okafor)
346	  body: |
347	    Messages the script writes go to a local alert log on the host — by convention,
348	    scripts/host-monitor-alerts.log next to the script itself — rather than anywhere off the
349	    machine. Nothing in this setup sends a message anywhere off the host; picking it up is a
350	    matter of a maintainer looking at that file, either directly or through whatever terminal
351	    prompt or desktop message tool they've set up locally to watch it. Teams that want something
352	    louder than a log line have wired their own local pop-up or sound onto changes in that file,
353	    but that wiring lives outside this page and outside the package entirely.
354	
355	    The line format is:
356	
357	      [<local timestamp>] <path> : <percent>% free (<free> of <total>) - <level> [<reason>]
358	
359	    with <level> one of OK, WARN, or ALARM. A WARN or ALARM line always includes which cutoff was
360	    crossed in parentheses, matching the key names in the threshold_values block above, so that
361	    reading the message alone is enough to know which number in this file to look at.
362	
363	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
364	# Section: Troubleshooting alerts that look wrong
365	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
366	troubleshooting_alerts_that_look_wrong:
367	  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
368	  body: |
369	    A few patterns come up often enough to note here directly rather than sending someone hunting.
370	
371	    - An alert fires but df or Get-PSDrive shows plenty of free space: check that the path in the
372	      alert matches a volume the maintainer thinks it does. On hosts with the database file moved
373	      to a mounted secondary drive, it's easy to check the wrong drive letter or mount point by
374	      habit.
375	    - No alert ever fires even though a volume looks tight by eye: confirm the monitoring script
376	      is actually scheduled and running — a missed cron entry or a disabled Task Scheduler job
377	      after a workstation rebuild is the most common cause, not a problem with the numbers in this
378	      file.
379	    - The same WARN condition seems to repeat every fifteen minutes instead of once a day: this
380	      usually means the "already alerted today" tracking file the script keeps
381	      (scripts/host-monitor-state.json, next to the script) was cleared or moved, often by a
382	      general clean-up of a scratch directory that didn't know to leave it alone.
383	    - Free space comes back on its own without anyone doing anything: on hosts where the -wal file
384	      described above had grown large, it folding back into the main database file naturally will
385	      account for this. It's worth confirming that's what happened rather than assuming the
386	      problem is simply gone.
387	
388	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
389	# Terminology
390	# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
391	terminology:
392	  - term: Loopback service
393	    definition: >
394	      The package's HTTP service, bound only to the loopback interface (127.0.0.1) rather than to
395	      any interface reachable from another machine.
396	  - term: Database file
397	    definition: >
398	      The local SQLite file the package reads from and writes to. Referred to throughout this
399	      page simply as the database file rather than by any internal name.
400	  - term: Console log file
401	    definition: >
402	      The plain text file the service writes its runtime output into while it runs, kept beside
403	      the console log directory rather than only shown in the terminal window it was started from.
404	  - term: Warn level
405	    definition: >
406	      The lower of the two free-space cutoffs tracked in this file. Crossing it produces one
407	      message per day rather than one every check.
408	  - term: Alarm level
409	    definition: >
410	      The higher of the two free-space cutoffs. Crossing it produces a message on every run of the
411	      monitoring script for as long as the condition holds, including during quiet hours.
412	  - term: Volume
413	    definition: >
414	      A disk or partition as seen by the operating system — what df reports on per line on Linux,
415	      or what a drive letter refers to on Windows.
416	  - term: Write-ahead log file
417	    definition: >
418	      SQLite's side file, ending in -wal, kept next to the database file while writes are in
419	      progress. Normally small; folds back into the main database file on its own under ordinary
420	      use.
421	  - term: Host-monitoring script
422	    definition: >
423	      The script (scripts/host-monitor.sh or scripts/host-monitor.ps1) that reads the values in
424	      this file on a timer and writes messages to the local alert log when a cutoff is crossed.
425	  - term: Loopback interface
426	    definition: >
427	      127.0.0.1, the network interface a machine uses to talk to itself. The service only listens
428	      here, never on an interface another machine could reach.
429	  - term: Quiet hours
430	    definition: >
431	      A local time window, set in this file, during which warn-level messages are held rather
432	      than written immediately. Alarm-level messages ignore this window.
433	  - term: Stray database file copy
434	    definition: >
435	      A copy of the database file made for a backup or a hand-off and then left sitting on the
436	      host's main volume rather than moved off, a common and easy-to-miss cause of a warn alert.
437

file.content:
title: Disk Usage Threshold Settings
version: v1.0.2
owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
last_updated: 2025-10-22
summary: >
  Holds the free-space threshold numbers a host-monitoring script reads before it
  warns a maintainer about the volume holding the package's files. This page is
  both the write-up and the live values file — the monitoring script parses the
  thresholds block below directly, so changes made here take effect the next time
  the script runs, typically within fifteen minutes. Covers where free space gets
  used up around the package on a workstation or small host, how the numbers below
  were chosen, and what to check when an alert looks wrong.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: Purpose and range
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
purpose_and_range:
  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
  body: |
    This page exists because the package, being nothing more than a Python standard-library
    program with a loopback service and a local database file, does not manage disk space for
    itself. Nothing in the package removes old console log lines, shrinks the database file, or
    warns anyone when a volume gets tight. All of that upkeep is left to whoever runs the host,
    which on our team usually means a workstation someone keeps a long-running copy of the
    service on, or a small shared host that a few people use for the same purpose.

    The thresholds below are read by the host-monitoring script (see scripts/host-monitor.sh, or
    scripts/host-monitor.ps1 on Windows workstations) on a fixed timer. The script does three
    things: it looks at free space on each watched path, compares the numbers against the values
    in this file, and writes a message to the host's local alert log when a threshold is crossed.
    It does not act on the numbers beyond that — it will not remove old console log files, will
    not shrink the database file, and will not stop the service. Those are jobs for a maintainer,
    covered in the sibling pages linked at the bottom of this page.

    Applies to any host running a long-lived copy of the service outside of a throwaway
    workstation setup — that is, any machine where the database file and console log files are
    expected to still be there next week.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: Threshold values (the numbers the script actually reads)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
threshold_values:
  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
  note: >
    These are the current numbers in place on team hosts as of this page's last update. Change
    them here, save the file, and the next scheduled run of the monitoring script will pick up
    the new values — there is no separate reload step.
  thresholds:
    warn_percent_free: 20
    alarm_percent_free: 8
    warn_free_megabytes: 6144
    alarm_free_megabytes: 1536
    check_interval_minutes: 15
    quiet_hours_local: "22:00-06:00"
    quiet_hours_still_alarm: true
  body: |
    Two kinds of cutoffs are tracked side by side: a percentage of the volume's total size, and
    an absolute number of free megabytes. The script checks both and fires on whichever one trips
    first. Percentage cutoffs matter more on small drives — 20% free on a 40 GB workstation volume
    is only about 8 GB, which a growing console log file and a couple of leftover database file
    copies can eat into surprisingly fast. Absolute cutoffs matter more on large drives, where 20%
    free might still be hundreds of gigabytes and not worth an alert.

    warn_percent_free and warn_free_megabytes together set the lower bar. Crossing either one
    produces a single message the next time the script runs, and then nothing further unless free
    space keeps dropping — the script does not re-alert every fifteen minutes for the same warn
    condition, only once per day it stays crossed.

    alarm_percent_free and alarm_free_megabytes set the higher bar. This one does re-alert on
    every run while the condition holds, including during quiet_hours_local, because
    quiet_hours_still_alarm is set to true. Warn-level messages are held until 06:00 if they land
    during quiet hours; alarm-level messages are not.

    check_interval_minutes controls how often the script runs, not how often it alerts — see
    above for the difference. Fifteen minutes was chosen because it is short enough to catch a
    console log file growing quickly after a busy day of local calls to the service, without
    running the free-space check so often that it shows up in process accounting on a shared
    host.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: Volumes and paths watched
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
volumes_and_paths_watched:
  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
  body: |
    On most of our workstations the package's install directory, its console log directory, and
    the directory holding the database file all sit on the same volume — usually the machine's
    main drive. The monitoring script only needs one watched path in that case. A few of the
    small hosts split these across volumes, most often to keep the database file on a mounted
    secondary drive with more room, so the script is given a list of paths there instead of one.
  table:
    - path: auditlog/ (repository install directory)
      typical_volume: Main system drive
      why_it_matters: >
        Holds the package's own files. Small and mostly static, but worth watching because a
        volume that's full here will also block writes to anything else on the same drive.
    - path: console log directory beneath auditlog/
      typical_volume: Main system drive, unless overridden at start-up
      why_it_matters: >
        The fastest-growing thing on the list. A service left running for weeks with a lot of
        local traffic can fill several gigabytes here before anyone looks.
    - path: directory holding the database file
      typical_volume: Main system drive on workstations; a mounted secondary drive on some small hosts
      why_it_matters: >
        Grows slowly under normal use but can jump suddenly when someone makes a working copy of
        the database file next to the original for a backup and forgets to move it off the host.
    - path: /tmp or a host-local scratch directory used during a database file copy
      typical_volume: Varies by host; sometimes the main drive, sometimes a separate scratch volume
      why_it_matters: >
        A short-lived spike. If a copy of the database file is staged here before being moved
        elsewhere, this path can briefly need as much free space as the database file itself.

  worked_example: |
    On dev-ws-14 (Owen's workstation), the install directory, console log directory, and database
    file directory are all on C:. The monitoring script therefore watches a single path,
    C:\Users\obaptiste\auditlog\, and rolls the free-space number for the whole C: volume up
    into that one check. On the shared host bramble (used by a few people for a longer-running
    copy of the service), the database file directory was moved to a second mounted volume back
    in early 2025 because the main volume was already tight, so bramble's monitoring script is
    given two paths and alerts separately for each.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: How the host-monitoring script reads this file
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
how_the_script_reads_this_file:
  owner: Infra Reliability (Sam Okafor)
  body: |
    The script loads this file at the start of every run, so edits here are picked up on the next
    scheduled pass rather than immediately. There is no in-memory copy kept between runs. If a
    change needs to take effect sooner than the next fifteen-minute window, run the script by hand
    once after saving the file.

    A minimal run, by hand, from a shell in the repository root looks like this on a host that
    uses cron or a similar scheduler:

      $ bash scripts/host-monitor.sh --config operations-runbooks/disk-usage-thresholds.yaml

    and the PowerShell equivalent on a Windows workstation:

      PS> .\scripts\host-monitor.ps1 -Config .\operations-runbooks\disk-usage-thresholds.yaml

    The script prints a one-line summary for each watched path even when nothing is crossed, so a
    quiet run still shows output — that's expected and is not itself a sign anything is wrong. A
    typical quiet run on dev-ws-14 looks like:

      [2026-09-24 09:15] C:\Users\obaptiste\auditlog\ : 61% free (24.4 GB of 40.0 GB) - OK

    and a run where the warn cutoff has been crossed looks like:

      [2026-09-24 22:03] C:\Users\obaptiste\auditlog\ : 17% free (6.8 GB of 40.0 GB) - WARN (below 20%)

    Scheduling itself is set up outside this file — cron on Linux hosts, Task Scheduler on Windows
    workstations — and is covered on the host-monitoring overview page rather than here. This page
    only covers the numbers the script compares against once it is already running.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: Choosing thresholds for a workstation versus a small host
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
choosing_thresholds_by_host_kind:
  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
  body: |
    The default numbers above were tuned for a mid-sized workstation drive, somewhere in the
    range of 250 GB to 1 TB with a fair amount of other, unrelated work already living on it. Two
    situations call for different numbers.

    Small, dedicated hosts with a drive under about 60 GB should generally raise
    warn_percent_free and alarm_percent_free rather than lower the absolute megabyte figures,
    since a small drive can drop from comfortable to full in a single busy day of local calls
    filling the console log file. A setting of warn_percent_free: 30 and alarm_percent_free: 12 is
    common on these hosts.

    Workstations that already run other, larger programs sharing the same drive — a database
    engine, a set of local Java projects, whatever else a given team member keeps on the machine —
    are better served by leaving the percentage cutoffs low and instead tightening the megabyte
    ones, since a large drive at 20% free might still be a comfortable margin in absolute terms.

    A short table of the values we've settled on for a few named hosts, for reference when setting
    up a new one:
  table:
    - host: dev-ws-14 (Owen's workstation)
      drive_size: "~476 GB"
      warn_percent_free: 20
      alarm_percent_free: 8
    - host: bramble (shared small host)
      drive_size: "~58 GB (main), ~120 GB (secondary)"
      warn_percent_free: 30
      alarm_percent_free: 12
    - host: dev-ws-07 (Priya's workstation)
      drive_size: "~1 TB"
      warn_percent_free: 15
      alarm_percent_free: 5

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: Port conflicts and disk space
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
port_conflicts_and_disk_space:
  owner: Infra Reliability (Dez Whitfield)
  body: |
    At first glance a bound-port problem and a free-space problem look unrelated, but they show up
    together often enough on our hosts to be worth a note here. When the service's usual loopback
    port is already taken by something else — another local copy of the service left running from
    an earlier session is the most common cause — a maintainer will sometimes start a second copy
    on a different port rather than stopping the first one. Two copies of the service, each with
    its own console log file and, if they're pointed at different database files, its own copy of
    the database file, use roughly twice the disk space of one. This is a common cause of a warn
    alert that doesn't line up with what the maintainer expects, since nothing about the volume
    itself has changed — there is just more running on it than intended.

    Before treating a warn or alarm message as a disk-space problem to fix by removing old files,
    it's worth a quick check for more than one copy of the service running on the host:

      $ netstat -ano | findstr 897

    (897x being the usual local port range the service defaults to — see the loopback port
    defaults page for the exact default and how it can be changed). Two listeners bound to the
    loopback interface at ports a few numbers apart is a strong hint that this is what happened.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: Console log files and disk growth
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
console_log_files_and_disk_growth:
  owner: Developer Experience (Priya Chandrasekaran)
  body: |
    The service writes its console output to a plain text file rather than only to the terminal
    it was started from, so that a maintainer can look back at what happened after closing the
    window it was launched in. Nothing in the package caps how large that file can get or starts a
    new one on its own — left running for a few weeks with steady local traffic, a console log
    file on a busy host can reach several hundred megabytes, and we've seen one on bramble pass 2
    GB before anyone rolled it over.

    Because this is the single fastest-growing thing the monitoring script watches, it's worth
    checking the current size directly rather than waiting for a warn alert:

      $ du -sh auditlog/logs/console.log

    or on a Windows workstation:

      PS> (Get-Item .\auditlog\logs\console.log).Length / 1MB

    When a console log file is the main reason a volume is tight, the usual fix is to stop the
    service, move the current file aside with a new name, gzip it, and start the service again so
    it opens a fresh file:

      $ gzip auditlog/logs/console.log.old

    Sizes we consider normal for a few common patterns of use are listed on the console log file
    size reference page; anything well past those numbers is worth rolling over even before a warn
    alert fires, since disk growth here tends to speed up rather than level off once local traffic
    on a host picks up.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: SQLite file locking and free space
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
sqlite_file_locking_and_free_space:
  owner: Platform Tools (Ines Carrow)
  body: |
    The database file is a standard SQLite file, and SQLite keeps a side file next to it while
    the service is writing — a file with the same name plus a -wal suffix, and usually a small
    -shm file alongside it. Both live in the same directory as the database file itself and are
    counted by the monitoring script as part of that path's usage, since du and similar tools
    don't distinguish them from any other file there.

    Under ordinary use the -wal file stays small, a few hundred kilobytes at most, because SQLite
    folds its contents back into the main database file on its own as the service runs. It only
    grows large enough to matter for disk space in two situations: a long-running local call that
    holds a write lock open far longer than usual, or a maintainer opening the database file with
    a separate copy of the sqlite3 command-line tool and leaving that session open while the
    service is also writing to it. Either one can let the -wal file grow to be as large as the
    main database file before it's folded back in.

    A quick way to check whether this is what's eating space, from the same directory as the
    database file:

      $ ls -lh auditlog.db auditlog.db-wal auditlog.db-shm

    If auditlog.db-wal is unexpectedly large, closing any separate sqlite3 sessions against the
    file and giving the service a few minutes usually lets it fold back down on its own without
    needing to stop the service. Lock errors that come up alongside this — rather than the disk
    space side of it — are covered in full on the SQLite lock troubleshooting page rather than
    here.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: Copying the database file for backup, and its temporary disk cost
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
copying_database_file_temporary_cost:
  owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
  body: |
    Making a copy of the database file for backup is the other common source of a sudden,
    short-lived jump in disk usage that the monitoring script will sometimes catch mid-way
    through. A straightforward copy of the file while the service is stopped briefly needs as
    much free space as the database file's own current size, plus a little more if the -wal file
    hasn't folded back in yet at the moment of the copy.

    A copy made using the sqlite3 command line's own backup command rather than a plain file copy
    is the safer choice while the service keeps running, since it takes a consistent copy without
    needing the service stopped:

      $ sqlite3 auditlog.db ".backup 'auditlog-copy-2026-09-27.db'"

    This still needs roughly the same amount of free space in the target directory as the
    database file's current size — the command does not compress or otherwise shrink anything
    along the way. On a host where the database file has grown past a gigabyte or two, it's worth
    checking free space in the target directory before starting a copy rather than after, since a
    copy that runs out of room part-way through leaves a partial file behind that then needs to be
    cleared out by hand.

    If the target directory for the copy is a different volume than the one the monitoring script
    watches for the database file's own directory, remember that a short-lived spike there won't
    show up in this page's numbers at all unless that target directory has separately been added
    to the paths the script watches. On bramble, the scratch directory used for staging these
    copies before they're moved off the host was added as a fourth watched path back in March
    2025 for exactly this reason.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: Worked example — a near-miss on dev-ws-07
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
worked_example_near_miss:
  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
  body: |
    On the afternoon of 2026-08-19, dev-ws-07 (Priya's workstation) crossed its warn cutoff for
    the first time in several months. The monitoring script's log showed the sequence below:

      [2026-08-19 13:15] C:\Users\pchandra\auditlog\ : 22% free - OK
      [2026-08-19 13:30] C:\Users\pchandra\auditlog\ : 19% free - WARN (below 20%)
      [2026-08-19 13:45] C:\Users\pchandra\auditlog\ : 17% free - WARN (below 20%, held, already alerted today)
      [2026-08-19 14:00] C:\Users\pchandra\auditlog\ : 12% free - ALARM (below 15%)

    A quick look at the two most likely causes found both at once: the console log file had grown
    to just under 900 MB after several days of a long-running local job hitting the service
    repeatedly, and a database file copy made the previous week for a hand-off had been left
    sitting in the console log directory rather than being moved off the workstation.

    The fix was to move the stray database file copy to a separate external drive, then stop the
    service, roll the console log file over and gzip the old one, and start the service again. Free
    space climbed back to 34% within the hour once both were dealt with, well clear of the alarm
    cutoff and comfortably above the warn line too. No change was made to the threshold numbers
    themselves afterward — the alerts had done their job and fired at the right point — the
    change made was to add a reminder on the weekly host monitoring walk-through to check for
    stray database file copies specifically, not just overall free space.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: Alert message format
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
alert_message_format:
  owner: Infra Reliability (Sam Okafor)
  body: |
    Messages the script writes go to a local alert log on the host — by convention,
    scripts/host-monitor-alerts.log next to the script itself — rather than anywhere off the
    machine. Nothing in this setup sends a message anywhere off the host; picking it up is a
    matter of a maintainer looking at that file, either directly or through whatever terminal
    prompt or desktop message tool they've set up locally to watch it. Teams that want something
    louder than a log line have wired their own local pop-up or sound onto changes in that file,
    but that wiring lives outside this page and outside the package entirely.

    The line format is:

      [<local timestamp>] <path> : <percent>% free (<free> of <total>) - <level> [<reason>]

    with <level> one of OK, WARN, or ALARM. A WARN or ALARM line always includes which cutoff was
    crossed in parentheses, matching the key names in the threshold_values block above, so that
    reading the message alone is enough to know which number in this file to look at.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section: Troubleshooting alerts that look wrong
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
troubleshooting_alerts_that_look_wrong:
  owner: Systems Engineering (Owen Baptiste)
  body: |
    A few patterns come up often enough to note here directly rather than sending someone hunting.

    - An alert fires but df or Get-PSDrive shows plenty of free space: check that the path in the
      alert matches a volume the maintainer thinks it does. On hosts with the database file moved
      to a mounted secondary drive, it's easy to check the wrong drive letter or mount point by
      habit.
    - No alert ever fires even though a volume looks tight by eye: confirm the monitoring script
      is actually scheduled and running — a missed cron entry or a disabled Task Scheduler job
      after a workstation rebuild is the most common cause, not a problem with the numbers in this
      file.
    - The same WARN condition seems to repeat every fifteen minutes instead of once a day: this
      usually means the "already alerted today" tracking file the script keeps
      (scripts/host-monitor-state.json, next to the script) was cleared or moved, often by a
      general clean-up of a scratch directory that didn't know to leave it alone.
    - Free space comes back on its own without anyone doing anything: on hosts where the -wal file
      described above had grown large, it folding back into the main database file naturally will
      account for this. It's worth confirming that's what happened rather than assuming the
      problem is simply gone.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Terminology
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
terminology:
  - term: Loopback service
    definition: >
      The package's HTTP service, bound only to the loopback interface (127.0.0.1) rather than to
      any interface reachable from another machine.
  - term: Database file
    definition: >
      The local SQLite file the package reads from and writes to. Referred to throughout this
      page simply as the database file rather than by any internal name.
  - term: Console log file
    definition: >
      The plain text file the service writes its runtime output into while it runs, kept beside
      the console log directory rather than only shown in the terminal window it was started from.
  - term: Warn level
    definition: >
      The lower of the two free-space cutoffs tracked in this file. Crossing it produces one
      message per day rather than one every check.
  - term: Alarm level
    definition: >
      The higher of the two free-space cutoffs. Crossing it produces a message on every run of the
      monitoring script for as long as the condition holds, including during quiet hours.
  - term: Volume
    definition: >
      A disk or partition as seen by the operating system — what df reports on per line on Linux,
      or what a drive letter refers to on Windows.
  - term: Write-ahead log file
    definition: >
      SQLite's side file, ending in -wal, kept next to the database file while writes are in
      progress. Normally small; folds back into the main database file on its own under ordinary
      use.
  - term: Host-monitoring script
    definition: >
      The script (scripts/host-monitor.sh or scripts/host-monitor.ps1) that reads the values in
      this file on a timer and writes messages to the local alert log when a cutoff is crossed.
  - term: Loopback interface
    definition: >
      127.0.0.1, the network interface a machine uses to talk to itself. The service only listens
      here, never on an interface another machine could reach.
  - term: Quiet hours
    definition: >
      A local time window, set in this file, during which warn-level messages are held rather
      than written immediately. Alarm-level messages ignore this window.
  - term: Stray database file copy
    definition: >
      A copy of the database file made for a backup or a hand-off and then left sitting on the
      host's main volume rather than moved off, a common and easy-to-miss cause of a warn alert.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Files and host paths referenced by this page
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
files_and_paths_referenced:
  - path: operations-runbooks/disk-usage-thresholds.yaml
    purpose: This page. Also the live values file the host-monitoring script reads directly.
  - path: operations-runbooks/disk-space-checks.md
    purpose: Manual, by-hand steps for checking free space around the database file without the script.
  - path: operations-runbooks/console-log-files.md
    purpose: Full write-up on managing the service's console log files, including rolling them over.

content.content:
1	================================================================================
2	Weekly Host Monitoring Checklist
3	================================================================================
4	Version: v1.4.0
5	Owner: Infra Reliability (Sam Okafor)
6	Last updated: 2026-03-15
7	
8	Summary: Lists the checks a maintainer should walk through each week on a host
9	that runs the auditlog package.
10	
11	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
12	1. Purpose and Range
13	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
14	
15	This page is the week-to-week companion to host-monitoring-overview.md. Where
16	that page explains why we watch these hosts at all, this one is the actual
17	walk-through: the order to run things in, what a healthy result looks like,
18	and what to do when a check comes back wrong. It's written for whoever is
19	covering host upkeep that week, whether that's a full-time maintainer or
20	someone filling in.
21	
22	The checklist below assumes a single host running one copy of the package,
23	either a workstation someone runs by hand or a small always-on host tucked
24	in a closet somewhere. It does not assume any particular OS; most steps are
25	given for both PowerShell and a POSIX shell, since our fleet has a mix of
26	Windows workstations and small Linux boxes.
27	
28	Section owner: Sam Okafor (Infra Reliability)
29	
30	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
31	2. Weekly Checklist at a Glance
32	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
33	
34	Run these roughly in this order. Each row links to the fuller section later
35	in this page.
36	
37	  Check                          | Typical time | Where to look
38	  --------------------------------|--------------|----------------------------
39	  Port availability check         | 2 min        | Section 3
40	  Disk space around the db file   | 3 min        | Section 4
41	  Console log folder size         | 3 min        | Section 5
42	  SQLite lock state               | 5 min        | Section 6
43	  Host-level monitoring status    | 5 min        | Section 7
44	  Backup copy of the database     | 10 min       | Section 8
45	
46	* If the host has been quiet all week (no restarts, no disk alerts), the
47	  whole pass takes under 20 minutes.
48	* If something looks off, budget extra time - most issues chain together
49	  (a full disk causes a stuck lock, a stuck lock causes a restart loop, a
50	  restart loop grows the console log folder, and so on).
51	- Keep a running note of what you found each week; three lines in a shared
52	  doc is enough. It saves the next person a repeat investigation.
53	
54	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
55	3. Port Conflicts
56	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
57	
58	Section owner: Dez Whitfield (Infra Reliability)
59	
60	The service listens on the loopback interface only, on a small range of
61	default ports (see loopback-port-defaults.md for the exact numbers and how
62	to change them - that page is the one place worth keeping open while you do
63	this check, since the defaults have moved before).
64	
65	What to check weekly:
66	
67	1. Confirm the service's port is actually bound and not silently sitting on
68	   a fallback port because the preferred one was taken at startup.
69	
70	   On Windows:
71	
72	       Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalAddress 127.0.0.1 -State Listen |
73	         Where-Object { $_.LocalPort -in 8987,8988,8989 }
74	
75	   On Linux/macOS:
76	
77	       lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -n -P | grep 127.0.0.1
78	
79	2. Check for a second local process fighting over the same port. This
80	   happens most often when someone starts a second copy of the service by
81	   hand for a one-off check and forgets to stop it, or when an old copy
82	   from before a restart never fully let go of the port.
83	
84	3. If the port is taken by something unrelated to auditlog (a dev server,
85	   a container's local forward, a stray shell someone left running), note
86	   what it was in your weekly log line. Repeat offenders are worth raising
87	   with whoever owns that other process.
88	
89	Worked example - what a conflict actually looks like:
90	
91	  A maintainer restarts the host after an OS update. The service's launch
92	  step starts on schedule, but a leftover process from before the restart
93	  (never fully torn down, still holding its old port) is still there for a
94	  few seconds during boot. The new copy fails its first bind attempt, falls
95	  back to the next port in its list, and quietly keeps running there. A week
96	  later someone points a local script at the "usual" port and gets nothing.
97	  The fix in this case wasn't a config change - the old process just needed
98	  to be found and stopped, and the new copy restarted so it took the
99	  intended port back.
100	
101	A short table of what you might see and what it usually means:
102	
103	  Symptom                                 | Likely cause
104	  -----------------------------------------|----------------------------------
105	  Bind fails at startup, log shows a repeated attempt  | Old copy of the service still up
106	  Port open, but wrong PID owns it          | Another local tool grabbed it first
107	  Port open on an unexpected number         | Service fell back per its port list
108	  Nothing listening at all                  | Service didn't start; check console log
109	
110	See port-conflicts.md for the full diagnostic walk-through, including how to
111	identify the owning process by PID on each OS and how to force a clean
112	restart without leaving anything half-stopped.
113	
114	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
115	4. Disk Space
116	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
117	
118	Section owner: Owen Baptiste (Systems Engineering)
119	
120	The database file, the console log folder, and any backup copies sitting on
121	the same host all draw from the same disk. A workstation that's otherwise
122	fine can still end up with a full volume because someone's downloads folder
123	is on the same drive as the database file.
124	
125	Weekly steps:
126	
127	1. Check free space on the volume that holds the database file, not just
128	   the system volume overall (they're sometimes different drives).
129	
130	   On Windows:
131	
132	       Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem |
133	         Select-Object Name, @{n='FreeGB';e={[math]::Round($_.Free/1GB,2)}}
134	
135	   On Linux/macOS:
136	
137	       df -h /home/svc-auditlog
138	
139	2. Compare the free space number against the thresholds in
140	   disk-usage-thresholds.yaml. As of this writing that file sets a warning
141	   level at 15% free and an urgent level at 5% free on the volume holding
142	   the database file; check the file itself for the current numbers rather
143	   than trusting a number written down here, since it gets adjusted per
144	   host.
145	
146	3. Check the database file's own size. It grows slowly under ordinary use,
147	   so a sudden jump week over week is worth a look on its own, separate from
148	   overall disk pressure.
149	
150	       ls -lh ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db
151	       Get-Item "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\auditlog\auditlog.db" | Select-Object Length
152	
153	4. Check for stray copies. A common cause of unexpected disk growth isn't
154	   the live database file at all - it's an old backup copy from Section 8
155	   that never got moved off the host, sitting in a home folder taking up
156	   several times the size of the current file.
157	
158	A rough size-to-action table, useful for a fast read:
159	
160	  Free space on volume    | Action
161	  -------------------------|---------------------------------------------
162	  Above 15%                | Nothing to do, note it and move on
163	  5% to 15%                | Look for stray backup copies and old console
164	                             log files before anything else
165	  Below 5%                 | Treat as urgent; free space today, don't wait
166	                             for the next weekly pass
167	
168	Note: disk-usage-thresholds.yaml is the source of truth for the actual
169	numbers used in day-to-day monitoring; the figures above are meant as a
170	sanity check, not a replacement for reading the config file.
171	
172	See disk-space-checks.md for a longer treatment, including how to work out
173	what's actually taking up space when the console log folder and the backup
174	folder are both suspects at once.
175	
176	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
177	5. Console Log Files
178	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
179	
180	Section owner: Priya Chandrasekaran (Developer Experience)
181	
182	The service writes its own console output to a folder of plain text log
183	files, separate from anything in the database file. These are useful for
184	working out why a port bind failed or why the service didn't come up after
185	a restart, but they're also the most common source of slow, creeping disk
186	growth on a workstation that's been running for a few months without anyone
187	looking at this folder.
188	
189	Where to look:
190	
191	  Linux/macOS:   ~/.auditlog/logs/
192	  Windows:       C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\  (some older hosts still use
193	                 %LOCALAPPDATA%\auditlog\logs\ - check both if the first is
194	                 empty)
195	
196	Weekly steps:
197	
198	1. Check the total size of the log folder and the size of the newest file
199	   in it.
200	
201	       du -sh ~/.auditlog/logs/
202	       Get-ChildItem C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\ |
203	         Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum
204	
205	2. Compare the newest file's size against the reference sizes in
206	   console-log-file-sizes.txt. A file well past the expected size for its
207	   age usually means the service is writing the same warning over and over,
208	   which is worth reading a page or two of before assuming it's harmless.
209	
210	3. Trim old files. There's no built-in turnover for these logs, so the
211	   folder only ever grows unless someone tidies it. A reasonable weekly
212	   habit is to set aside anything older than four weeks into a separate
213	   folder off the host (a shared drive or a cold storage folder), then
214	   remove what's left in the live logs folder older than that window.
215	
216	       Get-ChildItem C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\ |
217	         Where-Object { $_.LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-28) } |
218	         Move-Item -To D:\host-upkeep\old-console-logs\
219	
220	       find ~/.auditlog/logs/ -name '*.log' -mtime +28 \
221	         -exec mv {} ~/host-upkeep/old-console-logs/ \;
222	
223	4. Skim the newest file for anything unusual before moving on - repeated
224	   restart lines, repeated bind failures, or long gaps where nothing was
225	   written at all (a long gap usually means the service wasn't running
226	   during that window, which is worth cross-checking against Section 7).
227	
228	Worked example: a host that had been quietly rebooting itself once a day
229	for two weeks (an unrelated OS update setting) had a console log folder
230	that had grown past six hundred megabytes, almost entirely repeated startup
231	lines. Nothing in the database file was affected, but the log folder alone
232	had eaten most of the free space on that volume, which is what set off the
233	disk space check in Section 4 in the first place.
234	
235	See console-log-files.md for the full write-up on managing this folder,
236	and console-log-file-sizes.txt for the current reference sizes per log type.
237	
238	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
239	6. SQLite File Locking
240	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
241	
242	Section owner: Ines Carrow (Platform Tools)
243	
244	The database file is a single SQLite file, and SQLite's locking is
245	file-based rather than something the service manages on its own. On a
246	single-host setup this rarely bites anyone, but it does show up in two
247	fairly predictable ways: a second process opening the file at the same time
248	as the service, or a copy operation (see Section 8) started while the file
249	was still being written.
250	
251	Weekly steps:
252	
253	1. Confirm nothing else on the host has the database file open at the same
254	   time as the service. This is the single most common cause of "database
255	   is locked" style errors on a workstation - someone opens the file in a
256	   local SQLite viewer to poke around, forgets to close it, and leaves it
257	   open for days.
258	
259	       lsof ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db
260	       (On Windows, Process Explorer's "Find Handle" against the file path
261	       works, or Get-Process | Where-Object with a handle scan if you have
262	       that set up.)
263	
264	2. Check for a lingering journal or write-ahead file sitting next to the
265	   database file (same name, different suffix). Its presence isn't
266	   automatically a problem, but if it's still there hours after the service
267	   was last active, or it's grown unusually large, that's worth a closer
268	   look before it turns into an actual lock error.
269	
270	       ls -la ~/.auditlog/*.db-*
271	
272	3. If you do hit a lock error while running a manual check against the
273	   file, don't just try again right away - first confirm nothing still has
274	   the file open (step 1), and check the journal mode with a quick sqlite3
275	   session:
276	
277	       sqlite3 ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db "PRAGMA journal_mode;"
278	       sqlite3 ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db "PRAGMA busy_timeout;"
279	
280	   A short busy_timeout on a workstation that also runs a local viewer
281	   against the same file is a common, easy-to-fix cause of intermittent
282	   lock errors.
283	
284	4. If a lock persists after confirming nothing else has the file open, a
285	   full host restart clears it in every case we've seen so far. That's a
286	   blunt tool, though, so treat it as a last step, not a first one.
287	
288	A quick reference table:
289	
290	  Situation                                   | What it usually means
291	  ---------------------------------------------|-------------------------------
292	  Lock error, another process has file open     | Close the other viewer/tool
293	  Lock error, nothing else has it open           | Check busy_timeout, then try again
294	  Journal/WAL file present and growing           | Backup copy or check under way
295	  Journal/WAL file present, host has been idle   | Worth a closer look, see below
296	
297	See sqlite-file-locking.md for the fuller treatment of how this shows up in
298	practice, and sqlite-lock-troubleshooting.rst (v2.0) for step-by-step
299	restoration once a lock error has already happened rather than just being
300	watched for.
301	
302	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
303	7. Host Monitoring
304	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
305	
306	Section owner: Sam Okafor (Infra Reliability)
307	
308	This section is about the host itself staying up and the service staying
309	running on it - separate from any of the file-level checks above.
310	
311	Weekly steps:
312	
313	1. Confirm the service process is actually running, not just that the port
314	   check in Section 3 came back clean (a process can hold a port briefly on
315	   its way down, which can look fine for a moment and then vanish).
316	
317	       Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.ProcessName -like '*auditlog*' }
318	       ps aux | grep auditlog
319	
320	2. Check uptime on the host itself. An unexpectedly recent boot time on a
321	   host that's supposed to run unattended is worth investigating even if
322	   the service came back up fine afterward - it often points at an OS
323	   update, a power event, or something else worth knowing about before it
324	   happens again.
325	
326	       (Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem).LastBootUpTime
327	       uptime -s
328	
329	3. If the host has any general-purpose monitoring already set up (a simple
330	   heartbeat check, a small dashboard, whatever the team happens to use on
331	   that particular box), confirm it's actually still reporting and not
332	   quietly stuck showing last week's numbers. A monitoring dashboard that
333	   silently stopped updating three weeks ago is worse than having no
334	   dashboard at all, because it looks fine at a glance.
335	
336	4. Look back over the week for any alert that fired and was dealt with
337	   without being written down anywhere. If something happened and got
338	   fixed quietly, add a line to the shared weekly log mentioned in Section
339	   2 so the pattern is visible if it happens again.
340	
341	A short table of what "healthy" looks like on an ordinary week:
342	
343	  Signal                          | Healthy
344	  ---------------------------------|-----------------------------------
345	  Service process running          | Yes, one copy, expected PID age
346	  Port bound                       | Yes, on the expected number
347	  Host uptime                      | Matches the last known restart
348	  Local monitoring dashboard        | Recently updated, no stuck values
349	
350	As of v1.1.0 host-monitoring-overview.md covers the broader reasoning behind
351	why we watch these signals at all; this page only covers the weekly
352	mechanics of doing it.
353	
354	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
355	8. Copying the Database File for Backup
356	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
357	
358	Section owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools)
359	
360	Because the database file is a single flat file, copying it is
361	straightforward, but doing it while the service is mid-write can produce a
362	copy that's inconsistent or, worse, one that opens fine but is missing
363	whatever was being written at the moment of the copy.
364	
365	Weekly steps:
366	
367	1. Confirm the service isn't in the middle of anything heavy before
368	   copying. On a workstation this usually just means picking a quiet moment
369	   rather than stopping the service outright.
370	
371	2. Copy the file, and copy any journal/write-ahead file sitting next to it
372	   at the same time, using a tool that copies in one pass rather than
373	   streaming byte by byte over a slow link.
374	
375	       robocopy C:\ProgramData\auditlog C:\host-upkeep\backups\auditlog auditlog.db*
376	       rsync -a ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db* ~/host-upkeep/backups/auditlog/
377	
378	3. Check the copy's size against the original right after copying, then
379	   confirm with a hash value rather than trusting size alone (two files the
380	   same size aren't necessarily the same content).
381	
382	       Get-FileHash C:\ProgramData\auditlog\auditlog.db -Algorithm SHA256
383	       Get-FileHash C:\host-upkeep\backups\auditlog\auditlog.db -Algorithm SHA256
384	
385	       shasum -a 256 ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db
386	       shasum -a 256 ~/host-upkeep/backups/auditlog/auditlog.db
387	
388	4. Store the copy somewhere off the host - a shared drive, another host on
389	   the local network, whatever the team already uses. A backup copy sitting
390	   next to the original on the same disk doesn't help much if that disk is
391	   what fails.
392	
393	5. Name the copy with the date so it's obvious later which week it came
394	   from:
395	
396	       auditlog.db.2026-03-15
397	       auditlog.db.2026-03-08
398	
399	6. Keep the last four to six weekly copies and clear out anything older
400	   from the target location once you've confirmed the newer ones are good -
401	   this ties back into the disk space check in Section 4, since backup
402	   copies left unchecked are a common cause of slow disk growth on the host
403	   that holds them.
404	
405	Worked example: a maintainer copying the database file mid-write ended up
406	with a copy that opened without error in a local viewer but was missing the
407	last few minutes of activity compared to the live file. The fix was simply
408	to redo the copy a few minutes later, once the write had settled, and to
409	add the hash-value check above as a standing step so a short copy would be
410	caught immediately rather than discovered weeks later when it was needed.
411	
412	See database-file-backup-copy.md for the fuller write-up, and
413	backup-copy-verification.rst for a longer treatment of confirming a copy is
414	good beyond just matching size and hash value.
415	
416	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
417	9. Terminology
418	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
419	
420	Database file - The single SQLite file the service reads from and writes
421	to. On most hosts this is auditlog.db, though the exact path varies by OS.
422	
423	Console log file - A plain text file the service writes its own startup
424	and runtime output to, kept in a separate folder from the database file.
425	
426	Loopback interface - The local-only network interface (127.0.0.1) the
427	service binds to; nothing outside the host can reach it directly.
428	
429	Port conflict - A situation where the service's expected port is already
430	held by another process at startup, forcing a fallback or a failed bind.
431	
432	Lock error - An error surfaced by SQLite when the database file is opened
433	by more than one process in a way that its locking rules don't allow at
434	that moment.
435	
436	Journal file / write-ahead file - A small companion file SQLite keeps next
437	to the main database file while changes are being written; its presence
438	and size are useful signals during the checks in Section 6.
439	
440	Backup copy - A separate copy of the database file, taken at a point in
441	time and stored somewhere other than the host that produced it.
442	
443	Hash value - A short fixed-length value computed from a file's contents,
444	used here to confirm a backup copy matches its source exactly.
445	
446	Busy timeout - A SQLite setting controlling how long a process will wait
447	for a lock to clear before giving up and returning a lock error.
448	
449	Threshold - A configured free-space or size level (see
450	disk-usage-thresholds.yaml) that separates a "fine for now" reading from
451	one that calls for action.
452	
453	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
454	10. Files and Paths Referenced

465	  docs/operations-runbooks/host-monitoring-overview.md | Broader reasoning behind
