================================================================================
Weekly Host Monitoring Checklist
================================================================================
Version: v1.4.0
Owner: Infra Reliability (Sam Okafor)
Last updated: 2026-03-15

Summary: Lists the checks a maintainer should walk through each week on a host
that runs the auditlog package.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Purpose and Range
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This page is the week-to-week companion to host-monitoring-overview.md. Where
that page explains why we watch these hosts at all, this one is the actual
walk-through: the order to run things in, what a healthy result looks like,
and what to do when a check comes back wrong. It's written for whoever is
covering host upkeep that week, whether that's a full-time maintainer or
someone filling in.

The checklist below assumes a single host running one copy of the package,
either a workstation someone runs by hand or a small always-on host tucked
in a closet somewhere. It does not assume any particular OS; most steps are
given for both PowerShell and a POSIX shell, since our fleet has a mix of
Windows workstations and small Linux boxes.

Section owner: Sam Okafor (Infra Reliability)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Weekly Checklist at a Glance
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Run these roughly in this order. Each row links to the fuller section later
in this page.

  Check                          | Typical time | Where to look
  --------------------------------|--------------|----------------------------
  Port availability check         | 2 min        | Section 3
  Disk space around the db file   | 3 min        | Section 4
  Console log folder size         | 3 min        | Section 5
  SQLite lock state               | 5 min        | Section 6
  Host-level monitoring status    | 5 min        | Section 7
  Backup copy of the database     | 10 min       | Section 8

* If the host has been quiet all week (no restarts, no disk alerts), the
  whole pass takes under 20 minutes.
* If something looks off, budget extra time - most issues chain together
  (a full disk causes a stuck lock, a stuck lock causes a restart loop, a
  restart loop grows the console log folder, and so on).
- Keep a running note of what you found each week; three lines in a shared
  doc is enough. It saves the next person a repeat investigation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Port Conflicts
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Section owner: Dez Whitfield (Infra Reliability)

The service listens on the loopback interface only, on a small range of
default ports (see loopback-port-defaults.md for the exact numbers and how
to change them - that page is the one place worth keeping open while you do
this check, since the defaults have moved before).

What to check weekly:

1. Confirm the service's port is actually bound and not silently sitting on
   a fallback port because the preferred one was taken at startup.

   On Windows:

       Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalAddress 127.0.0.1 -State Listen |
         Where-Object { $_.LocalPort -in 8987,8988,8989 }

   On Linux/macOS:

       lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -n -P | grep 127.0.0.1

2. Check for a second local process fighting over the same port. This
   happens most often when someone starts a second copy of the service by
   hand for a one-off check and forgets to stop it, or when an old copy
   from before a restart never fully let go of the port.

3. If the port is taken by something unrelated to auditlog (a dev server,
   a container's local forward, a stray shell someone left running), note
   what it was in your weekly log line. Repeat offenders are worth raising
   with whoever owns that other process.

Worked example - what a conflict actually looks like:

  A maintainer restarts the host after an OS update. The service's launch
  step starts on schedule, but a leftover process from before the restart
  (never fully torn down, still holding its old port) is still there for a
  few seconds during boot. The new copy fails its first bind attempt, falls
  back to the next port in its list, and quietly keeps running there. A week
  later someone points a local script at the "usual" port and gets nothing.
  The fix in this case wasn't a config change - the old process just needed
  to be found and stopped, and the new copy restarted so it took the
  intended port back.

A short table of what you might see and what it usually means:

  Symptom                                 | Likely cause
  -----------------------------------------|----------------------------------
  Bind fails at startup, log shows a repeated attempt  | Old copy of the service still up
  Port open, but wrong PID owns it          | Another local tool grabbed it first
  Port open on an unexpected number         | Service fell back per its port list
  Nothing listening at all                  | Service didn't start; check console log

See port-conflicts.md for the full diagnostic walk-through, including how to
identify the owning process by PID on each OS and how to force a clean
restart without leaving anything half-stopped.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Disk Space
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Section owner: Owen Baptiste (Systems Engineering)

The database file, the console log folder, and any backup copies sitting on
the same host all draw from the same disk. A workstation that's otherwise
fine can still end up with a full volume because someone's downloads folder
is on the same drive as the database file.

Weekly steps:

1. Check free space on the volume that holds the database file, not just
   the system volume overall (they're sometimes different drives).

   On Windows:

       Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem |
         Select-Object Name, @{n='FreeGB';e={[math]::Round($_.Free/1GB,2)}}

   On Linux/macOS:

       df -h /home/svc-auditlog

2. Compare the free space number against the thresholds in
   disk-usage-thresholds.yaml. As of this writing that file sets a warning
   level at 15% free and an urgent level at 5% free on the volume holding
   the database file; check the file itself for the current numbers rather
   than trusting a number written down here, since it gets adjusted per
   host.

3. Check the database file's own size. It grows slowly under ordinary use,
   so a sudden jump week over week is worth a look on its own, separate from
   overall disk pressure.

       ls -lh ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db
       Get-Item "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\auditlog\auditlog.db" | Select-Object Length

4. Check for stray copies. A common cause of unexpected disk growth isn't
   the live database file at all - it's an old backup copy from Section 8
   that never got moved off the host, sitting in a home folder taking up
   several times the size of the current file.

A rough size-to-action table, useful for a fast read:

  Free space on volume    | Action
  -------------------------|---------------------------------------------
  Above 15%                | Nothing to do, note it and move on
  5% to 15%                | Look for stray backup copies and old console
                             log files before anything else
  Below 5%                 | Treat as urgent; free space today, don't wait
                             for the next weekly pass

Note: disk-usage-thresholds.yaml is the source of truth for the actual
numbers used in day-to-day monitoring; the figures above are meant as a
sanity check, not a replacement for reading the config file.

See disk-space-checks.md for a longer treatment, including how to work out
what's actually taking up space when the console log folder and the backup
folder are both suspects at once.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Console Log Files
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Section owner: Priya Chandrasekaran (Developer Experience)

The service writes its own console output to a folder of plain text log
files, separate from anything in the database file. These are useful for
working out why a port bind failed or why the service didn't come up after
a restart, but they're also the most common source of slow, creeping disk
growth on a workstation that's been running for a few months without anyone
looking at this folder.

Where to look:

  Linux/macOS:   ~/.auditlog/logs/
  Windows:       C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\  (some older hosts still use
                 %LOCALAPPDATA%\auditlog\logs\ - check both if the first is
                 empty)

Weekly steps:

1. Check the total size of the log folder and the size of the newest file
   in it.

       du -sh ~/.auditlog/logs/
       Get-ChildItem C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\ |
         Measure-Object -Property Length -Sum

2. Compare the newest file's size against the reference sizes in
   console-log-file-sizes.txt. A file well past the expected size for its
   age usually means the service is writing the same warning over and over,
   which is worth reading a page or two of before assuming it's harmless.

3. Trim old files. There's no built-in turnover for these logs, so the
   folder only ever grows unless someone tidies it. A reasonable weekly
   habit is to set aside anything older than four weeks into a separate
   folder off the host (a shared drive or a cold storage folder), then
   remove what's left in the live logs folder older than that window.

       Get-ChildItem C:\ProgramData\auditlog\logs\ |
         Where-Object { $_.LastWriteTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-28) } |
         Move-Item -To D:\host-upkeep\old-console-logs\

       find ~/.auditlog/logs/ -name '*.log' -mtime +28 \
         -exec mv {} ~/host-upkeep/old-console-logs/ \;

4. Skim the newest file for anything unusual before moving on - repeated
   restart lines, repeated bind failures, or long gaps where nothing was
   written at all (a long gap usually means the service wasn't running
   during that window, which is worth cross-checking against Section 7).

Worked example: a host that had been quietly rebooting itself once a day
for two weeks (an unrelated OS update setting) had a console log folder
that had grown past six hundred megabytes, almost entirely repeated startup
lines. Nothing in the database file was affected, but the log folder alone
had eaten most of the free space on that volume, which is what set off the
disk space check in Section 4 in the first place.

See console-log-files.md for the full write-up on managing this folder,
and console-log-file-sizes.txt for the current reference sizes per log type.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. SQLite File Locking
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Section owner: Ines Carrow (Platform Tools)

The database file is a single SQLite file, and SQLite's locking is
file-based rather than something the service manages on its own. On a
single-host setup this rarely bites anyone, but it does show up in two
fairly predictable ways: a second process opening the file at the same time
as the service, or a copy operation (see Section 8) started while the file
was still being written.

Weekly steps:

1. Confirm nothing else on the host has the database file open at the same
   time as the service. This is the single most common cause of "database
   is locked" style errors on a workstation - someone opens the file in a
   local SQLite viewer to poke around, forgets to close it, and leaves it
   open for days.

       lsof ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db
       (On Windows, Process Explorer's "Find Handle" against the file path
       works, or Get-Process | Where-Object with a handle scan if you have
       that set up.)

2. Check for a lingering journal or write-ahead file sitting next to the
   database file (same name, different suffix). Its presence isn't
   automatically a problem, but if it's still there hours after the service
   was last active, or it's grown unusually large, that's worth a closer
   look before it turns into an actual lock error.

       ls -la ~/.auditlog/*.db-*

3. If you do hit a lock error while running a manual check against the
   file, don't just try again right away - first confirm nothing still has
   the file open (step 1), and check the journal mode with a quick sqlite3
   session:

       sqlite3 ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db "PRAGMA journal_mode;"
       sqlite3 ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db "PRAGMA busy_timeout;"

   A short busy_timeout on a workstation that also runs a local viewer
   against the same file is a common, easy-to-fix cause of intermittent
   lock errors.

4. If a lock persists after confirming nothing else has the file open, a
   full host restart clears it in every case we've seen so far. That's a
   blunt tool, though, so treat it as a last step, not a first one.

A quick reference table:

  Situation                                   | What it usually means
  ---------------------------------------------|-------------------------------
  Lock error, another process has file open     | Close the other viewer/tool
  Lock error, nothing else has it open           | Check busy_timeout, then try again
  Journal/WAL file present and growing           | Backup copy or check under way
  Journal/WAL file present, host has been idle   | Worth a closer look, see below

See sqlite-file-locking.md for the fuller treatment of how this shows up in
practice, and sqlite-lock-troubleshooting.rst (v2.0) for step-by-step
restoration once a lock error has already happened rather than just being
watched for.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Host Monitoring
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Section owner: Sam Okafor (Infra Reliability)

This section is about the host itself staying up and the service staying
running on it - separate from any of the file-level checks above.

Weekly steps:

1. Confirm the service process is actually running, not just that the port
   check in Section 3 came back clean (a process can hold a port briefly on
   its way down, which can look fine for a moment and then vanish).

       Get-Process | Where-Object { $_.ProcessName -like '*auditlog*' }
       ps aux | grep auditlog

2. Check uptime on the host itself. An unexpectedly recent boot time on a
   host that's supposed to run unattended is worth investigating even if
   the service came back up fine afterward - it often points at an OS
   update, a power event, or something else worth knowing about before it
   happens again.

       (Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem).LastBootUpTime
       uptime -s

3. If the host has any general-purpose monitoring already set up (a simple
   heartbeat check, a small dashboard, whatever the team happens to use on
   that particular box), confirm it's actually still reporting and not
   quietly stuck showing last week's numbers. A monitoring dashboard that
   silently stopped updating three weeks ago is worse than having no
   dashboard at all, because it looks fine at a glance.

4. Look back over the week for any alert that fired and was dealt with
   without being written down anywhere. If something happened and got
   fixed quietly, add a line to the shared weekly log mentioned in Section
   2 so the pattern is visible if it happens again.

A short table of what "healthy" looks like on an ordinary week:

  Signal                          | Healthy
  ---------------------------------|-----------------------------------
  Service process running          | Yes, one copy, expected PID age
  Port bound                       | Yes, on the expected number
  Host uptime                      | Matches the last known restart
  Local monitoring dashboard        | Recently updated, no stuck values

As of v1.1.0 host-monitoring-overview.md covers the broader reasoning behind
why we watch these signals at all; this page only covers the weekly
mechanics of doing it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Copying the Database File for Backup
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Section owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools)

Because the database file is a single flat file, copying it is
straightforward, but doing it while the service is mid-write can produce a
copy that's inconsistent or, worse, one that opens fine but is missing
whatever was being written at the moment of the copy.

Weekly steps:

1. Confirm the service isn't in the middle of anything heavy before
   copying. On a workstation this usually just means picking a quiet moment
   rather than stopping the service outright.

2. Copy the file, and copy any journal/write-ahead file sitting next to it
   at the same time, using a tool that copies in one pass rather than
   streaming byte by byte over a slow link.

       robocopy C:\ProgramData\auditlog C:\host-upkeep\backups\auditlog auditlog.db*
       rsync -a ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db* ~/host-upkeep/backups/auditlog/

3. Check the copy's size against the original right after copying, then
   confirm with a hash value rather than trusting size alone (two files the
   same size aren't necessarily the same content).

       Get-FileHash C:\ProgramData\auditlog\auditlog.db -Algorithm SHA256
       Get-FileHash C:\host-upkeep\backups\auditlog\auditlog.db -Algorithm SHA256

       shasum -a 256 ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db
       shasum -a 256 ~/host-upkeep/backups/auditlog/auditlog.db

4. Store the copy somewhere off the host - a shared drive, another host on
   the local network, whatever the team already uses. A backup copy sitting
   next to the original on the same disk doesn't help much if that disk is
   what fails.

5. Name the copy with the date so it's obvious later which week it came
   from:

       auditlog.db.2026-03-15
       auditlog.db.2026-03-08

6. Keep the last four to six weekly copies and clear out anything older
   from the target location once you've confirmed the newer ones are good -
   this ties back into the disk space check in Section 4, since backup
   copies left unchecked are a common cause of slow disk growth on the host
   that holds them.

Worked example: a maintainer copying the database file mid-write ended up
with a copy that opened without error in a local viewer but was missing the
last few minutes of activity compared to the live file. The fix was simply
to redo the copy a few minutes later, once the write had settled, and to
add the hash-value check above as a standing step so a short copy would be
caught immediately rather than discovered weeks later when it was needed.

See database-file-backup-copy.md for the fuller write-up, and
backup-copy-verification.rst for a longer treatment of confirming a copy is
good beyond just matching size and hash value.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
9. Terminology
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Database file - The single SQLite file the service reads from and writes
to. On most hosts this is auditlog.db, though the exact path varies by OS.

Console log file - A plain text file the service writes its own startup
and runtime output to, kept in a separate folder from the database file.

Loopback interface - The local-only network interface (127.0.0.1) the
service binds to; nothing outside the host can reach it directly.

Port conflict - A situation where the service's expected port is already
held by another process at startup, forcing a fallback or a failed bind.

Lock error - An error surfaced by SQLite when the database file is opened
by more than one process in a way that its locking rules don't allow at
that moment.

Journal file / write-ahead file - A small companion file SQLite keeps next
to the main database file while changes are being written; its presence
and size are useful signals during the checks in Section 6.

Backup copy - A separate copy of the database file, taken at a point in
time and stored somewhere other than the host that produced it.

Hash value - A short fixed-length value computed from a file's contents,
used here to confirm a backup copy matches its source exactly.

Busy timeout - A SQLite setting controlling how long a process will wait
for a lock to clear before giving up and returning a lock error.

Threshold - A configured free-space or size level (see
disk-usage-thresholds.yaml) that separates a "fine for now" reading from
one that calls for action.

1	# Default Loopback Port Numbers and How to Change Them
2	
3	**Version:** 1.2
4	**Owner:** Infra Reliability (Dez Whitfield)
5	**Last updated:** 2024-05-11
6	
7	## Overview
8	
9	auditlog ships as a small standard-library-only Python package with a command line and a loopback HTTP service that keeps its records in a local SQLite file. On a workstation or a small shared host, the service binds to a fixed loopback interface and port at startup. Most of the time nobody thinks about the port at all — it's just there, quietly serving requests from the local machine — until something else on the host wants the same number, or until a maintainer needs to run two copies of the service side by side (one against a working database file, one against a day-old copy used for spot checks).
10	
11	This page documents the default port the service uses out of the box, the places on disk where that default is recorded, and the three supported ways a maintainer can move it aside. It also covers, at a lighter level, how the port choice interacts with the other pieces of host upkeep that this folder documents: port conflicts proper, disk space around the database file, the service's own console log files, SQLite file locking, host monitoring, and copying the database file for backup. Those topics each have their own page in this folder; this page only goes as deep into them as the port number touches.
12	
13	If you're new to the team, read `workstation-host-upkeep-overview.md` first — it frames all of the runbooks in this folder, including this one.
14	
15	## Terminology
16	
17	- **Loopback interface** — the network interface a host uses to talk to itself, conventionally 127.0.0.1 on IPv4. auditlog's HTTP service only ever binds here; it does not listen on any interface reachable from another host.
18	- **Bind** — the act of a process claiming a port number on a given interface so that it, and only it, can accept connections there.
19	- **Port** — a 16-bit number (1–65535) that, together with an interface, identifies where a process is listening.
20	- **Default port** — the port number the service uses when no override is present in the config file or the environment.
21	- **Override** — a config file setting or environment variable that replaces the default port with a maintainer-chosen one.
22	- **Ephemeral port** — a short-lived, operating-system-assigned port from the high end of the range (typically 49152–65535), used by outgoing connections; not what auditlog listens on, but sometimes confused with it.
23	- **Config file** — the small plain-text file auditlog reads at startup for host-specific settings, including the port.
24	- **Console log** — the plain-text file the service writes its own startup and shutdown lines to; covered in depth by `console-log-files.md`.
25	- **Database file** — the single SQLite file where auditlog keeps its records, referenced throughout this folder simply as "the database file."
26	- **Stale bind** — a port that appears occupied because a previous process instance did not shut down cleanly, even though nothing is currently listening.
27	- **Instance** — one running copy of the service; a host can run more than one instance at a time as long as each uses a distinct port and a distinct database file.
28	
29	## Default Port Assignment
30	
31	Out of the box, the service binds to the loopback interface on port **8765**. This has been the default since the package's early releases and has not changed in the current major line.
32	
33	| Setting | Value | Where it lives |
34	|---|---|---|
35	| Default interface | 127.0.0.1 | hard-coded in the package; not overridable |
36	| Default port | 8765 | `auditlog/` package defaults |
37	| Config file override key | `port` | `~/.auditlog/service.cfg` (Linux/macOS) or `%USERPROFILE%\.auditlog\service.cfg` (Windows) |
38	| Environment variable override | `LOGSVC_PORT` | shell environment, takes precedence over the config file |
39	| Console log line at startup | `listening on 127.0.0.1:<port>` | first line the service writes after the config file is read |
40	
41	Note that the interface itself is not configurable — logsvc will never bind to a non-loopback interface on this host class, by design of the package, and that falls outside what this page covers.
42	
43	If port 8765 is already bound by something else when the service starts, the service does not try again and does not fall back to a nearby port on its own; it exits and the console log records why. See "Interaction with the Console Log Files" below for what that line looks like.
44	
45	## Why the Service Binds Only to Loopback
46	
47	The service is meant to be reached only from processes running on the same workstation or small host — the command line, a local script, or a browser open on that same machine. Binding to loopback rather than to all interfaces keeps the service out of the picture entirely for anything arriving over the network, which simplifies host upkeep considerably: there's no port to open in a host firewall, no interface to pick among several, and no interaction with whatever else the host's network configuration is doing. It also means port conflicts on this host are strictly local — two processes on the *same* machine fighting over the *same* number — rather than something that could show up differently depending on which network interface a caller used.
48	
49	## Changing the Port
50	
51	*(Section owner: Dez Whitfield)*
52	
53	There are two supported ways to move the port, in order of how the service resolves them:
54	
55	1. Environment variable `LOGSVC_PORT` — checked first, wins if set.
56	2. `port` key in the config file — checked if the environment variable is absent.
57	
58	If neither is present, the service falls back to 8765.
59	
60	### Through the Config File
61	
62	The config file is a small INI-style file. On most workstations it lives at:
63	
64	- Linux/macOS: `~/.auditlog/service.cfg`
65	- Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.auditlog\service.cfg`
66	
67	A minimal entry that moves the port to 8901 looks like this:
68	
69	```
70	[service]
71	port = 8901
72	```
73	
74	If the file or the `[service]` section doesn't exist yet, create it — the service reads whatever is present and applies its own defaults for anything missing. Save the file, then restart the service through whatever your usual startup method is on this host (scheduled task, startup item, or manual start from a terminal — this varies by workstation and isn't standardized across the team yet).
75	
76	Worked example — moving a workstation off the default because a local Jupyter install has claimed 8765 on port bump day:
77	
78	1. Open `~/.auditlog/service.cfg` in a text editor.
79	2. Add or edit the `[service]` block:
80	   ```
81	   [service]
82	   port = 8801
83	   ```
84	3. Save and close the file.
85	4. Restart the auditlog service.
86	5. Confirm the new port is listening (see verification steps below).
87	6. Update any local scripts or shortcuts that assumed 8765.
88	
89	### Through an Environment Variable
90	
91	Setting `LOGSVC_PORT` is useful for a one-off run — for example, spinning up a second instance temporarily against a copied database file without touching the config file that the primary instance reads.
92	
93	On PowerShell, for the current session only:
94	
95	```powershell
96	$env:LOGSVC_PORT = "8902"
97	```
98	
99	On a POSIX shell:
100	
101	```bash
102	export LOGSVC_PORT=8902
103	```
104	
105	Because the environment variable takes precedence over the config file, this is also the fastest way to check whether a port problem is coming from a stale config file entry — set the variable to a known-free port, restart, and see if the problem follows.
106	
107	To make the override stick across reboots on Windows, set it as a user environment variable through System Properties rather than only in a single PowerShell session, or add the `export` line to your shell's startup file on Linux/macOS.
108	
109	### Picking a New Number
110	
111	There's no team-wide convention yet for which numbers to use when moving off 8765 — pick anything outside the well-known range (below 1024) and outside your host's ephemeral range. A loose convention some of us follow, worth writing down here even though it isn't enforced:
112	
113	- 8765 — default, leave alone unless it's occupied.
114	- 8766–8770 — reserved informally for a second, third, etc. instance on the same host (spot-check copies, side-by-side version comparisons).
115	- Anything else above 1024 and below 49152 — fine for a workstation-specific override, as long as it doesn't collide with something else that host runs regularly.
116	
117	### Running Two Instances on One Host
118	
119	Each instance needs its own port *and* its own database file — pointing two instances at the same database file while using two different ports does not avoid the file-locking behavior described in `sqlite-file-locking.md`; it just adds a second process contending for the same file lock in addition to the port question. If you need a second instance for a side-by-side check, copy the database file first (see "Backup Copy Considerations" below) and point the second instance's config file or environment variable at both the copy and a distinct port.
120	
121	## Verifying What's Listening
122	
123	Before changing anything, and after, it's worth confirming what's actually bound to a given port on the loopback interface. These are general operating-system utilities, not auditlog commands.
124	
125	On Windows (PowerShell):
126	
127	```powershell
128	Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8765 -LocalAddress 127.0.0.1
129	```
130	
131	or the older but still common:
132	
133	```powershell
134	netstat -ano | findstr "8765"
135	```
136	
137	The trailing number in the `netstat` output is the process ID; cross-reference it with Task Manager or `Get-Process -Id <pid>` to confirm which process actually holds the port.
138	
139	On Linux/macOS:
140	
141	```bash
142	lsof -i :8765
143	```
144	
145	or
146	
147	```bash
148	ss -ltnp | grep 8765
149	```
150	
151	A stale bind — where the port looks occupied but the process behind it is long dead — usually clears on its own within a short interval after the operating system reclaims the socket, but if it persists, ending the stale process is the more reliable fix over waiting.
152	
153	## Interaction with Port Conflicts
154	
155	This page covers what the default is and how to move it; the deeper diagnostic steps for figuring out *what else* has taken 8765 (or any override) live in `port-conflicts.md`. The short version worth repeating here: on a typical developer workstation, the numbers most likely to collide with a hand-picked override are ones used by other local tooling — notebook servers, small local web frameworks, and container tooling all tend to cluster in the 3000–9000 range. A quick table of common local occupants, kept here because it's useful at the moment of picking a new port and not everyone reads the conflicts page first:
156	
157	| Port | Commonly used by |
158	|---|---|
159	| 3000 | Node-based local dev servers |
160	| 5000 | Local Flask-style dev servers |
161	| 8000 | Simple local static file servers |
162	| 8080 | Various local proxies and management consoles |
163	| 8888 | Jupyter notebook servers |
164	| 9000 | Various local build/watch tooling |
165	
166	None of these are reserved for auditlog in any way; they're listed only because they're the numbers most likely to already be busy when you go looking for a free one.
167	
168	## Interaction with Disk Space
169	
170	The port number itself takes essentially no disk space — the config file that holds the override is a handful of bytes. The connection worth noting here is indirect: a maintainer running a second instance to inspect a copied database file (which requires picking a second port, per "Running Two Instances on One Host" above) has now also doubled the number of console log files and added a full copy of the database file to disk. On a small host where `disk-space-checks.md` already flags the database file's directory as worth watching, a temporary second instance temporarily draws on that same disk budget and should be cleaned up — config file entry, database file copy, and console log — once the side-by-side check is done.
171	
172	## Interaction with the Console Log Files
173	
174	Every time the service starts, the very first thing it writes to its console log is the interface and port it bound to, for example:
175	
176	```
177	2026-09-14 09:02:11 listening on 127.0.0.1:8765
178	```
179	
180	If the port was already bound by something else, the console log instead records a line describing the bind failure and the process exits without ever writing the "listening on" line at all. This is the fastest way to confirm, after the fact, which port a given run actually used — more reliable than trusting memory or an old note taped to a monitor, especially on a host that's had its config file edited more than once.
181	
182	Because the console log records the port on every single startup, a host that restarts the service often (for instance, during repeated port changes while troubleshooting) will accumulate a lot of very short-lived log entries. `console-log-files.md` covers the file sizes and format in full; the only note worth adding here is that a burst of startup/shutdown cycles while hunting for a free port is a normal, expected source of a temporarily busier console log, not a sign of a problem with the service itself.
183	
184	## Interaction with SQLite File Locking
185	
186	The port and the database file's lock are two independent mechanisms, and it's worth being explicit about that because the two are easy to conflate. Binding a port does not, by itself, lock the database file, and holding the database file's lock does not reserve any port. In practice they move together because a single instance normally does both at once, but the failure modes are different:
187	
188	- A **port conflict** stops the service from starting at all — you never get as far as the database file being opened.
189	- A **file lock conflict** (covered in `sqlite-file-locking.md`) can happen even after the service has successfully bound its port, if some other process — a second instance, a manual `sqlite3` session, a backup script — is holding the database file open at the same moment.
190	
191	When two instances are run deliberately (see "Running Two Instances on One Host"), giving each a distinct port is necessary but not sufficient — each also needs its own database file, or its own copy, to avoid file-locking contention. A quick way to confirm a database file isn't already open elsewhere before starting a second instance:
192	
193	```bash
194	fuser ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db
195	```
196	
197	or on Windows, check the handle through Resource Monitor's "Associated Handles" search for the file name.
198	
199	## Host Monitoring Hooks
200	
201	If this host has any local monitoring set up per `host-monitoring-overview.md`, a check that confirms the service is listening on its expected port is one of the simplest and most useful things to include. A minimal PowerShell check suitable for a scheduled task:
202	
203	```powershell
204	$conn = Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8765 -LocalAddress 127.0.0.1 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
205	if (-not $conn) {
206	    Write-Warning "auditlog is not listening on 127.0.0.1:8765"
207	}
208	```
209	
210	If the host has been moved to a non-default port through a config file override, remember to update the port number in this check as well — a stale monitoring check that still watches 8765 after everyone agreed to move the host to 8801 will fire a false warning every time it runs and eventually get ignored, which defeats the point of having it. During the March 2026 workstation sweep, two hosts were found running happily on 8766 (the service had, in fact, fallen back to the next free port automatically that quarter) while their local monitoring checks were still pointed at 8765 and had been quietly failing for weeks — worth keeping in mind if a check on this host seems to be reporting the service down when it clearly isn't.
211	
212	`host-monitoring-checklist.txt` includes a line item for confirming the expected port on a weekly basis; this page is the source of truth for what "expected" should mean for a given host.
213	
214	## Backup Copy Considerations
215	
216	Copying the database file for backup, per `database-file-backup-copy.md`, doesn't touch the port at all, but there's a sequencing point worth calling out here: if the service is stopped before the copy (the safer of the two documented approaches on the backup page), restarting it afterward should bind the same port it had before, as long as neither the config file nor the environment variable changed in between. It's easy, when stopping a service for a backup copy, to also decide "while it's down, let's move the port too" — resist doing both at once. If the copy needs to be verified afterward and the port also changed at the same moment, it becomes harder to tell whether an unexpected result came from the copy itself or from the port change, and separating the two makes troubleshooting either one considerably simpler.
217	
218	If a second instance is started against the copied database file to verify it (see `backup-copy-verification.rst`), that instance needs its own port per "Running Two Instances on One Host" above — pointing the verification instance at the same port as the primary instance will simply fail to bind, and the console log will record that failure rather than anything about the copy itself.
219	
220	## Files and Paths Referenced
221	
222	| Path | Purpose |
223	|---|---|
224	| `auditlog/` | package directory; holds the built-in default port value, not edited for routine port changes |
225	| `README.md` | repository root readme; general package overview |
226	| `~/.auditlog/service.cfg` (Linux/macOS) | per-user config file; holds the `port` override key |
227	| `%USERPROFILE%\.auditlog\service.cfg` (Windows) | same config file, Windows path |
228	| `~/.auditlog/auditlog.db` | default database file location |
229	| `~/.auditlog/logs/console.log` | default console log file; first line of each run records the bound port |
230	| `docs/operations-runbooks/` | folder holding this page and its sibling runbooks |
231	| `scripts/set-loopback-port.ps1` | local helper script some maintainers use to edit the config file's `port` key without opening an editor by hand |
232	| `scripts/check-loopback-port.ps1` | local helper script wrapping `Get-NetTCPConnection` for a quick pass/fail on the expected port |
233	| `host-monitoring-checklist.txt` | weekly checklist; includes the "confirm expected port" line item this page defines |
234	
235	## Tools and Packages
236	
237	| Tool / package | Version used on team workstations | Purpose |
238	|---|---|---|
239	| Python | 3.11.8 | runs the package; no third-party dependencies required |
240	| auditlog | current internal build | the package this whole folder documents |
241	| PowerShell | 7.4 | verification and helper scripts on Windows hosts |
242	| sqlite3 CLI | 3.45.1 | manual inspection of the database file when checking file locks alongside a port change |
243	| lsof | 4.94.0 (macOS/Linux builds vary) | confirming what process holds a port or a file handle |
244	| Resource Monitor | built into Windows 10/11 | Windows equivalent for checking file handles when `lsof` isn't available |
245	
246	## Change Log
247	
248	| Date | Version | Change |
249	|---|---|---|
250	| 2023-01-16 | 1.0 | Initial page: documented default port 8765 and the config file override. |
251	| 2023-06-02 | 1.0.1 | Added environment variable override (`LOGSVC_PORT`) after several maintainers asked for a way to override without editing the config file. |
252	| 2023-11-20 | 1.1 | Added "Running Two Instances on One Host" following recurring questions during side-by-side database file checks. |
253	| 2024-02-08 | 1.1.1 | Added verification commands for Windows and Linux/macOS. |
254	| 2024-04-30 | 1.1.2 | Added the common local port table under "Interaction with Port Conflicts." |
255	| 2024-05-11 | 1.2 | Added host monitoring hook example and the note about the March 2026 workstation sweep; clarified backup copy sequencing. |
256	
257	## Related Pages
258	
259	- "operations-runbooks Overview" — folder-level index for this and every sibling page.
260	- "Diagnosing Port Conflicts for the Loopback Service" (v1.4) — deeper diagnostic steps when a port, default or overridden, turns out to be occupied.

If you need a second instance for a side-by-side check, copy the database file first (see "Backup Copy Considerations" below) and point the second instance's config file or environment variable at both the copy and a distinct port.

## Verifying What's Listening

Before changing anything, and after, it's worth confirming what's actually bound to a given port on the loopback interface. These are general operating-system utilities, not auditlog commands.

On Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8765 -LocalAddress 127.0.0.1
```

or the older but still common:

```powershell
netstat -ano | findstr "8765"
```

The trailing number in the `netstat` output is the process ID; cross-reference it with Task Manager or `Get-Process -Id <pid>` to confirm which process actually holds the port.

On Linux/macOS:

```bash
lsof -i :8765
```

or

```bash
ss -ltnp | grep 8765
```

A stale bind — where the port looks occupied but the process behind it is long dead — usually clears on its own within a short interval after the operating system reclaims the socket, but if it persists, ending the stale process is the more reliable fix over waiting.

## Interaction with Port Conflicts

This page covers what the default is and how to move it; the deeper diagnostic steps for figuring out *what else* has taken 8765 (or any override) live in `port-conflicts.md`. The short version worth repeating here: on a typical developer workstation, the numbers most likely to collide with a hand-picked override are ones used by other local tooling — notebook servers, small local web frameworks, and container tooling all tend to cluster in the 3000–9000 range. A quick table of common local occupants, kept here because it's useful at the moment of picking a new port and not everyone reads the conflicts page first:

| Port | Commonly used by |
|---|---|
| 3000 | Node-based local dev servers |
| 5000 | Local Flask-style dev servers |
| 8000 | Simple local static file servers |
| 8080 | Various local proxies and management consoles |
| 8888 | Jupyter notebook servers |
| 9000 | Various local build/watch tooling |

None of these are reserved for auditlog in any way; they're listed only because they're the numbers most likely to already be busy when you go looking for a free one.

## Interaction with Disk Space

The port number itself takes essentially no disk space — the config file that holds the override is a handful of bytes. The connection worth noting here is indirect: a maintainer running a second instance to inspect a copied database file (which requires picking a second port, per "Running Two Instances on One Host" above) has now also doubled the number of console log files and added a full copy of the database file to disk. On a small host where `disk-space-checks.md` already flags the database file's directory as worth watching, a temporary second instance temporarily draws on that same disk budget and should be cleaned up — config file entry, database file copy, and console log — once the side-by-side check is done.

## Interaction with the Console Log Files

Every time the service starts, the very first thing it writes to its console log is the interface and port it bound to, for example:

```
2026-09-14 09:02:11 listening on 127.0.0.1:8765
```

If the port was already bound by something else, the console log instead records a line describing the bind failure and the process exits without ever writing the "listening on" line at all. This is the fastest way to confirm, after the fact, which port a given run actually used — more reliable than trusting memory or an old note taped to a monitor, especially on a host that's had its config file edited more than once.

Because the console log records the port on every single startup, a host that restarts the service often (for instance, during repeated port changes while troubleshooting) will accumulate a lot of very short-lived log entries. `console-log-files.md` covers the file sizes and format in full; the only note worth adding here is that a burst of startup/shutdown cycles while hunting for a free port is a normal, expected source of a temporarily busier console log, not a sign of a problem with the service itself.

## Interaction with SQLite File Locking

The port and the database file's lock are two independent mechanisms, and it's worth being explicit about that because the two are easy to conflate. Binding a port does not, by itself, lock the database file, and holding the database file's lock does not reserve any port. In practice they move together because a single instance normally does both at once, but the failure modes are different:

- A **port conflict** stops the service from starting at all — you never get as far as the database file being opened.
- A **file lock conflict** (covered in `sqlite-file-locking.md`) can happen even after the service has successfully bound its port, if some other process — a second instance, a manual `sqlite3` session, a backup script — is holding the database file open at the same moment.

When two instances are run deliberately (see "Running Two Instances on One Host"), giving each a distinct port is necessary but not sufficient — each also needs its own database file, or its own copy, to avoid file-locking contention. A quick way to confirm a database file isn't already open elsewhere before starting a second instance:

```bash
fuser ~/.auditlog/auditlog.db
```

or on Windows, check the handle through Resource Monitor's "Associated Handles" search for the file name.

## Host Monitoring Hooks

If this host has any local monitoring set up per `host-monitoring-overview.md`, a check that confirms the service is listening on its expected port is one of the simplest and most useful things to include. A minimal PowerShell check suitable for a scheduled task:

```powershell
$conn = Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 8765 -LocalAddress 127.0.0.1 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
if (-not $conn) {
    Write-Warning "auditlog is not listening on 127.0.0.1:8765"
}
```

If the host has been moved to a non-default port through a config file override, remember to update the port number in this check as well — a stale monitoring check that still watches 8765 after everyone agreed to move the host to 8801 will fire a false warning every time it runs and eventually get ignored, which defeats the point of having it. During the March 2026 workstation sweep, two hosts were found running happily on 8766 (the service had, in fact, fallen back to the next free port automatically that quarter) while their local monitoring checks were still pointed at 8765 and had been quietly failing for weeks — worth keeping in mind if a check on this host seems to be reporting the service down when it clearly isn't.

`host-monitoring-checklist.txt` includes a line item for confirming the expected port on a weekly basis; this page is the source of truth for what "expected" should mean for a given host.

## Backup Copy Considerations

Copying the database file for backup, per `database-file-backup-copy.md`, doesn't touch the port at all, but there's a sequencing point worth calling out here: if the service is stopped before the copy (the safer of the two documented approaches on the backup page), restarting it afterward should bind the same port it had before, as long as neither the config file nor the environment variable changed in between. It's easy, when stopping a service for a backup copy, to also decide "while it's down, let's move the port too" — resist doing both at once. If the copy needs to be verified afterward and the port also changed at the same moment, it becomes harder to tell whether an unexpected result came from the copy itself or from the port change, and separating the two makes troubleshooting either one considerably simpler.

If a second instance is started against the copied database file to verify it (see `backup-copy-verification.rst`), that instance needs its own port per "Running Two Instances on One Host" above — pointing the verification instance at the same port as the primary instance will simply fail to bind, and the console log will record that failure rather than anything about the copy itself.

## Files and Paths Referenced

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `auditlog/` | package directory; holds the built-in default port value, not edited for routine port changes |
| `README.md` | repository root readme; general package overview |
| `~/.auditlog/service.cfg` (Linux/macOS) | per-user config file; holds the `port` override key |
| `%USERPROFILE%\.auditlog\service.cfg` (Windows) | same config file, Windows path |
| `~/.auditlog/auditlog.db` | default database file location |
| `~/.auditlog/logs/console.log` | default console log file; first line of each run records the bound port |
| `docs/operations-runbooks/` | folder holding this page and its sibling runbooks |
| `scripts/set-loopback-port.ps1` | local helper script some maintainers use to edit the config file's `port` key without opening an editor by hand |
| `scripts/check-loopback-port.ps1` | local helper script wrapping `Get-NetTCPConnection` for a quick pass/fail on the expected port |
| `host-monitoring-checklist.txt` | weekly checklist; includes the "confirm expected port" line item this page defines |

## Tools and Packages

| Tool / package | Version used on team workstations | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11.8 | runs the package; no third-party dependencies required |
| auditlog | current internal build | the package this whole folder documents |
| PowerShell | 7.4 | verification and helper scripts on Windows hosts |
| sqlite3 CLI | 3.45.1 | manual inspection of the database file when checking file locks alongside a port change |
| lsof | 4.94.0 (macOS/Linux builds vary) | confirming what process holds a port or a file handle |
| Resource Monitor | built into Windows 10/11 | Windows equivalent for checking file handles when `lsof` isn't available |

| 2023-11-20 | 1.1 | Added "Running Two Instances on One Host" following recurring questions during side-by-side database file checks. |

| 2024-05-11 | 1.2 | Added host monitoring hook example and the note about the March 2026 workstation sweep; clarified backup copy sequencing. |

1	# Diagnosing Port Conflicts for the Loopback Service
2	
3	| Field | Value |
4	|-------|-------|
5	| **Title** | Diagnosing Port Conflicts for the Loopback Service |
6	| **Version** | v1.3.0 |
7	| **Owner** | Infra Reliability (Dez Whitfield) |
8	| **Last Updated** | 2025-11-14 |
9	
10	## Summary
11	
12	This page explains how to identify when another process is already using the network port that the service listens on, and how to resolve the conflict. Port conflicts prevent the service from starting or binding correctly, resulting in startup failures or degraded functionality. This guide covers detection, diagnosis, remediation, and prevention of port conflicts on workstations and small host environments.
13	
14	## What Is a Port Conflict?
15	
16	The service uses a loopback HTTP interface to accept requests from local applications. It binds to a specific port on the local network interface (typically `127.0.0.1`). A port conflict occurs when:
17	
18	- Another process is already listening on that port
19	- The port is in a TIME_WAIT state and the service cannot rebind quickly
20	- The port reservation from a previous service run has not yet cleared
21	
22	When the service cannot bind to its configured port, it either fails to start or logs a binding error and exits. Requests from local applications will fail with connection refused or timeout errors.
23	
24	## Detecting a Port Conflict
25	
26	### Startup Failure Indicators
27	
28	The most common scenario is that the service fails to start when you attempt to run it. Check for these signs:
29	
30	1. **Service does not remain running** — The service exits immediately after launch with a port binding error message in the console output
31	2. **Local applications cannot connect** — Applications trying to reach the service receive immediate connection errors
32	3. **Port already in use error** — The console output contains a message such as `Port binding already in use` or `Only one usage of each socket is normally permitted`
33	
34	### Checking Which Port Is in Use
35	
36	To identify which port the service is attempting to use, check the service configuration or review the loopback-port-defaults.md page. The default loopback port is 9127, but this can be changed. You can also review startup logs or the console output from the last service run.
37	
38	**On Windows:**
39	
40	Use the netstat utility to list all listening ports and the process IDs that own them:
41	
42	```
43	netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING
44	```
45	
46	This command returns output similar to:
47	
48	```
49	The output shows the protocol, local binding location, connection state, and process identifier
50	TCP    127.0.0.1:9127         LISTENING       4208
51	TCP    127.0.0.1:9128         LISTENING       2104
52	```
53	
54	Look for the configured port number and note the PID (process ID) of the process that is listening. In this example, PID 4208 is listening on port 9127.
55	
56	**On Linux or macOS:**
57	
58	Use the netstat or ss command:
59	
60	```
61	netstat -tlnp | grep 9127
62	```
63	
64	Or with ss (socket statistics):
65	
66	```
67	ss -tlnp | grep 9127
68	```
69	
70	The output will show the process name and PID bound to the port.
71	
72	## Identifying the Conflicting Process
73	
74	Once you know which process ID is using the port, look up what process it is.
75	
76	**On Windows:**
77	
78	1. Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc)
79	2. Go to the **Details** tab
80	3. Look for the PID in the rightmost column (you may need to scroll right to see it)
81	4. The process name and description are shown in adjacent columns
82	
83	Alternatively, use the command line:
84	
85	```
86	tasklist /fi "PID eq 4208"
87	```
88	
89	This will return the executable name and memory usage of the process.
90	
91	**On Linux or macOS:**
92	
93	```
94	ps -p 4208 -o comm=
95	```
96	
97	Or for more detail:
98	
99	```
100	ps -p 4208 -o pid,user,comm,args
101	```
102	
103	### Common Conflicting Processes
104	
105	The following table shows processes that frequently conflict with the service port:
106	
107	| Process | Typical Port | Reason |
108	|---------|--------------|--------|
109	| Another auditlog instance | 9127 | Service running twice, or running after a previous crash |
110	| Python REPL or notebook server | 9128–9200 | Jupyter, IPython, or other development tools |
111	| Third-party monitoring agent | varies | Monitoring or observability software using adjacent ports |
112	| System service or daemon | varies | Windows/Linux service running on a reserved port |
113	| Stale service process | 9127 | Previous service run did not terminate cleanly |
114	
115	## Resolving Port Conflicts
116	
117	### Step 1: Verify the Conflicting Process
118	
119	Before terminating a process, confirm:
120	
121	- You are terminating the correct process (not a critical system service)
122	- You have the capability to end it (if you are the owner or system manager)
123	- No important work is in progress (close any open files or applications)
124	
125	### Step 2: Stop the Conflicting Process
126	
127	**On Windows:**
128	
129	If the process is safe to stop, use the command line:
130	
131	```
132	taskkill /PID 4208 /F
133	```
134	
135	The `/F` flag forces termination. Omit `/F` for a graceful shutdown:
136	
137	```
138	taskkill /PID 4208
139	```
140	
141	Wait a few seconds after terminating the process before attempting to start the service. This allows the port to fully release.
142	
143	**On Linux or macOS:**
144	
145	```
146	kill -TERM 4208
147	```
148	
149	Or force kill if needed:
150	
151	```
152	kill -KILL 4208
153	```
154	
155	Wait for the kernel to release the port. If the port remains in TIME_WAIT state, you may need to wait 30–60 seconds before the service can rebind.
156	
157	### Step 3: Attempt Service Startup
158	
159	Try starting the service again. If it starts successfully, the port conflict has been resolved. Verify that the service is running and accepting requests by checking the console output or attempting a connection from a local application.
160	
161	### Step 4: If the Conflict Persists
162	
163	If the port is still in use after stopping the identified process:
164	
165	1. Run the port check command again to see if a different process is now using the port
166	2. Verify you are checking the correct port (review the configuration file again)
167	3. Check whether the port is in TIME_WAIT state and may need additional wait time
168	4. Restart the host if all else fails (this will clear all port reservations and reset TCP state tables)
169	
170	## Preventing Port Conflicts
171	
172	### Changing the Loopback Port
173	
174	If a particular port is frequently conflicted on your host, you can change the service's loopback port to an unused port. Refer to loopback-port-defaults.md for configuration instructions. Common alternatives are 9128, 9129, 9200, or any port above 1024 that is not in use.
175	
176	After changing the port:
177	
178	- Update any applications or scripts that connect to the service
179	- Update monitoring systems to check the new port
180	- Document the port change in your host-specific notes
181	
182	### Regular Port Monitoring
183	
184	Include a port-in-use check in your regular host monitoring routine. The host-monitoring-checklist.txt provides a template for weekly checks.
185	
186	Consider adding a cron job (Linux/macOS) or scheduled task (Windows) to monitor the port:
187	
188	**Linux/macOS cron entry:**
189	
190	```
191	0 9 * * * netstat -tlnp 2>/dev/null | grep -q 9127 && echo "Port 9127 in use" || true
192	```
193	
194	This runs every day at 9:00 AM and logs if the port is in use.
195	
196	**Windows Task Scheduler:**
197	
198	Create a scheduled task that runs:
199	
200	```
201	netstat -ano | findstr 9127
202	```
203	
204	And logs the output to a file for review.
205	
206	### Multiple Service Instances
207	
208	Ensure only one instance of the service runs on each host. Common mistakes:
209	
210	- Starting the service twice from different terminals
211	- Leaving the service running when you think you stopped it
212	- Automated startup scripts conflicting with manual starts
213	
214	Check process listings regularly if this has been an issue on your host.
215	
216	## Service Restoration Following Port Conflicts
217	
218	If the service fails to start due to a port conflict, the service may not have created any console output or log file entries. After resolving the port conflict and restarting the service, review the console output to ensure the service bound successfully and is running normally.
219	
220	Refer to console-log-files.md for guidance on examining the service's console log files and cycling them if they grow large.
221	
222	If a port conflict has caused the service to exit unexpectedly, check:
223	
224	1. Whether any in-flight requests were lost
225	2. Whether the database file is still in a consistent state (see sqlite-file-locking.md for repair procedures)
226	3. Whether disk space was used during the failed startup attempts
227	
228	## Interplay with Other Host Maintenance
229	
230	Port conflicts often occur alongside other host upkeep issues:
231	
232	- **Disk space:** A host running out of disk space may cause background services to fail, freeing up ports. See disk-space-checks.md for details.
233	- **SQLite locking:** If the service cannot start due to a port conflict, the database file may remain locked. See sqlite-file-locking.md.
234	- **Console log files:** Port conflict errors are logged to console output, which may need to be cycled. See console-log-files.md.
235	- **Host monitoring:** Automated host monitoring should alert on service startup failures. See host-monitoring-overview.md.
236	
237	## Troubleshooting Special Cases
238	
239	### TIME_WAIT Port State
240	
241	On some systems, a port may appear "in use" even after the process using it has terminated. The port is in TIME_WAIT state, a TCP state that persists for 30–120 seconds to prevent packet confusion. You cannot immediately rebind to this port.
242	
243	If you encounter this:
244	
245	1. Wait 60 seconds and try starting the service again
246	2. Verify that no process is actually still listening on the port using netstat
247	3. Change to a different loopback port (see loopback-port-defaults.md)
248	4. On Windows, you can adjust the TIME_WAIT period (advanced configuration)
249	
250	To reduce the TIME_WAIT timeout on Windows (requires system manager capabilities):
251	
252	```
253	reg add HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters /v TcpTimedWaitDelay /t REG_DWORD /d 30
254	```
255	
256	This sets the TIME_WAIT duration to 30 seconds. The Windows default is 240 seconds. After this change, you must restart the host for the setting to take effect. Use caution when modifying Windows registry settings, as errors can affect system stability.
257	
258	### IPv6 vs. IPv4
259	
260	If your host has IPv6 enabled, both IPv4 and IPv6 loopback ports may need to be available. The service listens on `127.0.0.1` (IPv4), but some monitoring or firewall tools may also reserve IPv6 loopback locations `::1`.
261	
262	Check for IPv6 listeners:
263	
264	```
265	netstat -ano | findstr ":9127" | findstr IPv6
266	```
267	
268	If an IPv6 listener is using the port, resolve it using the same process as IPv4 conflicts.
269	
270	### Persistent Processes
271	
272	Some system services and background monitoring agents are designed to restart themselves automatically if terminated. If you kill a conflicting process and it immediately starts again, the process may be managed by a supervisor or scheduled task.
273	
274	On Windows, check:
275	
276	- Task Scheduler for recurring tasks
277	- Services snap-in for service auto-restart settings
278	- Startup folders in `C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup` and user startup folders
279	
280	On Linux/macOS, check:
281	
282	- Cron jobs or systemd timers
283	- Supervisor or systemd unit files in `/etc/systemd/system/` and `/usr/lib/systemd/system/`
284	- LaunchDaemons or LaunchAgents on macOS
285	
286	Disable the auto-restart setting if the process is non-critical, or change the service's loopback port instead.
287	
288	## Terminology and Glossary
289	
290	**Loopback interface** — A virtual network interface (`127.0.0.1` on IPv4, `::1` on IPv6) that allows local applications to communicate as if over a real network. Used for validation and local-only services.
291	
292	**Port** — A 16-bit number (0–65535) that identifies a communication socket on a host. Ports 0–1023 are reserved for system services; ports 1024–65535 are user-allocatable. The service typically uses port 9127.
293	
294	**Port conflict** — A situation in which two or more processes attempt to listen on the same port simultaneously. Only one process can hold exclusive access to a given port at a time.
295	
296	**Socket** — An operating-system-level abstraction representing one side of network communication. A socket is defined by a protocol (TCP or UDP), an IP location, and a port.
297	
298	**TIME_WAIT state** — A TCP socket state in which the socket remains reserved for 30–120 seconds after connection closure to prevent lingering packets from interfering with a new connection on the same port.
299	
300	**Process ID (PID)** — A unique integer assigned by the operating system to identify a running process. Used by system management tools to look up or terminate a process.
301	
302	**netstat** — A command-line utility (network statistics) that displays active network connections, listening ports, and associated process information. Supported on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
303	
304	**HTTP service** — A network service that accepts incoming HTTP requests and returns responses. The service exposes a loopback HTTP interface on port 9127 for local communication.
