db_op.description: Database operation: 'get', 'list' or 'query' for read_db; 'set', 'update' or 'delete' for write_db, or 'batch' to send up to 50 of those in `writes` under one approval. Required for both database actions; meaningless for every other action.

writes.description: write_db with db_op 'batch' only: the writes to apply together, 1-50 entries of {op: 'set'|'update'|'delete', collection, doc_id, and for set/update exactly one of data (inline object) or file_path (a local JSON file)}. Each document is addressed at most once; the batch commits all-or-nothing where the server supports it, else in order one at a time (the result says which). Prefer it over separate write_db calls whenever you write more than a couple of documents.

collection.description: Database collection path: an odd number (1-15) of "/"-separated segments (letters, digits, _ - . ~ : @ + per segment). Paths alternate collection/document, so "boards/b1/columns" is a collection and, with `doc_id` "c2", names the document "boards/b1/columns/c2". Per-user data: "data/users/<id>" (3 segments) is the collection holding that user's documents, "data/users/<id>/decks" is one document in it, and "data/users/<id>/decks/cards" a collection under that; "me" as the <id> means the current user. Required for read_db and write_db.

doc_id.description: Document id (one path segment). Required for db_op 'get', 'set', 'update' and 'delete'; not accepted with 'list' or 'query'.

as_level.description: read_db and write_db only: act at this access level instead of your own — 'interact' is any signed-in viewer who can use the page, 'admin' a co-owner — to check what the page's access rules let such a user do. It narrows, never raises, your access; the call still reads and writes your own data/users subtree. At a lowered level a write the rules refuse reads as not found and a refused read as empty. Omit it to act as yourself.

query.description: Options for db_op 'list' and 'query': `limit` (1-1000, default 100) and `cursor` (from a prior result's `next_cursor`) page through a collection; `where` clauses ([field, operator, value] triples) and `order_by` filter and order a 'query' only. A query with `order_by` is a single page: it returns at most `limit` documents in that order and never a `next_cursor`, so pass the `limit` you mean (up to 1000), or drop `order_by` and page with `cursor` to read a whole collection.

data.description: write_db: document fields to write, as a JSON object — db_op 'set' (replaces the document) and 'update' (merges into it; a field given as `{"__delete__": true}` is removed) take exactly one of `data` or `file_path`; not accepted with any other db_op.

file_path.description: Path to the .html file to render. Required to publish (the default action). Use a short, distinctive basename — it is the last-resort title when the HTML has no <title> and no `title` parameter is given. For 'upload_asset', the local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet (CSS), script (JS), or text (CSV, Markdown, JSON, plain text) file to upload. For 'write_db' (db_op 'set' or 'update'), a local JSON file whose top-level object is sent as the document — an alternative to inline `data`, so a large document need not pass through the conversation.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map — a plain signifier, not a product or brand name. Include it on every page's first publish; omit when republishing to keep the current icon, and pass a new one only when the user asks.

limit.description: list only: maximum artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list only: 'mine' (default) lists artifacts the user owns; 'shared' lists artifacts other people shared with the user; 'all' lists both. Rows are labeled (mine)/(shared) whenever scope is not 'mine'.

title.description: Title for the artifact — the name shown in the browser tab and gallery. A short, distinctive noun-phrase name — not a generic label, a summary, or a name with an appended explainer. Prefer a <title> tag at the top of the HTML itself; this parameter fills in only when the file lacks one in the first 8KB of the file, and never overrides the tag. HTML publishes only — Markdown pages keep their filename identity. Content always comes from file_path — there is no inline content parameter.

description.description: One-sentence subtitle shown on the gallery card. Say what the page is or does.

label.description: A short name for this publish, max 60 chars (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional — a few words, not a description.

url.description: Existing artifact URL to update in place. Pass whenever the user wants to update an artifact this conversation did not publish — "update my artifact", "keep the same link", a pasted artifact URL — and find the URL with action: "list" or ask the user for the link if you don't have it; without this, the publish creates a separate artifact instead of updating the existing one. Omit for new artifacts and same-conversation redeploys. Must be an artifact the user owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). For 'read' and the other url-addressed actions: the artifact to act on.

prompt.description: read only: what to extract from an artifact shared with the user — its content reaches you as an isolated summary answering this. Ignored for artifacts the user owns and for a page published in this session's own Slack channel (raw content is returned); optional.

force.description: Last-resort overwrite that DISCARDS the newer published version's page — another session's publish, or someone's save from a page that can publish new versions of itself. On a conflict the fix is to merge your changes onto the newer content (handed to you in the rejection, or re-read) and publish again — not force. Pass force:true only when the user has explicitly said to discard that specific version; never to get past a conflict on your own judgment. The tracked baseVersion is still sent; with force:true the server treats it as informational and overwrites, unless it refuses force over a version saved from inside the page. Omit (or false) so a concurrent write conflicts instead of being silently clobbered.

out_dir.description: read_asset: directory to save into — default: this artifact’s folder in your scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval and which you can Read from. read_asset names the file by the asset id plus the extension for its type; saving to any directory other than the default is an ordinary file save the user may be asked to approve. read_db: when given, each returned document is written as pretty-printed JSON to <out_dir>/<collection path>/<doc_id>.json (directories created as needed) and the result lists the files instead of the document contents — use it for large documents or many of them.

file_paths.description: upload_asset: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

asset_id.description: read_asset and delete_asset: the asset's id (32 hex characters), from a list_assets or upload_asset result.

after.description: list_assets only: the `next` value from a previous list_assets result, to continue that listing.

capabilities.description: Runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. The control plane is the authority on valid names and config shapes. An empty object clears any previously stored declaration; omit the field on a redeploy to carry the stored declaration forward unchanged. Before declaring any capability, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill for the current contract and per-capability guidance.

contract.description: The artifact's runtime version. Omit to keep its current version (the default); 'latest' to upgrade; a specific version to pin or roll back. Changing it changes how the published page behaves — pass only when the author explicitly intends the change, never as a side effect of editing.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `find`, `grep`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - File search: Use Glob (NOT find or ls)
 - Content search: Use Grep (NOT grep or rg)
 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - If you must poll an external process, use a check command (e.g. `gh run view`) rather than sleeping first.
  - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacements in files.

Usage:
- You must use your `Read` tool at least once in the conversation before editing. This tool will error if you attempt an edit without reading the file.
- When editing text from Read tool output, ensure you preserve the exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as it appears AFTER the line number prefix. The line number prefix format is: line number + tab. Everything after that is the actual file content to match. Never include any part of the line number prefix in the old_string or new_string.
- ALWAYS prefer editing existing files in the codebase. NEVER write new files unless explicitly required.
- Only use emojis if the user explicitly requests it. Avoid adding emojis to files unless asked.
- The edit will FAIL if `old_string` is not unique in the file. Either provide a larger string with more surrounding context to make it unique or use `replace_all` to change every instance of `old_string`.
- Use `replace_all` for replacing and renaming strings across the file. This parameter is useful if you want to rename a variable for instance.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.
- This tool can read Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb files) and returns all cells with their outputs, combining code, text, and visualizations.
- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

"""Small starting model for the audit log.

It defines an audit entry and the canonical rule for deriving its id from its
own recorded content.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

# The fields that constitute an entry's identity. Anything outside this tuple
# is descriptive: it may differ between two records of the same event without
# making them different events.
IDENTIFYING_FIELDS: tuple[str, ...] = ("actor", "action", "outcome", "recorded_at")


def content_digest(actor: str, action: str, outcome: str, recorded_at: str) -> str:
    """Return the deterministic event id for this entry's recorded content.

    Identity is the recorded content itself, so the same event recorded twice
    collapses to one id and any later edit to a stored entry is detectable by
    recomputing this. The separator cannot appear in a field value, so distinct
    inputs cannot collide by concatenation.
    """

    joined = "\x1f".join((actor, action, outcome, recorded_at))
    return hashlib.sha256(joined.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AuditEvent:
    """One recorded entry in the append-only trail.

    ``sequence`` is the entry's gapless position in the trail and ``event_id``
    is its content digest. ``source_version`` records which store format the
    entry was read from, and ``metadata`` carries caller-supplied context such
    as an archive's own reference. Both are descriptive context and are not
    part of the entry's identity.
    """

    event_id: str
    sequence: int
    actor: str
    action: str
    outcome: str
    recorded_at: str
    source_version: int = 2
    metadata: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def recomputed_id(self) -> str:
        """The id this entry's current content implies; compare to ``event_id``."""

        return content_digest(self.actor, self.action, self.outcome, self.recorded_at)

"""Command-line shell for the audit log service.

The starter only defines the stable top-level parser; every command errors out
until it is implemented.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
from typing import IO

from .models import AuditEvent
from .store import AuditLogStore, LogStoreError


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    """Return the stable top-level parser.

    The ``record``/``query``/``repair`` commands and their required
    ``--log-store`` option are the documented contract; keep them.
    """

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="auditlog")
    subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    record = subparsers.add_parser("record", help="append an entry to the trail")
    record.add_argument("actor")
    record.add_argument("action")
    record.add_argument("outcome")
    record.add_argument(
        "--metadata",
        action="append",
        default=[],
        metavar="KEY=VALUE",
        help="descriptive context to store with the entry; repeatable",
    )
    record.add_argument("--log-store", required=True)

    query = subparsers.add_parser("query", help="read entries from the trail")
    query.add_argument("--actor")
    query.add_argument("--action")
    query.add_argument("--log-store", required=True)

    repair = subparsers.add_parser("repair", help="rebuild derived indexes")
    repair.add_argument("--log-store", required=True)
    return parser


def _parse_metadata(pairs: list[str]) -> dict[str, str]:
    metadata: dict[str, str] = {}
    for pair in pairs:
        key, sep, value = pair.partition("=")
        if not sep or not key:
            raise ValueError(f"invalid --metadata value {pair!r}; expected KEY=VALUE")
        metadata[key] = value
    return metadata


def _entry_to_json(entry: AuditEvent) -> dict:
    return {
        "event_id": entry.event_id,
        "sequence": entry.sequence,
        "actor": entry.actor,
        "action": entry.action,
        "outcome": entry.outcome,
        "recorded_at": entry.recorded_at,
        "metadata": entry.metadata,
    }


def _run_record(args: argparse.Namespace, out: IO[str]) -> int:
    metadata = _parse_metadata(args.metadata)
    store = AuditLogStore(args.log_store)
    entry = store.record(args.actor, args.action, args.outcome, metadata)
    print(json.dumps(_entry_to_json(entry)), file=out)
    return 0


def _run_query(args: argparse.Namespace, out: IO[str]) -> int:
    store = AuditLogStore(args.log_store)
    for entry in store.query(actor=args.actor, action=args.action):
        print(json.dumps(_entry_to_json(entry)), file=out)
    return 0


def _run_repair(args: argparse.Namespace, out: IO[str]) -> int:
    store = AuditLogStore(args.log_store)
    report = store.repair()
    print(
        json.dumps(
            {
                "migrated_from_version": report.migrated_from_version,
                "entry_count": report.entry_count,
                "tampered_event_ids": report.tampered_event_ids,
            }
        ),
        file=out,
    )
    return 1 if report.tampered_event_ids else 0


_HANDLERS = {"record": _run_record, "query": _run_query, "repair": _run_repair}


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    """Parse the command line and dispatch to the requested command."""

    parser = build_parser()
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    try:
        return _HANDLERS[args.command](args, sys.stdout)
    except (LogStoreError, ValueError) as exc:
        parser.error(str(exc))
        return 2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

# Example events

Ten JSON Lines files, one per fictional business team, for trying the
`record` and `query` commands (see the top-level `README.md`). Each line is
one JSON object with the four fields `record` accepts: `actor`, `action`,
`outcome`, and `metadata` (a flat string-to-string map, matching what the
CLI's `--metadata KEY=VALUE` and the server's `/v1/events` endpoint both
require). None of the files include `event_id`, `sequence`, or `recorded_at`
-- the store assigns those itself when an event is recorded.

Every file has between 120 and 160 events with varied, realistic actors,
actions, and metadata for that team's domain.

To feed a file through the CLI, one event at a time:

```text
python - <<'PY'
import json, subprocess
with open("examples/billing.jsonl") as f:
    for line in f:
        event = json.loads(line)
        args = ["python", "-m", "auditlog.cli", "record",
                event["actor"], event["action"], event["outcome"],
                "--log-store", "trail.db"]
        for key, value in event["metadata"].items():
            args += ["--metadata", f"{key}={value}"]
        subprocess.run(args, check=True)
PY
```

Then try a query against the same store, for example
`python -m auditlog.cli query --actor billing.svc-billing-worker --log-store trail.db`.

## Files

- **billing.jsonl** -- Invoicing, payments, subscriptions, credit notes,
  dunning, and chargebacks. Actions include `invoice.issued`,
  `payment.refunded`, `subscription.renewed`, and `chargeback.filed`.
  Metadata carries `invoice_id`, `customer_id`, `amount`, `currency`,
  `payment_method`, `plan`, and similar billing context.

- **warehouse.jsonl** -- Receiving, stock adjustments, cycle counts, picking,
  packing, and shipment staging across four warehouses. Actions include
  `stock.received`, `stock.adjusted`, `pick.completed`, and
  `cycle_count.completed`. Metadata carries `sku`, `warehouse_id`,
  `bin_location`, and `quantity`.

- **catalog.jsonl** -- Product catalog maintenance: item creation, pricing,
  images, categorization, publishing, and bulk imports. Actions include
  `catalog.item_created`, `catalog.price_changed`, and
  `catalog.bulk_import_processed`. Metadata carries `sku`, `category`,
  `old_price`/`new_price`, and `editor_id`.

- **support.jsonl** -- Ticket lifecycle for a customer support desk: opening,
  assignment, escalation, resolution, SLA breaches, and CSAT. Actions include
  `ticket.opened`, `ticket.escalated`, `sla.breached`, and
  `refund_request.submitted`. Metadata carries `ticket_id`, `customer_id`,
  `priority`, `channel`, and `agent_id`.

- **payroll.jsonl** -- Paycheck issuance and corrections, timesheets,
  deductions, tax withholding, direct deposit, bonuses, garnishments, and
  onboarding/offboarding. Actions include `paycheck.issued`,
  `garnishment.applied`, and `benefits.enrollment_updated`. Metadata carries
  `employee_id`, `pay_period`, `amount`, and `department`.

- **shipping.jsonl** -- Outbound shipment handling: label generation, carrier
  assignment, dispatch, tracking, delivery, delays, and returns. Actions
  include `shipment.dispatched`, `shipment.delayed`, and
  `delivery_exception.logged`. Metadata carries `shipment_id`, `carrier`,
  `tracking_number`, and `destination`.

- **procurement.jsonl** -- Purchase orders, supplier lifecycle, invoice
  matching, goods receipt, contracts, RFQs, and budget flags. Actions
  include `purchase_order.approved`, `supplier.onboarded`, and
  `budget.exceeded_flagged`. Metadata carries `po_number`, `supplier_id`,
  `amount`, and `department`.

- **marketing.jsonl** -- Campaign management: launches, pauses, email sends,
  segmentation, A/B tests, lead capture, and budget moves. Actions include
  `campaign.launched`, `ab_test.concluded`, and `lead.qualified`. Metadata
  carries `campaign_id`, `channel`, `audience_segment`, and `variant`.

- **fraud.jsonl** -- Transaction review and case handling: flagging,
  clearing, account suspension, risk scoring, chargebacks, and watchlist
  updates. Actions include `transaction.flagged`, `account.suspended`, and
  `case.closed`. Metadata carries `case_id`, `account_id`, `risk_score`, and
  `amount`.

- **facilities.jsonl** -- Workorders, badge issuance, visitor management,
  scheduled maintenance, incidents, HVAC adjustments, and room access across
  several sites. Actions include `workorder.escalated`, `badge.issued`, and
  `access.denied`. Metadata carries `site`, `room`, `ticket_id`, and
  `equipment_id`.

1	# docs-style Folder Overview
2	
3	**Title:** docs-style Folder Overview
4	**Version:** v1.4.0
5	**Owner:** Docs Program (Kara Voss)
6	**Last updated:** 2026-05-14
7	
8	## Purpose
9	
10	This page is the index for the `docs-style/` folder, which is the internal documentation program for auditlog. auditlog is a small standard-library Python package with a command line and a loopback HTTP service, and its own working parts are described elsewhere in the wiki, not here. This folder is only about how we write, template, check, and publish the pages that describe those parts — the words, the layout, and the process, not the package itself.
11	
12	Anyone opening `docs-style/` for the first time should start here. The rest of this page explains how the folder is organized, gives a short glossary of terms the other pages assume you already know, lists every file the docs program touches, names the tools the program runs on, and closes with a change log and a short guide for contributing an edit.
13	
14	## How This Folder Is Organized
15	
16	The folder mixes formats on purpose. Most guidance pages are Markdown, two of the older reference pages are reStructuredText left over from when the wiki was still Sphinx-based, one worksheet is a flat text file that predates all of it, and the front matter rules are written as YAML because that's the format they describe. Nobody has gotten around to converting the holdouts, and honestly there's no strong push to — Style Checklist and Changelog Notes Format work fine as `.rst`, and the Glossary Terms Worksheet is small enough that a text file is still the easiest thing to diff.
17	
18	Below, pages are grouped under four headings that roughly follow the order a new writer would need them: style and voice first, then structure and templates, then terminology, then review and publishing. A short onboarding section sits at the end for people who are new to the docs program itself rather than new to a single page.
19	
20	### Style and Voice Pages
21	
22	| Title | Version | Owner | Last updated | Link |
23	|---|---|---|---|---|
24	| Voice and Tone Guide | 2.3 | Docs Program (Kara Voss) | 2025-11-02 | [voice-and-tone.md](./voice-and-tone.md) |
25	| Markdown Conventions | 2.6 | Docs Program (Kara Voss) | 2025-04-28 | [markdown-conventions.md](./markdown-conventions.md) |
26	| Code Block Standards | 1.5 | Developer Experience (Priya Nair) | 2025-09-30 | [code-block-standards.md](./code-block-standards.md) |
27	| Screenshots and Diagrams | v1.0.0 | Developer Experience (Priya Nair) | 2024-10-11 | [screenshots-and-diagrams.md](./screenshots-and-diagrams.md) |
28	
29	Voice and Tone covers word choice, sentence length, and how much personality a page is allowed to have. Markdown Conventions is the syntax-level companion — heading depth, list markers, table formatting. Code Block Standards governs how snippets are labeled and fenced, and Screenshots and Diagrams covers image capture, alt text, and when a diagram is preferred over a screenshot.
30	
31	### Structure and Templates

# docs-style Folder Overview

**Title:** docs-style Folder Overview
**Version:** v1.4.0
**Owner:** Docs Program (Kara Voss)
**Last updated:** 2026-05-14

## Purpose

This page is the index for the `docs-style/` folder, which is the internal documentation program for auditlog. auditlog is a small standard-library Python package with a command line and a loopback HTTP service, and its own working parts are described elsewhere in the wiki, not here. This folder is only about how we write, template, check, and publish the pages that describe those parts — the words, the layout, and the process, not the package itself.

Anyone opening `docs-style/` for the first time should start here. The rest of this page explains how the folder is organized, gives a short glossary of terms the other pages assume you already know, lists every file the docs program touches, names the tools the program runs on, and closes with a change log and a short guide for contributing an edit.

## How This Folder Is Organized

The folder mixes formats on purpose. Most guidance pages are Markdown, two of the older reference pages are reStructuredText left over from when the wiki was still Sphinx-based, one worksheet is a flat text file that predates all of it, and the front matter rules are written as YAML because that's the format they describe. Nobody has gotten around to converting the holdouts, and honestly there's no strong push to — Style Checklist and Changelog Notes Format work fine as `.rst`, and the Glossary Terms Worksheet is small enough that a text file is still the easiest thing to diff.

Below, pages are grouped under four headings that roughly follow the order a new writer would need them: style and voice first, then structure and templates, then terminology, then review and publishing. A short onboarding section sits at the end for people who are new to the docs program itself rather than new to a single page.

### Style and Voice Pages

| Title | Version | Owner | Last updated | Link |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Voice and Tone covers word choice, sentence length, and how much personality a page is allowed to have. Markdown Conventions is the syntax-level companion — heading depth, list markers, table formatting. This one is aimed at people joining the docs program itself, not people writing their first auditlog page. It's short and a little dated but still gets people oriented on who owns what.

## Terminology and Glossary (Section owner: Mara Olsen)

This is a working glossary for the docs-style folder itself — the words the other pages in this folder assume a reader already knows. For terms about the words used inside the published documentation (like what to call a stored record or the local file the package writes to), see the Terminology Glossary page instead.

## Files and Paths (Section owner: Kara Voss)

Paths below are relative to the repository root unless noted. The docs program does not touch anything under `auditlog/` — that folder belongs to the package's own maintainers.

1	Changelog Notes Format
2	========================
3	
4	:Title: Changelog Notes Format
5	:Version: 1.3
6	:Owner: Support Enablement (Theo Bram)
7	:Last updated: 2026-02-25
8	
9	Summary
10	-------
11	
12	This page describes how to phrase short changelog entries whenever a
13	documentation page in this repository is updated alongside a new package
14	release. It covers the entry template, dating and version-numbering
15	conventions, how entries get tagged to a specific release, and how the
16	change log fits into the wider review and publishing cycle described on
17	the sibling pages listed at the bottom of this page.
18	
19	Purpose and Coverage
20	---------------------
21	
22	The package ships without any built-in way to tell a reader what changed
23	between one version and the next beyond reading the code directly, so the
24	short prose changelog kept in ``docs/changelog.rst`` is the only record
25	most readers will ever look at. Because several people touch that file —
26	sometimes the person who changed the package, sometimes whoever spotted it
27	the docs were stale — the entries drift in tone and length unless
28	everyone follows the same shape. This page exists to keep that shape
29	consistent from one entry to the next, the same way the Voice and Tone
30	Guide keeps sentence-level phrasing consistent across the rest of the
31	wiki.
32	
33	A changelog entry, for our purposes, is a single dated line or short
34	paragraph that says what a documentation page gained, lost, or had
35	corrected, tied to a specific package release number. It is not a
36	description of what the underlying feature does — that belongs on the
37	page the feature is documented on — and it is not a summary of every
38	small wording fix made during a normal review pass. Save the change log
39	for changes that a reader who skipped straight to the newest docs would
40	otherwise miss.
41	
42	Where Changelog Notes Live
43	----------------------------
44	
45	There are two files that hold changelog text, and people confuse them
46	more often than you'd expect:
47	
48	- ``docs/changelog.rst`` is the file that gets built and published with
49	  the rest of the docs. Every entry described on this page belongs here.
50	- ``docs/CHANGES.rst`` is an older file from before the docs site had a
51	  proper build step. It still exists at the repository root's ``docs/``
52	  folder and a few older links point at it, but new entries should not
53	  be added there. If you find yourself editing it, that's usually a sign
54	  a stale bookmark somewhere needs fixing rather than a sign the file is
55	  still current.
56	
57	Do not add changelog text to ``README.md`` at the repository root. The
58	readme sometimes gets a single line added by whoever cuts a release
59	saying "see the changelog for details," but the readme itself is not a
60	changelog and should not accumulate dated entries over time.
61	
62	Writing Style for Entries (Owner: Kara Voss)
63	----------------------------------------------
64	
65	Changelog entries follow the same sentence-level rules as the rest of
66	the wiki — see the Voice and Tone Guide for the general rules on
67	contractions, second person, and sentence length — with a few
68	extra constraints that are specific to this format:
69	
70	1. Start with a verb in the past tense: Added, Updated, Fixed, Removed,
71	   Renamed, Clarified. Do not start with "This entry" or "We."
72	2. Keep the whole entry to one sentence where possible. Two is the
73	   practical ceiling; if you need three, the entry is probably two
74	   entries.
75	3. Name the page or section that changed, not just "the docs." A reader
76	   scanning the change log should be able to tell which page to open
77	   without following a link.
78	4. Do not restate the release notes for the package itself. If the
79	   package gained a new command-line option, the changelog entry says
80	   the reference page was updated to cover it — it does not explain what
81	   the option does. That explanation lives on the reference page.
82	5. Avoid vague verbs like "improved" or "cleaned up." Say what changed:
83	   "reworded," "added a table," "removed the outdated paragraph about."
84	
85	One inconsistency worth flagging for anyone editing this section later:
86	some older entries in ``docs/changelog.rst`` are written in present
87	tense ("Adds a section on...") because that's what the Markdown
88	Conventions page recommended at the time. Present tense is no longer the
89	house style for this file; new entries use past tense. Old entries are
90	not being rewritten just to match.
91	
92	Entry Template
93	----------------
94	
95	Every entry follows this shape, whether it's typed directly into
96	``docs/changelog.rst`` with an editor or drafted first as a note:
97	
98	.. code-block:: text
99	
100	   YYYY-MM-DD — Release X.Y.Z
101	     Verb + page or section + what changed, in one sentence.
102	     (Owner initials in parentheses, optional for minor wording fixes.)
103	
104	The table below spells out each field:
105	
106	.. list-table:: Entry Template Fields
107	   :header-rows: 1
108	
109	   * - Field
110	     - Required
111	     - Notes
112	   * - Date
113	     - Yes
114	     - The day the entry was written, not the day the release shipped.
115	       These are usually close together but are not always the same day.
116	   * - Release
117	     - Yes
118	     - The package's own version number, matched exactly to the tag used
119	       for that release. Do not shorten "1.4.0" to "1.4."
120	   * - Verb
121	     - Yes
122	     - One of: Added, Updated, Fixed, Removed, Renamed, Clarified.
123	   * - Page or section
124	     - Yes
125	     - The docs page title as it appears in that page's own header block,
126	       not the file name.
127	   * - Owner initials
128	     - Optional
129	     - Included for anything more than a small wording fix, so a later
130	       reader knows who to ask.
131	
132	Worked Examples
133	------------------
134	
135	Here is a short run of entries as they actually appear in
136	``docs/changelog.rst``, taken from around the 1.3.0 and 1.4.0 releases:
137	
138	.. code-block:: text
139	
140	   2025-09-18 — Release 1.3.0
141	     Updated the installation page to cover the new local folder default
142	     for the database file. (TB)
143	
144	   2025-09-22 — Release 1.3.0
145	     Fixed a broken cross-link on the command-line reference page that
146	     pointed at the old glossary location.
147	
148	   2026-02-21 — Release 1.4.0
149	     Added a section to the command-line reference page for the new
150	     output option. (TB)
151	
152	   2026-02-25 — Release 1.4.0
153	     Clarified the quickstart page's description of where the database
154	     file is created when no folder is given.
155	
156	See that the second entry above has no owner initials — that's fine
157	for a link fix, which is the kind of small tweak the style allows
158	to skip that field. The first and third entries name the page and the
159	specific thing that changed, without explaining what the output option
160	does; that explanation is left to the reference page itself.
161	
162	A common mistake is writing an entry like this instead:
163	
164	.. code-block:: text
165	
166	   2026-02-21 — Release 1.4.0
167	     Docs updated for the new release.
168	
169	That entry tells a reader nothing about which page changed or what to
170	look for, and it will be sent back during review (see Review Cadence for
171	Changelog Notes below).
172	
173	Dating and Version Numbers
174	------------------------------
175	
176	Use the ISO date format, ``YYYY-MM-DD``, for every entry. This matches
177	the convention used on every other page's header block in this folder,
178	so a reader scanning across pages sees the same date shape everywhere.
179	
180	The version number in an entry is always the package's release number,
181	never this documentation page's own version number. It is easy to
182	confuse the two, especially since this page's own header block also
183	carries a version field. When in doubt: the number in a changelog entry
184	answers "what package release does this describe," and the number in a
185	page's header block answers "how many times has this page itself been
186	updated."
187	
188	Entries are ordered newest first within ``docs/changelog.rst``. When two
189	entries share a date, order them by the order the underlying page
190	changes were made, which is usually traceable from the commit log:
191	
192	.. code-block:: shell
193	
194	   git log --oneline -- docs/changelog.rst | head -10
195	
196	Tagging Entries to Releases
197	-------------------------------
198	
199	Every entry names exactly one release. If a documentation change
200	answers something that was true across several releases — for example,
201	a wording fix that applies equally well to 1.2.0 through 1.3.4 — tag it
202	to the release during which the fix was actually made, not the earliest
203	release it happens to also be true for.
204	
205	When a release is skipped entirely for documentation purposes (nothing
206	about the docs changed), no entry is written for it. The change log is
207	not expected to have one line per package release; it has one line per
208	documentation change.
209	
210	To confirm which release a change belongs to, compare the page's edit
211	against the package's own tags:
212	
213	.. code-block:: shell
214	
215	   git diff v1.3.0..v1.4.0 -- docs/changelog.rst
216	   git log --oneline --decorate | grep -E "^[a-f0-9]+ \(tag:" | head -5
217	
218	Review Cadence for Changelog Notes (Owner: Theo Bram)
219	--------------------------------------------------------
220	
221	Changelog entries get reviewed on a shorter cycle than most of the rest
222	of the wiki, because they go stale fast — a wrong release number in a
223	changelog entry is confusing in a way that most other wording problems
224	are not. Support Enablement reviews the change log every second Friday,
225	independent of the monthly full-page review cycle described on the
226	Review Cadence page (currently at v1.8, last we checked).
227	
228	The Friday review does three things:
229	
230	- Reads every entry added since the previous review and checks it
231	  against the template above.
232	- Confirms the release number in each new entry actually matches a
233	  package tag that exists.
234	- Moves any entry that turns out to describe a change to the package
235	  itself, rather than to the docs, out of the change log and flags it
236	  for whoever is tracking the package's own release notes separately.
237	
238	A small SQLite file at ``scripts/changelog-review.db`` is used to keep
239	track of which entries have gone through this Friday check. It is a
240	docs-tooling file, unrelated to the package's own database file, and it
241	only ever holds a short list of dates and release numbers:
242	
243	.. code-block:: shell
244	
245	   sqlite3 scripts/changelog-review.db
246	   sqlite3> .headers on
247	   sqlite3> .mode column
248	   sqlite3> .tables
249	
250	That file is checked in alongside the scripts that use it so anyone can
251	open it locally with the same ``sqlite3`` settings shown above.
252	
253	Publishing Workflow Integration (Owner: Mara Olsen)
254	------------------------------------------------------
255	
256	The change log is built as part of the same pass that builds the rest
257	of the docs site, described in full on the Docs Publishing Workflow
258	page (v3.9). The build step that turns ``docs/changelog.rst`` into a
259	published page is nothing special — it is picked up by the same
260	Sphinx build as every other ``.rst`` file in ``docs/`` — but a few
261	things about the change log specifically are worth calling out here:
262	
263	- The change log is excluded from the "page freshness" check that flags
264	  pages that haven't been touched in a while, since by nature it is
265	  touched constantly and briefly.
266	- Entries are never edited after publishing except to fix a factual
267	  error (wrong date, wrong release number, wrong page name). Wording
268	  polish on an already-published entry is left alone, even if a later
269	  reviewer would have phrased it differently.
270	- The build step does not check that every release actually has an
271	  entry — that check is a manual part of the Friday review above, not
272	  an automated one.
273	
274	Common Mistakes to Watch For
275	--------------------------------
276	
277	- Writing the entry as if it were release notes for the package rather
278	  than a note about the documentation. If the sentence would make sense
279	  even if the docs page in question had never been touched, it's in the
280	  wrong file.
281	- Using "we" or "I" instead of a plain verb-first sentence.
282	- Forgetting the release number entirely, or using a release number
283	  that was never actually tagged.
284	- Mixing the two changelog files described above — always
285	  ``docs/changelog.rst``, never ``docs/CHANGES.rst``.
286	- Bundling several unrelated page changes into a single entry. Write one
287	  entry per page per change, even if it means three short lines instead
288	  of one long one.
289	- Copying the exact wording of a commit message into the entry. Commit
290	  messages answer a different question ("what did I change in the
291	  repository") than a changelog entry does ("what will a reader
292	  note").
293	
294	Terminology
295	-------------
296	
297	Changelog entry
298	    A single dated line in ``docs/changelog.rst`` describing one
299	    documentation change tied to one package release.
300	
301	Release
302	    A tagged version of the package, identified by its version number
303	    (for example, 1.4.0), independent of any documentation page's own
304	    version field.
305	
306	Entry template
307	    The fixed shape — date, release, verb, page name, optional owner —
308	    that every changelog entry follows, defined in the Entry Template
309	    section above.
310	
311	Owner initials
312	    A short two- or three-letter mark added to an entry to show who
313	    wrote or is responsible for the underlying page change.
314	
315	Friday review
316	    The every-second-week check of new changelog entries run by Support
317	    Enablement, separate from the monthly full-page review cycle.
318	
319	Page freshness check
320	    The automated part of the publishing build that flags pages that
321	    have not been touched in a set number of weeks; the change log is
322	    excluded from it.
323	
324	Stale bookmark
325	    An old link, kept somewhere in the repository or elsewhere, that
326	    still points at ``docs/CHANGES.rst`` instead of the current
327	    ``docs/changelog.rst``.
328	
329	Tagged release
330	    A release of the package that has a corresponding tag in the
331	    repository, which changelog entries are matched against during
332	    review.
333	
334	Sibling page
335	    Any other page in the ``docs-style/`` folder, referenced by title
336	    rather than file name in cross-links and in the Related Pages
337	    section below.
338	
339	Files and Paths Referenced
340	------------------------------
341	
342	.. list-table::
343	   :header-rows: 1
344	
345	   * - Path
346	     - Function
347	   * - ``docs/changelog.rst``
348	     - The published change log. All new entries go here.
349	   * - ``docs/CHANGES.rst``
350	     - An older changelog file kept for old links; no longer receives
351	       new entries.
352	   * - ``docs-style/changelog-notes.rst``
353	     - This page.
354	   * - ``docs-style/page-templates.md``
355	     - Source of the general page-header block used at the top of this
356	       page.
357	   * - ``docs-style/terminology-glossary.md``
358	     - The canonical term list; new terms defined here should be checked
359	       against it before being added.
360	   * - ``docs-style/review-cadence.md``
361	     - Describes the monthly full-page review cycle that the Friday
362	       changelog check runs alongside but does not replace.
363	   * - ``scripts/changelog-review.db``
364	     - Small SQLite file used by Support Enablement to track which
365	       changelog entries have been through the Friday check.
366	   * - ``scripts/check-changelog.sh``
367	     - Shell script that checks a group of new entries against the
368	       template's field order and date format.
369	   * - ``README.md``
370	     - Repository root readme; may reference the change log by name but
371	       does not itself hold changelog entries.
372	   * - ``auditlog/``
373	     - The package directory; changelog entries name files changed here
374	       only by page, not by internal file name.
375	
376	Tools and Libraries
377	-----------------------
378	
379	.. list-table::
380	   :header-rows: 1
381	
382	   * - Tool or library
383	     - Version
384	     - Used for
385	   * - git
386	     - 2.43.0
387	     - Checking commit order and comparing tagged releases when dating
388	       entries.
389	   * - Sphinx
390	     - 7.2.6
391	     - Building the published docs site, including ``docs/changelog.rst``.
392	   * - docutils
393	     - 0.20.1
394	     - The RST parser underneath Sphinx.
395	   * - rstcheck
396	     - 6.2.0
397	     - Catches broken RST syntax in new changelog entries before they're
398	       committed.
399	   * - sqlite3 (CLI)
400	     - 3.45.1
401	     - Reading ``scripts/changelog-review.db`` during the Friday check.
402	   * - shellcheck
403	     - 0.9.0
404	     - Linting ``scripts/check-changelog.sh`` and related shell scripts.
405	
406	Change Log
407	------------
408

411	    template alongside the package's first tagged minor release.
412	
413	2024-11-14 — Release 1.2.0

415	    guidance on not restating package release notes inside changelog
416	    entries.
417

421

424	    the worked examples pulled from that release's own change log.

427	    Updated to v1.2.1, aligning the Friday review description with the
428	    current Review Cadence page and adding the ``scripts/changelog-review.db``
429	    reference.
430	
431	2026-02-25 — Release 1.4.0

Changelog Notes Format
========================

:Title: Changelog Notes Format
:Version: 1.3
:Owner: Support Enablement (Theo Bram)
:Last updated: 2026-02-25

Summary
-------

This page describes how to phrase short changelog entries whenever a
documentation page in this repository is updated alongside a new package
release. It covers the entry template, dating and version-numbering
conventions, how entries get tagged to a specific release, and how the
change log fits into the wider review and publishing cycle described on
the sibling pages listed at the bottom of this page.

Purpose and Coverage
---------------------

The package ships without any built-in way to tell a reader what changed
between one version and the next beyond reading the code directly, so the
short prose changelog kept in ``docs/changelog.rst`` is the only record
most readers will ever look at. Because several people touch that file —
sometimes the person who changed the package, sometimes whoever spotted it
the docs were stale — the entries drift in tone and length unless
everyone follows the same shape. This page exists to keep that shape
consistent from one entry to the next, the same way the Voice and Tone
Guide keeps sentence-level phrasing consistent across the rest of the
wiki.

A changelog entry, for our purposes, is a single dated line or short
paragraph that says what a documentation page gained, lost, or had
corrected, tied to a specific package release number. It is not a
description of what the underlying feature does — that belongs on the
page the feature is documented on — and it is not a summary of every
small wording fix made during a normal review pass. Save the change log
for changes that a reader who skipped straight to the newest docs would
otherwise miss.

Where Changelog Notes Live
----------------------------

There are two files that hold changelog text, and people confuse them
more often than you'd expect:

- ``docs/changelog.rst`` is the file that gets built and published with
  the rest of the docs. Every entry described on this page belongs here.
- ``docs/CHANGES.rst`` is an older file from before the docs site had a
  proper build step. It still exists at the repository root's ``docs/``
  folder and a few older links point at it, but new entries should not
  be added there. If you find yourself editing it, that's usually a sign
  a stale bookmark somewhere needs fixing rather than a sign the file is
  still current.

Do not add changelog text to ``README.md`` at the repository root. The
readme sometimes gets a single line added by whoever cuts a release
saying "see the changelog for details," but the readme itself is not a
changelog and should not accumulate dated entries over time.

Writing Style for Entries (Owner: Kara Voss)
----------------------------------------------

Changelog entries follow the same sentence-level rules as the rest of
the wiki — see the Voice and Tone Guide for the general rules on
contractions, second person, and sentence length — with a few
extra constraints that are specific to this format:

1. Start with a verb in the past tense: Added, Updated, Fixed, Removed,
   Renamed, Clarified. Do not start with "This entry" or "We."
2. Keep the whole entry to one sentence where possible. Two is the
   practical ceiling; if you need three, the entry is probably two
   entries.
3. Name the page or section that changed, not just "the docs." A reader
   scanning the change log should be able to tell which page to open
   without following a link.
4. Do not restate the release notes for the package itself. If the
   package gained a new command-line option, the changelog entry says
   the reference page was updated to cover it — it does not explain what
   the option does. That explanation lives on the reference page.
5. Avoid vague verbs like "improved" or "cleaned up." Say what changed:
   "reworded," "added a table," "removed the outdated paragraph about."

One inconsistency worth flagging for anyone editing this section later:
some older entries in ``docs/changelog.rst`` are written in present
tense ("Adds a section on...") because that's what the Markdown
Conventions page recommended at the time. Present tense is no longer the
house style for this file; new entries use past tense. Old entries are
not being rewritten just to match.

Entry Template
----------------

Every entry follows this shape, whether it's typed directly into
``docs/changelog.rst`` with an editor or drafted first as a note:

.. code-block:: text

   YYYY-MM-DD — Release X.Y.Z
     Verb + page or section + what changed, in one sentence.
     (Owner initials in parentheses, optional for minor wording fixes.)

The table below spells out each field:

.. list-table:: Entry Template Fields
   :header-rows: 1

   * - Field
     - Required
     - Notes
   * - Date
     - Yes
     - The day the entry was written, not the day the release shipped.
       These are usually close together but are not always the same day.
   * - Release
     - Yes
     - The package's own version number, matched exactly to the tag used
       for that release. Do not shorten "1.4.0" to "1.4."
   * - Verb
     - Yes
     - One of: Added, Updated, Fixed, Removed, Renamed, Clarified.
   * - Page or section
     - Yes
     - The docs page title as it appears in that page's own header block,
       not the file name.
   * - Owner initials
     - Optional
     - Included for anything more than a small wording fix, so a later
       reader knows who to ask.

Worked Examples
------------------

Here is a short run of entries as they actually appear in
``docs/changelog.rst``, taken from around the 1.3.0 and 1.4.0 releases:

.. code-block:: text

   2025-09-18 — Release 1.3.0
     Updated the installation page to cover the new local folder default
     for the database file. (TB)

   2025-09-22 — Release 1.3.0
     Fixed a broken cross-link on the command-line reference page that
     pointed at the old glossary location.

   2026-02-21 — Release 1.4.0
     Added a section to the command-line reference page for the new
     output option. (TB)

   2026-02-25 — Release 1.4.0
     Clarified the quickstart page's description of where the database
     file is created when no folder is given.

See that the second entry above has no owner initials — that's fine
for a link fix, which is the kind of small tweak the style allows
to skip that field. The first and third entries name the page and the
specific thing that changed, without explaining what the output option
does; that explanation is left to the reference page itself.

A common mistake is writing an entry like this instead:

.. code-block:: text

   2026-02-21 — Release 1.4.0
     Docs updated for the new release.

That entry tells a reader nothing about which page changed or what to
look for, and it will be sent back during review (see Review Cadence for
Changelog Notes below).

Dating and Version Numbers
------------------------------

Use the ISO date format, ``YYYY-MM-DD``, for every entry. This matches
the convention used on every other page's header block in this folder,
so a reader scanning across pages sees the same date shape everywhere.

The version number in an entry is always the package's release number,
never this documentation page's own version number. It is easy to
confuse the two, especially since this page's own header block also
carries a version field. When in doubt: the number in a changelog entry
answers "what package release does this describe," and the number in a
page's header block answers "how many times has this page itself been
updated."

Entries are ordered newest first within ``docs/changelog.rst``. When two
entries share a date, order them by the order the underlying page
changes were made, which is usually traceable from the commit log:

.. code-block:: shell

   git log --oneline -- docs/changelog.rst | head -10

Tagging Entries to Releases
-------------------------------

Every entry names exactly one release. If a documentation change
answers something that was true across several releases — for example,
a wording fix that applies equally well to 1.2.0 through 1.3.4 — tag it
to the release during which the fix was actually made, not the earliest
release it happens to also be true for.

When a release is skipped entirely for documentation purposes (nothing
about the docs changed), no entry is written for it. The change log is
not expected to have one line per package release; it has one line per
documentation change.

To confirm which release a change belongs to, compare the page's edit
against the package's own tags:

.. code-block:: shell

   git diff v1.3.0..v1.4.0 -- docs/changelog.rst
   git log --oneline --decorate | grep -E "^[a-f0-9]+ \(tag:" | head -5

Review Cadence for Changelog Notes (Owner: Theo Bram)
--------------------------------------------------------

Changelog entries get reviewed on a shorter cycle than most of the rest
of the wiki, because they go stale fast — a wrong release number in a
changelog entry is confusing in a way that most other wording problems
are not. Support Enablement reviews the change log every second Friday,
independent of the monthly full-page review cycle described on the
Review Cadence page (currently at v1.8, last we checked).

The Friday review does three things:

- Reads every entry added since the previous review and checks it
  against the template above.
- Confirms the release number in each new entry actually matches a
  package tag that exists.
- Moves any entry that turns out to describe a change to the package
  itself, rather than to the docs, out of the change log and flags it
  for whoever is tracking the package's own release notes separately.

A small SQLite file at ``scripts/changelog-review.db`` is used to keep
track of which entries have gone through this Friday check. It is a
docs-tooling file, unrelated to the package's own database file, and it
only ever holds a short list of dates and release numbers:

.. code-block:: shell

   sqlite3 scripts/changelog-review.db
   sqlite3> .headers on
   sqlite3> .mode column
   sqlite3> .tables

That file is checked in alongside the scripts that use it so anyone can
open it locally with the same ``sqlite3`` settings shown above.

Publishing Workflow Integration (Owner: Mara Olsen)
------------------------------------------------------

The change log is built as part of the same pass that builds the rest
of the docs site, described in full on the Docs Publishing Workflow
page (v3.9). The build step that turns ``docs/changelog.rst`` into a
published page is nothing special — it is picked up by the same
Sphinx build as every other ``.rst`` file in ``docs/`` — but a few
things about the change log specifically are worth calling out here:

- The change log is excluded from the "page freshness" check that flags
  pages that haven't been touched in a while, since by nature it is
  touched constantly and briefly.
- Entries are never edited after publishing except to fix a factual
  error (wrong date, wrong release number, wrong page name). Wording
  polish on an already-published entry is left alone, even if a later
  reviewer would have phrased it differently.
- The build step does not check that every release actually has an
  entry — that check is a manual part of the Friday review above, not
  an automated one.

Common Mistakes to Watch For
--------------------------------

- Writing the entry as if it were release notes for the package rather
  than a note about the documentation. If the sentence would make sense
  even if the docs page in question had never been touched, it's in the
  wrong file.
- Using "we" or "I" instead of a plain verb-first sentence.
- Forgetting the release number entirely, or using a release number
  that was never actually tagged.
- Mixing the two changelog files described above — always
  ``docs/changelog.rst``, never ``docs/CHANGES.rst``.
- Bundling several unrelated page changes into a single entry. Write one
  entry per page per change, even if it means three short lines instead
  of one long one.
- Copying the exact wording of a commit message into the entry. Commit
  messages answer a different question ("what did I change in the
  repository") than a changelog entry does ("what will a reader
  note").

Terminology
-------------

Changelog entry
    A single dated line in ``docs/changelog.rst`` describing one
    documentation change tied to one package release.

Release
    A tagged version of the package, identified by its version number
    (for example, 1.4.0), independent of any documentation page's own
    version field.

Entry template
    The fixed shape — date, release, verb, page name, optional owner —
    that every changelog entry follows, defined in the Entry Template
    section above.

Owner initials
    A short two- or three-letter mark added to an entry to show who
    wrote or is responsible for the underlying page change.

Friday review
    The every-second-week check of new changelog entries run by Support
    Enablement, separate from the monthly full-page review cycle.

Page freshness check
    The automated part of the publishing build that flags pages that
    have not been touched in a set number of weeks; the change log is
    excluded from it.

Stale bookmark
    An old link, kept somewhere in the repository or elsewhere, that

73	
74

80

98

101	```bash

103	  --config docs/docs-style/assets/code-samples/example.ini \
104	  --dry-run
105	```
106	
107	(That example name is illustrative only — it is not a real command from this repository, just a stand-in shape for how a long invocation should wrap.)

110	|---|---|---|
111	| Shell / command line | 100 characters | trailing `\`, two-space indent |

113	| sqlite3 session | 100 characters | none; long queries stay on one line |

128	c. show a return value or printed value as a trailing comment line starting with `# output:` rather than pasting an interpreter's own echo;
129	d. avoid import lines entirely unless the import itself is the point of the snippet;
130	e. never include a real file path, host name, or anything drawn from a contributor's own working checkout.
131
