1	==========================================================================
2	GLOSSARY TERMS WORKSHEET
3	==========================================================================
4	Title: Glossary Terms Worksheet
5	Version: 1.0
6	Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
7	Last updated: 2026-06-19
8	
9	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
10	1. Purpose
11	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
12	This page is the working scratchpad for the auditlog documentation program's
13	glossary. It exists because terminology-glossary.md is meant to be a stable,
14	citable reference — writers should not be dropping half-formed definitions
15	into it mid-draft. Instead, every new term, every disputed wording, and
16	every "wait, do we call it X or Y" thread starts here, gets argued over for
17	a while, and only moves into the published Glossary once it has settled.
18	
19	Mara Olsen (Platform Tools) owns this worksheet because Platform Tools also
20	owns the published Glossary page and the Docs Publishing Workflow, so the
21	same person can fold a term through all three steps without waiting on a
22	handoff. That said, day-to-day wording questions are frequently raised by
23	whoever is writing the page that needs the term — this worksheet is meant
24	to be low-friction and anyone on the docs program can add a row.
25	
26	What this page covers:
27	  - the submission process for candidate glossary terms
28	  - the format a draft entry must follow before it can be reviewed
29	  - the open wording-questions log
30	  - the cadence on which the worksheet itself gets cleared out
31	  - how an accepted entry gets folded into the published Glossary and
32	    carried through the publishing pipeline
33	
34	Out of bounds: this page does not attempt to restate the Voice and Tone
35	Guide's rules on sentence length, contractions, or heading capitalization.
36	Those live on their own page. If a wording question turns out to really be
37	a tone question, move it there instead of arguing it out on this worksheet.
38	
39	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
40	2. Relationship To The Published Glossary
41	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
42	terminology-glossary.md is where anything logged here ends up. As of
43	this writing the published Glossary sits at version 3.0 and is the
44	authoritative source for how we define package concepts, service behavior,
45	and database-file terminology across every other docs-style page. Nothing
46	on this worksheet is citable outside the docs program — if you find a link
47	pointing at glossary-terms.txt from a customer-facing page, that's a bug,
48	flag it to Mara.
49	
50	The two pages are deliberately different shapes:
51	  * terminology-glossary.md is alphabetized, one definition per term, no
52	    debate, no attribution.
53	  * glossary-terms.txt (this page) is chronological, keeps the back-and-
54	    forth, and keeps the name of whoever proposed the wording, because
55	    that context is useful when a term gets revisited six months later.
56	
57	A term should never live in both places for long. If an entry has been
58	sitting in the "Accepted" state on this worksheet for more than one review
59	cycle without being folded in, that's a process failure on Mara's part, not
60	a reason to start using the worksheet as a second glossary.
61	
62	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
63	3. Worksheet Entry Template (Page Templates section owner: Kara Voss)
64	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
65	Every candidate term added to Section 5 below must use this shape. This
66	mirrors the general docs-style templates described on page-templates.md,
67	narrowed down for a single term. Kara maintains the canonical version of
68	this template; Mara's copy here should match it, but the two have drifted
69	before, so if in doubt check page-templates.md (v1.2.0, updated 2025-08-01)
70	first.
71	
72	    Term:            <the candidate word or phrase, exactly as it would
73	                      appear in the Glossary>
74	    Proposed by:     <name or contact>
75	    Date proposed:   <YYYY-MM-DD>
76	    Draft definition:
77	        <one to three sentences, present tense, no examples>
78	    Used on pages:   <comma-separated list of docs-style pages that already
79	                      use this term informally>
80	    Status:          Open | Discussed | Accepted | Rejected | Folded
81	    Target section:  <the alphabetical section of terminology-glossary.md
82	                      this entry would land in>
83	    Notes:
84	        <anything a reviewer should know — conflicting existing usage,
85	        a synonym that's already taken, etc.>
86	
87	Worked example, as it would actually appear in Section 5:
88	
89	    Term:            "collection window"
90	    Proposed by:     Theo Bram
91	    Date proposed:   2026-04-02
92	    Draft definition:
93	        The span of local time during which the service is actively
94	        writing new rows to the database file.
95	    Used on pages:   review-cadence.md, publishing-workflow.md
96	    Status:          Discussed
97	    Target section:  C
98	    Notes:
99	        Kara pointed out "window" already gets used loosely on three
100	        pages to mean different things. Might need to rename before
101	        this goes in.
102	
103	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
104	4. Style Rules For Draft Entries
105	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
106	These narrow the Voice and Tone Guide down to glossary-specific rules.
107	Section owner: Kara Voss.
108	
109	  1. Definitions are written in the present tense, third person, no "you."
110	  2. A definition may not use the term it is defining, even inside a
111	     different tense or plural form.
112	  3. One sentence is preferred. Two is acceptable if the second sentence
113	     narrows the topic rather than adding an example. Three is the hard limit.
114	  4. Do not define a term by pointing at another undefined term — if
115	     definition A needs term B, term B needs its own worksheet row first.
116	  5. Avoid adjectives that imply a value judgment ("simple," "just,"
117	     "merely"). A definition states what something is, not how easy it
118	     is to use.
119	  6. Capitalize the term only if it is capitalized everywhere else it's
120	     used. Most terms in this Glossary are lowercase; a few, like "the
121	     Docs Program" itself, are conventionally capitalized. When unsure,
122	     check three existing pages and go with the majority.
123	  7. Do not smuggle a code sample, a configuration key, or a path into a
124	     definition. If the term needs an example to make sense, the example
125	     belongs on the page that uses the term, not in the Glossary.
126	
127	Worked before/after, taken from an actual worksheet row (2026-03-11):
128	
129	    Draft (rejected):
130	        "A build tag is basically a little label we slap on a docs build
131	        so you can tell which one is live."
132	
133	    Revised (accepted):
134	        "A build tag identifies a specific docs build produced during a
135	        single run of the publishing pipeline."
136	
137	The first draft breaks rules 5 and 6 (second person, "basically," "little
138	label," casual tone). The change was accepted on 2026-03-18 and folded
139	into terminology-glossary.md the same week.
140	
141	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
142	5. Proposed Additions Queue
143	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
144	This table is the live queue. Rows are appended in date order and never
145	reordered — if a term's status changes, edit the Status column in place,
146	don't move the row. When a row reaches Folded, it stays here for one more
147	review cycle (see Section 7) as a paper trail, then gets cut.
148	
149	Term                  | Proposed by       | Date       | Status    | Target section
150	----------------------|--------------------|------------|-----------|----------------
151	collection window      | Theo Bram          | 2026-04-02 | Discussed | C
152	build tag               | Priya Nair         | 2026-03-11 | Folded    | B
153	loopback bind           | Owen Petrakis      | 2026-02-14 | Accepted  | L
154	local file handle       | Kara Voss          | 2026-05-30 | Open      | L
155	draft state              | bgigurtsis@gmail.com | 2026-06-10 | Open      | D
156	worksheet cycle          | Mara Olsen         | 2026-06-18 | Discussed | W
157	publish pass             | Theo Bram          | 2026-06-19 | Open      | P
158	
159	Note on the "draft state" row: this was submitted through the shared docs
160	feedback form rather than added directly by a writer, which is why the
161	Proposed-by field holds a personal contact rather than a name — that's
162	allowed, the field just needs to be someone reachable if a reviewer has
163	questions.
164	
165	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
166	6. Open Wording Questions Log
167	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
168	Not every worksheet item is a new term — some rows are just unresolved
169	disagreements about wording that already exists somewhere. These get
170	logged here so the same argument doesn't happen twice.
171	
172	Question                                               | Raised by     | Date       | Resolution
173	--------------------------------------------------------|----------------|------------|------------
174	"local database file" vs. "local file database"          | Priya Nair     | 2026-01-09 | "local database file" wins, matches 4 of 5 existing uses
175	Should "loopback service" be one term or two?             | Owen Petrakis  | 2026-02-20 | Kept as two words, treated as a phrase not a compound
176	Is "the CLI" acceptable shorthand, or spell out each time?| Kara Voss      | 2026-03-04 | Spell out on first use per page, shorthand after
177	"host path" vs. "filesystem path"                         | Theo Bram      | 2026-05-02 | Open — waiting on Mara's input
178	Capitalize "Docs Program" or not?                          | Mara Olsen     | 2026-05-15 | Capitalize when referring to the team, lowercase when referring to the general activity
179	
180	The fourth row has been open longer than one review cycle, which is out of
181	line with the rule in Section 2 — Mara has it flagged for the next
182	worksheet cycle.
183	
184	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
185	7. Review Cadence For This Worksheet
186	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
187	Section owner: Theo Bram (Support Enablement), matching his ownership of
188	review-cadence.md.
189	
190	The worksheet is cleared out on a two-week cycle, timed to land the Monday
191	after each publishing window described in publishing-workflow.md. During a
192	clearing pass, whoever is running it should:
193	
194	  1. Read every row currently in "Accepted" state.
195	  2. Confirm the draft definition still follows the style rules in
196	     Section 4 — wording sometimes drifts during discussion.
197	  3. Copy the entry into terminology-glossary.md, in its correct
198	     alphabetical position, and mark the worksheet row "Folded."
199	  4. For rows still in "Discussed," post a one-line prompt in the docs
200	     channel asking for a call; if none comes in within the cycle,
201	     the row rolls forward untouched.
202	  5. Cut any row that has sat in "Folded" for a full extra cycle.
203	
204	In practice this ends up closer to a monthly pass — the two-week cadence
205	is the goal but the last three clearing passes landed on 2026-04-02,
206	2026-05-14, and 2026-06-19, which is roughly six weeks apart rather than
207	two. Nobody has updated this section to reflect that yet.
208	
209	Worked example of a clearing pass, using git to show the fold:
210	
211	    git status
212	    git diff --stat docs-style/terminology-glossary.md
213	    git add docs-style/terminology-glossary.md docs-style/glossary-terms.txt
214	    git commit -m "Glossary: fold 'build tag' from worksheet, cycle 2026-03-18"
215	
216	Kara's preference is one commit per folded term rather than grouping a
217	whole clearing pass into one commit, so that terminology-glossary.md's
218	Log reads as a list of individual additions rather than one large
219	diff every six weeks.
220	
221	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
222	8. Folding A Term Into The Publishing Pipeline
223	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
224	Once a term is folded into terminology-glossary.md, it still has to travel
225	through the same build that every other docs-style page goes through
226	before it's visible on the published site. This worksheet doesn't own that
227	pipeline — publishing-workflow.md does — but a folded term needs one extra
228	step that other edits don't: the local search index has to be told a new
229	term exists.
230	
231	    sqlite3 docs/search-index.db
232	    .tables
233	    .headers on
234	    .mode column
235	    .schema glossary_terms
236	
237	That's a read-only check, not a write — confirming the table the build
238	step will update actually exists before triggering a rebuild. The rebuild
239	itself is triggered by the publishing pipeline on its own schedule and is
240	not something anyone runs by hand from this worksheet.
241	
242	If a folded term needs to show up in the next published build immediately
243	(rare — usually only for a term that's actively causing confusion in a
244	live page), the writer should say so explicitly in the commit message so
245	whoever runs the next scheduled publish knows to prioritize it. There is
246	no fast-track publish step specific to glossary terms; it goes through the
247	same queue as everything else.
248	
249	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
250	9. Common Mistakes Seen In This Worksheet
251	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
252	  - Reordering rows in the Proposed Additions Queue instead of editing
253	    Status in place. This breaks the "logged in the order raised" property
254	    that makes the worksheet useful as a paper trail.
255	  - Skipping the Notes field on a rejected entry. If a term is rejected,
256	    the reason needs to be written down, otherwise it gets re-proposed by
257	    someone else in three months.
258	  - Writing the draft definition in the imperative ("Use this to mean...")
259	    rather than declarative ("This means..."). Definitions describe, they
260	    don't instruct.
261	  - Adding a term directly to terminology-glossary.md without a worksheet
262	    row first. This has happened at least twice; both times the term had
263	    to be pulled back out because it conflicted with an existing entry
264	    that the writer hadn't checked against.
265	  - Confusing this worksheet with the Style Checklist. The checklist
266	    (style-checklist.rst) is a pass/fail list applied to a finished page;
267	    this worksheet is a running log applied to a single category of
268	    content across many pages.
269	
270	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
271	10. Terminology
272	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
273	These terms describe the worksheet's own vocabulary — how the docs program
274	talks about the process of managing terms, not terms describing the
275	package itself.
276	
277	  worksheet row
278	      A single entry in either the Proposed Additions Queue or the Open
279	      Wording Questions Log, uniquely identified by its term or question
280	      text plus its date.
281	
282	  fold / folding
283	      The act of moving an accepted worksheet row into
284	      terminology-glossary.md and marking the row Folded.
285	
286	  clearing pass
287	      A scheduled pass through the worksheet, described in Section 7,
288	      during which rows are folded, prompted, or cut.
289	
290	  target section
291	      The alphabetical section letter a candidate term is expected to
292	      land under once it is folded into the published Glossary.
293	
294	  draft definition
295	      The proposed wording for a term, subject to the style rules in
296	      Section 4, before it is accepted.
297	
298	  wording question
299	      An unresolved disagreement about phrasing that does not itself
300	      introduce a new term — logged in Section 6 rather than Section 5.
301	
302	  status field
303	      One of Open, Discussed, Accepted, Rejected, or Folded, tracked per
304	      row in the Proposed Additions Queue.
305	
306	  used-on list
307	      The comma-separated set of docs-style pages a candidate term already
308	      appears on informally, recorded so a reviewer can check consistency
309	      before accepting the wording.
310	
311	  cut
312	      Removing a Folded row from this worksheet once it has served its
313	      purpose as a paper trail for one extra clearing pass.
314	
315	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
316	11. Files And Paths Referenced
317	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
318	Path                              | Purpose
319	----------------------------------|--------------------------------------
320	docs-style/glossary-terms.txt      | This page — the worksheet itself
321	docs-style/terminology-glossary.md | Published Glossary that accepted terms are folded into
322	docs-style/page-templates.md       | Canonical entry template Section 3 is copied from
323	docs-style/voice-and-tone.md       | Parent style rules narrowed by Section 4
324	docs-style/review-cadence.md       | Docs-program-wide review scheduling this worksheet's cadence is meant to follow
325	docs-style/publishing-workflow.md  | Describes the build/publish pipeline referenced in Section 8
326	docs-style/style-checklist.rst     | Pass/fail checklist for finished pages, distinct from this running log
327	docs-style/front-matter-schema.yaml| Defines the header-block fields used at the top of this page
328	docs/                              | Published docs site output, where folded terms eventually become visible
329	docs/search-index.db               | Local sqlite file backing the docs site's search feature, checked in Section 8
330	scripts/glossary-worksheet-check   | Shell helper that greps this file for duplicate terms against terminology-glossary.md before a clearing pass
331	docs/build-logs/                   | Folder holding logs from each publishing run, useful for confirming a folded term made it into a build
332	
333	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
334	12. Tools And Packages
335	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
336	Tool / package        | Version   | Used for
337	------------------------|-----------|------------------------------------
338	git                     | 2.45.1    | Version control for all docs-style pages
339	sqlite3 (CLI)           | 3.45.1    | Inspecting docs/search-index.db during a clearing pass
340	Vale                    | 3.4.1     | Prose linting against the style rules in Section 4
341	markdownlint-cli        | 0.41.0    | Linting sibling Markdown pages this worksheet's terms feed into
342	codespell               | 2.2.6     | Catching typos in draft definitions before folding
343	pandoc                  | 3.1.11    | Converting terminology-glossary.md for the published site build
344	lychee                  | 0.14.3    | Checking that "Used on pages" references in Section 5 still resolve
345	
346	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
347	13. Change Log
348	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
349	  2025-11-20 (v0.1) — First draft of the worksheet, plain list of terms
350	      with no template, no status field. Owner: Mara Olsen.
351	
352	  2026-01-09 (v0.4) — Added the Open Wording Questions Log as a separate
353	      section after three separate wording arguments happened in three
354	      separate page reviews the same week.
355	
356	  2026-02-14 (v0.6) — Introduced the Status field (Open/Discussed/
357	      Accepted/Rejected) to the Proposed Additions Queue. Folded was added
358	      later.
359	
360	  2026-03-18 (v0.8) — Added the worked before/after example in Section 4
361	      after the "build tag" definition needed two rounds of rework.
362	
363	  2026-05-02 (v0.9) — Split the entry template out into its own section
364	      (Section 3) and pointed it at page-templates.md as the source of
365	      truth rather than duplicating the fields independently.
366	
367	  2026-06-19 (v1.0) — Added Section 8 covering the fold into the
368	      publishing pipeline, added the tools table, and brought the Files
369	      And Paths section in line with the current docs-style layout.
370	
371	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
372	14. Related Pages
373	--------------------------------------------------------------------------
374	  - "docs-style Folder Overview" — orientation for this whole folder
375	  - "Terminology Glossary" — the published target this worksheet feeds
376	  - "Page Templates" — source of the entry template used in Section 3
377	  - "Voice and Tone Guide" — parent style rules narrowed in Section 4
378	  - "Review Cadence" — docs-program-wide scheduling this worksheet's
379	    clearing passes are meant to follow
380	  - "Docs Publishing Workflow" — the build/publish pipeline referenced
381	    in Section 8
382	  - "Style Checklist" — the pass/fail list applied to finished pages,
383	    distinct from this running worksheet

385	    top of this page

same person can fold a term through all three steps without waiting on a
handoff. That said, day-to-day wording questions are frequently raised by
whoever is writing the page that needs the term — this worksheet is meant
to be low-friction and anyone on the docs program can add a row.

What this page covers:
  - the submission process for candidate glossary terms
  - the format a draft entry must follow before it can be reviewed
  - the open wording-questions log
  - the cadence on which the worksheet itself gets cleared out
  - how an accepted entry gets folded into the published Glossary and
    carried through the publishing pipeline

Out of bounds: this page does not attempt to restate the Voice and Tone
Guide's rules on sentence length, contractions, or heading capitalization.
Those live on their own page. If a wording question turns out to really be
a tone question, move it there instead of arguing it out on this worksheet.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Relationship To The Published Glossary
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
terminology-glossary.md is where anything logged here ends up. As of
this writing the published Glossary sits at version 3.0 and is the
authoritative source for how we define package concepts, service behavior,
and database-file terminology across every other docs-style page. Nothing
on this worksheet is citable outside the docs program — if you find a link
pointing at glossary-terms.txt from a customer-facing page, that's a bug,
flag it to Mara.

The two pages are deliberately different shapes:
  * terminology-glossary.md is alphabetized, one definition per term, no
    debate, no attribution.
  * glossary-terms.txt (this page) is chronological, keeps the back-and-
    forth, and keeps the name of whoever proposed the wording, because
    that context is useful when a term gets revisited six months later.

A term should never live in both places for long. If an entry has been
sitting in the "Accepted" state on this worksheet for more than one review
cycle without being folded in, that's a process failure on Mara's part, not
a reason to start using the worksheet as a second glossary.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Worksheet Entry Template (Page Templates section owner: Kara Voss)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
Every candidate term added to Section 5 below must use this shape. This
mirrors the general docs-style templates described on page-templates.md,
narrowed down for a single term. Kara maintains the canonical version of
this template; Mara's copy here should match it, but the two have drifted
before, so if in doubt check page-templates.md (v1.2.0, updated 2025-08-01)
first.

    Term:            <the candidate word or phrase, exactly as it would
                      appear in the Glossary>
    Proposed by:     <name or contact>
    Date proposed:   <YYYY-MM-DD>
    Draft definition:
        <one to three sentences, present tense, no examples>
    Used on pages:   <comma-separated list of docs-style pages that already
                      use this term informally>
    Status:          Open | Discussed | Accepted | Rejected | Folded
    Target section:  <the alphabetical section of terminology-glossary.md
                      this entry would land in>
    Notes:
        <anything a reviewer should know — conflicting existing usage,
        a synonym that's already taken, etc.>

Worked example, as it would actually appear in Section 5:

    Term:            "collection window"
    Proposed by:     Theo Bram
    Date proposed:   2026-04-02
    Draft definition:
        The span of local time during which the service is actively
        writing new rows to the database file.
    Used on pages:   review-cadence.md, publishing-workflow.md
    Status:          Discussed
    Target section:  C
    Notes:
        Kara pointed out "window" already gets used loosely on three
        pages to mean different things. Might need to rename before
        this goes in.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Style Rules For Draft Entries
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
These narrow the Voice and Tone Guide down to glossary-specific rules.
Section owner: Kara Voss.

  1. Definitions are written in the present tense, third person, no "you."
  2. A definition may not use the term it is defining, even inside a
     different tense or plural form.
  3. One sentence is preferred. Two is acceptable if the second sentence
     narrows the topic rather than adding an example. Three is the hard limit.
  4. Do not define a term by pointing at another undefined term — if
     definition A needs term B, term B needs its own worksheet row first.
  5. Avoid adjectives that imply a value judgment ("simple," "just,"
     "merely"). A definition states what something is, not how easy it
     is to use.
  6. Capitalize the term only if it is capitalized everywhere else it's
     used. Most terms in this Glossary are lowercase; a few, like "the
     Docs Program" itself, are conventionally capitalized. When unsure,
     check three existing pages and go with the majority.
  7. Do not smuggle a code sample, a configuration key, or a path into a
     definition. If the term needs an example to make sense, the example
     belongs on the page that uses the term, not in the Glossary.

Worked before/after, taken from an actual worksheet row (2026-03-11):

    Draft (rejected):
        "A build tag is basically a little label we slap on a docs build
        so you can tell which one is live."

    Revised (accepted):
        "A build tag identifies a specific docs build produced during a
        single run of the publishing pipeline."

The first draft breaks rules 5 and 6 (second person, "basically," "little
label," casual tone). The change was accepted on 2026-03-18 and folded
into terminology-glossary.md the same week.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Proposed Additions Queue
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
This table is the live queue. Rows are appended in date order and never
reordered — if a term's status changes, edit the Status column in place,
don't move the row. When a row reaches Folded, it stays here for one more
review cycle (see Section 7) as a paper trail, then gets cut.

Term                  | Proposed by       | Date       | Status    | Target section
----------------------|--------------------|------------|-----------|----------------
collection window      | Theo Bram          | 2026-04-02 | Discussed | C
build tag               | Priya Nair         | 2026-03-11 | Folded    | B
loopback bind           | Owen Petrakis      | 2026-02-14 | Accepted  | L
local file handle       | Kara Voss          | 2026-05-30 | Open      | L
draft state              | bgigurtsis@gmail.com | 2026-06-10 | Open      | D

Note on the "draft state" row: this was submitted through the shared docs
feedback form rather than added directly by a writer, which is why the
Proposed-by field holds a personal contact rather than a name — that's
allowed, the field just needs to be someone reachable if a reviewer has
questions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Open Wording Questions Log
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
Not every worksheet item is a new term — some rows are just unresolved
disagreements about wording that already exists somewhere. These get
logged here so the same argument doesn't happen twice.

Question                                               | Raised by     | Date       | Resolution
--------------------------------------------------------|----------------|------------|------------
"local database file" vs. "local file database"          | Priya Nair     | 2026-01-09 | "local database file" wins, matches 4 of 5 existing uses
Should "loopback service" be one term or two?             | Owen Petrakis  | 2026-02-20 | Kept as two words, treated as a phrase not a compound
Is "the CLI" acceptable shorthand, or spell out each time?| Kara Voss      | 2026-03-04 | Spell out on first use per page, shorthand after
"host path" vs. "filesystem path"                         | Theo Bram      | 2026-05-02 | Open — waiting on Mara's input
Capitalize "Docs Program" or not?                          | Mara Olsen     | 2026-05-15 | Capitalize when referring to the team, lowercase when referring to the general activity

The fourth row has been open longer than one review cycle, which is out of
line with the rule in Section 2 — Mara has it flagged for the next
worksheet cycle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Review Cadence For This Worksheet
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
Section owner: Theo Bram (Support Enablement), matching his ownership of
review-cadence.md.

The worksheet is cleared out on a two-week cycle, timed to land the Monday
after each publishing window described in publishing-workflow.md. During a
clearing pass, whoever is running it should:

  1. Read every row currently in "Accepted" state.
  2. Confirm the draft definition still follows the style rules in
     Section 4 — wording sometimes drifts during discussion.
  3. Copy the entry into terminology-glossary.md, in its correct
     alphabetical position, and mark the worksheet row "Folded."
  4. For rows still in "Discussed," post a one-line prompt in the docs
     channel asking for a call; if none comes in within the cycle,
     the row rolls forward untouched.
  5. Cut any row that has sat in "Folded" for a full extra cycle.

In practice this ends up closer to a monthly pass — the two-week cadence
is the goal but the last three clearing passes landed on 2026-04-02,
2026-05-14, and 2026-06-19, which is roughly six weeks apart rather than
two. Nobody has updated this section to reflect that yet.

Worked example of a clearing pass, using git to show the fold:

    git status
    git diff --stat docs-style/terminology-glossary.md
    git add docs-style/terminology-glossary.md docs-style/glossary-terms.txt
    git commit -m "Glossary: fold 'build tag' from worksheet, cycle 2026-03-18"

Kara's preference is one commit per folded term rather than grouping a
whole clearing pass into one commit, so that terminology-glossary.md's
Log reads as a list of individual additions rather than one large
diff every six weeks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Folding A Term Into The Publishing Pipeline
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
Once a term is folded into terminology-glossary.md, it still has to travel
through the same build that every other docs-style page goes through
before it's visible on the published site. This worksheet doesn't own that
pipeline — publishing-workflow.md does — but a folded term needs one extra
step that other edits don't: the local search index has to be told a new
term exists.

    sqlite3 docs/search-index.db
    .tables
    .headers on
    .mode column
    .schema glossary_terms

That's a read-only check, not a write — confirming the table the build
step will update actually exists before triggering a rebuild. The rebuild
itself is triggered by the publishing pipeline on its own schedule and is
not something anyone runs by hand from this worksheet.

If a folded term needs to show up in the next published build immediately
(rare — usually only for a term that's actively causing confusion in a
live page), the writer should say so explicitly in the commit message so
whoever runs the next scheduled publish knows to prioritize it. There is
no fast-track publish step specific to glossary terms; it goes through the
same queue as everything else.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
9. Common Mistakes Seen In This Worksheet
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
  - Reordering rows in the Proposed Additions Queue instead of editing
    Status in place. This breaks the "logged in the order raised" property
    that makes the worksheet useful as a paper trail.
  - Skipping the Notes field on a rejected entry. If a term is rejected,
    the reason needs to be written down, otherwise it gets re-proposed by
    someone else in three months.
  - Writing the draft definition in the imperative ("Use this to mean...")
    rather than declarative ("This means..."). Definitions describe, they
    don't instruct.
  - Adding a term directly to terminology-glossary.md without a worksheet
    row first. This has happened at least twice; both times the term had
    to be pulled back out because it conflicted with an existing entry
    that the writer hadn't checked against.
  - Confusing this worksheet with the Style Checklist. The checklist
    (style-checklist.rst) is a pass/fail list applied to a finished page;
    this worksheet is a running log applied to a single category of
    content across many pages.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
10. Terminology
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
These terms describe the worksheet's own vocabulary — how the docs program
talks about the process of managing terms, not terms describing the
package itself.

  worksheet row
      A single entry in either the Proposed Additions Queue or the Open
      Wording Questions Log, uniquely identified by its term or question
      text plus its date.

  fold / folding
      The act of moving an accepted worksheet row into
      terminology-glossary.md and marking the row Folded.

  clearing pass
      A scheduled pass through the worksheet, described in Section 7,
      during which rows are folded, prompted, or cut.

  target section
      The alphabetical section letter a candidate term is expected to
      land under once it is folded into the published Glossary.

  draft definition
      The proposed wording for a term, subject to the style rules in
      Section 4, before it is accepted.

  wording question
      An unresolved disagreement about phrasing that does not itself
      introduce a new term — logged in Section 6 rather than Section 5.

  status field
      One of Open, Discussed, Accepted, Rejected, or Folded, tracked per
      row in the Proposed Additions Queue.

  used-on list
      The comma-separated set of docs-style pages a candidate term already
      appears on informally, recorded so a reviewer can check consistency
      before accepting the wording.

  cut
      Removing a Folded row from this worksheet once it has served its
      purpose as a paper trail for one extra clearing pass.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
11. Files And Paths Referenced
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
Path                              | Purpose
----------------------------------|--------------------------------------
docs-style/glossary-terms.txt      | This page — the worksheet itself
docs-style/terminology-glossary.md | Published Glossary that accepted terms are folded into

docs/                              | Published docs site output, where folded terms eventually become visible
docs/search-index.db               | Local sqlite file backing the docs site's search feature, checked in Section 8
scripts/glossary-worksheet-check   | Shell helper that greps this file for duplicate terms against terminology-glossary.md before a clearing pass
docs/build-logs/                   | Folder holding logs from each publishing run, useful for confirming a folded term made it into a build

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

1	# Markdown Conventions
2	
3	| Field | Value |
4	|---|---|
5	| Title | Markdown Conventions |
6	| Version | 2.6 |
7	| Owner | Docs Program (Kara Voss) |
8	| Last updated | 2025-04-28 |
9	| Summary | Lists the Markdown syntax choices, heading depths, and list styles that keep auditlog pages visually consistent across the folder. |
10	
11	## Purpose and Reach of This Page
12	
13	This page is the syntax-level companion to the [Voice and Tone Guide](voice-and-tone.md). Where that page tells a writer how a sentence should sound, this one tells them how the sentence should be marked up: which heading level to reach for, whether a list gets numbers or hyphens, how wide a table column is allowed to get before it should become a list instead. Every Markdown file under `docs-style/` and every published page under `docs/` is expected to follow the choices below. `.rst` and `.txt` files in the folder are out of reach for this page — they follow their own format's conventions, not Markdown's — but where a `.rst` page is later converted to Markdown, this page becomes the target style.
14	
15	The guide is intentionally narrow. It does not tell you what to write, only how to format what you've already decided to write. For voice, sentence length, and terminology choice, see the sibling pages listed at the end of this page.
16	
17	## Header Block Requirements
18	
19	Owner: Kara Voss (Docs Program)
20	
21	Every page in `docs-style/`, and every page it governs in `docs/`, opens with a small metadata table directly under the H1 title, exactly like the one at the top of this page. The fields, in order, are:
22	
23	1. Title — the human-readable page name, matched to the H1 exactly (including capitalization).
24	2. Version — a plain decimal number (`2.6`) for pages owned by Docs Program, or a semantic-style tag (`v1.2.0`) for pages owned by other teams. Both are acceptable inside the folder; we have not standardized on one, and a proposal to do so has been open since late 2024 without a final call.
25	3. Owner — a team name followed by a person's name in parentheses, e.g. `Docs Program (Kara Voss)`. Use the team's current name, not a person's name alone.
26	4. Last updated — an ISO date, `YYYY-MM-DD`. Do not use month names.
27	5. Summary — one sentence, present tense, describing what the page covers.
28	
29	The block is written as a Markdown table (pipe syntax), not as a bullet list, so that it renders consistently in the folder's various viewers — GitHub's renderer, the internal `docs/` build, and a plain-text `cat`. A bullet-list header block was used on a few older pages before version 1.8 of this guide and has since been converted everywhere it was found.
30	
31	```markdown
32	| Field | Value |
33	|---|---|
34	| Title | Example Page Title |
35	| Version | 1.0 |
36	| Owner | Docs Program (Kara Voss) |
37	| Last updated | 2026-01-05 |
38	| Summary | One sentence describing the page in the present tense. |
39	```
40	
41	Do not add extra rows to this table (no "Status," no "Audience," no "Reviewers"). If a page needs to track reviewers, that belongs in the Review Cadence section of the page itself, or in the change log at the bottom — not in the header.
42	
43	## Heading Depth and Structure
44	
45	Owner: Kara Voss (Docs Program)
46	
47	Eventlog docs pages use three heading levels and no more:
48	
49	- `#` (H1) — exactly once per page, the title, matching the header block's Title field.
50	- `##` (H2) — top-level sections. Most pages have between six and twelve of these.
51	- `###` (H3) — subsections inside an H2, used sparingly. A page with more than three H3s under a single H2 usually means that H2 should be split into two H2s instead.
52	
53	We do not use `####` (H4) or deeper in `docs-style/` pages. The folder's build step (see Publishing Workflow Hooks, below) flattens H4 and deeper into bold run-in text rather than rendering them as headings, so a fourth level simply disappears visually — it does not error, it just goes unnoticed, which is worse. If a section feels like it needs a fourth level, it almost always needs a table or a numbered procedure instead.
54	
55	Heading text is sentence case for H2 and H3 ("Review cadence for this guide," not "Review Cadence For This Guide"), except this page, which — for reasons no one now remembers — has always used title case for its own H2s. New pages should use sentence case; do not "fix" this page to match, since the inconsistency is tracked separately and touching it triggers a wider rename across the folder's cross-links.
56	
57	Do not put punctuation at the end of a heading, with one exception: a heading phrased as a question may end in a question mark ("What counts as a glossary term?").
58	
59	## List Styles
60	
61	Owner: Kara Voss (Docs Program)
62	
63	Three list shapes appear across the folder, and each has a job:
64	
65	- **Unordered lists** use a hyphen (`-`), never an asterisk (`*`) and never a plus (`+`). This is the most commonly broken rule in the folder — asterisks creep in from copy-pasted content written elsewhere — and it's the first thing a reviewer should flag.
66	- **Ordered lists** use `1.` for every item, not incrementing numbers (`1.`, `2.`, `3.`). Markdown renders the numbers correctly regardless of what you type, and using `1.` throughout means inserting a step in the middle of a procedure never requires renumbering every line below it.
67	- **Definition-style lists** (a term, a dash, a short description) are written as a bold term followed by an em dash, inside a normal unordered list item, since Markdown has no native definition-list syntax that renders consistently across our tools:
68	
69	```markdown
70	- **Header block** — the metadata table at the top of every page.
71	- **Section owner** — the person named as responsible for a section's content.
72	```
73	
74	Nesting is allowed to two levels. A nested list uses two-space indentation, not four, and not a tab:
75	
76	```markdown
77	- Top-level step
78	  - A clarifying sub-point
79	  - Another sub-point
80	- Next top-level step
81	```
82	
83	Mixed nesting — an ordered list inside an unordered one, or the reverse — is fine when the content calls for it, such as a numbered procedure that includes a short list of options at one step:
84	
85	```markdown
86	1. Open the page in an editor.
87	2. Update the header block's Last updated field, and, if this is a version bump, the Version field:
88	   - Minor wording fixes do not change the version.
89	   - New sections or worked examples get a minor version bump.
90	   - A change to required page structure (see Page Templates) gets a major version bump.
91	3. Add a change log entry describing the edit.
92	```
93	
94	Do not mix hyphens and asterisks within the same list, even across nested levels — pick hyphens and stay with them for the whole block.
95	
96	## Emphasis, Inline Code, and Line Length
97	
98	Owner: Kara Voss (Docs Program)
99	
100	- Use `**bold**` for UI-adjacent terms, field names, and the first mention of a glossary term inside a section. Use `*italic*` sparingly, mainly for the titles of other pages when a full link isn't warranted, or for a single word carrying stress in a sentence.
101	- Use single backticks for inline code spans: file names, folder paths, flag-like values, and short configuration snippets that live inside a sentence, e.g. `docs-style/.markdownlint.jsonc`. Do not bold and code-format the same span at once.
102	- Fenced code blocks (triple backtick) always declare a language tag — `bash`, `powershell`, `yaml`, `json`, `markdown`, `text` — even when the block is a plain file listing, in which case `text` is the correct tag. An untagged fenced block is treated the same as a missing header block during review: it gets sent back.
103	- Lines in the source Markdown should wrap at roughly 100 characters where the editor makes that convenient, but this is a soft guideline, not something a reviewer should block a change over. Several long-standing pages, including this one, run well past that in places and have not been reflowed, because reflowing a whole page just to fix line length creates a large, hard-to-review change for no reader-visible benefit.
104	
105	## Tables and Column Alignment
106	
107	Owner: Kara Voss (Docs Program)
108	
109	Tables use pipe syntax with a header separator row. Left-align by default; only add alignment colons (`:---`, `:---:`, `---:`) when a column genuinely benefits from it, such as a numeric column that reads better right-aligned:
110	
111	```markdown
112	| Tool | Version | Notes |
113	|---|---|---|
114	| markdownlint-cli | 0.39.0 | Run before every push to docs-style/ |
115	| Pandoc | 3.1.11 | Used by the docs/ build step |
116	```
117	
118	Keep tables to a width a reader can scan without horizontal scrolling in a typical Markdown viewer — in practice, no more than five columns, and cell contents short enough to stay on one visual line. A table cell that needs a full sentence with punctuation is usually better as a bullet list item instead. If a table would need to break that rule to hold all its information, split it into two smaller tables rather than widening it.
119	
120	Do not use HTML `<table>` markup anywhere in these pages, even for tricky merged-cell layouts. If a table genuinely needs a merged cell, restructure the content instead — auditlog's docs build strips inline HTML from Markdown source before rendering, and an HTML table will simply vanish from the published page, which is a confusing failure mode to debug after the fact.
121	
122	## Links and Cross-References
123	
124	Owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools)
125	
126	Links between pages in the same folder use relative Markdown links with the file name, not a full path and not a bare page title:
127	
128	```markdown
129	See the [Page Templates](page-templates.md) page for the section order a new
130	page should follow.
131	```
132	
133	Link text should match the target page's Title field from its header block, word for word, so that a reader scanning link text can tell exactly which page they'll land on. When a link points at a specific section rather than the top of a page, use the section's heading text lowercased and hyphenated as the fragment, matching how the `docs/` build generates its anchors:
134	
135	```markdown
136	[list styles](markdown-conventions.md#list-styles)
137	```
138	
139	External links (outside the auditlog documentation folder) are written the same way but should include a short parenthetical noting what the reader will find there if the link text alone doesn't make it obvious. Do not leave bare URLs in running text; wrap them in link syntax even if the link text is just the URL itself, since a bare URL breaks the folder's automated link check.
140	
141	## Front Matter and Metadata Fields
142	
143	Owner: Owen Petrakis (Field Guides)
144	
145	Some pages, mainly the longer field-facing guides outside `docs-style/`, carry a YAML front matter block above the header table, used by the `docs/` build to generate side navigation. Pages inside `docs-style/` itself do not currently use front matter — the header table alone is sufficient for this folder's size — but a writer copying a `docs-style/` page as a starting point for a page elsewhere should add one. A minimal block looks like this:
146	
147	```yaml
148	---
149	title: Example Page Title
150	owner: docs-program
151	updated: 2026-01-05
152	---
153	```
154	
155	Field names in front matter are lowercase and hyphenated where needed (`last-updated`, not `Last Updated`), which is a deliberate difference from the header table's field names — front matter is machine-read, and the header table is human-read, so their casing conventions diverge on purpose. # Markdown Conventions

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Title | Markdown Conventions |
| Version | 2.6 |
| Owner | Docs Program (Kara Voss) |
| Last updated | 2025-04-28 |
| Summary | Lists the Markdown syntax choices, heading depths, and list styles that keep auditlog pages visually consistent across the folder. |

## Purpose and Reach of This Page

This page is the syntax-level companion to the [Voice and Tone Guide](voice-and-tone.md). Where that page tells a writer how a sentence should sound, this one tells them how the sentence should be marked up: which heading level to reach for, whether a list gets numbers or hyphens, how wide a table column is allowed to get before it should become a list instead. Every Markdown file under `docs-style/` and every published page under `docs/` is expected to follow the choices below. `.rst` and `.txt` files in the folder are out of reach for this page — they follow their own format's conventions, not Markdown's — but where a `.rst` page is later converted to Markdown, this page becomes the target style.

The guide is intentionally narrow. It does not tell you what to write, only how to format what you've already decided to write. For voice, sentence length, and terminology choice, see the sibling pages listed at the end of this page.

## Header Block Requirements

Owner: Kara Voss (Docs Program)

Every page in `docs-style/`, and every page it governs in `docs/`, opens with a small metadata table directly under the H1 title, exactly like the one at the top of this page. The fields, in order, are:

1. Title — the human-readable page name, matched to the H1 exactly (including capitalization).
2. Version — a plain decimal number (`2.6`) for pages owned by Docs Program, or a semantic-style tag (`v1.2.0`) for pages owned by other teams. Both are acceptable inside the folder; we have not standardized on one, and a proposal to do so has been open since late 2024 without a final call.
3. Owner — a team name followed by a person's name in parentheses, e.g. `Docs Program (Kara Voss)`. Use the team's current name, not a person's name alone.
4. Last updated — an ISO date, `YYYY-MM-DD`. Do not use month names.
5. Summary — one sentence, present tense, describing what the page covers.

The block is written as a Markdown table (pipe syntax), not as a bullet list, so that it renders consistently in the folder's various viewers — GitHub's renderer, the internal `docs/` build, and a plain-text `cat`. A bullet-list header block was used on a few older pages before version 1.8 of this guide and has since been converted everywhere it was found.

```markdown
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Title | Example Page Title |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Owner | Docs Program (Kara Voss) |
| Last updated | 2026-01-05 |
| Summary | One sentence describing the page in the present tense. |
```

Do not add extra rows to this table (no "Status," no "Audience," no "Reviewers"). If a page needs to track reviewers, that belongs in the Review Cadence section of the page itself, or in the change log at the bottom — not in the header.

## Heading Depth and Structure

Owner: Kara Voss (Docs Program)

Eventlog docs pages use three heading levels and no more:

- `#` (H1) — exactly once per page, the title, matching the header block's Title field.
- `##` (H2) — top-level sections. Most pages have between six and twelve of these.
- `###` (H3) — subsections inside an H2, used sparingly. A page with more than three H3s under a single H2 usually means that H2 should be split into two H2s instead.

We do not use `####` (H4) or deeper in `docs-style/` pages. The folder's build step (see Publishing Workflow Hooks, below) flattens H4 and deeper into bold run-in text rather than rendering them as headings, so a fourth level simply disappears visually — it does not error, it just goes unnoticed, which is worse. If a section feels like it needs a fourth level, it almost always needs a table or a numbered procedure instead.

Heading text is sentence case for H2 and H3 ("Review cadence for this guide," not "Review Cadence For This Guide"), except this page, which — for reasons no one now remembers — has always used title case for its own H2s. New pages should use sentence case; do not "fix" this page to match, since the inconsistency is tracked separately and touching it triggers a wider rename across the folder's cross-links.

Do not put punctuation at the end of a heading, with one exception: a heading phrased as a question may end in a question mark ("What counts as a glossary term?").

## List Styles

Owner: Kara Voss (Docs Program)

Three list shapes appear across the folder, and each has a job:

- **Unordered lists** use a hyphen (`-`), never an asterisk (`*`) and never a plus (`+`). This is the most commonly broken rule in the folder — asterisks creep in from copy-pasted content written elsewhere — and it's the first thing a reviewer should flag.
- **Ordered lists** use `1.` for every item, not incrementing numbers (`1.`, `2.`, `3.`). Markdown renders the numbers correctly regardless of what you type, and using `1.` throughout means inserting a step in the middle of a procedure never requires renumbering every line below it.
- **Definition-style lists** (a term, a dash, a short description) are written as a bold term followed by an em dash, inside a normal unordered list item, since Markdown has no native definition-list syntax that renders consistently across our tools:

```markdown
- **Header block** — the metadata table at the top of every page.
- **Section owner** — the person named as responsible for a section's content.
```

Nesting is allowed to two levels. A nested list uses two-space indentation, not four, and not a tab:

```markdown
- Top-level step
  - A clarifying sub-point
  - Another sub-point
- Next top-level step
```

Mixed nesting — an ordered list inside an unordered one, or the reverse — is fine when the content calls for it, such as a numbered procedure that includes a short list of options at one step:

```markdown
1. Open the page in an editor.
2. Update the header block's Last updated field, and, if this is a version bump, the Version field:
   - Minor wording fixes do not change the version.
   - New sections or worked examples get a minor version bump.
   - A change to required page structure (see Page Templates) gets a major version bump.
3. Add a change log entry describing the edit.
```

Do not mix hyphens and asterisks within the same list, even across nested levels — pick hyphens and stay with them for the whole block.

## Emphasis, Inline Code, and Line Length

Owner: Kara Voss (Docs Program)

- Use `**bold**` for UI-adjacent terms, field names, and the first mention of a glossary term inside a section. Use `*italic*` sparingly, mainly for the titles of other pages when a full link isn't warranted, or for a single word carrying stress in a sentence.
- Use single backticks for inline code spans: file names, folder paths, flag-like values, and short configuration snippets that live inside a sentence, e.g. `docs-style/.markdownlint.jsonc`. Do not bold and code-format the same span at once.
- Fenced code blocks (triple backtick) always declare a language tag — `bash`, `powershell`, `yaml`, `json`, `markdown`, `text` — even when the block is a plain file listing, in which case `text` is the correct tag. An untagged fenced block is treated the same as a missing header block during review: it gets sent back.
- Lines in the source Markdown should wrap at roughly 100 characters where the editor makes that convenient, but this is a soft guideline, not something a reviewer should block a change over. Several long-standing pages, including this one, run well past that in places and have not been reflowed, because reflowing a whole page just to fix line length creates a large, hard-to-review change for no reader-visible benefit.

## Tables and Column Alignment

Owner: Kara Voss (Docs Program)

Tables use pipe syntax with a header separator row. Left-align by default; only add alignment colons (`:---`, `:---:`, `---:`) when a column genuinely benefits from it, such as a numeric column that reads better right-aligned:

```markdown
| Tool | Version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| markdownlint-cli | 0.39.0 | Run before every push to docs-style/ |
| Pandoc | 3.1.11 | Used by the docs/ build step |
```

Keep tables to a width a reader can scan without horizontal scrolling in a typical Markdown viewer — in practice, no more than five columns, and cell contents short enough to stay on one visual line. A table cell that needs a full sentence with punctuation is usually better as a bullet list item instead. If a table would need to break that rule to hold all its information, split it into two smaller tables rather than widening it.

Do not use HTML `<table>` markup anywhere in these pages, even for tricky merged-cell layouts. If a table genuinely needs a merged cell, restructure the content instead — auditlog's docs build strips inline HTML from Markdown source before rendering, and an HTML table will simply vanish from the published page, which is a confusing failure mode to debug after the fact.

## Links and Cross-References

Owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools)

Links between pages in the same folder use relative Markdown links with the file name, not a full path and not a bare page title:

```markdown
See the [Page Templates](page-templates.md) page for the section order a new
page should follow.
```

Link text should match the target page's Title field from its header block, word for word, so that a reader scanning link text can tell exactly which page they'll land on. When a link points at a specific section rather than the top of a page, use the section's heading text lowercased and hyphenated as the fragment, matching how the `docs/` build generates its anchors:

```markdown
[list styles](markdown-conventions.md#list-styles)
```

External links (outside the auditlog documentation folder) are written the same way but should include a short parenthetical noting what the reader will find there if the link text alone doesn't make it obvious. Do not leave bare URLs in running text; wrap them in link syntax even if the link text is just the URL itself, since a bare URL breaks the folder's automated link check.

## Front Matter and Metadata Fields

Owner: Owen Petrakis (Field Guides)

Some pages, mainly the longer field-facing guides outside `docs-style/`, carry a YAML front matter block above the header table, used by the `docs/` build to generate side navigation.
```yaml
---
title: Example Page Title
owner: docs-program
updated: 2026-01-05
---
```

- **Cross-reference** — a relative Markdown link from one page in the folder to another, or to a specific section of one.
- **Glossary entry** — a bold term followed by an em dash and a short, present-tense definition, alphabetized within its section.
- **Lint pass** — the automated check, run by markdownlint-cli, that enforces this page's formatting rules before a change is published.

A note on the schema file: `front-matter-schema.yaml` is owned by Field Guides, not by Docs Program, which surprises people. It was written for a different purpose originally and got adopted here because nobody wanted to write a second one.

| Python                 | 3.11     | Running any snippet in a procedure template             |

## Common Mistakes

A running list, added to as reviewers catch the same problems repeatedly:

- Skipping the glossary section because "this page's terms are already in the main glossary." They still need to be here — see above.
- Version numbers that don't match the `vX.Y.Z` pattern used by this page itself. Inconsistent, yes, but new pages should use the `v` prefix going forward.
- Change log entries with no release name attached, just a date and a one-line description. Every entry needs a version.
- Numbered steps in a procedure page rewritten as bullets during a copyedit pass. Don't.
- Section owner names left stale after someone changes teams.

1	# Screenshots and Diagrams
2	
3	**Version:** v1.1.0
4	**Owner:** Developer Experience (Priya Nair)
5	**Last updated:** 2024-10-11
6	
7	## Summary
8	
9	This page covers image sizing, alt text, and diagram labeling conventions for illustrating how pieces of the package and the service fit together. If you're adding a terminal capture, a window screenshot, or a box-and-arrow diagram to any page under docs/, the conventions here apply. 10	
11	## Why this page exists
12	
13	Screenshots and diagrams rot faster than prose. A terminal capture showing the shell prompt style from two laptops ago, a diagram with a box labeled with a term the glossary no longer uses, a PNG that's 4000px wide and blows out the layout on a phone — these are the recurring complaints in doc reviews. Priya Nair put this page together after the Q2 2024 review cycle turned up eleven stale screenshots across six pages. The goal isn't to make images pretty. It's to make them replaceable without archaeology.
14	
15	## Coverage
16	
17	This page applies to:
18	
19	- Terminal/shell capture screenshots showing CLI-style output panes
20	- Screenshots of the loopback service responding in a browser or in an HTTP request tool
21	- Diagrams showing how the package's pieces relate to each other (component diagrams, sequence-style flow diagrams, folder/file diagrams)
22	- Any embedded image in a page under docs/, including this docs-style/ folder itself
23	
24	It does not apply to inline code blocks (see code-block-standards.md) or to plain-text file tree listings, which should stay as text, not screenshots, per markdown-conventions.md.
25	
26	## When to use a screenshot vs. a diagram vs. nothing
27	
28	Not every concept needs a picture. Use this rough guideline list:
29	
30	1. If the reader needs to recognize what something looks like on their own screen (an error dialog, a specific pane layout) → screenshot.
31	2. If the reader needs to understand how components relate, or a sequence of steps across more than two actors → diagram.
32	3. If the concept is a single command's output and the output is short (under ~15 lines) → prefer a code block over a screenshot. Screenshots of short text output are almost always unnecessary and go stale faster than the text they replace.
33	4. If you're documenting a folder layout or file relationships → text tree in a code block, not a screenshot.
34	
35	Owner note (Priya Nair): I still see people screenshot a config file's contents instead of pasting the text. Don't do that. If it's text, it goes in a code block.
36	
37	## Image sizing
38	
39	**Section owner: Priya Nair**
40	
41	Screenshots should be captured and cropped to a maximum of 1200px wide. Anything wider gets scaled down awkwardly by our renderer and text inside the screenshot becomes unreadable on a laptop screen at 100% zoom.
42	
43	| Asset type | Max width | Max height | Notes |
44	|---|---|---|---|
45	| Terminal capture | 1000px | 700px | Crop trailing blank lines; don't capture the whole terminal window chrome |
46	| Browser/HTTP request screenshot | 1200px | 900px | Crop browser chrome unless the chrome itself is relevant |
47	| Component diagram | 1200px | no hard limit | Tall diagrams should be split into two images rather than shrunk |
48	| Sequence/flow diagram | 1100px | 1000px | Prefer landscape orientation |
49	
50	Steps to resize on macOS or Linux without a paid tool:
51	
52	1. Take the capture at native resolution.
53	2. Open a shell and check the current dimensions:
54	   ```
55	   sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight capture.png
56	   ```
57	3. Resize to the target width, keeping aspect ratio:
58	   ```
59	   sips --resampleWidth 1000 capture.png
60	   ```
61	4. On Linux, the equivalent with ImageMagick:
62	   ```
63	   convert capture.png -resize 1000x capture-resized.png
64	   ```
65	5. Re-check dimensions before committing. If height still exceeds the max in the table above, crop rather than squash — squashing distorts text.
66	
67	File format: PNG for screenshots (lossless, text stays crisp), SVG for diagrams where the diagramming tool supports export to SVG. Avoid JPEG; compression artifacts make small terminal text blurry.
68	
69	## Alt text
70	
71	**Section owner: Priya Nair**
72	
73	Every embedded image needs alt text. This isn't optional and it isn't a one-line afterthought — alt text is read by screen readers and also shows up as a tooltip and in broken-image fallback, so it has to actually describe content, not just repeat the filename.
74	
75	Bad alt text:
76	```
77	![screenshot](img/shot1.png)
78	```
79	
80	Better:
81	```
82	![Terminal window showing the record count after a lookup, with the count printed on the last line](img/lookup-count-2024-09.png)
83	```
84	
85	Guidelines for alt text:
86	
87	- Describe what the image shows, not why you included it. "Diagram of the package's three components" is fine; "diagram explaining the architecture" is vague.
88	- Keep it under ~125 characters where possible. Screen readers will read all of it, so don't write a paragraph.
89	- For diagrams, name the components shown, in the order they appear left-to-right or top-to-bottom.
90	- For screenshots, mention the pane or window type and the one detail that matters (a count, a status word, a shape of output) — not every pixel.
91	- Don't start with "Image of" or "Screenshot of" redundantly if the surrounding image markdown or caption already says so; but if there's no caption, do include that framing word.
92	
93	Caption vs. alt text: alt text is for accessibility and must always be present. A caption (a line of italic text below the image) is optional and used when you want to add commentary that isn't strictly a description, e.g. *Captured on the September 2024 build; loopback service running on the default local port.*
94	
95	## Diagram labeling conventions
96	
97	**Section owner: Priya Nair**
98	
99	Diagrams in the docs generally show one of three things: how the CLI tool, the loopback service, and the database file relate to each other; a sequence of steps a request or a record takes through the package; or a folder/file layout (though as noted above, folder layouts are usually better as text).
100	
101	Labeling rules:
102	
103	1. **Box labels are nouns, not verbs.** Label a box "Database file" not "Storing records."
104	2. **Use the same term the glossary uses.** If terminology-glossary.md calls something "the service," don't label a diagram box "HTTP server" — pick one term and match it. This is the single most common diagram bug we catch in review: a diagram drawn in 2025 using a term that's since been superseded in the glossary.
105	3. **Arrows get short labels, not sentences.** "reads from," "writes to," "starts" — three words max.
106	4. **Number sequence steps if order matters.** Use small numbered circles or numbered labels (1, 2, 3) rather than relying on arrow direction alone; readers scanning quickly miss directionality.
107	5. **One diagram, one idea.** If you're tempted to show both the component relationships and a sequence of steps in the same image, split it into two diagrams.
108	6. **Color is decoration, not information.** Never rely on color alone to distinguish elements — some readers view docs in grayscale or have color vision differences. Pair color with a label or shape difference.
109	7. **Include a one-line title inside the diagram image itself**, top-left, restating what the diagram shows. This helps when the image is viewed outside its page context (e.g., pasted into a support message).
110	
111	### Worked example: component diagram
112	
113	A minimal text description of what a compliant component diagram should contain (the actual image is drawn in a diagramming tool, not in markdown):
114	
115	```
116	Title: How the package's pieces fit together
117	
118	[Command-line tool] --invokes--> [Package core]
119	[Package core] --reads/writes--> [Database file]
120	[Loopback service] --reads/writes--> [Database file]
121	[Command-line tool] and [Loopback service] both sit above [Package core]
122	```
123	
124	Box labels: "Command-line tool," "Package core," "Database file," "Loopback service" — these four terms should match exactly what's defined in the glossary section below and in terminology-glossary.md.
125	
126	### Worked example: sequence diagram
127	
128	```
129	Title: Sequence when a record is written
130	
131	1. Caller invokes the command-line tool
132	2. Command-line tool calls into the package core
133	3. Package core opens the database file
134	4. Package core writes the record
135	5. Package core closes the database file
136	6. Command-line tool prints a confirmation line
137	```
138	
139	Each numbered step becomes one labeled arrow or box in the actual diagram. Don't compress steps 3–5 into one box just to save space; readers use this diagram to understand ordering, and collapsing steps defeats the purpose.
140	
141	## File naming and storage
142	
143	**Section owner: Priya Nair**
144	
145	Store image assets under `docs/img/`, organized by the page they belong to where practical:
146	
147	- `docs/img/quickstart-terminal-2024-09.png`
148	- `docs/img/service-response-browser.png`
149	- `docs/img/component-diagram-v2.svg`
150	
151	Naming conventions:
152	
153	- Lowercase, hyphen-separated, no spaces.
154	- Include a rough date stamp (YYYY-MM) in the filename for screenshots that show a moving target (terminal output, browser views), since these are the ones most likely to go stale and need a diff-friendly replacement name.
155	- Diagrams that get updated should bump a version suffix (`-v2`, `-v3`) rather than overwrite the old file silently — this keeps the git log reviewable and lets a reviewer diff old vs. new in a pull request.
156	- Do not put images in the same folder as the page markdown files directly; keep `docs/img/` separate so page-listing scripts don't pick up binary files.
157	
158	When you replace a screenshot, remove the old file in the same change rather than leaving orphaned images in `docs/img/` — a script in `scripts/` periodically flags images not referenced by any markdown page, and cleaning up proactively saves a review cycle.
159	
160	## Accessibility checklist before committing an image
161	
162	- [ ] Alt text present and descriptive (not just the filename)
163	- [ ] Image width within the table above
164	- [ ] Diagram box labels match current glossary terms
165	- [ ] Diagram has a one-line title embedded top-left
166	- [ ] File named with hyphens, lowercase, and a date stamp if it's a moving-target screenshot
167	- [ ] Old version of the image removed if this is a replacement
168	- [ ] Caption added if there's context the alt text doesn't cover
169	
170	## Common mistakes seen in review
171	
172	- Alt text that just says "screenshot" or "diagram" with nothing else.
173	- Screenshots at native resolution (often 2500px+ wide from a retina display) committed without resizing.
174	- Diagrams with box labels that predate a glossary term change — most often "HTTP server" instead of "the service," or "log file" instead of "database file."
175	- JPEG screenshots of terminal text, blurry enough that small numbers are unreadable.
176	- Two ideas crammed into one diagram (component relationships plus a sequence), making it hard to caption briefly.
177	- Images committed directly into the page's folder instead of `docs/img/`.
178	
179	## Terminology
180	
181	- **Screenshot** — A captured image of an actual screen, window, or terminal pane, as opposed to a drawn diagram.
182	- **Diagram** — A drawn illustration (boxes, arrows, labels) representing a relationship or sequence, not a literal screen capture.
183	- **Alt text** — The descriptive text attached to an image for accessibility and fallback display, set inside the `![...]()` markdown brackets.
184	- **Caption** — Optional italic text below an image adding context beyond what the alt text covers.
185	- **Component diagram** — A diagram showing how pieces of the package and service relate to one another, without implying a strict order.
186	- **Sequence diagram** — A diagram showing an ordered series of steps, typically numbered.
187	- **Moving-target screenshot** — A screenshot of output likely to change in appearance over time (terminal captures, browser views), as opposed to a static diagram.
188	- **Box label** — The short noun phrase inside a diagram shape identifying what it represents.
189	- **Arrow label** — The short verb phrase on a diagram connector describing the relationship between two boxes.
190	- **Docs/img/ folder** — The dedicated storage location for all embedded image assets, kept separate from markdown page files.
191	
192	## Files referenced on this page
193	
194	| Path | Purpose |
195	|---|---|
196	| `docs/img/` | Storage folder for all screenshot and diagram image assets |
197	| `docs/img/quickstart-terminal-2024-09.png` | Example moving-target screenshot naming pattern |
198	| `docs/img/component-diagram-v2.svg` | Example versioned diagram file |
199	| `scripts/` | Contains the script that flags orphaned images not referenced by any page |
200	| `docs-style/markdown-conventions.md` | Sibling page covering general markdown formatting, including when to use code blocks instead of images |
201	| `docs-style/terminology-glossary.md` | Canonical source of terms that diagram box labels must match |
202	| `docs-style/code-block-standards.md` | Sibling page covering formatting for text/code output, the alternative to screenshotting short output |
203	
204	## Tools and libraries
205	
206	| Tool | Version | Purpose |
207	|---|---|---|
208	| ImageMagick | 7.1.1 | Command-line image resizing and format conversion on Linux |
209	| sips | (built-in, macOS) | Command-line image resizing on macOS |
210	| draw.io desktop | 24.7.5 | Primary diagramming tool for component and sequence diagrams |
211	| Inkscape | 1.3.2 | SVG editing for diagrams needing manual touch-up |
212	| Optipng | 0.7.7 | Lossless PNG compression pass before committing screenshots |
213	| git | 2.43.0 | Version control for image assets, same as page content |
214	
215	Diagram source files (the editable `.drawio` versions, not just exported PNG/SVG) should be kept alongside the exported image in `docs/img/` when the tool supports it, so future edits don't start from scratch.
216	
217	## Review cadence for images specifically
218	
219	Images get reviewed on the same cadence as the page they belong to — see review-cadence.md for the general schedule (owned by Support Enablement). There isn't a separate standalone review pass just for images; instead, reviewers checking a page for content accuracy also check that embedded screenshots still match current terminal/browser appearance and that diagram labels match the glossary. As of the 2025 review cycle, that shared-review approach replaced an earlier standalone quarterly image check that Priya Nair ran through most of 2024.
220	
221	## Related pages
222	
223	- [docs-style Folder Overview](./README.md)
224	- [Voice and Tone Guide](./voice-and-tone.md)
225	- [Terminology Glossary](./terminology-glossary.md)
226	- [Page Templates](./page-templates.md)
227	- [Review Cadence](./review-cadence.md)
228	- [Docs Publishing Workflow](./publishing-workflow.md)
229	- [Markdown Conventions](./markdown-conventions.md)
230	- [Code Block Standards](./code-block-standards.md)
231	
232	## Change log
233	
234	- **2023-11-08** — v1.0.0 — Initial page created by Priya Nair, covering basic image width limits.
235	- **2024-02-14** — v1.0.1 — Added alt text guidelines section after two pages shipped with empty alt attributes.
236	- **2024-05-02** — v1.0.2 — Added the docs/img/ naming convention and date-stamp recommendation for moving-target screenshots.
237	- **2024-07-19** — v1.0.3 — Added diagram labeling rules 1–5; rule 6 (color) and rule 7 (embedded title) added later.
238	- **2024-09-03** — v1.0.4 — Added worked examples for component and sequence diagrams; retired the old "screenshot everything" habit from early 2023 pages.
239	- **2024-10-11** — v1.1.0 — Folded the standalone quarterly image check into the general page review cadence; added the Tools and libraries table; updated ImageMagick version reference from 6.9 to 7.1.1.
