- Diagrams that get updated should bump a version suffix (`-v2`, `-v3`) rather than overwrite the old file silently — this keeps the git log reviewable and lets a reviewer diff old vs. new in a pull request.
- Do not put images in the same folder as the page markdown files directly; keep `docs/img/` separate so page-listing scripts don't pick up binary files.

When you replace a screenshot, remove the old file in the same change rather than leaving orphaned images in `docs/img/` — a script in `scripts/` periodically flags images not referenced by any markdown page, and cleaning up proactively saves a review cycle.

## Accessibility checklist before committing an image

- [ ] Alt text present and descriptive (not just the filename)
- [ ] Image width within the table above
- [ ] Diagram box labels match current glossary terms
- [ ] Diagram has a one-line title embedded top-left
- [ ] File named with hyphens, lowercase, and a date stamp if it's a moving-target screenshot
- [ ] Old version of the image removed if this is a replacement
- [ ] Caption added if there's context the alt text doesn't cover

## Common mistakes seen in review

- Alt text that just says "screenshot" or "diagram" with nothing else.
- Screenshots at native resolution (often 2500px+ wide from a retina display) committed without resizing.
- Diagrams with box labels that predate a glossary term change — most often "HTTP server" instead of "the service," or "log file" instead of "database file."
- JPEG screenshots of terminal text, blurry enough that small numbers are unreadable.
- Two ideas crammed into one diagram (component relationships plus a sequence), making it hard to caption briefly.
- Images committed directly into the page's folder instead of `docs/img/`.

## Terminology

- **Screenshot** — A captured image of an actual screen, window, or terminal pane, as opposed to a drawn diagram.
- **Diagram** — A drawn illustration (boxes, arrows, labels) representing a relationship or sequence, not a literal screen capture.
- **Alt text** — The descriptive text attached to an image for accessibility and fallback display, set inside the `![...]()` markdown brackets.
- **Caption** — Optional italic text below an image adding context beyond what the alt text covers.
- **Component diagram** — A diagram showing how pieces of the package and service relate to one another, without implying a strict order.
- **Sequence diagram** — A diagram showing an ordered series of steps, typically numbered.
- **Moving-target screenshot** — A screenshot of output likely to change in appearance over time (terminal captures, browser views), as opposed to a static diagram.
- **Box label** — The short noun phrase inside a diagram shape identifying what it represents.
- **Arrow label** — The short verb phrase on a diagram connector describing the relationship between two boxes.
- **Docs/img/ folder** — The dedicated storage location for all embedded image assets, kept separate from markdown page files.

## Files referenced on this page

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docs/img/` | Storage folder for all screenshot and diagram image assets |
| `docs/img/quickstart-terminal-2024-09.png` | Example moving-target screenshot naming pattern |
| `docs/img/component-diagram-v2.svg` | Example versioned diagram file |
| `scripts/` | Contains the script that flags orphaned images not referenced by any page |
| `docs-style/markdown-conventions.md` | Sibling page covering general markdown formatting, including when to use code blocks instead of images |
| `docs-style/terminology-glossary.md` | Canonical source of terms that diagram box labels must match |
| `docs-style/code-block-standards.md` | Sibling page covering formatting for text/code output, the alternative to screenshotting short output |

## Tools and libraries

| Tool | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| ImageMagick | 7.1.1 | Command-line image resizing and format conversion on Linux |
| sips | (built-in, macOS) | Command-line image resizing on macOS |
| draw.io desktop | 24.7.5 | Primary diagramming tool for component and sequence diagrams |
| Inkscape | 1.3.2 | SVG editing for diagrams needing manual touch-up |
| Optipng | 0.7.7 | Lossless PNG compression pass before committing screenshots |
| git | 2.43.0 | Version control for image assets, same as page content |

Diagram source files (the editable `.drawio` versions, not just exported PNG/SVG) should be kept alongside the exported image in `docs/img/` when the tool supports it, so future edits don't start from scratch.

## Review cadence for images specifically

Images get reviewed on the same cadence as the page they belong to — see review-cadence.md for the general schedule (owned by Support Enablement). There isn't a separate standalone review pass just for images; instead, reviewers checking a page for content accuracy also check that embedded screenshots still match current terminal/browser appearance and that diagram labels match the glossary. As of the 2025 review cycle, that shared-review approach replaced an earlier standalone quarterly image check that Priya Nair ran through most of 2024.

## Related pages

- [docs-style Folder Overview](./README.md)
- [Voice and Tone Guide](./voice-and-tone.md)
- [Terminology Glossary](./terminology-glossary.md)
- [Page Templates](./page-templates.md)
- [Review Cadence](./review-cadence.md)
- [Docs Publishing Workflow](./publishing-workflow.md)
- [Markdown Conventions](./markdown-conventions.md)
- [Code Block Standards](./code-block-standards.md)

## Change log

- **2023-11-08** — v1.0.0 — Initial page created by Priya Nair, covering basic image width limits.
- **2024-02-14** — v1.0.1 — Added alt text guidelines section after two pages shipped with empty alt attributes.
- **2024-05-02** — v1.0.2 — Added the docs/img/ naming convention and date-stamp recommendation for moving-target screenshots.
- **2024-07-19** — v1.0.3 — Added diagram labeling rules 1–5; rule 6 (color) and rule 7 (embedded title) added later.
- **2024-09-03** — v1.0.4 — Added worked examples for component and sequence diagrams; retired the old "screenshot everything" habit from early 2023 pages.
- **2024-10-11** — v1.1.0 — Folded the standalone quarterly image check into the general page review cadence; added the Tools and libraries table; updated ImageMagick version reference from 6.9 to 7.1.1.

1	.. title: Style Checklist
2	.. version: 2.0
3	.. owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)
4	.. last-updated: 2025-12-05
5	
6	Style Checklist
7	===============
8	
9	Summary
10	-------
11	Offers a short pass or fail checklist writers run through before marking a documentation page ready for review.
12	
13	This checklist ensures that documentation pages meet the established standards for content, structure, formatting, and metadata before entering the review process. Writers use this guide to catch common issues early and avoid delays in peer review.
14	
15	About This Page
16	---------------
17	*Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*
18	
19	The Style Checklist is the final validation gate before requesting review. It captures the accumulated best practices from our documentation program, distilled into verifiable criteria. Each criterion supports readability, maintainability, and consistency across the auditlog documentation set.
20	
21	This page assumes you have already reviewed the Voice and Tone Guide and Page Templates documentation. It focuses on the specific, checkable aspects of a finished page before handoff to reviewers.
22	
23	
24	Pre-Review Checklist
25	--------------------
26	*Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*
27	
28	Use this checklist in order. A page must pass all checks before review request.
29	
30	**Metadata and Header Requirements**
31	
32	- [ ] Title is present and descriptive (3–8 words)
33	- [ ] Version number follows semantic versioning (v1.0, 2.0, etc.)
34	- [ ] Owner name and team are listed
35	- [ ] Last-updated date is today's date or earlier (YYYY-MM-DD format)
36	- [ ] Summary statement is 1–3 sentences and describes purpose, not content
37	- [ ] No unfilled sections remain anywhere in the page
38	
39	**Structure and Navigation**
40	
41	- [ ] At least 4 section headings are present
42	- [ ] Section owners are named for major sections (in italics)
43	- [ ] Section headings follow hierarchy (H2, H3, etc., not skipped levels)
44	- [ ] Related pages section lists 3 or more sibling pages with exact titles
45	- [ ] Glossary section defines at least 8 terms used in the page
46	- [ ] Changelog includes at least 6 entries with dates and version names
47	- [ ] Files and Paths section lists every repository location mentioned
48	
49	**Content Requirements**
50	
51	- [ ] All file paths and repository locations are listed with purpose descriptions
52	- [ ] All tools, packages, or libraries have version numbers in a table
53	- [ ] All procedures include concrete steps, not vague descriptions
54	- [ ] All examples are runnable or clearly demonstrable (not pseudocode)
55	- [ ] Technical terms are defined on first use or in glossary
56	- [ ] Links to sibling pages use exact titles, not "see also" or similar
57	- [ ] Paragraph length does not exceed 7 sentences
58	
59	**Formatting and Consistency**
60	
61	- [ ] Numbered lists and bullet lists are used consistently within sections
62	- [ ] Code blocks are marked with language (e.g., ``bash``, ``yaml``)
63	- [ ] Tables have headers and consistent column alignment
64	- [ ] Inline code uses backticks, not quotes or other delimiters
65	- [ ] Line length does not exceed 100 characters in source
66	- [ ] Acronyms are spelled out on first mention
67	- [ ] No trailing whitespace on any line
68	
69	**Voice, Tone, and Clarity**
70	
71	- [ ] Language avoids marketing jargon and vague qualifiers
72	- [ ] Sentences use active voice where possible
73	- [ ] Recommendations use "should" or "must," not "might" or "can"
74	- [ ] Instructions use imperative verb forms (e.g., "Open the file," not "You should open")
75	- [ ] No undefined acronyms remain in the document
76	- [ ] Consistent capitalization of terms and titles throughout
77	
78	
79	Documentation Content Standards
80	--------------------------------
81	*Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*
82	
83	Page Header Block
84	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
85	
86	Every page must contain a machine-readable header block at the very top. In reStructuredText, use comment syntax:
87	
88	::
89	
90	  .. title: Your Page Title Here
91	  .. version: 2.0
92	  .. owner: Team Name (Person Name)
93	  .. last-updated: 2025-12-05
94	
95	The title field must match the main title heading exactly. The version field uses semantic versioning; choose one format and maintain it throughout the page's lifetime. Do not mix v2.0 and 2.0 formats.
96	
97	The owner field lists a team or group, followed by a primary point person in parentheses. Update the last-updated date every time you make a material change to the page. If you add a changelog entry, update the header date to match. If you correct only a typo or formatting issue, the date may remain unchanged.
98	
99	Section Ownership Model
100	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
101	
102	Sections with substantive instructional or procedural content must list an owner in italics at the start of the section. For example:
103	
104	::
105	
106	  Pre-Review Checklist
107	  --------------------
108	  *Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*
109	
110	If the entire page has a single owner, you may still list owners on major sections for clarity. If different teams maintain different sections, each section must list its owner. This allows readers to know whom to contact with questions or feedback.
111	
112	When multiple people share ownership, list the team name only, not every individual. Avoid listing owners on subsections (H3 and below) unless the subsection has a distinctly different owner than its parent section.
113	
114	Summary and Purpose Statement
115	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
116	
117	The Summary section should appear immediately after the title and should be 1–3 sentences. It must explain the page's purpose and audience, not describe its contents. Good summaries answer: "Who should read this?" and "What problem does this page solve?" Bad summaries say, "This page covers X, Y, and Z." Readers can see the section headings; they need to know why they should care.
118	
119	
120	Terminology and Glossary
121	------------------------
122	*Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*
123	
124	Each page must include a glossary section with definitions for at least 8 terms used within that page. Terms should be ordered alphabetically. Each definition should be 1–3 sentences and contextualized for the page's domain.
125	
126	**Inclusion guideline:** If a term appears more than once in the page and might be unfamiliar to readers, it should appear in the glossary. If a term is ambiguous (e.g., "service" can mean HTTP service or customer support), define it explicitly in the glossary.
127	
128	**Example glossary entry:**
129	
130	  **Checklist item:** A single criterion or question in a verification list that must pass for a page to advance to the next stage. Checklist items are atomic (they cannot be subdivided) and binary (pass or fail).
131	
132	The glossary section must have its own heading (H2 or H3 depending on page structure) and be positioned after the main content sections, before the "Files and Paths" section. Do not include terms that are already defined in the shared Terminology Glossary document, unless you need to provide a page-specific definition.
133	
134	Glossary Terms and Definitions
135	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
136	
137	**Author:** The primary writer responsible for creating and maintaining a page. May differ from the owner, who represents the team or domain responsible for keeping the page accurate.
138	
139	**Changelog:** A dated log of changes to a page, including the version, release name (if applicable), and a brief description of what changed. Entries are ordered from newest to oldest.
140	
141	**Checksum:** A hash or fingerprint computed from file content, used to verify that a file has not been modified since its generation or publication.
142	
143	**Consistency:** The degree to which a page follows the same formatting, tone, capitalization, and structural patterns as other pages in the documentation set.
144	
145	**Front matter:** Structured metadata at the top of a page, often in YAML, Markdown, or reStructuredText comment syntax, containing title, version, author, and date fields.
146	
147	**Glossary:** An alphabetical list of terms defined in the context of a single page or document set. Differs from a shared terminology reference by being local to a specific page or folder.
148	
149	**Maintainability:** The ease with which a future writer can find, update, and verify the accuracy of information on a page. High maintainability means clear section ownership and explicit file path references.
150	
151	**Peer review:** A process in which one or more writers read a page before publication to verify accuracy, tone, consistency, and completeness. Distinct from technical review by subject matter experts.
152	
153	**Semantic versioning:** A versioning scheme in which a version number consists of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., 2.3.1), where MAJOR indicates breaking changes, MINOR indicates new features, and PATCH indicates bug fixes.
154	
155	**Section owner:** The team or individual responsible for keeping a section of a page up to date and accurate. Different sections of a single page may have different owners.
156	
157	
158	Files and Paths Referenced
159	---------------------------
160	
161	This page refers to the following files and directories in the auditlog documentation repository:
162	
163	| Path | Purpose |
164	|------|------|
165	| ``docs-style/style-checklist.rst`` | This file. Contains standards and checklist for all documentation pages. |
166	| ``docs-style/`` | Parent directory. Holds all style guides, templates, and writing standards for the documentation program. |
167	| ``docs-style/voice-and-tone.md`` | Voice and Tone Guide. Defines the writing voice, perspective, and tone for technical documentation. |
168	| ``docs-style/page-templates.md`` | Page Templates. Provides boilerplate and suggested structures for common documentation page types. |
169	| ``docs-style/terminology-glossary.md`` | Shared Terminology Glossary. Central reference for terms used across multiple pages; page-specific glossaries supplement this. |
170	| ``docs-style/review-cadence.md`` | Review Cadence. Specifies how often sections must be reviewed, by whom, and when to schedule reviews. |
171	| ``docs-style/publishing-workflow.md`` | Docs Publishing Workflow. Outlines the steps from draft to published documentation, including merge and deployment. |
172	| ``docs-style/markdown-conventions.md`` | Markdown Conventions. Formatting rules for pages in Markdown format, complementing this reStructuredText page. |
173	| ``docs-style/code-block-standards.md`` | Code Block Standards. Rules for displaying code examples and command output, including language tags. |
174	| ``docs-style/screenshots-and-diagrams.md`` | Screenshots and Diagrams. Guidelines for creating, sizing, and embedding visual assets in documentation. |
175	| ``docs-style/front-matter-schema.yaml`` | Front Matter Schema. Machine-readable definition of required metadata fields and their format constraints. |
176	| ``docs-style/README.md`` | docs-style Folder Overview. Index and description of all pages in the style guides folder. |
177	
178	
179	Tools, Packages, and Library Versions
180	--------------------------------------
181	
182	This page references the following tools and utilities for documentation authoring and validation:
183	
184	| Tool | Version | Purpose |
185	|------|---------|---------|
186	| reStructuredText | N/A | Markup language used for documentation pages in .rst format. |
187	| Markdown | N/A | Lightweight markup language used for some documentation pages in .md format. |
188	| Git | 2.40+ | Version control for documentation source and tracking changes over time. |
189	| PowerShell | 7.2+ | Command shell used for file operations and script execution on Windows systems. |
190	| Bash | 4.4+ | Command shell used for POSIX-based file operations and scripting on Unix-like systems. |
191	| sqlite3 | 3.33+ | Command-line tool for inspecting and validating database example queries in documentation. |
192	| rst2html | 1.0.0 | Converts reStructuredText to HTML for preview and validation before publishing. |
193	| nano or vi | Current | Text editors available on all systems for quick file edits during documentation work. |
194	
195	
196	Writing and Style Verification
197	-------------------------------
198	*Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*
199	
200	**Paragraph length:** Paragraphs should be 3–7 sentences. Shorter paragraphs (1–2 sentences) are acceptable for emphasis or list introductions; longer paragraphs (8+ sentences) usually indicate a section should be divided into subsections.
201	
202	**Sentence structure:** Aim for 15–25 words per sentence. Sentences exceeding 30 words often need rephrasing into two sentences or simplification.
203	
204	**Capitalization:** Capitalize proper nouns (team names, file names, page titles as shown in headers) and the first word of sentences. Use lowercase for common nouns (page, section, owner, checklist) except at sentence start.
205	
206	**Abbreviations and acronyms:** Spell out acronyms on first mention in a page. After the first mention, the acronym alone is acceptable. In a glossary entry, spell it out once; do not abbreviate it in the definition.
207	
208	**Links to sibling pages:** In reStructuredText, use the format ``Page Title`_`` with a reference link at the end of the document. In Markdown, use ``[Page Title](path/to/file.md)``. Always link using the exact title from the related page's header block.
209	
210	**Inline code:** Use backticks for code, command names, file names, variable names, and configuration keys: "Run the ``checkout`` command," "Edit the ``config.yaml`` file," "Set ``max_retries`` to 10."
211	
212	**Emphasis:** Use italics (*like this*) for emphasis, to introduce a defined term, or to mark section owners. Use bold (**like this**) for strong directives, section headers in tables, or when introducing defined terms as headings.
213	
214	**Tables:** Always include a header row. Align columns consistently. Use pipes (|) for column separators and dashes for row separators. Ensure the source is readable even in plain text.
215	
216	
217	Common Issues to Watch For
218	--------------------------
219	
220	**Missing version information:** The most common failure is omitting tool or package versions. Every tool, library, or dependency mentioned in the page must have a version number in either the header block (for the page's own version) or a versions table (for dependencies and tools).
221	
222	**Inconsistent list formatting:** If a page mixes numbered lists and bullet lists without clear reason, it signals to readers that order or structure differs unexpectedly. Use numbered lists only when sequence or priority matters. Use bullets for equal-weight items.
223	
224	**Glossary gaps:** Do not assume readers know specialized terms like "checklist item," "changelog," or "front matter." If you write it more than once, define it in the glossary.
225	
226	**Dangling references:** Avoid phrases like "See the page on publishing" or "Refer to the guide," which may go out of date if page titles change. Use exact page titles: "See `Docs Publishing Workflow`_." Broken links are easy to spot in a pre-review checklist.
227	
228	**Stale dates:** The last-updated date must reflect actual edits. If you edited a page in September 2025, do not leave the date as August 2025. Readers rely on this date to assess the page's freshness.
229	
230	**Undefined acronyms:** Spell out acronyms on first mention, even if they seem obvious. RST means reStructuredText; API means application programming interface. Do not assume readers know every acronym.
231	
232	**File paths without purpose descriptions:** Every file path in a section must be accompanied by a one-line description of its function. Bare file paths confuse readers about why that file matters.
233	
234	**Inconsistent section ownership:** If two sections have similar coverage and authority, both should list owners. If only some sections list owners and others do not, readers may assume unowned sections are less official or out of date.
235	
236	
237	Worked Example: Creating a New Documentation Page
238	--------------------------------------------------
239	
240	This example walks through writing and checking a new documentation page from start to finish.
241	
242	**Step 1: Create the file**
243	
244	Create a new file in the ``docs-style/`` folder with a descriptive name using hyphens (not underscores or spaces):
245	
246	::
247	
248	  $ touch docs-style/new-page.rst
249	
250	**Step 2: Add the header block**
251	
252	Open the file in your text editor (nano, vi, or your preferred editor) and add the metadata block at the very top:
253	
254	::
255	
256	  .. title: New Documentation Page
257	  .. version: 1.0
258	  .. owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)
259	  .. last-updated: 2026-09-27
260	
261	The version should start at 1.0 for a new page. Use today's date in the last-updated field.
262	
263	**Step 3: Write the title and introduction**
264	
265	Add the main title using the reStructuredText H1 format (equals signs above and below):
266	
267	::
268	
269	  New Documentation Page
270	  ======================
271	
272	  Summary
273	  -------
274	  Describes how to write, structure, and validate new documentation pages in the auditlog project.
275	
276	**Step 4: Add the main content sections with owners**
277	
278	Write the main content sections, assigning owners to sections that are instructional or procedural:
279	
280	::
281	
282	  Getting Started
283	  ---------------
284	  *Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*
285	
286	  This section covers the initial setup steps needed before writing documentation.
287	
288	  Main Workflow
289	  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
290	
291	  [Subsections below an owner section inherit that owner unless explicitly marked otherwise.]
292	
293	**Step 5: Create the glossary section**
294	
295	After the main content, add a Glossary section with at least 8 terms used in your page:
296	
297	::
298	
299	  Glossary
300	  --------
301	
302	  **Checklist:** A list of criteria or questions that must all pass for a task to be complete.
303	
304	  **Front matter:** Structured metadata at the top of a page containing title, version, owner, and date.
305	
306	  [Continue with 6 more terms, ordered alphabetically...]
307	
308	**Step 6: Add Files and Paths section**
309	
310	Create a table listing every file path or directory mentioned in the page:
311	
312	::
313	
314	  Files and Paths Referenced
315	  ---------------------------
316	
317	  | Path | Purpose |
318	  |------|------|
319	  | ``docs-style/new-page.rst`` | This file. Contains documentation on creating new pages. |
320	  | ``docs-style/`` | Parent directory holding all style guides and templates. |
321	  | ``docs/`` | Main documentation folder containing all published pages and guides. |
322	
323	**Step 7: Add tools and versions table**
324	
325	List all tools and packages mentioned in the page:
326	
327	::
328	
329	  Tools and Versions
330	  ------------------
331	
332	  | Tool | Version |
333	  |------|---------|
334	  | reStructuredText | N/A |
335	  | Git | 2.40+ |
336	  | rst2html | 1.0.0 |
337	
338	**Step 8: Run through the pre-review checklist**
339	
340	Go through each item in the Pre-Review Checklist section at the top of this page. Mark off each item with a mental note or physical check as you verify it. Do not request review until all items pass. If you cannot pass an item, fix the page or add clarification.
341	
342	**Step 9: Add a changelog section**
343	
344	Before requesting review, add an entry to your changelog section:
345	
346	::
347	
348	  Changelog
349	  ---------
350	
351	  | Date | Version | Release | Changes |
352	  |------|---------|---------|---------|
353	  | 2026-09-27 | 1.0 | Initial Publication | Page created with full structure, nine glossary terms, and worked example section. |
354	  | [Earlier entries below...] |
355	
356	**Step 10: Link from the related pages section**
357	
358	Add a Related Pages section that links to sibling pages using exact titles:
359	
360	::
361	
362	  Related Pages
363	  ---------
364	
365	  - `Page Templates`_
366	  - `Voice and Tone Guide`_
367	  - `Docs Publishing Workflow`_
368	
369	**Step 11: Request peer review**
370	
371	Ask a peer from another team to work through the same checklist. Do not merge or publish until the assessment is complete and all feedback is incorporated.
372	
373	
374	Changelog
375	---------
376	
377	| Date | Version | Release | Changes |
378	|------|---------|---------|---------|
379	| 2025-12-05 | 2.0 | Winter 2025 | Expanded glossary section to 10 terms, added common issues section, refined checklist pass/fail criteria. |
380	| 2025-09-15 | 1.9 | Fall 2025 | Added worked example section, updated tool versions to 2.40+ for Git. |
381	| 2025-06-22 | 1.8 | Summer 2025 | Added paragraph and sentence length guidance, expanded style verification section, clarified section ownership model. |
382	| 2025-03-10 | 1.7 | Spring 2025 | Refined inline code formatting guidance, added table formatting standards. |
383	| 2024-12-08 | 1.6 | Winter 2024 | Added file paths section with purpose descriptions, expanded related pages list. |
384	| 2024-09-01 | v1.0 | Initial Release | Initial framework for style checklist, established baseline requirements for all documentation pages. |
385	
386	
387	Related Pages
388	-------------
389	
390	The following pages in the ``docs-style/`` folder complement this checklist and provide additional guidance:
391	
392	- `Voice and Tone Guide`_
393	- `Page Templates`_
394	- `Terminology Glossary`_
395	- `Review Cadence`_
396	- `Docs Publishing Workflow`_
397	- `Markdown Conventions`_
398	- `Code Block Standards`_
399	- `Screenshots and Diagrams`_
400	- `docs-style Folder Overview`_

.. title: Style Checklist
.. version: 2.0
.. owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)
.. last-updated: 2025-12-05

Style Checklist
===============

Summary
-------
Offers a short pass or fail checklist writers run through before marking a documentation page ready for review.

This checklist ensures that documentation pages meet the established standards for content, structure, formatting, and metadata before entering the review process. Writers use this guide to catch common issues early and avoid delays in peer review.

About This Page
---------------
*Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*

The Style Checklist is the final validation gate before requesting review. It captures the accumulated best practices from our documentation program, distilled into verifiable criteria. Each criterion supports readability, maintainability, and consistency across the auditlog documentation set.

This page assumes you have already reviewed the Voice and Tone Guide and Page Templates documentation. It focuses on the specific, checkable aspects of a finished page before handoff to reviewers.


Pre-Review Checklist
--------------------
*Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*

Use this checklist in order. A page must pass all checks before review request.

**Metadata and Header Requirements**

- [ ] Title is present and descriptive (3–8 words)
- [ ] Version number follows semantic versioning (v1.0, 2.0, etc.)
- [ ] Owner name and team are listed
- [ ] Last-updated date is today's date or earlier (YYYY-MM-DD format)
- [ ] Summary statement is 1–3 sentences and describes purpose, not content
- [ ] No unfilled sections remain anywhere in the page

**Structure and Navigation**

- [ ] At least 4 section headings are present
- [ ] Section owners are named for major sections (in italics)
- [ ] Section headings follow hierarchy (H2, H3, etc., not skipped levels)
- [ ] Related pages section lists 3 or more sibling pages with exact titles
- [ ] Glossary section defines at least 8 terms used in the page
- [ ] Changelog includes at least 6 entries with dates and version names
- [ ] Files and Paths section lists every repository location mentioned

**Content Requirements**

- [ ] All file paths and repository locations are listed with purpose descriptions
- [ ] All tools, packages, or libraries have version numbers in a table
- [ ] All procedures include concrete steps, not vague descriptions
- [ ] All examples are runnable or clearly demonstrable (not pseudocode)
- [ ] Technical terms are defined on first use or in glossary
- [ ] Links to sibling pages use exact titles, not "see also" or similar
- [ ] Paragraph length does not exceed 7 sentences

**Formatting and Consistency**

- [ ] Numbered lists and bullet lists are used consistently within sections
- [ ] Code blocks are marked with language (e.g., ``bash``, ``yaml``)
- [ ] Tables have headers and consistent column alignment
- [ ] Inline code uses backticks, not quotes or other delimiters
- [ ] Line length does not exceed 100 characters in source
- [ ] Acronyms are spelled out on first mention
- [ ] No trailing whitespace on any line

**Voice, Tone, and Clarity**

- [ ] Language avoids marketing jargon and vague qualifiers
- [ ] Sentences use active voice where possible
- [ ] Recommendations use "should" or "must," not "might" or "can"
- [ ] Instructions use imperative verb forms (e.g., "Open the file," not "You should open")
- [ ] No undefined acronyms remain in the document
- [ ] Consistent capitalization of terms and titles throughout


Documentation Content Standards
--------------------------------
*Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*

Page Header Block
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Every page must contain a machine-readable header block at the very top. In reStructuredText, use comment syntax:

::

  .. title: Your Page Title Here
  .. version: 2.0
  .. owner: Team Name (Person Name)
  .. last-updated: 2025-12-05

The title field must match the main title heading exactly. The version field uses semantic versioning; choose one format and maintain it throughout the page's lifetime. Do not mix v2.0 and 2.0 formats.

The owner field lists a team or group, followed by a primary point person in parentheses. Update the last-updated date every time you make a material change to the page. If you add a changelog entry, update the header date to match. If you correct only a typo or formatting issue, the date may remain unchanged.

Section Ownership Model
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Sections with substantive instructional or procedural content must list an owner in italics at the start of the section. For example:

::

  Pre-Review Checklist
  --------------------
  *Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*

If the entire page has a single owner, you may still list owners on major sections for clarity. If different teams maintain different sections, each section must list its owner. This allows readers to know whom to contact with questions or feedback.

When multiple people share ownership, list the team name only, not every individual. Avoid listing owners on subsections (H3 and below) unless the subsection has a distinctly different owner than its parent section.

Summary and Purpose Statement
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The Summary section should appear immediately after the title and should be 1–3 sentences. It must explain the page's purpose and audience, not describe its contents. Good summaries answer: "Who should read this?" and "What problem does this page solve?" Bad summaries say, "This page covers X, Y, and Z." Readers can see the section headings; they need to know why they should care.


Terminology and Glossary
------------------------
*Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*

Each page must include a glossary section with definitions for at least 8 terms used within that page. Terms should be ordered alphabetically. Each definition should be 1–3 sentences and contextualized for the page's domain.

**Inclusion guideline:** If a term appears more than once in the page and might be unfamiliar to readers, it should appear in the glossary. If a term is ambiguous (e.g., "service" can mean HTTP service or customer support), define it explicitly in the glossary.

**Example glossary entry:**

  **Checklist item:** A single criterion or question in a verification list that must pass for a page to advance to the next stage. Checklist items are atomic (they cannot be subdivided) and binary (pass or fail).

The glossary section must have its own heading (H2 or H3 depending on page structure) and be positioned after the main content sections, before the "Files and Paths" section. Do not include terms that are already defined in the shared Terminology Glossary document, unless you need to provide a page-specific definition.

Glossary Terms and Definitions
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

**Author:** The primary writer responsible for creating and maintaining a page. May differ from the owner, who represents the team or domain responsible for keeping the page accurate.

**Changelog:** A dated log of changes to a page, including the version, release name (if applicable), and a brief description of what changed. Entries are ordered from newest to oldest.

**Checksum:** A hash or fingerprint computed from file content, used to verify that a file has not been modified since its generation or publication.

**Consistency:** The degree to which a page follows the same formatting, tone, capitalization, and structural patterns as other pages in the documentation set.

**Front matter:** Structured metadata at the top of a page, often in YAML, Markdown, or reStructuredText comment syntax, containing title, version, author, and date fields.

**Glossary:** An alphabetical list of terms defined in the context of a single page or document set. Differs from a shared terminology reference by being local to a specific page or folder.

**Maintainability:** The ease with which a future writer can find, update, and verify the accuracy of information on a page. High maintainability means clear section ownership and explicit file path references.

**Peer review:** A process in which one or more writers read a page before publication to verify accuracy, tone, consistency, and completeness. Distinct from technical review by subject matter experts.

**Semantic versioning:** A versioning scheme in which a version number consists of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., 2.3.1), where MAJOR indicates breaking changes, MINOR indicates new features, and PATCH indicates bug fixes.

**Section owner:** The team or individual responsible for keeping a section of a page up to date and accurate. Different sections of a single page may have different owners.


Files and Paths Referenced
---------------------------

This page refers to the following files and directories in the auditlog documentation repository:

| Path | Purpose |
|------|------|
| ``docs-style/style-checklist.rst`` | This file. Contains standards and checklist for all documentation pages. |
| ``docs-style/`` | Parent directory. Holds all style guides, templates, and writing standards for the documentation program. |
| ``docs-style/voice-and-tone.md`` | Voice and Tone Guide. Defines the writing voice, perspective, and tone for technical documentation. |
| ``docs-style/page-templates.md`` | Page Templates. Provides boilerplate and suggested structures for common documentation page types. |
| ``docs-style/terminology-glossary.md`` | Shared Terminology Glossary. Central reference for terms used across multiple pages; page-specific glossaries supplement this. |
| ``docs-style/review-cadence.md`` | Review Cadence. Specifies how often sections must be reviewed, by whom, and when to schedule reviews. |
| ``docs-style/publishing-workflow.md`` | Docs Publishing Workflow. Outlines the steps from draft to published documentation, including merge and deployment. |
| ``docs-style/markdown-conventions.md`` | Markdown Conventions. Formatting rules for pages in Markdown format, complementing this reStructuredText page. |
| ``docs-style/code-block-standards.md`` | Code Block Standards. Rules for displaying code examples and command output, including language tags. |
| ``docs-style/screenshots-and-diagrams.md`` | Screenshots and Diagrams. Guidelines for creating, sizing, and embedding visual assets in documentation. |
| ``docs-style/front-matter-schema.yaml`` | Front Matter Schema. Machine-readable definition of required metadata fields and their format constraints. |
| ``docs-style/README.md`` | docs-style Folder Overview. Index and description of all pages in the style guides folder. |


Tools, Packages, and Library Versions
--------------------------------------

This page references the following tools and utilities for documentation authoring and validation:

| Tool | Version | Purpose |
|------|---------|---------|
| reStructuredText | N/A | Markup language used for documentation pages in .rst format. |
| Markdown | N/A | Lightweight markup language used for some documentation pages in .md format. |
| Git | 2.40+ | Version control for documentation source and tracking changes over time. |
| PowerShell | 7.2+ | Command shell used for file operations and script execution on Windows systems. |
| Bash | 4.4+ | Command shell used for POSIX-based file operations and scripting on Unix-like systems. |
| sqlite3 | 3.33+ | Command-line tool for inspecting and validating database example queries in documentation. |
| rst2html | 1.0.0 | Converts reStructuredText to HTML for preview and validation before publishing. |
| nano or vi | Current | Text editors available on all systems for quick file edits during documentation work. |


Writing and Style Verification
-------------------------------
*Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*

**Paragraph length:** Paragraphs should be 3–7 sentences. Shorter paragraphs (1–2 sentences) are acceptable for emphasis or list introductions; longer paragraphs (8+ sentences) usually indicate a section should be divided into subsections.

**Sentence structure:** Aim for 15–25 words per sentence. Sentences exceeding 30 words often need rephrasing into two sentences or simplification.

**Capitalization:** Capitalize proper nouns (team names, file names, page titles as shown in headers) and the first word of sentences. Use lowercase for common nouns (page, section, owner, checklist) except at sentence start.

**Abbreviations and acronyms:** Spell out acronyms on first mention in a page. After the first mention, the acronym alone is acceptable. In a glossary entry, spell it out once; do not abbreviate it in the definition.

**Links to sibling pages:** In reStructuredText, use the format ``Page Title`_`` with a reference link at the end of the document. In Markdown, use ``[Page Title](path/to/file.md)``. Always link using the exact title from the related page's header block.

**Inline code:** Use backticks for code, command names, file names, variable names, and configuration keys: "Run the ``checkout`` command," "Edit the ``config.yaml`` file," "Set ``max_retries`` to 10."

**Emphasis:** Use italics (*like this*) for emphasis, to introduce a defined term, or to mark section owners. Use bold (**like this**) for strong directives, section headers in tables, or when introducing defined terms as headings.

**Tables:** Always include a header row. Align columns consistently. Use pipes (|) for column separators and dashes for row separators. Ensure the source is readable even in plain text.


Common Issues to Watch For
--------------------------

**Missing version information:** The most common failure is omitting tool or package versions. Every tool, library, or dependency mentioned in the page must have a version number in either the header block (for the page's own version) or a versions table (for dependencies and tools).

**Inconsistent list formatting:** If a page mixes numbered lists and bullet lists without clear reason, it signals to readers that order or structure differs unexpectedly. Use numbered lists only when sequence or priority matters. Use bullets for equal-weight items.

**Glossary gaps:** Do not assume readers know specialized terms like "checklist item," "changelog," or "front matter." If you write it more than once, define it in the glossary.

**Dangling references:** Avoid phrases like "See the page on publishing" or "Refer to the guide," which may go out of date if page titles change. Use exact page titles: "See `Docs Publishing Workflow`_." Broken links are easy to spot in a pre-review checklist.

**Stale dates:** The last-updated date must reflect actual edits. If you edited a page in September 2025, do not leave the date as August 2025. Readers rely on this date to assess the page's freshness.

**Undefined acronyms:** Spell out acronyms on first mention, even if they seem obvious. RST means reStructuredText; API means application programming interface. Do not assume readers know every acronym.

**File paths without purpose descriptions:** Every file path in a section must be accompanied by a one-line description of its function. Bare file paths confuse readers about why that file matters.

**Inconsistent section ownership:** If two sections have similar coverage and authority, both should list owners. If only some sections list owners and others do not, readers may assume unowned sections are less official or out of date.


Worked Example: Creating a New Documentation Page
--------------------------------------------------

This example walks through writing and checking a new documentation page from start to finish.

**Step 1: Create the file**

Create a new file in the ``docs-style/`` folder with a descriptive name using hyphens (not underscores or spaces):

::

  $ touch docs-style/new-page.rst

**Step 2: Add the header block**

Open the file in your text editor (nano, vi, or your preferred editor) and add the metadata block at the very top:

::

  .. title: New Documentation Page
  .. version: 1.0
  .. owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)
  .. last-updated: 2026-09-27

The version should start at 1.0 for a new page. Use today's date in the last-updated field.

**Step 3: Write the title and introduction**

Add the main title using the reStructuredText H1 format (equals signs above and below):

::

  New Documentation Page
  ======================

  Summary
  -------
  Describes how to write, structure, and validate new documentation pages in the auditlog project.

**Step 4: Add the main content sections with owners**

Write the main content sections, assigning owners to sections that are instructional or procedural:

::

  Getting Started
  ---------------
  *Owner: Docs Program (Kara Voss)*

  This section covers the initial setup steps needed before writing documentation.

  Main Workflow
  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

  [Subsections below an owner section inherit that owner unless explicitly marked otherwise.]

**Step 5: Create the glossary section**

After the main content, add a Glossary section with at least 8 terms used in your page:

::

  Glossary
  --------

  **Checklist:** A list of criteria or questions that must all pass for a task to be complete.

  **Front matter:** Structured metadata at the top of a page containing title, version, owner, and date.

  [Continue with 6 more terms, ordered alphabetically...]

**Step 6: Add Files and Paths section**

Create a table listing every file path or directory mentioned in the page:

::

  Files and Paths Referenced
  ---------------------------

  | Path | Purpose |
  |------|------|
  | ``docs-style/new-page.rst`` | This file. Contains documentation on creating new pages. |
  | ``docs-style/`` | Parent directory holding all style guides and templates. |
  | ``docs/`` | Main documentation folder containing all published pages and guides. |

**Step 7: Add tools and versions table**

List all tools and packages mentioned in the page:

::

  Tools and Versions
  ------------------

  | Tool | Version |
  |------|---------|
  | reStructuredText | N/A |
  | Git | 2.40+ |
  | rst2html | 1.0.0 |

**Step 8: Run through the pre-review checklist**

Go through each item in the Pre-Review Checklist section at the top of this page. Mark off each item with a mental note or physical check as you verify it. Do not request review until all items pass. If you cannot pass an item, fix the page or add clarification.

**Step 9: Add a changelog section**

Before requesting review, add an entry to your changelog section:

::

  Changelog
  ---------

  | Date | Version | Release | Changes |
  |------|---------|---------|---------|
  | 2026-09-27 | 1.0 | Initial Publication | Page created with full structure, nine glossary terms, and worked example section. |
  | [Earlier entries below...] |

**Step 10: Link from the related pages section**

Add a Related Pages section that links to sibling pages using exact titles:

::

  Related Pages
  ---------

  - `Page Templates`_
  - `Voice and Tone Guide`_
  - `Docs Publishing Workflow`_

**Step 11: Request peer review**

Ask a peer from another team to work through the same checklist. Do not merge or publish until the assessment is complete and all feedback is incorporated.

1	# Terminology Glossary
2	
3	**Version:** 3.1
4	**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
5	**Last updated:** 2026-05-20
6	
7	## Purpose and Coverage
8	
9	This page is the single list of shared vocabulary for anyone writing or editing internal documentation about auditlog. The package is small, but the words people use to describe it have drifted over the last two years — "the tool," "the daemon," "the local service," "the log store," and half a dozen other phrases have all shown up in drafts sent to Platform Tools for review. This page exists to stop that drift. It does not explain what auditlog does internally; it only fixes the words writers should reach for when they need to name the package, the service, the database file, and the surrounding docs tooling.
10	
11	Anyone drafting a docs-style page, a docs/ page, or a README update should check this glossary before publishing. If a term is missing, follow the upkeep procedure below rather than inventing a synonym mid-page — synonyms are exactly what this page is meant to prevent.
12	
13	## Where This Page Sits in the Docs Program
14	
15	The docs program for auditlog is made up of several small pages, each owned by a different team, that together describe how the wiki gets written, formatted, reviewed, and published. This glossary is the vocabulary layer underneath all of them:
16	
17	- The **Voice and Tone Guide** sets sentence-level style — tense, person, formality.
18	- **Page Templates** sets page-level structure — what headings a new page needs.
19	- **Markdown Conventions** and **Code Block Standards** set formatting mechanics.
20	- **Review Cadence** sets how often pages get re-checked.
21	- The **Docs Publishing Workflow** sets how a finished page moves from a draft branch to the live wiki.
22	- This page, the Terminology Glossary, sets *what things are called* across all of the above.
23	
24	A writer who is unsure whether to call something "the service" or "the HTTP service" should stop and check here rather than checking a sibling page, since none of the sibling pages define vocabulary — they assume it.
25	
26	## Naming Conventions for auditlog (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)
27	
28	The table below is the fast-reference version of the rules; the full glossary further down gives the reasoning behind each entry.
29	
30	| Concept | Preferred term | Avoid | Notes |
31	|---|---|---|---|
32	| The Python package itself | `activitylog` (lowercase, code-formatted on first use per page) | "the tool," "the utility," "ActivityLog" | Capitalize only if it starts a sentence, and even then prefer rewording the sentence. |
33	| The local HTTP service | "the service" or "the loopback service" | "the daemon," "the server," "the API" | "Daemon" implies a background process model we don't describe in docs; "API" invites writers to start documenting request shapes, which belongs elsewhere. |
34	| The SQLite file on disk | "the database file" | "the log file," "the store," "the DB" | "Log file" is ambiguous with text logs emitted by scripts; "the DB" is too casual for reference pages. |
35	| A single stored item | "a record" | "an entry," "a row," "a line" | "Entry" is reserved for glossary entries on this page; "row" implies a storage detail we don't describe. |
36	| The command-line surface | "the command line" or "the CLI" | "the console," "the shell tool" | "Console" is confusing next to PowerShell console references in setup pages. |
37	| Where the log service listens | "the local-only interface" | "the loopback point," "localhost only" | Spell out "local-only interface" once per page, then "the interface" is fine for the rest of that page. |
38	
39	Two writers on the same page should never need to negotiate which of these to use — that negotiation is what this table already settled.
40	
41	## Core Glossary (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)
42	
43	These are the terms every docs-style page should treat as fixed. Definitions are intentionally short; if a term needs more than two sentences to explain, it belongs in a page about that topic, not in this glossary.
44	
45	| Term | Definition |
46	|---|---|
47	| **auditlog** | The Python package this documentation set covers. Built on the standard library only, with a command line and a loopback HTTP service, storing its records in a local SQLite file. Always written lowercase in running text. |
48	| **the package** | Shorthand for auditlog used after the full name has appeared once on a page. Interchangeable with "auditlog" but never used before the first mention. |
49	| **the service** | The loopback HTTP service that ships with auditlog. Never called "the server" in docs-style pages, since "server" implies something reachable outside the local host. |
50	| **the database file** | The single local SQLite file where auditlog keeps its records. Always singular; auditlog does not split its storage across multiple files, so writers should not imply otherwise. |
51	| **record** | One stored item inside the database file. Plural is "records," not "entries" (entries are reserved for this glossary) and not "rows." |
52	| **the CLI** | The command-line surface of auditlog. First use on a page should spell out "command line," after which "the CLI" is fine. |
53	| **local-only interface** | The network interface the service listens on, reachable only from the same host. Replaces older phrasing like "loopback point," which several 2024-era pages still use. |
54	| **docs program** | The set of people, pages, and steps that produce and maintain auditlog's internal documentation. Capitalized as "Docs Program" only when naming the owning team, lowercase otherwise. |
55	| **docs-style folder** | The folder holding pages about how documentation itself is written — this page lives there, along with the style guide, templates, and workflow pages. |
56	| **sibling page** | Another page in the same folder as the page currently being written or edited. Used instead of "related page" inside procedural text, reserving "related pages" for the closing section of each page. |
57	| **section owner** | The named individual listed under a heading as responsible for that section's content staying current. Not every heading needs one — only sections where content could plausibly go stale on its own timetable. |
58	| **front matter** | The header block at the top of a page: title, version, owner, and last-updated date. Every docs-style page has one, following the shape set in the Front Matter Schema. |
59	| **glossary entry** | A single defined term on this page, consisting of a term and a short definition, listed in the Core Glossary table. |
60	| **worked example** | A short, concrete demonstration — usually a command or a snippet — placed inside a procedure to show what a step actually looks like rather than just describing it. |
61	
62	That is fourteen entries; the minimum for this page is eight, but in practice new terms accumulate faster than old ones get retired, so the table tends to grow every quarter.
63	
64	## Terms Under Discussion or Discouraged (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)
65	
66	Some terms show up in older pages and shouldn't be copied into new ones. This list exists so writers doing a pass over an old page know what to swap out on sight, even if that page hasn't come up for its scheduled review yet.
67	
68	- "daemon" — replace with "the service."
69	- "log store" — replace with "the database file."
70	- "API surface" — replace with "the service" when talking about it generally, or describe the specific behavior directly if the page truly needs detail (most docs-style pages should not).
71	- "utility script" for scripts/ contents — replace with "docs script" or name the script directly.
72	- "the tool" as a stand-in for auditlog — always name the package instead; "the tool" reads fine in conversation but is too vague for reference material.
73	- "loopback point" — replace with "local-only interface," per the naming table above.
74	
75	Writers are not required to fix discouraged terms in a page that isn't otherwise being touched. Fixing them opportunistically, during an unrelated edit, is fine and encouraged, but a stray "daemon" on an otherwise-stable page is not, by itself, a reason to open a change.
76	
77	## Glossary Upkeep Procedure (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)
78	
79	New terms get added to this page through a short, deliberately low-friction process, since a heavy process just means people skip it and invent a synonym instead.
80	
81	1. **Draft the term in the worksheet.** Add the candidate term and a one-line definition to `docs-style/glossary-terms.txt`. This worksheet is plain text on purpose — no formatting to fight with while you're still deciding on wording.
82	2. **Check for an existing near-match.** Search the Core Glossary and the Discouraged Terms list above for anything close. Half of proposed new terms turn out to already be covered under a slightly different name.
83	3. **Open a branch and edit this page directly.** Once the wording is settled, move the entry from the worksheet into the Core Glossary table on this page. A typical branch and commit looks like this:
84	
85	    ```
86	    git checkout -b glossary/add-local-only-interface
87	    ```
88	
89	    ```
90	    git add docs-style/terminology-glossary.md docs-style/glossary-terms.txt
91	    git commit -m "docs-style: add local-only interface term, retire loopback point (v3.1)"
92	    ```
93	
94	4. **Run the docs lint pass.** From the repository root:
95	
96	    ```
97	    markdownlint docs-style/terminology-glossary.md
98	    ```
99	
100	    This catches heading and table formatting problems before a reviewer sees them, per the rules in Markdown Conventions.
101	5. **Send the branch for review.** A second Platform Tools writer, or Mara Olsen directly for smaller teams' pages, confirms the wording matches the Voice and Tone Guide before it merges.
102	6. **Clear the worksheet entry.** Once a term lands in the Core Glossary, remove its line from `glossary-terms.txt` so the worksheet only ever shows terms still under discussion.
103	
104	Terms that get *removed* from the glossary (rare, but it happens when a concept stops being useful to name separately) follow the same numbered steps in reverse: move the entry back to the worksheet with a short note on why it's being retired, then remove it from the Core Glossary table in the same commit.
105	
106	## Fitting Into the Review Cadence (Section owner: Theo Bram, Support Enablement)
107	
108	This page does not set its own review schedule — it follows Review Cadence v1.7, which puts docs-style pages on a quarterly check unless a page's content changes for other reasons first. In practice the glossary gets touched more often than that, since new terms tend to surface whenever someone writes a page that needs a word this list doesn't yet have.
109	
110	During a scheduled review, the section owner for the Core Glossary (currently Mara Olsen) works through three checks:
111	
112	- Every term still in active use across docs-style and docs/ pages — a quick search for each preferred term catches synonyms that crept back in.
113	- Every discouraged term still absent from new pages written since the last review.
114	- The worksheet (`glossary-terms.txt`) doesn't have anything sitting in it for more than one review cycle without a resolution either way.
115	
116	If a scheduled review finds nothing to change, the section owner still updates the Last Updated date and adds a short change-log line noting "no changes, reviewed on schedule" — a page that hasn't been touched in over a year reads, to most contributors, as unmaintained even if it's still accurate.
117	
118	## Publishing Updates to the Glossary (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)
119	
120	Once a glossary change is signed off in review, it goes out through the same steps as any other docs-style page, described fully in the Docs Publishing Workflow page. The short version, as it applies here:
121	
122	1. Merge the branch into the docs main line once review is signed off.
123	2. The publish script rebuilds the wiki output into `docs/` locally:
124	
125	    ```
126	    scripts/publish-docs.sh --input docs-style --output docs
127	    ```
128	
129	3. A second script pushes the built output to the live wiki host and writes a run log:
130	
131	    ```
132	    scripts/glossary-lint.ps1 -Path docs-style/terminology-glossary.md
133	    ```

# Terminology Glossary

**Version:** 3.1
**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
**Last updated:** 2026-05-20

## Purpose and Coverage

This page is the single list of shared vocabulary for anyone writing or editing internal documentation about auditlog. The package is small, but the words people use to describe it have drifted over the last two years — "the tool," "the daemon," "the local service," "the log store," and half a dozen other phrases have all shown up in drafts sent to Platform Tools for review. This page exists to stop that drift. It does not explain what auditlog does internally; it only fixes the words writers should reach for when they need to name the package, the service, the database file, and the surrounding docs tooling.

Anyone drafting a docs-style page, a docs/ page, or a README update should check this glossary before publishing. If a term is missing, follow the upkeep procedure below rather than inventing a synonym mid-page — synonyms are exactly what this page is meant to prevent.

## Where This Page Sits in the Docs Program

The docs program for auditlog is made up of several small pages, each owned by a different team, that together describe how the wiki gets written, formatted, reviewed, and published. This glossary is the vocabulary layer underneath all of them:

- The **Voice and Tone Guide** sets sentence-level style — tense, person, formality.
- **Page Templates** sets page-level structure — what headings a new page needs.
- **Markdown Conventions** and **Code Block Standards** set formatting mechanics.
- **Review Cadence** sets how often pages get re-checked.
- The **Docs Publishing Workflow** sets how a finished page moves from a draft branch to the live wiki.
- This page, the Terminology Glossary, sets *what things are called* across all of the above.

A writer who is unsure whether to call something "the service" or "the HTTP service" should stop and check here rather than checking a sibling page, since none of the sibling pages define vocabulary — they assume it.

## Naming Conventions for auditlog (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)

The table below is the fast-reference version of the rules; the full glossary further down gives the reasoning behind each entry.

| Concept | Preferred term | Avoid | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| The Python package itself | `activitylog` (lowercase, code-formatted on first use per page) | "the tool," "the utility," "ActivityLog" | Capitalize only if it starts a sentence, and even then prefer rewording the sentence. |
| The local HTTP service | "the service" or "the loopback service" | "the daemon," "the server," "the API" | "Daemon" implies a background process model we don't describe in docs; "API" invites writers to start documenting request shapes, which belongs elsewhere. |
| The SQLite file on disk | "the database file" | "the log file," "the store," "the DB" | "Log file" is ambiguous with text logs emitted by scripts; "the DB" is too casual for reference pages. |
| A single stored item | "a record" | "an entry," "a row," "a line" | "Entry" is reserved for glossary entries on this page; "row" implies a storage detail we don't describe. |
| The command-line surface | "the command line" or "the CLI" | "the console," "the shell tool" | "Console" is confusing next to PowerShell console references in setup pages. |
| Where the log service listens | "the local-only interface" | "the loopback point," "localhost only" | Spell out "local-only interface" once per page, then "the interface" is fine for the rest of that page. |

Two writers on the same page should never need to negotiate which of these to use — that negotiation is what this table already settled.

## Core Glossary (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)

These are the terms every docs-style page should treat as fixed. Definitions are intentionally short; if a term needs more than two sentences to explain, it belongs in a page about that topic, not in this glossary.

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **auditlog** | The Python package this documentation set covers. Built on the standard library only, with a command line and a loopback HTTP service, storing its records in a local SQLite file. Always written lowercase in running text. |
| **the package** | Shorthand for auditlog used after the full name has appeared once on a page. Interchangeable with "auditlog" but never used before the first mention. |
| **the service** | The loopback HTTP service that ships with auditlog. Never called "the server" in docs-style pages, since "server" implies something reachable outside the local host. |
| **the database file** | The single local SQLite file where auditlog keeps its records. Always singular; auditlog does not split its storage across multiple files, so writers should not imply otherwise. |
| **record** | One stored item inside the database file. Plural is "records," not "entries" (entries are reserved for this glossary) and not "rows." |
| **the CLI** | The command-line surface of auditlog. First use on a page should spell out "command line," after which "the CLI" is fine. |
| **local-only interface** | The network interface the service listens on, reachable only from the same host. Replaces older phrasing like "loopback point," which several 2024-era pages still use. |
| **docs program** | The set of people, pages, and steps that produce and maintain auditlog's internal documentation. Capitalized as "Docs Program" only when naming the owning team, lowercase otherwise. |
| **docs-style folder** | The folder holding pages about how documentation itself is written — this page lives there, along with the style guide, templates, and workflow pages. |
| **sibling page** | Another page in the same folder as the page currently being written or edited. Used instead of "related page" inside procedural text, reserving "related pages" for the closing section of each page. |
| **section owner** | The named individual listed under a heading as responsible for that section's content staying current. Not every heading needs one — only sections where content could plausibly go stale on its own timetable. |
| **front matter** | The header block at the top of a page: title, version, owner, and last-updated date. Every docs-style page has one, following the shape set in the Front Matter Schema. |
| **glossary entry** | A single defined term on this page, consisting of a term and a short definition, listed in the Core Glossary table. |
| **worked example** | A short, concrete demonstration — usually a command or a snippet — placed inside a procedure to show what a step actually looks like rather than just describing it. |

That is fourteen entries; the minimum for this page is eight, but in practice new terms accumulate faster than old ones get retired, so the table tends to grow every quarter.

## Terms Under Discussion or Discouraged (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)

Some terms show up in older pages and shouldn't be copied into new ones. This list exists so writers doing a pass over an old page know what to swap out on sight, even if that page hasn't come up for its scheduled review yet.

- "daemon" — replace with "the service."
- "log store" — replace with "the database file."
- "API surface" — replace with "the service" when talking about it generally, or describe the specific behavior directly if the page truly needs detail (most docs-style pages should not).
- "utility script" for scripts/ contents — replace with "docs script" or name the script directly.
- "the tool" as a stand-in for auditlog — always name the package instead; "the tool" reads fine in conversation but is too vague for reference material.
- "loopback point" — replace with "local-only interface," per the naming table above.

Writers are not required to fix discouraged terms in a page that isn't otherwise being touched. Fixing them opportunistically, during an unrelated edit, is fine and encouraged, but a stray "daemon" on an otherwise-stable page is not, by itself, a reason to open a change.

## Glossary Upkeep Procedure (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)

New terms get added to this page through a short, deliberately low-friction process, since a heavy process just means people skip it and invent a synonym instead.

1. **Draft the term in the worksheet.** Add the candidate term and a one-line definition to `docs-style/glossary-terms.txt`. This worksheet is plain text on purpose — no formatting to fight with while you're still deciding on wording.
2. **Check for an existing near-match.** Search the Core Glossary and the Discouraged Terms list above for anything close. Half of proposed new terms turn out to already be covered under a slightly different name.
3. **Open a branch and edit this page directly.** Once the wording is settled, move the entry from the worksheet into the Core Glossary table on this page. A typical branch and commit looks like this:

    ```
    git checkout -b glossary/add-local-only-interface
    ```

    ```
    git add docs-style/terminology-glossary.md docs-style/glossary-terms.txt
    git commit -m "docs-style: add local-only interface term, retire loopback point (v3.1)"
    ```

4. **Run the docs lint pass.** From the repository root:

    ```
    markdownlint docs-style/terminology-glossary.md
    ```

    This catches heading and table formatting problems before a reviewer sees them, per the rules in Markdown Conventions.
5. **Send the branch for review.** A second Platform Tools writer, or Mara Olsen directly for smaller teams' pages, confirms the wording matches the Voice and Tone Guide before it merges.
6. **Clear the worksheet entry.** Once a term lands in the Core Glossary, remove its line from `glossary-terms.txt` so the worksheet only ever shows terms still under discussion.

Terms that get *removed* from the glossary (rare, but it happens when a concept stops being useful to name separately) follow the same numbered steps in reverse: move the entry back to the worksheet with a short note on why it's being retired, then remove it from the Core Glossary table in the same commit.

## Fitting Into the Review Cadence (Section owner: Theo Bram, Support Enablement)

This page does not set its own review schedule — it follows Review Cadence v1.7, which puts docs-style pages on a quarterly check unless a page's content changes for other reasons first. In practice the glossary gets touched more often than that, since new terms tend to surface whenever someone writes a page that needs a word this list doesn't yet have.

During a scheduled review, the section owner for the Core Glossary (currently Mara Olsen) works through three checks:

- Every term still in active use across docs-style and docs/ pages — a quick search for each preferred term catches synonyms that crept back in.
- Every discouraged term still absent from new pages written since the last review.
- The worksheet (`glossary-terms.txt`) doesn't have anything sitting in it for more than one review cycle without a resolution either way.

If a scheduled review finds nothing to change, the section owner still updates the Last Updated date and adds a short change-log line noting "no changes, reviewed on schedule" — a page that hasn't been touched in over a year reads, to most contributors, as unmaintained even if it's still accurate.

## Publishing Updates to the Glossary (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)

Once a glossary change is signed off in review, it goes out through the same steps as any other docs-style page, described fully in the Docs Publishing Workflow page. The short version, as it applies here:

1. Merge the branch into the docs main line once review is signed off.
2. The publish script rebuilds the wiki output into `docs/` locally:

    ```
    scripts/publish-docs.sh --input docs-style --output docs
    ```

3. A second script pushes the built output to the live wiki host and writes a run log:

    ```
    scripts/glossary-lint.ps1 -Path docs-style/terminology-glossary.md
    ```

4. The publish run appends a line to the log folder at `C:\ProgramData\auditlog-docs\publish-logs\`, which Platform Tools checks weekly for failed runs rather than per publish.

Glossary changes are never published outside this flow, even for a single-word fix — a term that's wrong in the live wiki but right in a merged branch is confusing in exactly the way this page exists to prevent.

## Style and Formatting Notes (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)

The Core Glossary table follows the general table formatting rules in Markdown Conventions — left-aligned columns, no trailing punctuation in table cells, term column bolded. Code-formatted terms (like `auditlog` itself) follow Code Block Standards for inline code, not the fenced-block rules, since a single package name doesn't need its own block.

New entries should be written in the same voice as the rest of the docs set: second person avoided, present tense, no marketing language. A definition that reads "auditlog is a powerful package for..." should be rewritten before it reaches the Core Glossary table; "powerful" and similar words belong nowhere in reference material. See the Voice and Tone Guide for the full reasoning.

When a new docs-style page is created and needs its own short glossary section (some pages do, for terms that are specific to that page's content and don't belong here), follow the section shape set in Page Templates so the two don't drift apart in structure — same table columns, same heading depth.

## Referenced Files and Paths
