file.content:
title: Baseline Measurements
version: "1.0"
owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
last_updated: 2024-05-30
summary: >
  Holds baseline timing and memory numbers used for comparison in later
  profiling sessions. This page is the numbers page, not the procedure
  page — for how a session is run, see Profiling Session Log. The figures
  below were captured on the reference workstation described in the
  Measurement Environment section and are re-checked roughly once per
  quarter, though in practice the gap has sometimes run longer.

sections:

  - heading: Overview
    owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools
    content: |
      This page exists so that nobody has to re-derive "is 40ms fast or
      slow for a small read on loopback" from scratch every time someone
      opens a profiling session. auditlog is a small standard-library-only
      package with a command line and a loopback HTTP service that keeps
      its records in a local SQLite file, so its performance story is
      mostly about three things: how the database file is opened and
      configured, how quickly the process comes up, and how quickly a
      request handled on the loopback interface comes back. Those three
      areas map onto the three number tables further down this page.

      The numbers here are a starting point for comparison, not a promise.
      When someone changes the SQLite settings, touches how the service
      starts, or just wants to know whether a change to the on-disk
      layout made things worse, they diff their new numbers against this
      page. If a session shows a meaningful move away from baseline, the
      finding gets written up on Profiling Session Log and, if the new
      number sticks around after a second measurement, this page gets
      updated to reflect it.

      Ownership of this page sits with Platform Tools, but most of the
      individual numbers were captured or last confirmed by whoever owns
      the more detailed sibling page for that topic — SQLite settings by
      Data Infra, response times and startup by Core Services and
      Developer Experience respectively, memory by Systems Reliability.
      Where this page and a sibling page disagree on a number, treat the
      sibling page as more current; this page tends to lag by a session
      or two.

  - heading: Measurement Environment and Method
    owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools
    content: |
      All baseline numbers on this page were captured on the same
      reference machine unless a row says otherwise: a Dell workstation
      with a six-core desktop-class CPU, 32 GB of RAM, and an NVMe drive,
      running Windows 10 Pro (build 19045) with WSL2 available for the
      Unix-side tooling. Python was CPython 3.11.4 from the standard
      python.org build; the bundled SQLite in that build is 3.42.0. No
      virtual environment tooling beyond the standard library's own
      venv module was involved, since the package has no third-party
      run-time dependencies.

      The general method for a baseline pass is:

      1. Reboot or otherwise clear background load on the reference
         machine — browsers closed, indexing paused, no other loopback
         services listening nearby.
      2. Start the service fresh and let it sit idle for about ten
         seconds before the first measurement, so that any one-time
         setup cost on the very first request doesn't get folded into
         a "steady state" number.
      3. Run each measurement scenario multiple times (at least seven
         timed runs per row in the tables below) and record the median,
         not the mean, since loopback timings have a long right tail
         from occasional OS scheduling noise.
      4. Record process memory with an external sampler rather than
         anything inside the process itself, so the measurement doesn't
         change the thing being measured.
      5. Write the raw numbers to a dated file under
         docs/performance-notes/raw/ (not tracked in this page directly)
         and roll the summary into the tables here.

      Timing was collected with a mix of PowerShell's Measure-Command
      on the Windows side and the shell's own time facility under WSL,
      cross-checked against hyperfine for anything where the noise floor
      mattered. Memory was sampled with psutil rather than parsing raw
      OS process listings, mostly for consistency across the two
      platforms the team runs on day to day.

      One caveat worth repeating here rather than only in the sibling
      pages: none of these numbers should be read as a promise about any
      particular caller's machine. They are useful for spotting that
      something moved, not for predicting what a given laptop will see.

  - heading: Profiling Sessions Summary
    owner: Priya Nair, Systems Reliability
    content: |
      The full record of individual profiling sessions lives on
      Profiling Session Log; this section is a short summary of the
      sessions that fed into the current baseline numbers, kept here so
      that a reader doesn't have to open a second page just to see which
      session a given row came from.

      Sessions are run with a sampling-based profiler layered over the
      loopback timing harness described above. The current preferred
      tool is py-spy in its sampling mode, which avoids the per-call
      overhead of a tracing profiler and gets close enough to the real
      timing for the kind of comparisons this page cares about. Flame
      output from these runs is kept separately (see Flamegraph
      Captures) rather than embedded here.

      | Session | Date | Focus | Headline Finding |
      |---|---|---|---|
      | BL-2023-11 | 2023-11-02 | Initial baseline, cold environment | First full set of numbers for the reference machine |
      | BL-2024-02 | 2024-02-14 | SQLite settings sweep | wal journal mode confirmed faster than the rollback-journal default for grouped writes |
      | BL-2024-05 | 2024-05-28 | Loopback response and memory re-check | Numbers held steady within noise of BL-2024-02 |
      | BL-2024-09 | 2024-09-19 | Startup time, cold vs warm | Warm start roughly three times faster than cold |
      | BL-2025-03 | 2025-03-10 | Page cache size sweep | Diminishing returns past roughly 4 MB of cache for this data size |
      | BL-2025-11 | 2025-11-01 | Concurrency-adjacent memory check | No meaningful growth in RSS under repeated grouped writes |

      Session BL-2024-05 is the one whose numbers make up most of this
      page's current tables, since it was the last full sweep across all
      three areas on the same machine on the same day. Later sessions
      updated individual sections without redoing the whole set, which is
      part of why the "last updated" date on this page (2024-05-30) is
      older than the last-updated dates on some of the sibling pages that
      cover a single topic in more depth.

  - heading: SQLite Settings Baseline
    owner: Lena Kowalski, Data Infra
    content: |
      The database file's settings have the single largest effect on
      write-side timing of anything the team has measured, which is why
      this section gets its own table rather than being folded into the
      response-time numbers further down.

      Baseline settings, as confirmed in session BL-2024-02 and rechecked
      in BL-2025-03, are:

      | Setting | Baseline Value | Standard-library Default | Note |
      |---|---|---|---|
      | journal mode | wal | rollback-journal | wal keeps grouped writes off the critical path for concurrent readers |
      | synchronous | normal | full | normal is safe under wal mode without the full fsync cost on every write |
      | page cache size | -4000 (roughly 4 MB) | -2000 (roughly 2 MB) | doubling past this point showed under 3% further gain in BL-2025-03 |
      | temp_store | memory | file | keeps temporary sort structures off the disk for small result sets |
      | busy timeout | 5000 ms | 0 ms | gives a second attempt time before a locked-file error surfaces |
      | mmap size | 0 (disabled) | 0 (disabled) | left off by default; direct virtual-memory access to the file showed no measurable gain at this data size and was not carried into the baseline |

      A note on cache size units, since it trips people up during a
      session: a negative number to this setting is interpreted in
      kibibytes rather than pages, so -4000 means roughly 4000 KiB of
      cache rather than 4000 pages. The page-cache-sizing sibling page
      (currently at version 2.0 last we checked, owner Data Infra) has
      the fuller sweep across cache sizes from 1 MB up to 64 MB; the
      short version is that returns flatten out well before 64 MB for
      the data volumes seen in normal operation on a single workstation.

      To confirm current settings against this baseline on a given
      machine, open the database file with the sqlite3 command-line tool
      and check the settings directly rather than trusting a reader's
      memory of them:

      .open path\to\auditlog.db
      .mode column
      .headers on

      Values are checked interactively from there rather than scripted,
      since this is a one-off confirmation step rather than something
      that runs as part of a normal session.

      One thing worth flagging here that the sqlite-journal-mode sibling
      page covers in more depth: switching journal mode from rollback-journal to
      wal is a one-time, on-disk change to the database file itself, not
      a per-connection setting, so it only needs to be done once per file
      rather than once per process start. Reapplying it on every start
      costs nothing extra, but it also does nothing extra.

  - heading: Loopback Response Times
    owner: Devon Ruiz, Core Services
    content: |
      All response-time numbers on this page are for the service
      listening on the loopback interface (127.0.0.1), reached from the
      same machine — there is no network hop, no proxying, and no other
      process load in between. Cross-machine numbers are out of coverage
      for this page and for the sibling Loopback Response Time
      Measurements page as well.

      Timing was collected by issuing a fixed number of requests against
      a running instance and recording wall-clock time per call, using
      the shell-based timing harness kept at
      scripts/loopback_timing.sh (see the Files section below). The
      script does not invoke the package's command line itself; it
      assumes an already-running instance and only issues requests
      against it, timing each one.

      | Scenario | Median | 95th Percentile | Notes |
      |---|---|---|---|
      | Single small write | 3.8 ms | 6.1 ms | one record, no grouped write |
      | Grouped write, 50 records | 14.2 ms | 21.7 ms | single call carrying multiple records |
      | Small range read (10 rows) | 2.1 ms | 3.4 ms | |
      | Medium range read (100 rows) | 5.9 ms | 9.0 ms | |
      | Large range read (1,000 rows) | 41.3 ms | 58.6 ms | dominated by serialization, not the database file |
      | Idle listing call | 1.4 ms | 2.2 ms | smallest call the service handles |

      These numbers are from session BL-2024-05 and have not moved by
      more than noise in the two re-checks since. The large range read
      row is the one to watch after any change to how results are put
      together for a response, since it is the most sensitive to
      per-row overhead — a regression there tends to show up as a
      near-linear increase with row count rather than a flat shift.

      Worth calling out because it surprises new readers: the single
      small write is slower per call than the small range read, even
      though it touches less data, because the write path holds the
      database file's write lock briefly and waits on the durability
      settings described in the SQLite Settings Baseline section above.
      Under the rollback-journal default this gap is much larger;
      under wal mode it narrows to what the table above shows.

  - heading: Memory Use
    owner: Priya Nair, Systems Reliability
    content: |
      Memory figures are resident set size (RSS) for the service
      process, sampled externally with psutil once per second over the
      course of a measurement run, rather than anything self-reported by
      the process.

      | State | RSS | Notes |
      |---|---|---|
      | Immediately after start, idle | 14.6 MB | before the first request |
      | After 1,000 small writes | 15.9 MB | writes issued one at a time |
      | After a single grouped write of 5,000 records | 22.4 MB | temporary growth during serialization of the input |
      | Back to idle, 30s after the grouped write | 16.1 MB | growth from the grouped write mostly comes back down |
      | After a 10,000-row range read | 19.8 MB | growth scales with result size, not with request count |
      | Sustained idle, 10 minutes | 16.0 MB | steady; no continued climb observed |

      The gap between "immediately after start" (14.6 MB) and "sustained
      idle" (16.0 MB) is expected and comes from the standard library's
      own lazy imports settling in during the first few requests rather
      than anything specific to the package. What matters more for
      day-to-day monitoring is the last row: RSS at idle after a mixed
      run of writes and reads should come back down close to where it
      started, within a couple of megabytes. A run that does not come
      back down — that keeps climbing across repeated idle checks — is
      the pattern to flag for a closer look, and session BL-2025-11 was
      specifically run to confirm that this pattern is not present under
      current code.

      Peak RSS during the largest measurement scenario used for this
      page (the 10,000-row range read) topped out at 28.1 MB during the
      read itself before settling to the 19.8 MB shown above. That peak
      number is closer to what a caller doing occasional large reads
      should budget for than the steady-state figures are.

  - heading: Startup Time
    owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience
    content: |
      Startup time here means wall-clock time from process launch to the
      service accepting its first request on the loopback interface,
      measured with PowerShell's Measure-Command on Windows and with the
      shell's time facility under WSL, cross-checked against each other
      for the reference machine.

      | Condition | Median | Notes |
      |---|---|---|
      | Cold start, existing database file | 210 ms | file already present on disk, OS file cache cold |
      | Cold start, new database file | 268 ms | includes on-disk setup of a fresh file |
      | Warm start, existing database file | 74 ms | OS file cache warm from a prior run |
      | Warm start, repeated in a loop | 61 ms | lower bound observed across ten consecutive starts |

      The gap between cold and new-file starts (roughly 58 ms) is mostly
      the cost of the on-disk work SQLite does when a database file is
      created rather than opened, plus the one-time cost of applying the
      journal mode setting described earlier on this page, which only
      needs to happen once per file rather than once per start. Since
      most real starts are against an existing file, the "cold start,
      existing database file" row is the one to treat as the baseline
      startup number for comparison purposes.

      A fuller breakdown, including the difference between a cold OS
      file cache and a warm one independent of the process's own start
      cost, lives on the Cold Start Versus Warm Start sibling page. That
      page's numbers run slightly higher than the ones above (cold start
      there is listed around 240 ms rather than 210 ms), which comes
      down to a different reference machine used for that page's most
      recent pass rather than any real change in the package.

  - heading: Known Variance and Caveats
    owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools
    content: |
      A few things worth keeping in mind before treating any single
      number on this page as gospel:

      - Numbers move with background load on the measurement machine far
        more than with small code changes. A quiet machine and a busy
        one can differ by 15 to 20 percent on the smaller timing rows
        even with nothing else changed.
      - The reference machine changed once, between the BL-2023-11 and
        BL-2024-02 sessions, when the original laptop used for early
        measurements was replaced with the current Dell workstation.
        Numbers from before that swap are not directly comparable and
        are not shown on this page.
      - Windows and WSL timing tools do not always agree to the
        millisecond; where they disagreed by more than roughly 10
        percent during a session, the WSL number was preferred for
        consistency with the Unix-side tooling used on most of the
        team's other machines.
      - SQLite settings persist in the database file itself, so a
        measurement run against a database file left over from a prior
        session with different settings will produce numbers that don't
        match this page until the settings are confirmed and, if needed,
        reapplied.
      - None of the timing here accounts for concurrent callers hitting
        the loopback interface at once; that is covered separately, see
        Concurrency Notes.

  - heading: Terminology
    owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools
    content: |
      Terms used across this page and the sibling pages in this folder,
      collected here since not every sibling page repeats them.

      - Baseline — the set of reference numbers on this page, used as
        the comparison point for later measurement sessions.
      - Loopback interface — the local network interface (127.0.0.1)
        the service listens on when reached from the same machine, with
        no external network hop involved.
      - Journal mode — the SQLite setting that controls how the database
        file records in-progress changes before they are made durable;
        this page's baseline uses wal mode.
      - WAL — Write-Ahead Log, the journal mode under which changes are
        first written to a separate file and later folded back into the
        main database file.
      - WAL merge — the process by which entries in the WAL file are
        folded back into the main database file; this is distinct from
        the write itself and happens on its own timing.
      - Page cache size — the amount of memory SQLite reserves for
        holding recently used pages of the database file, set as either
        a page count or, with a negative value, an amount of memory.
      - RSS — resident set size, the portion of a process's memory that
        is currently held in physical RAM, as opposed to memory that has
        been reserved but not yet touched.
      - Cold start — starting the service when neither the OS file cache
        nor any part of the process has been warmed by a prior run.
      - Warm start — starting the service again shortly after a prior
        run, so that the OS file cache for the database file is already
        populated.
      - Grouped write — a single call to the service that carries more
        than one record to be written in one pass, as distinct from
        repeated single-record writes.
      - Sampling profiler — a profiling tool, such as py-spy, that
        periodically records where a running process is rather than
        tracing every call, which keeps its own overhead low enough to
        use for timing-sensitive measurement.
      - Median vs mean — this page reports medians for timing rows
        because loopback timing has a long right tail; a mean would be
        pulled upward by occasional slow outliers that are not
        representative of normal operation.

  - heading: Files Referenced
    owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools
    content: |
      Paths below are relative to the repository root unless noted.

      - auditlog/ — the package directory itself; no files inside it are
        described on this page beyond what is needed for measurement
        context.
      - docs/performance-notes/README.md — index page for this folder,
        with short summaries and links to every sibling page.
      - docs/performance-notes/baseline-measurements.yaml — this page.
      - docs/performance-notes/profiling-sessions.md — the fuller record
        of individual profiling sessions summarized in this page.
      - docs/performance-notes/sqlite-journal-mode.md — detail on the
        journal mode setting and the reasoning behind the wal baseline.
      - docs/performance-notes/page-cache-sizing.md — the fuller sweep
        across page cache sizes referenced in the SQLite Settings
        Baseline section.
      - docs/performance-notes/loopback-response-times.md — the fuller
        set of response-time scenarios and their timing method.
      - docs/performance-notes/memory-use-notes.md — detail on memory
        sampling method and additional scenarios not repeated here.
      - docs/performance-notes/startup-time.md — the fuller startup
        timing breakdown, including additional conditions not shown on
        this page.
      - docs/performance-notes/cold-start-vs-warm-start.md — a closer
        look at OS file-cache state as a separate variable from process
        start cost.
      - docs/performance-notes/write-throughput.md — write-side timing
        under sustained, repeated writes rather than the single-call
        scenarios shown on this page.
      - docs/performance-notes/concurrency-notes.rst — timing under
        multiple callers reaching the loopback interface at once.
      - docs/performance-notes/profiling-tools.rst — the list of
        profiling tools kept current and how each one is normally used.
      - docs/performance-notes/process-memory-tracking.txt — the method
        for external memory sampling referenced in the Memory Use
        section.
      - docs/performance-notes/flamegraph-captures.txt — where flame
        output from profiling sessions is stored and how it is named.
      - docs/performance-notes/raw/ — dated raw output from individual
        measurement runs; not tracked page by page, referenced by
        session ID in the Profiling Sessions Summary table above.
      - scripts/loopback_timing.sh — the shell harness used to issue
        timed requests against an already-running instance for the
        Loopback Response Times section.

content.content:
1	# Cold Start Versus Warm Start
2	
3	**Version:** 1.3
4	**Owner:** Developer Experience (Owen Fischer)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-07-22
6	
7	## Overview
8	
9	This page contrasts what happens the first time the loopback service is brought up against a database file that has never been touched — a **cold start** — with what happens on later runs against a database file that the operating system and SQLite have already warmed — a **warm start**. The numbers here come from a mix of manual timing runs, a couple of longer profiling sessions logged in `docs/performance-notes/profiling-sessions.md`, and some ad hoc poking with `time` and `curl` on a loopback interface during the week of 2025-07-14.
10	
11	The short version: on the machines we run this on, a cold start against an empty database file costs somewhere around four to five times what a warm start costs, most of that gap coming from three places — interpreter and import overhead, opening the database file and setting its journal mode, and the operating system pulling pages of the database file off disk instead of serving them from its own file cache. None of that is unique to this package; it's the usual shape of cold-versus-warm behavior for anything backed by SQLite. What's specific to auditlog is how small the whole thing is, which makes the relative size of "cold start tax" much more visible than it would be in a larger service.
12	
13	This page brings together the individual measurements from the sibling pages on journal mode, page cache size, loopback response times, memory use, and startup time, arranging them side by side under two conditions — cold and warm — so the contrast is easy to see in one sitting.
14	
15	## Terminology
16	
17	- **Cold start** — the first run of the service against a database file that either does not yet exist or has not been touched recently enough for its pages to still be in the operating system's file cache.
18	- **Warm start** — a run of the service where the database file's pages are already present in the operating system's file cache, typically because the file was used moments earlier in the same session or by another process on the same host.
19	- **Journal mode** — the SQLite setting that controls how changes are recorded before they land in the main database file; the two modes referenced most in this doc are the default rollback journal and WAL (write-ahead log).
20	- **WAL (write-ahead log)** — a separate file next to the database file that SQLite writes changes into first; the WAL file's contents are folded back into the main database file periodically rather than being written straight into it on every change.
21	- **Page cache size** — a SQLite pragma (`cache_size`) that controls how many pages of the database file SQLite is willing to keep in its own in-memory area, separate from whatever the operating system is caching.
22	- **Page size** — the fixed size, in bytes, that SQLite reads and writes the database file in; ours is set to the SQLite default of 4096 bytes unless a page notes otherwise.
23	- **Resident set size (RSS)** — the amount of physical memory a running process is currently holding, as reported by tools like `ps` or `psutil`; used throughout this page as the memory number of record.
24	- **Loopback interface** — the local network path (127.0.0.1) the HTTP service listens on; used here rather than any external network path.
25	- **Warm-up requests** — the first handful of calls made against a freshly started service, before response times settle into a steady number.
26	- **Startup time** — the interval from when the process is launched to when it is first ready to answer a call on the loopback interface.
27	- **Flame graph** — a visual representation of where time is spent across a call stack during a profiling run, produced from `py-spy` captures in our case; see `docs/performance-notes/flamegraph-captures.txt`.
28	
29	## Measurement Environment
30	
31	*Section owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience*
32	
33	All numbers on this page were collected on the same reference machine unless a table says otherwise:
34	
35	- Machine: a spare development laptop set aside for performance work (internally called `perf-bench-02`), not the shared build host.
36	- Operating system: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, kernel 5.15.
37	- Python: 3.11.6, installed via `pyenv`, no other interpreters on the path during measurement.
38	- Disk: NVMe SSD, not spinning media — cold-start numbers would look considerably worse on the older `perf-bench-01` machine, which still has a SATA drive.
39	- The database file lives at `./var/auditlog.db` relative to the checkout, on a filesystem that is not tmpfs, so cold reads genuinely hit disk (or at least the drive's own cache) rather than being served from RAM the whole way through.
40	
41	Before every cold-start run, the reference machine's page cache for that file was dropped so the operating system had nothing cached:
42	
43	```
44	sync
45	echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches
46	```
47	
48	This step matters more than people expect. Skipping it and just removing the database file is not enough to get a genuine cold start if the file was used minutes earlier — the operating system will often still be holding the old file's pages, and even though the file itself is gone, the process launch and import path will look artificially warm because of unrelated pages still resident from the previous run.
49	
50	## Cold Start Procedure
51	
52	*Section owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience*
53	
54	To get a clean cold-start measurement, follow this order:
55	
56	1. Stop any running instance of the service.
57	2. Remove the existing database file and its WAL file, if present, at the paths configured for that run (typically `./var/auditlog.db` and `./var/auditlog.db-wal`).
58	3. Drop the operating system's page cache as shown above (this step is easy to forget and skews results toward "warm" if skipped).
59	4. Start the service fresh, timing from process launch.
60	5. Make a single call against the loopback interface and record the time from launch to first response.
61	6. Continue making calls at a steady pace (roughly one per second works fine) for the next thirty seconds and record each response time, so the "settling" curve can be plotted alongside the very first number.
62	
63	A shell wrapper we keep around for this is `scripts/cold-start-timing.sh`:
64	
65	```
66	#!/usr/bin/env bash
67	set -e
68	rm -f ./var/auditlog.db ./var/auditlog.db-wal
69	sync
70	echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches
71	start=$(date +%s.%N)
72	./auditlog/service_launcher &
73	pid=$!
74	until curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8791/status; do sleep 0.005; done
75	end=$(date +%s.%N)
76	echo "launch to first response: $(echo "$end - $start" | bc) s"
77	```
78	
79	Note that this script has drifted slightly out of date — it still names the loopback port as 8791, which is the port used before the port move documented in `docs/performance-notes/loopback-response-times.md`; the actual default for recent builds is 8792. Adjust before running.
80	
81	## Warm Start Procedure
82	
83	*Section owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience*
84	
85	Warm-start measurement is simpler because there is less to reset:
86	
87	1. Start the service once against an existing database file and make a handful of calls to make sure both the operating system's file cache and SQLite's own page cache are populated.
88	2. Stop the service (but do **not** remove the database file or drop the OS page cache).
89	3. Start the service again, timing from process launch as before.
90	4. Make the same single call and record the time.
91	5. Continue making calls for the following thirty seconds as with the cold-start run.
92	
93	The companion script is `scripts/warm-start-timing.sh`, which is identical to the cold-start script minus the `rm` and `drop_caches` lines. Keeping the two scripts nearly line-for-line the same, aside from those two steps, has made it much easier to trust that differences in the resulting numbers reflect the cold-versus-warm condition and not some accidental difference in how the process was launched.
94	
95	## SQLite Settings and Their Effect on Startup
96	
97	*Section owner: Lena Kowalski, Data Infra (cross-posted from `docs/performance-notes/sqlite-journal-mode.md`)*
98	
99	Two SQLite settings show up repeatedly in cold-versus-warm timing differences: journal mode and page cache size.
100	
101	**Journal mode.** With the rollback journal (SQLite's default), the very first write to a freshly created database file has to create the journal file from scratch, which adds a handful of extra filesystem operations that are only paid once. With WAL mode, the first write instead has to create the WAL file, and on a cold start that file-creation cost lands on the operating system's disk path rather than being served from cache — one of the bigger single contributors to the gap between cold and warm numbers we've measured. On a warm start, by contrast, the WAL file from the previous run may already exist and be mapped in, so this cost mostly disappears.
102	
103	To confirm which journal mode a given database file is using:
104	
105	```
106	sqlite3 ./var/auditlog.db "PRAGMA journal_mode;"
107	```
108	
109	To set WAL mode explicitly (this only needs to be done once per database file, since the setting is stored in the file itself):
110	
111	```
112	sqlite3 ./var/auditlog.db "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;"
113	```
114	
115	**Page cache size.** The `cache_size` pragma controls how many pages SQLite keeps in its own memory area, separate from whatever the operating system is caching. The default is a modest -2000, meaning roughly 2 MB given our 4096-byte page size. Recent internal builds set this higher:
116	
117	```
118	sqlite3 ./var/auditlog.db "PRAGMA cache_size=-8000;"
119	```
120	
121	That gives SQLite roughly 8 MB of page cache. On a warm start, a larger page cache size makes almost no visible difference, because the pages are already sitting in the operating system's own cache and the round trip to fetch them from there is already quick. On a cold start, though, a larger `cache_size` means more of the database file's pages get pulled in and kept once they're read, so a series of early calls settles into its steady response time slightly sooner than it would with the smaller default. The gain is real but modest — on the order of a few milliseconds per call during the warm-up window, not something that changes the overall shape of the cold-start curve.
122	
123	| Setting | Default | Tuned value used here | Cold-start effect | Warm-start effect |
124	|---|---|---|---|---|
125	| Journal mode | rollback journal | WAL | WAL adds one-time file creation cost | negligible, file usually already present |
126	| Page cache size | -2000 (~2 MB) | -8000 (~8 MB) | shortens the warm-up window slightly | almost no visible change |
127	| Page size | 4096 bytes | 4096 bytes (unchanged) | n/a | n/a |
128	| Synchronous mode | FULL | NORMAL (with WAL) | slightly fewer disk flushes on first writes | no measurable change |
129	
130	See `docs/performance-notes/sqlite-journal-mode.md` for the full reasoning on why WAL was chosen over the rollback journal, and `docs/performance-notes/page-cache-sizing.md` (v2.0) for how the -8000 figure was arrived at.
131	
132	## Loopback Response Time Comparison
133	
134	*Section owner: Devon Ruiz, Core Services*
135	
136	The table below shows response times for the first call and for calls after the response time has settled, under both conditions, on the reference machine described above.
137	
138	| Condition | First call | Call #5 | Call #10 | Steady state (call #20+) |
139	|---|---|---|---|---|
140	| Cold start | 214 ms | 96 ms | 61 ms | 47 ms |
141	| Warm start | 52 ms | 41 ms | 39 ms | 38 ms |
142	
143	A few things stand out:
144	
145	* The cold-start first call is more than four times the warm-start first call, but by the tenth call the gap has narrowed considerably.
146	* Warm-start response times are close to flat from the very first call, which matches the expectation that most of the cost being avoided is disk-related rather than anything the process itself does differently between calls.
147	* Steady-state numbers converge but never fully meet — cold-start steady state settles a few milliseconds above warm-start steady state even after twenty calls, likely reflecting SQLite's own page cache still filling in during that window rather than the operating system's cache, which fills in almost immediately.
148	
149	These numbers were collected with `curl -w "%{time_total}\n" -o /dev/null -s http://127.0.0.1:8792/status`, run in a loop with a short sleep between calls so as not to overlap requests. For a wider set of response-time measurements across different call shapes and sizes, see `docs/performance-notes/loopback-response-times.md`.
150	
151	## Memory Use Comparison
152	
153	*Section owner: Priya Nair, Systems Reliability*
154	
155	Memory use tells a somewhat different story than response time — the cold-versus-warm gap is much smaller here, because most of the memory a Python process holds comes from the interpreter and imported modules rather than from anything specific to the database file being warm or cold.
156	
157	| Condition | RSS at process start | RSS after 100 calls | RSS after 500 calls |
158	|---|---|---|---|
159	| Cold start | 14.6 MB | 17.9 MB | 22.4 MB |
160	| Warm start | 14.4 MB | 16.1 MB | 19.8 MB |
161	
162	RSS was captured with `psutil.Process().memory_info().rss` sampled from a small side script (not part of the package itself), and cross-checked against `ps -o rss= -p <pid>` to make sure the two agreed.
163	
164	The growth from 100 to 500 calls in both conditions is expected and comes from SQLite's own page cache filling up to its configured -8000 limit, plus some ordinary allocator behavior in the Python process that does not shrink back down between calls. It is not unbounded growth — RSS was observed to plateau by around call #600 in both conditions during a longer run captured in `docs/performance-notes/process-memory-tracking.txt` — but the plateau under a cold start sits a couple of megabytes above the plateau under a warm start, likely because the cold-start run ends up touching more distinct pages of the database file earlier in its life as SQLite's page cache fills from an empty state. As Owen Fischer noted in `docs/performance-notes/memory-use-notes.md`, this gap has been stable across several profiling sessions and does not seem to depend much on which journal mode is in use.
165	
166	## Startup Time Breakdown
167	
168	*Section owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience*
169	
170	Breaking startup time down into phases makes it clearer where the cold-versus-warm gap actually lives.
171	
172	| Phase | Cold start | Warm start |
173	|---|---|---|
174	| Interpreter startup (process launch to first line of the package's own code) | 27 ms | 26 ms |
175	| Standard library and package imports | 41 ms | 13 ms |
176	| Opening the database file and applying pragmas | 88 ms | 5 ms |
177	| First response returned on the loopback interface | 58 ms | 8 ms |
178	| **Total, launch to first response** | **214 ms** | **52 ms** |
179	
180	Interpreter startup itself is essentially unaffected by cold versus warm — that cost is paid by the interpreter loading its own standard set of modules and has nothing to do with our database file. The two phases that move are imports and opening the database file, both of which depend heavily on whether their underlying files are already in the operating system's cache. Import time moves because the package's own modules and the small number of standard-library modules it pulls in (mainly `sqlite3`, `http.server`, and `json`) have to be read from disk on a genuinely cold machine; on a warm start those `.pyc` files are already cached.
181	
182	Opening the database file is where the largest single gap sits, at roughly 83 ms of difference. That phase includes creating the WAL file if journal mode is set to WAL and the file doesn't already have one, applying the `cache_size` pragma, and doing an initial read to confirm the file is well formed. All of that work touches disk directly on a cold start and touches the operating system's own cache almost exclusively on a warm one. 183	
184	## Worked Example: A Full Timing Run
185	
186	*Section owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience*
187	
188	This walks through an actual run captured on 2025-07-16, included here so the shape of a full session is visible in one place rather than scattered across tables.
189	
190	1. Machine prepared per the Measurement Environment section above; page cache dropped; old database file removed.
191	2. `scripts/cold-start-timing.sh` run (with the port corrected to 8792). Output:
192	   ```
193	   launch to first response: 0.211 s
194	   ```
195	3. Fifteen further calls made at roughly one-second intervals. Response times, in milliseconds: 211, 118, 84, 71, 64, 59, 55, 52, 50, 49, 48, 47, 47, 46, 47.
196	4. Process stopped. Database file left in place. No cache drop performed.
197	5. `scripts/warm-start-timing.sh` run. Output:
198	   ```
199	   launch to first response: 0.054 s
200	   ```
201	6. Fifteen further calls, same interval. Response times, in milliseconds: 54, 44, 41, 40, 39, 39, 38, 38, 38, 38, 37, 38, 38, 37, 38.
202	
203	Plotting the two curves side by side, the cold-start curve looks roughly like a decaying exponential settling toward the warm-start curve's flat line — it never quite reaches it within thirty seconds, and the small residual gap is consistent with the SQLite page-cache-fill effect discussed above rather than anything the operating system is still doing.
204	
205	A memory sample was taken alongside this run: RSS at the fifteenth cold-start call was 17.1 MB, versus 15.9 MB at the corresponding point in the warm-start run — a smaller gap than the earlier 100-call comparison, which is expected since fewer calls had been made by this point.
206	
207	## Common Pitfalls
208	
209	* Forgetting to drop the operating system's page cache before a cold-start run — the single most common cause of a "cold" measurement that quietly comes back looking half-warm.
210	* Reusing a database file's WAL sidecar file without removing it, which can leave a cold-start run partially warm on the SQLite side even though the main database file itself was freshly created.
211	* Running warm-start and cold-start measurements on different machines and drawing conclusions from the difference — always keep both runs on the same host during the same sitting.
212	* Measuring only the very first call and skipping the warm-up curve, which hides the fact that even a "cold" run settles to something close to warm-start performance within a dozen calls or so.
213	* Comparing numbers gathered months apart without noting the Python version or SQLite library version in use at the time — a Python upgrade alone has moved our interpreter-startup number by several milliseconds in the past.
214

220	| SQLite (bundled with Python's `sqlite3` module) | 3.42.0 | underlying database engine |

# Cold Start Versus Warm Start

**Version:** 1.3
**Owner:** Developer Experience (Owen Fischer)
**Last updated:** 2025-07-22

## Overview

This page contrasts what happens the first time the loopback service is brought up against a database file that has never been touched — a **cold start** — with what happens on later runs against a database file that the operating system and SQLite have already warmed — a **warm start**. The numbers here come from a mix of manual timing runs, a couple of longer profiling sessions logged in `docs/performance-notes/profiling-sessions.md`, and some ad hoc poking with `time` and `curl` on a loopback interface during the week of 2025-07-14.

The short version: on the machines we run this on, a cold start against an empty database file costs somewhere around four to five times what a warm start costs, most of that gap coming from three places — interpreter and import overhead, opening the database file and setting its journal mode, and the operating system pulling pages of the database file off disk instead of serving them from its own file cache. None of that is unique to this package; it's the usual shape of cold-versus-warm behavior for anything backed by SQLite. What's specific to auditlog is how small the whole thing is, which makes the relative size of "cold start tax" much more visible than it would be in a larger service.

This page brings together the individual measurements from the sibling pages on journal mode, page cache size, loopback response times, memory use, and startup time, arranging them side by side under two conditions — cold and warm — so the contrast is easy to see in one sitting.

## Terminology

- **Cold start** — the first run of the service against a database file that either does not yet exist or has not been touched recently enough for its pages to still be in the operating system's file cache.
- **Warm start** — a run of the service where the database file's pages are already present in the operating system's file cache, typically because the file was used moments earlier in the same session or by another process on the same host.
- **Journal mode** — the SQLite setting that controls how changes are recorded before they land in the main database file; the two modes referenced most in this doc are the default rollback journal and WAL (write-ahead log).
- **WAL (write-ahead log)** — a separate file next to the database file that SQLite writes changes into first; the WAL file's contents are folded back into the main database file periodically rather than being written straight into it on every change.
- **Page cache size** — a SQLite pragma (`cache_size`) that controls how many pages of the database file SQLite is willing to keep in its own in-memory area, separate from whatever the operating system is caching.
- **Page size** — the fixed size, in bytes, that SQLite reads and writes the database file in; ours is set to the SQLite default of 4096 bytes unless a page notes otherwise.
- **Resident set size (RSS)** — the amount of physical memory a running process is currently holding, as reported by tools like `ps` or `psutil`; used throughout this page as the memory number of record.
- **Loopback interface** — the local network path (127.0.0.1) the HTTP service listens on; used here rather than any external network path.
- **Warm-up requests** — the first handful of calls made against a freshly started service, before response times settle into a steady number.
- **Startup time** — the interval from when the process is launched to when it is first ready to answer a call on the loopback interface.
- **Flame graph** — a visual representation of where time is spent across a call stack during a profiling run, produced from `py-spy` captures in our case; see `docs/performance-notes/flamegraph-captures.txt`.

## Measurement Environment

*Section owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience*

All numbers on this page were collected on the same reference machine unless a table says otherwise:

- Machine: a spare development laptop set aside for performance work (internally called `perf-bench-02`), not the shared build host.
- Operating system: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, kernel 5.15.
- Python: 3.11.6, installed via `pyenv`, no other interpreters on the path during measurement.
- Disk: NVMe SSD, not spinning media — cold-start numbers would look considerably worse on the older `perf-bench-01` machine, which still has a SATA drive.
- The database file lives at `./var/auditlog.db` relative to the checkout, on a filesystem that is not tmpfs, so cold reads genuinely hit disk (or at least the drive's own cache) rather than being served from RAM the whole way through.

Before every cold-start run, the reference machine's page cache for that file was dropped so the operating system had nothing cached:

```
sync
echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches
```

This step matters more than people expect. Skipping it and just removing the database file is not enough to get a genuine cold start if the file was used minutes earlier — the operating system will often still be holding the old file's pages, and even though the file itself is gone, the process launch and import path will look artificially warm because of unrelated pages still resident from the previous run.

## Cold Start Procedure

*Section owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience*

To get a clean cold-start measurement, follow this order:

1. Stop any running instance of the service.
2. Remove the existing database file and its WAL file, if present, at the paths configured for that run (typically `./var/auditlog.db` and `./var/auditlog.db-wal`).
3. Drop the operating system's page cache as shown above (this step is easy to forget and skews results toward "warm" if skipped).
4. Start the service fresh, timing from process launch.
5. Make a single call against the loopback interface and record the time from launch to first response.
6. Continue making calls at a steady pace (roughly one per second works fine) for the next thirty seconds and record each response time, so the "settling" curve can be plotted alongside the very first number.

A shell wrapper we keep around for this is `scripts/cold-start-timing.sh`:

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
rm -f ./var/auditlog.db ./var/auditlog.db-wal
sync
echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches
start=$(date +%s.%N)
./auditlog/service_launcher &
pid=$!
until curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8791/status; do sleep 0.005; done
end=$(date +%s.%N)
echo "launch to first response: $(echo "$end - $start" | bc) s"
```

Note that this script has drifted slightly out of date — it still names the loopback port as 8791, which is the port used before the port move documented in `docs/performance-notes/loopback-response-times.md`; the actual default for recent builds is 8792. Adjust before running.

## Warm Start Procedure

*Section owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience*

Warm-start measurement is simpler because there is less to reset:

1. Start the service once against an existing database file and make a handful of calls to make sure both the operating system's file cache and SQLite's own page cache are populated.
2. Stop the service (but do **not** remove the database file or drop the OS page cache).
3. Start the service again, timing from process launch as before.
4. Make the same single call and record the time.
5. Continue making calls for the following thirty seconds as with the cold-start run.

The companion script is `scripts/warm-start-timing.sh`, which is identical to the cold-start script minus the `rm` and `drop_caches` lines. Keeping the two scripts nearly line-for-line the same, aside from those two steps, has made it much easier to trust that differences in the resulting numbers reflect the cold-versus-warm condition and not some accidental difference in how the process was launched.

## SQLite Settings and Their Effect on Startup

*Section owner: Lena Kowalski, Data Infra (cross-posted from `docs/performance-notes/sqlite-journal-mode.md`)*

Two SQLite settings show up repeatedly in cold-versus-warm timing differences: journal mode and page cache size.

**Journal mode.** With the rollback journal (SQLite's default), the very first write to a freshly created database file has to create the journal file from scratch, which adds a handful of extra filesystem operations that are only paid once. With WAL mode, the first write instead has to create the WAL file, and on a cold start that file-creation cost lands on the operating system's disk path rather than being served from cache — one of the bigger single contributors to the gap between cold and warm numbers we've measured. On a warm start, by contrast, the WAL file from the previous run may already exist and be mapped in, so this cost mostly disappears.

To confirm which journal mode a given database file is using:

```
sqlite3 ./var/auditlog.db "PRAGMA journal_mode;"
```

To set WAL mode explicitly (this only needs to be done once per database file, since the setting is stored in the file itself):

```
sqlite3 ./var/auditlog.db "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;"
```

**Page cache size.** The `cache_size` pragma controls how many pages SQLite keeps in its own memory area, separate from whatever the operating system is caching. The default is a modest -2000, meaning roughly 2 MB given our 4096-byte page size. Recent internal builds set this higher:

```
sqlite3 ./var/auditlog.db "PRAGMA cache_size=-8000;"
```

That gives SQLite roughly 8 MB of page cache. On a warm start, a larger page cache size makes almost no visible difference, because the pages are already sitting in the operating system's own cache and the round trip to fetch them from there is already quick. On a cold start, though, a larger `cache_size` means more of the database file's pages get pulled in and kept once they're read, so a series of early calls settles into its steady response time slightly sooner than it would with the smaller default. The gain is real but modest — on the order of a few milliseconds per call during the warm-up window, not something that changes the overall shape of the cold-start curve.

| Setting | Default | Tuned value used here | Cold-start effect | Warm-start effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Journal mode | rollback journal | WAL | WAL adds one-time file creation cost | negligible, file usually already present |
| Page cache size | -2000 (~2 MB) | -8000 (~8 MB) | shortens the warm-up window slightly | almost no visible change |
| Page size | 4096 bytes | 4096 bytes (unchanged) | n/a | n/a |
| Synchronous mode | FULL | NORMAL (with WAL) | slightly fewer disk flushes on first writes | no measurable change |

See `docs/performance-notes/sqlite-journal-mode.md` for the full reasoning on why WAL was chosen over the rollback journal, and `docs/performance-notes/page-cache-sizing.md` (v2.0) for how the -8000 figure was arrived at.

## Loopback Response Time Comparison

*Section owner: Devon Ruiz, Core Services*

The table below shows response times for the first call and for calls after the response time has settled, under both conditions, on the reference machine described above.

| Condition | First call | Call #5 | Call #10 | Steady state (call #20+) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cold start | 214 ms | 96 ms | 61 ms | 47 ms |
| Warm start | 52 ms | 41 ms | 39 ms | 38 ms |

A few things stand out:

* The cold-start first call is more than four times the warm-start first call, but by the tenth call the gap has narrowed considerably.
* Warm-start response times are close to flat from the very first call, which matches the expectation that most of the cost being avoided is disk-related rather than anything the process itself does differently between calls.
* Steady-state numbers converge but never fully meet — cold-start steady state settles a few milliseconds above warm-start steady state even after twenty calls, likely reflecting SQLite's own page cache still filling in during that window rather than the operating system's cache, which fills in almost immediately.

For a wider set of response-time measurements across different call shapes and sizes, see `docs/performance-notes/loopback-response-times.md`.

*Section owner: Priya Nair, Systems Reliability*

Memory use tells a somewhat different story than response time — the cold-versus-warm gap is much smaller here, because most of the memory a Python process holds comes from the interpreter and imported modules rather than from anything specific to the database file being warm or cold.

As Owen Fischer noted in `docs/performance-notes/memory-use-notes.md`, this gap has been stable across several profiling sessions and does not seem to depend much on which journal mode is in use.

1. Machine prepared per the Measurement Environment section above; page cache dropped; old database file removed.

   ```

4. Process stopped. Database file left in place. No cache drop performed.
5. `scripts/warm-start-timing.sh` run. Output:
   ```
   launch to first response: 0.054 s
   ```
6. Fifteen further calls, same interval. Response times, in milliseconds: 54, 44, 41, 40, 39, 39, 38, 38, 38, 38, 37, 38, 38, 37, 38.

## Common Pitfalls

* Forgetting to drop the operating system's page cache before a cold-start run — the single most common cause of a "cold" measurement that quietly comes back looking half-warm.
* Reusing a database file's WAL sidecar file without removing it, which can leave a cold-start run partially warm on the SQLite side even though the main database file itself was freshly created.
* Running warm-start and cold-start measurements on different machines and drawing conclusions from the difference — always keep both runs on the same host during the same sitting.
* Measuring only the very first call and skipping the warm-up curve, which hides the fact that even a "cold" run settles to something close to warm-start performance within a dozen calls or so.
* Comparing numbers gathered months apart without noting the Python version or SQLite library version in use at the time — a Python upgrade alone has moved our interpreter-startup number by several milliseconds in the past.

## Tools and Package Versions

1	.. RST Documentation Page: Concurrency Notes
2	
3	Concurrency Notes
4	=================
5	
6	| **Version:** 2.4
7	| **Owner:** Systems Reliability (Priya Nair)
8	| **Last Updated:** 2026-02-09
9	
10	Summary
11	-------
12	
13	This page documents observations and recommendations from profiling sessions where the package handles multiple simultaneous writers against the same SQLite database file. We cover settings that affect concurrent write performance, measurement procedures, observed response time distributions, and memory behavior under load. The page captures accumulated findings from production deployments and lab profiling runs over the past year.
14	
15	
16	Coverage and Audience
17	------------------
18	
19	This documentation is intended for:
20	
21	- Systems engineers deploying the package in multi-writer scenarios
22	- Developers optimizing database access patterns
23	- Operations staff interpreting performance metrics during incidents
24	
25	We assume familiarity with SQLite transaction concepts and the package's HTTP service model. This page focuses on empirical observations under concurrent load; for detailed configuration guidance, see the sibling pages on journal mode and page cache sizing.
26	
27	
28	Concurrent Write Patterns
29	--------------------------
30	
31	*Owner: Priya Nair*
32	
33	The package's loopback HTTP service can receive multiple simultaneous requests from different processes. Each request typically performs one or more database writes, which can compete for locks on the same database file. SQLite handles this through its locking protocol, but behavior varies significantly based on configuration.
34	
35	We have observed three dominant patterns in production deployments:
36	
37	1. **Low-contention scenario** (fewer than 5 concurrent writers): Lock wait times remain under 10 milliseconds. Requests complete with minimal queueing. Memory use remains flat across all writer instances.
38	
39	2. **Moderate-contention scenario** (5 to 15 concurrent writers): Lock conflicts occur regularly. Response time variation increases; some requests take 50 to 200 milliseconds while others complete in 5 milliseconds. Database file grows at a measurable rate.
40	
41	3. **High-contention scenario** (more than 15 concurrent writers): Lock timeouts begin appearing in logs. Response time distribution becomes bimodal—most requests complete quickly or after extended wait. Memory use shows periodic spikes correlating with transaction log merges.
42	
43	The transition between patterns is not sharp. We have measured intermediate states where behavior degrades gradually from pattern 1 to pattern 2 over the course of several hours as writer load accumulates.
44	
45	
46	Profiling Under Load
47	---------------------
48	
49	*Owner: Devon Ruiz (on behalf of Core Services)*
50	
51	Profiling sessions follow a standard protocol:
52	
53	1. Start the loopback service with default settings on a clean database file
54	2. Launch a pool of writer processes, each sending requests at a fixed interval
55	3. Capture system metrics (CPU, memory, I/O) and service metrics (response times, lock waits)
56	4. Run for 15 minutes, then measure startup time on a warm database file
57	5. Preserve logs and database file for analysis
58	
59	**Example profiling run setup:**
60	
61	Launch writer processes with staggered start times over 30 seconds. Each writer sends a request every 100 milliseconds. Capture response time samples at 1-second intervals. Record peak memory use and minimum free heap size.
62	
63	```
64	Writer count: 8
65	Request interval per writer: 100 ms
66	Measurement duration: 15 minutes
67	Sample rate: 1 second (response times), 5 seconds (memory)
68	Database file location: /tmp/bench-concurrent-8w.db
69	```
70	
71	After a completed run, the database file typically grows to 2.5 to 4.2 megabytes. The logfile records approximately 7,200 requests under normal conditions.
72	
73	One inconsistency we have noted: runs on the same hardware with identical writer counts produce different peak response times on alternate days, suggesting filesystem caching effects that we have not fully characterized. Restarting the system and clearing the filesystem cache (by other means) has not resolved the variance completely.
74	
75	
76	SQLite Configuration for Concurrency
77	-------------------------------------
78	
79	*Owner: Lena Kowalski (Data Infra)*
80	
81	Three SQLite settings have the largest measurable impact on concurrent write behavior:
82	
83	**Journal Mode**
84	
85	The journal mode determines how SQLite manages transaction state. We recommend Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode for concurrent scenarios; it reduces lock contention compared to the default Standard mode. In WAL mode, writes go to a separate log file first, and the main database file is updated asynchronously. This allows readers to continue while writes are in progress.
86	
87	Measured lock wait time comparison (8 concurrent writers, 15-minute run):
88	
89	- Standard mode: Mean 42 ms, P95 180 ms, P99 420 ms
90	- WAL mode: Mean 8 ms, P95 35 ms, P99 95 ms
91	
92	WAL mode introduces additional CPU overhead during log-merge operations (when the log is merged back into the main file). We observe CPU spikes lasting 2 to 5 seconds every 5 to 10 minutes during sustained load.
93	
94	**Page Cache Size**
95	
96	The page cache (or buffer pool) holds in-memory copies of database pages. Larger caches reduce disk I/O for frequently accessed data but increase memory usage per process. The setting is specified in pages; each page is typically 4 kilobytes.
97	
98	Recommended settings:
99	
100	- Low-contention (fewer than 5 writers): 2000 pages (8 MB per process)
101	- Moderate-contention (5 to 15 writers): 5000 pages (20 MB per process)
102	- High-contention (more than 15 writers): 10000 pages (40 MB per process)
103	
104	Increasing page cache beyond 10000 pages shows diminishing returns; we have not observed measurable improvement with 20000-page caches.
105	
106	**Synchronous Mode**
107	
108	The synchronous mode controls how aggressively SQLite writes to disk. FULL mode ensures all writes reach the disk before returning to the caller; NORMAL mode is less strict. Switching from FULL to NORMAL reduces mean response time by approximately 35 percent in our measurements, but introduces risk of data loss in case of power failure or crash during a transaction.
109	
110	For the package's use cases, we recommend FULL mode for reliability, accepting the response time cost.
111	
112	
113	Response Time Measurement Methodology
114	--------------------------------------
115	
116	*Owner: Devon Ruiz*
117	
118	Response times are measured from the HTTP caller's perspective: the elapsed time from sending the request to receiving the complete response body. We do not include caller-side processing or network delay on the loopback interface (which is negligible, typically under 1 millisecond).
119	
120	Measurement is performed using a simple timing wrapper around the service caller library. Samples are collected continuously and written to a flat file with nanosecond precision. Post-processing aggregates these into percentile distributions.
121	
122	**Sample measurement output format:**
123	
124	```
125	request_id=12847, method=PUT, path=/entries, elapsed_ns=4156000, lock_wait_ns=892000
126	request_id=12848, method=GET, path=/summary, elapsed_ns=2341000, lock_wait_ns=0
127	request_id=12849, method=PUT, path=/entries, elapsed_ns=156291000, lock_wait_ns=151834000
128	...
129	```
130	
131	The lock_wait_ns field is an estimate derived from system call tracing (when available) or inferred from response time spikes.
132	
133	**Typical response time distribution under moderate load (8 concurrent writers):**
134	
135	| Percentile | Time (ms) | Notes                                        |
136	|------------|-----------|----------------------------------------------|
137	| P50        | 6.2       | Most requests complete quickly               |
138	| P75        | 12.1      | Some lock contention visible                 |
139	| P90        | 47.3      |                                              |
140	| P95        | 156.8     | Lock waits become frequent                    |
141	| P99        | 312.5     | Occasional very long waits                    |
142	| P99.9      | 1847.2    | Rare timeout-adjacent behavior                |
143	
144	Response time variance decreases when journal mode is switched to WAL and page cache is increased to 5000 pages.
145	
146	
147	Memory Use Under Concurrent Load
148	---------------------------------
149	
150	*Owner: Priya Nair*
151	
152	The package's process memory use in concurrent scenarios consists of:
153	
154	1. Base memory: typically 8 to 12 MB at startup
155	2. Page cache: proportional to the configured cache size (e.g., 5000 pages = ~20 MB)
156	3. Connection buffers: each concurrent request allocates temporary buffers (~500 KB each)
157	4. Python interpreter overhead: grows with the number of active threads or async tasks
158	
159	Under sustained load with 8 concurrent writers, we observe:
160	
161	- Initial memory: 12 MB
162	- Steady-state memory (after 1 minute): 35 to 45 MB
163	- Peak memory (during log-merge operations in WAL mode): 50 to 65 MB
164	
165	The memory spike during log-merge operations is temporary and lasts 1 to 3 seconds. It correlates with the CPU spike mentioned earlier.
166	
167	**Memory use with different writer counts:**
168	
169	| Writers | Steady-State Memory | Peak Memory | Notes                           |
170	|---------|-------------------|-------------|--------------------------------|
171	| 2       | 22 MB             | 28 MB       | Minimal contention              |
172	| 4       | 28 MB             | 35 MB       |                                 |
173	| 8       | 40 MB             | 60 MB       | Log-merge overhead visible     |
174	| 12      | 50 MB             | 85 MB       |                                 |
175	| 16      | 58 MB             | 110 MB      | Lock timeout behavior begins    |
176	
177	These figures assume default page cache settings. Reducing page cache to 2000 pages lowers steady-state memory by approximately 12 MB across all writer counts, with corresponding increase in response time variability.
178	
179	
180	Startup Time Under Different Database Conditions
181	-------------------------------------------------
182	
183	*Owner: Owen Fischer (Developer Experience)*
184	
185	Startup time varies based on whether the database file is cold (freshly created, zero size) or warm (existing file with prior data).
186	
187	**Cold startup:**
188	- Empty database file: ~220 ms
189	- Service listening on loopback: ~240 ms
190	
191	**Warm startup (with existing database):**
192	- 2 MB database file: ~320 ms
193	- 5 MB database file: ~410 ms
194	- 10 MB database file: ~480 ms
195	
196	The additional time during warm startup is spent performing consistency checks and building in-memory indexes. These operations are I/O-bound and sensitive to filesystem cache state.
197	
198	Startup time does not increase linearly with database file size. A 10 MB file takes roughly 2x longer to open than a 2 MB file, not 5x. This suggests that most of the cost is amortized over the first few megabytes.
199	
200	**Effect of prior journal mode:**
201	
202	If the database was previously running in WAL mode, startup time increases by approximately 15 to 20 percent as the service performs additional repair procedures. This penalty is one-time; subsequent restarts are fast.
203	
204	We have observed one edge case: if the database is corrupted (e.g., file truncated during an unclean shutdown), startup can take 5 to 10 seconds while repair procedures attempt to restore the file. This is rare but has occurred in production during hardware failures.
205	
206	
207	Contention Mitigation Strategies
208	---------------------------------
209	
210	*Owner: Priya Nair*
211	
212	Several operational strategies can reduce observed lock contention:
213	
214	1. **Stagger writer schedules:** If writer processes can adjust their request timing, spreading requests over time rather than clustering them reduces peak lock contention. Even random jitter of ±20 milliseconds helps measurably.
215	
216	2. **Increase page cache:** Discussed above. A page cache of 5000 to 10000 pages reduces both response time and variance for moderate loads.
217	
218	3. **Enable WAL mode:** Reduces lock hold times. The log-merge overhead is worthwhile for scenarios with 4 or more concurrent writers.
219	
220	4. **Reduce request frequency per writer:** If individual writers can wait longer between requests without violating business requirements, total lock contention decreases linearly.
221	
222	5. **Partition data across multiple database files:** If the application can logically separate data by writer (or by some other dimension), using separate database files for each partition eliminates cross-partition lock conflicts. This approach requires application-level changes.
223	
224	Strategy 1 and 2 are easiest to implement without code changes. We have seen production deployments adopt strategy 1 as a first step, followed by strategy 2 if contention remains problematic.
225	
226	
227	Profiling Tools and Instrumentation
228	------------------------------------
229	
230	*Owner: Mara Olsen (Platform Tools)*
231	
232	Standard tools used for profiling concurrent load:
233	
234	- **System metrics:** The vmstat and iostat utilities on Linux; Task Manager and Resource Monitor on Windows. Sample interval: 2 to 5 seconds.
235	- **Process metrics:** Process Explorer (Windows) or top/htop (Linux) for memory and CPU tracking per process.
236	- **Service metrics:** Built-in service logging (response times, request counts) written to structured format.
237	- **Database inspection:** The sqlite3 command-line tool for querying database statistics (file size, table record counts, index usage).
238	
239	A typical profiling session uses a dedicated measurement script that orchestrates these tools, collects output, and produces a summary report. Scripts are stored in the scripts/ directory; consult the baseline-measurements.yaml file for example run configurations.
240	
241	**Lock wait estimation:** Under Linux, strace can trace system calls and identify lock wait syscalls. This provides high-precision measurement of database lock hold times. On Windows, Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) provides similar information but requires additional setup.
242	
243	
244	Terminology and Glossary
245	------------------------
246	
247	**Journal Mode:** SQLite's mechanism for recording transaction state and ensuring durability. Standard mode writes transaction state to a journal file, then removes it after the transaction completes; WAL mode uses a Write-Ahead Log file that is merged into the main database file later.
248	
249	**Page Cache (Buffer Pool):** In-memory storage for database pages. Larger caches reduce disk I/O but increase memory usage. The size is configured in units of pages (typically 4 KB per page).
250	
251	**Lock Wait Time:** The elapsed time from when a process attempts to acquire a database lock to when the lock is granted. High lock wait times indicate contention.
252	
253	**Log-Merge (WAL):** The operation in WAL mode where the write-ahead log is merged back into the main database file, freeing space in the log file. Log merges are performed periodically and can cause brief CPU spikes.
254	
255	**Cold Start:** Starting the service with a database file that is not in the filesystem cache (or using a newly created, zero-size database file).
256	
257	**Warm Start:** Starting the service with a database file that is already in the filesystem cache or has been recently accessed.
258	
259	**Contention:** Competition for the same resource (in this context, database locks). High contention means multiple processes are frequently waiting for locks held by other processes.
260	
261	**Synchronous Mode:** SQLite setting controlling how aggressively writes are flushed to disk. FULL mode ensures all writes reach disk before returning; NORMAL mode is less strict and faster but riskier.
262	
263
