1	# Profiling Session Log
2	
3	**Version:** 2.3
4	**Owner:** Systems Reliability (Priya Nair)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-11-02
6	
7	This page chronicles individual profiling sessions run against the package's command line and its loopback service. It records what tool was used, what SQLite settings were in effect on the database file at the time, what was measured, and what came out of it. It is meant to be read chronologically — later entries assume you've read the earlier ones — but the tables can be skimmed on their own if you just need a number.
8	
9	Sessions logged here feed the sibling pages that cover single topics in more depth (journal mode, page cache sizing, loopback timings, memory, and startup). This page is the raw notebook; those pages are the distilled write-ups. If a number here disagrees with one of those pages, the sibling page is usually the more current source, since it gets revisited more often than this log does.
10	
11	## Purpose and Coverage
12	
13	The intent of this log is to give future contributors a record of *how* a measurement was taken, not just what the measurement was. Numbers without a method attached age badly — six months later nobody remembers whether a response time figure included connection setup or not. Each entry below tries to include:
14	
15	- the date and who ran it,
16	- the machine and OS,
17	- the exact tool invocation (or a close paraphrase of it),
18	- the SQLite settings on the database file used for that pass,
19	- what was observed, and
20	- any follow-up question it raised.
21	
22	This page documents the results of trying various SQLite journal mode and page cache configurations. We focus on what was attempted and what resulted — for explanations of why the package behaves as it does, see the SQLite journal mode and page cache documentation pages.
23	
24	## Terminology
25	
26	**Journal mode** — the SQLite setting that controls how the database file records in-flight changes before they land in the main file body. The two modes referenced most in this log are the default rollback mode and the write-ahead mode.
27	
28	**Page cache size** — the number of database pages SQLite is allowed to hold in memory before it has to go back to the file on disk for more. Larger values trade memory for fewer disk reads.
29	
30	**Write-ahead log** — a companion file next to the main database file, used when the write-ahead journal mode is active. Changes are recorded there first and folded back into the main file on a schedule.
31	
32	**Page size** — the size, in bytes, of one unit of storage inside the database file. This is fixed when the file is first created and cannot be changed afterward without rebuilding the file.
33	
34	**Cold start** — the first launch of a process after the host has not run it recently, so nothing related to it is warm in any operating-system cache.
35	
36	**Warm start** — a launch that follows shortly after a prior one, where the operating system still has relevant pages of the executable and shared libraries in memory.
37	
38	**Resident set size (RSS)** — the portion of a process's memory that is actually held in physical RAM at a point in time, as opposed to memory that has been reserved but not yet touched.
39	
40	**Sampling profiler** — a profiling tool that periodically interrupts a running process to record where it currently is, building up a statistical picture of where time goes rather than tracing every call.
41	
42	**Loopback interface** — the local, host-only network interface (127.0.0.1) that the package's HTTP service listens on; calls to it never leave the machine.
43	
44	**Percentile latency (p50 / p95 / p99)** — a way of describing a distribution of response times by the value below which a given fraction of samples fall. p95 means 95 out of 100 calls finished at or under that time.
45	
46	**Flame graph** — a visual rendering of sampled call stacks, stacked so that wider bars mean more samples spent in that stack.
47	
48	**Wall-clock time** — elapsed real time as measured by a clock on the wall, as distinct from CPU time, which excludes time spent waiting.
49	
50	## Environment and Tooling Setup
51	
52	*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*
53	
54	Most sessions in this log were run on one of two machines, referred to below by short names:
55	
56	| Short name | Description | OS |
57	|---|---|---|
58	| bench-a | Desktop workstation, 6-core, 32 GB RAM, local SSD | Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS |
59	| bench-w | Laptop, 4-core, 16 GB RAM | Windows 10 Pro 10.0.19045 |
60	
61	Python was 3.11.6 on bench-a and 3.12.1 on bench-w for most of 2025; a handful of early sessions (before March) used 3.11.4 on bench-a before it was patched. This matters because the bundled SQLite version travels with the interpreter build — 3.11.6 ships SQLite 3.42.0, while 3.12.1 ships 3.43.2. A few numbers in this log therefore come from slightly different SQLite builds, which is worth remembering before treating two rows in a table as directly comparable.
62	
63	The general shape of a profiling session is:
64	
65	1. Check out the package at the target commit and confirm the working tree is clean.
66	2. Remove any stale database file left over from the previous pass — sessions use a fresh file each time rather than reusing one from a prior run, so page counts and cache warmth start from a known point.
67	3. Start the harness script for the mode being profiled (command line or loopback).
68	4. Attach the profiling tool to the running process, or wrap the harness invocation in the profiling tool if it is the kind that launches its own subprocess.
69	5. Drive a fixed amount of work through it.
70	6. Collect the tool's output into the day's folder under `logs/profiling/`.
71	7. Write up what was found, here.
72	
73	A typical harness invocation, wrapped in a sampling profiler, looks like this on bench-a:
74	
75	```
76	py-spy record -o logs/profiling/2025-10-14/loopback.svg -- \
77	  scripts/run_profile_session.sh --mode loopback --port 8642 --duration 90
78	```
79	
80	And the equivalent on bench-w, using a timing harness rather than a sampler:
81	
82	```
83	hyperfine --warmup 3 --min-runs 20 `
84	  'scripts\run_profile_session.ps1 -Mode cli -Iterations 1'
85	```
86	
87	Neither of these lines invokes the package directly — both call a wrapper script that in turn starts the process being measured, so the profiling tool always sees a subprocess it launched itself rather than one it had to find and attach to after the fact. For sampling passes against an already-running loopback service, the harness prints the process id to standard output so it can be handed to `py-spy record --pid`.
88	
89	## Command Line Profiling Sessions
90	
91	*(Section owner: Priya Nair, Systems Reliability)*
92	
93	The command line surface is short-lived by nature — one call, one exit — so most of the profiling effort here goes into flame graphs of a single pass rather than sustained sampling, plus repeated timing passes to get a distribution rather than one number.
94	
95	| Date | Machine | Tool | Focus | Finding |
96	|---|---|---|---|---|
97	| 2025-02-11 | bench-a | py-spy (native profile) | overall shape of a single pass | most of the wall-clock time sits in interpreter start-up, not in anything the package itself does |
98	| 2025-04-03 | bench-a | hyperfine, 50 runs | wall-clock distribution, default journal mode | median 61 ms, p95 89 ms |
99	| 2025-04-04 | bench-a | hyperfine, 50 runs | wall-clock distribution, write-ahead mode | median 58 ms, p95 84 ms — small but consistent improvement |
100	| 2025-06-19 | bench-w | Measure-Command (PowerShell) | wall-clock distribution on Windows | median 104 ms, p95 151 ms; Windows process start-up overhead dominates the difference from bench-a |
101	| 2025-09-02 | bench-a | py-spy (native + Python frames combined) | check for stack imbalance after a dependency bump | no change of note |
102	| 2025-10-14 | bench-a | py-spy record, flame graph | confirm the earlier finding still holds after several months of small changes | still true — most of the flame graph is under interpreter start-up, module import, and stdlib parsing of arguments |
103	
104	A worked example, in case someone wants to reproduce the 2025-10-14 pass: the harness script builds a fresh database file, then times ten sequential invocations under a wrapping sampling profiler with a short sample interval, then merges the resulting profiles into one flame graph with the vendor tool that ships alongside py-spy. The merged graph is kept as `logs/profiling/2025-10-14/cli-merged.svg`.
105	
106	One recurring note across these sessions: because the command line path is short, jitter from anything else running on the machine at the same time (a background update, a browser tab doing something, whatever) has an outsized effect on the tail. Several early numbers in this table were thrown out and re-run because a background process on bench-w was clearly interfering with the p95 figure. If a number in this table looks suspiciously high, check the raw log folder for that date before trusting it.
107	
108	## Loopback Service Profiling Sessions
109	
110	*(Section owner: Devon Ruiz, Core Services)*
111	
112	The loopback service holds state across many calls, which makes it a better subject for sustained sampling than the command line is. Sessions here generally start the service once, drive it for a fixed window with a load-generating shell loop, and sample throughout.
113	
114	Load generation is a small shell loop rather than anything fancier:
115	
116	```
117	for i in $(seq 1 2000); do
118	  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8642/ >> \
119	    logs/profiling/2025-10-21/timings.txt
120	done
121	```
122	
123	(The loopback service does have more than one thing you can call against it, but for the purpose of these sessions a single representative call, repeated, is enough to characterize typical latency. Sessions that specifically wanted to compare across the different kinds of calls the service handles are logged separately below.)
124	
125	| Date | Machine | Tool | Calls issued | Notes |
126	|---|---|---|---|---|
127	| 2025-03-08 | bench-a | py-spy top (live view) | ~500 | first look, mostly to confirm the service starts cleanly under a profiler attached |
128	| 2025-05-02 | bench-a | py-spy record, 60 s window | 2,000 | default journal mode; most samples land in the standard library's socket handling, a small fraction in the database file access path |
129	| 2025-05-02 | bench-a | py-spy record, 60 s window | 2,000 | write-ahead mode, same call shape; sampling picture is nearly identical, database-file-related samples shrink slightly |
130	| 2025-08-11 | bench-w | py-spy record | 1,500 | first Windows-side sampling pass; confirms shape matches bench-a, just shifted upward by overall slower socket handling on this machine |
131	| 2025-10-21 | bench-a | curl timing loop + concurrent py-spy | 2,000 | used to cross-check the response time numbers reported on the loopback response time page |
132	| 2025-11-01 | bench-a | py-spy record, 120 s window, mixed call shapes | ~5,000 | longest sustained sampling pass logged so far; used to look for anything that only shows up under longer sustained load |
133	
134	The 2025-11-01 session is worth a note of its own. It ran for two minutes rather than the usual one, specifically to see whether anything drifted over a longer window — memory growth, slowdown, anything. Nothing did. The flame graph for that session (`logs/profiling/2025-11-01/loopback-sustained.svg`) looks essentially the same at the two-minute mark as it does at the thirty-second mark, just with proportionally more samples in each bucket.
135	
136	## SQLite Journal Mode and Page Cache Observations
137	
138	*(Section owner: Lena Kowalski, Data Infra)*
139	
140	Every profiling session records the SQLite settings in effect on the database file at the time, because both journal mode and page cache size visibly move the numbers elsewhere on this page. The settings tried across sessions logged here are:
141	
142	| Setting | Values tried | Notes |
143	|---|---|---|
144	| Journal mode | rollback (default), write-ahead | write-ahead consistently shows lower tail latency on the loopback path |
145	| Page cache size | 2,000 pages (default, roughly 8 MB at the standard 4,096-byte page size), 8,000 pages (roughly 32 MB), 20,000 pages (roughly 80 MB) | gains beyond 8,000 pages were not measurable in these sessions — the database file used in profiling is small enough that most of it fits in an 8,000-page cache already |
146	| Page size | 4,096 bytes (default) | never varied in these sessions; changing it means rebuilding the file, which none of these sessions attempted |
147	
148	Settings were applied by opening the database file directly with the sqlite3 command-line shell before the harness started the process being profiled, then confirming the applied values with the shell's own inspection commands rather than trusting that the setting "took":
149	
150	```
151	sqlite3 logs/profiling/2025-05-02/session.db
152	sqlite> .timeout 3000
153	sqlite> .dbinfo
154	```
155	
156	The `.dbinfo` output was checked by hand against what was expected before the harness was allowed to proceed — this caught one early mistake in April 2025 where a session intended to run under write-ahead mode was actually still on the default rollback mode because the setting had been applied to a different file than the one the harness ended up using. That session's numbers were discarded rather than corrected.
157	
158	A recurring observation: on bench-w, the gap between rollback mode and write-ahead mode is smaller than on bench-a. The working guess is that Windows's own file system caching narrows the advantage that write-ahead mode gets from avoiding certain kinds of file locking overhead, but nobody has profiled deeply enough to say that with confidence — it's a guess written down here so the next person doesn't have to start from zero.
159	
160	Page cache size above roughly 20,000 pages was never tried in these sessions and is flagged as an open question — the database file used for profiling tops out around 4,000 pages of content, so a cache larger than the file itself was assumed to be pointless, though nobody has actually confirmed that assumption against a larger generated file.
161	
162	## Response Time Measurements
163	
164	*(Section owner: Devon Ruiz, Core Services)*
165	
166	Response times reported here are measured over the loopback interface using the curl timing loop shown above, unless otherwise noted. All figures are wall-clock, single caller, no concurrent load unless the row says otherwise.
167	
168	| Date | Journal mode | Cache pages | p50 | p95 | p99 | Sample size |
169	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
170	| 2025-05-02 | rollback | 2,000 | 5.1 ms | 13.2 ms | 27.9 ms | 2,000 |
171	| 2025-05-02 | write-ahead | 2,000 | 4.4 ms | 11.0 ms | 22.1 ms | 2,000 |
172	| 2025-08-11 | write-ahead | 2,000 | 7.6 ms | 18.4 ms | 34.0 ms | 1,500 (bench-w) |
173	| 2025-09-30 | write-ahead | 8,000 | 4.2 ms | 10.6 ms | 21.4 ms | 2,000 |
174	| 2025-10-21 | write-ahead | 8,000 | 4.2 ms | 11.8 ms | 24.3 ms | 2,000 |
175	
176	The 2025-09-30 and 2025-10-21 rows use the same settings and are close but not identical — this is the ordinary run-to-run noise you get on a shared workstation and not a sign that anything changed between the two dates.
177	
178	Two things worth flagging for anyone reading this table quickly:
179	
180	- The bench-w row (2025-08-11) is not directly comparable to the bench-a rows above and below it. Windows loopback handling in general shows higher overhead than Linux loopback handling in these sessions, independent of anything the package does.
181	- The 2025-10-21 row was cross-checked against a concurrent py-spy session (see the loopback profiling table above) specifically to make sure the extra profiling overhead of running curl and py-spy at the same time wasn't inflating the p99 figure. It appeared to add roughly one millisecond to the tail, which is within the noise already visible between the two write-ahead rows above.
182	
183	For a more complete treatment of loopback timings, including different call shapes, see the loopback response time page. As of that page's last update it reported a p95 figure in the same range as the numbers above, though it was last revised several weeks before the most recent session logged here, so a small amount of drift between the two is expected.
184	
185	## Memory Use Observations
186	
187	*(Section owner: Priya Nair, Systems Reliability)*
188	
189	Memory figures below are resident set size, sampled at intervals during a loopback session using the operating system's own process inspection (`ps` on bench-a, Process Explorer 17.05 on bench-w) alongside the standard library's own memory tracking, which was enabled for a handful of sessions to see where memory was actually being used rather than just how much.
190	
191	| Date | Machine | Journal mode | Cache pages | RSS at start | RSS after 2,000 calls | Growth |
192	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
193	| 2025-05-02 | bench-a | rollback | 2,000 | 16.8 MB | 19.2 MB | 2.4 MB |
194	| 2025-05-02 | bench-a | write-ahead | 2,000 | 17.1 MB | 20.5 MB | 3.4 MB |
195	| 2025-08-11 | bench-w | write-ahead | 2,000 | 22.0 MB | 28.6 MB | 6.6 MB |
196	| 2025-09-30 | bench-a | write-ahead | 8,000 | 17.3 MB | 34.1 MB | 16.8 MB |
197	| 2025-11-01 | bench-a | write-ahead | 8,000 | 17.5 MB | 33.9 MB | 16.4 MB (over ~5,000 calls, 2 minute window) |
198	
199	The larger growth figure on 2025-09-30 and 2025-11-01 is expected and not treated as a sign of unbounded growth — an 8,000-page cache means SQLite is allowed to hold up to roughly 32 MB of page data in memory, and the growth observed lines up with the cache filling up as more of the database file is touched during the session, then staying roughly flat afterward. The 2025-11-01 session specifically ran twice as long as the 2025-09-30 one and ended up with a slightly *lower* RSS figure, which is more evidence that the growth plateaus rather than continuing — if it were still climbing at the two-minute mark you'd expect it to be higher, not about the same.
200	
201	The Windows figures (bench-w, 2025-08-11) run several megabytes higher throughout, which the team currently attributes to baseline overhead in how the Windows build of the interpreter maps shared libraries rather than anything specific to the package. This has not been investigated further.
202	
203	A note for anyone repeating these sessions: `ps` reports RSS in kilobytes and Process Explorer reports it in the units its column is set to display, which defaults to bytes on a fresh install. The 2025-08-11 figures above were converted by hand from a byte reading and are trusted to two significant figures at most.
204	
205	## Startup Time Observations
206	
207	*(Section owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience)*
208	
209	Startup timing sessions distinguish cold start (first launch after the host hasn't run the process recently) from warm start (a launch shortly after a prior one, with relevant pages of the interpreter and shared libraries still resident from the operating system's point of view). All figures below are wall-clock from process launch to the point the harness detects the process is ready to receive a call.
210	
211	| Date | Machine | Start kind | Median | p95 | Notes |
212	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
213	| 2025-01-15 | bench-a | cold | 210 ms | 260 ms | first host reboot of the year, used deliberately to get a clean cold reading |
214	| 2025-01-15 | bench-a | warm | 48 ms | 61 ms | measured immediately after the cold pass above, ten repeats |
215	| 2025-06-30 | bench-a | cold | 178 ms | 224 ms | after an interpreter patch bump; faster than January, likely unrelated to the package itself |
216	| 2025-06-30 | bench-a | warm | 44 ms | 58 ms | consistent with January |
217	| 2025-08-11 | bench-w | cold | 340 ms | 410 ms | first Windows cold-start reading logged |
218	| 2025-08-11 | bench-w | warm | 95 ms | 118 ms | roughly double the bench-a warm figure |
219	
220	Cold-start readings are hard to get cleanly on a machine that isn't rebooted for each one — several attempts on bench-a earlier in 2025 were discarded because the operating system's own file cache had clearly kept enough of the interpreter warm from an unrelated process to make the "cold" reading indistinguishable from a warm one. The two cold-start rows above were both taken within a few minutes of a full host reboot specifically to avoid that problem.
221	
222	A more detailed comparison between cold and warm behavior, including a breakdown of where the time actually goes during a cold start, lives on the cold start versus warm start page. That page's figures were last checked in the middle of 2025 and should be read alongside the rows above rather than instead of them, since a few months separate the two write-ups.
223	
224	## Files and Host Paths Referenced
225	
226	- `auditlog/` — the package directory; the thing being profiled in every session on this page.
227	- `docs/performance-notes/` — this page's own folder, holding this log and its sibling pages.
228	- `scripts/run_profile_session.sh` — the shell harness used on bench-a (Linux) to start the command line or loopback path under a profiling tool and tear it down afterward.
229	- `scripts/run_profile_session.ps1` — the PowerShell equivalent, used on bench-w.
230	- `scripts/gen_load.sh` — the small curl loop used to drive repeated calls against a running loopback service.
231	- `logs/profiling/` — the directory holding raw output from every session in this log, one date-stamped folder per session.
232	- a fresh database file created inside each date-stamped session folder — never the same file reused across sessions, so cache warmth and page counts start from a known point each time.
233	
234	## Tools and Libraries
235	
236	| Tool / library | Version | Used for |
237	|---|---|---|
238	| Python | 3.11.6 (bench-a), 3.12.1 (bench-w) | interpreter running the package during every session |
239	| SQLite (bundled with Python) | 3.42.0 (under 3.11.6), 3.43.2 (under 3.12.1) | the database engine backing the file being profiled |
240	| py-spy | 0.3.14 | sampling profiler used for flame graphs and live views |
241	| hyperfine | 1.18.0 | repeated wall-clock timing passes for the command line path |
242	| curl | 8.4.0 | driving individual calls against the loopback service and timing them |
243	| sqlite3 command-line shell | bundled with the Python build in use | applying and confirming journal mode and page cache settings on the database file before a session |
244	| Process Explorer | 17.05 | Windows-side process memory inspection |
245	| ps (procps) | 3.3.17 | Linux-side process memory inspection |
246	| standard library memory tracking | (part of the Python standard library) | occasional in-process memory sampling during longer loopback sessions |
247	| Measure-Command (PowerShell) | built into PowerShell 7.4 | wall-clock timing on bench-w where hyperfine was not used |
248

253	- **2.1** — 2025-05-30 — added the write-ahead versus rollback comparison sessions from May; expanded the terminology section to include page cache and page size.
254	- **2.0** — 2025-02-14 — restructured the page from a flat list of dated notes into the current section layout with named section owners.

# Profiling Session Log

**Version:** 2.3
**Owner:** Systems Reliability (Priya Nair)
**Last updated:** 2025-11-02

This page chronicles individual profiling sessions run against the package's command line and its loopback service. It records what tool was used, what SQLite settings were in effect on the database file at the time, what was measured, and what came out of it. It is meant to be read chronologically — later entries assume you've read the earlier ones — but the tables can be skimmed on their own if you just need a number.

Sessions logged here feed the sibling pages that cover single topics in more depth (journal mode, page cache sizing, loopback timings, memory, and startup). This page is the raw notebook; those pages are the distilled write-ups. If a number here disagrees with one of those pages, the sibling page is usually the more current source, since it gets revisited more often than this log does.

## Purpose and Coverage

The intent of this log is to give future contributors a record of *how* a measurement was taken, not just what the measurement was. Numbers without a method attached age badly — six months later nobody remembers whether a response time figure included connection setup or not. Each entry below tries to include:

- the date and who ran it,
- the machine and OS,
- the exact tool invocation (or a close paraphrase of it),
- the SQLite settings on the database file used for that pass,
- what was observed, and
- any follow-up question it raised.

This page documents the results of trying various SQLite journal mode and page cache configurations. We focus on what was attempted and what resulted — for explanations of why the package behaves as it does, see the SQLite journal mode and page cache documentation pages.

## Terminology

**Journal mode** — the SQLite setting that controls how the database file records in-flight changes before they land in the main file body. The two modes referenced most in this log are the default rollback mode and the write-ahead mode.

**Page cache size** — the number of database pages SQLite is allowed to hold in memory before it has to go back to the file on disk for more. Larger values trade memory for fewer disk reads.

**Write-ahead log** — a companion file next to the main database file, used when the write-ahead journal mode is active. Changes are recorded there first and folded back into the main file on a schedule.

**Page size** — the size, in bytes, of one unit of storage inside the database file. This is fixed when the file is first created and cannot be changed afterward without rebuilding the file.

**Cold start** — the first launch of a process after the host has not run it recently, so nothing related to it is warm in any operating-system cache.

**Warm start** — a launch that follows shortly after a prior one, where the operating system still has relevant pages of the executable and shared libraries in memory.

**Resident set size (RSS)** — the portion of a process's memory that is actually held in physical RAM at a point in time, as opposed to memory that has been reserved but not yet touched.

**Sampling profiler** — a profiling tool that periodically interrupts a running process to record where it currently is, building up a statistical picture of where time goes rather than tracing every call.

**Loopback interface** — the local, host-only network interface (127.0.0.1) that the package's HTTP service listens on; calls to it never leave the machine.

**Percentile latency (p50 / p95 / p99)** — a way of describing a distribution of response times by the value below which a given fraction of samples fall. p95 means 95 out of 100 calls finished at or under that time.

**Flame graph** — a visual rendering of sampled call stacks, stacked so that wider bars mean more samples spent in that stack.

**Wall-clock time** — elapsed real time as measured by a clock on the wall, as distinct from CPU time, which excludes time spent waiting.

## Environment and Tooling Setup

*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*

Most sessions in this log were run on one of two machines, referred to below by short names:

| Short name | Description | OS |
|---|---|---|
| bench-a | Desktop workstation, 6-core, 32 GB RAM, local SSD | Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS |
| bench-w | Laptop, 4-core, 16 GB RAM | Windows 10 Pro 10.0.19045 |

Python was 3.11.6 on bench-a and 3.12.1 on bench-w for most of 2025; a handful of early sessions (before March) used 3.11.4 on bench-a before it was patched. This matters because the bundled SQLite version travels with the interpreter build — 3.11.6 ships SQLite 3.42.0, while 3.12.1 ships 3.43.2. A few numbers in this log therefore come from slightly different SQLite builds, which is worth remembering before treating two rows in a table as directly comparable.

The general shape of a profiling session is:

1. Check out the package at the target commit and confirm the working tree is clean.
2. Remove any stale database file left over from the previous pass — sessions use a fresh file each time rather than reusing one from a prior run, so page counts and cache warmth start from a known point.
3. Start the harness script for the mode being profiled (command line or loopback).
4. Attach the profiling tool to the running process, or wrap the harness invocation in the profiling tool if it is the kind that launches its own subprocess.
5. Drive a fixed amount of work through it.
6. Collect the tool's output into the day's folder under `logs/profiling/`.
7. Write up what was found, here.

A typical harness invocation, wrapped in a sampling profiler, looks like this on bench-a:

```
py-spy record -o logs/profiling/2025-10-14/loopback.svg -- \
  scripts/run_profile_session.sh --mode loopback --port 8642 --duration 90
```

And the equivalent on bench-w, using a timing harness rather than a sampler:

```
hyperfine --warmup 3 --min-runs 20 `
  'scripts\run_profile_session.ps1 -Mode cli -Iterations 1'
```

Neither of these lines invokes the package directly — both call a wrapper script that in turn starts the process being measured, so the profiling tool always sees a subprocess it launched itself rather than one it had to find and attach to after the fact. For sampling passes against an already-running loopback service, the harness prints the process id to standard output so it can be handed to `py-spy record --pid`.

## Command Line Profiling Sessions

*(Section owner: Priya Nair, Systems Reliability)*

The command line surface is short-lived by nature — one call, one exit — so most of the profiling effort here goes into flame graphs of a single pass rather than sustained sampling, plus repeated timing passes to get a distribution rather than one number.

| Date | Machine | Tool | Focus | Finding |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-02-11 | bench-a | py-spy (native profile) | overall shape of a single pass | most of the wall-clock time sits in interpreter start-up, not in anything the package itself does |
| 2025-04-03 | bench-a | hyperfine, 50 runs | wall-clock distribution, default journal mode | median 61 ms, p95 89 ms |
| 2025-04-04 | bench-a | hyperfine, 50 runs | wall-clock distribution, write-ahead mode | median 58 ms, p95 84 ms — small but consistent improvement |
| 2025-06-19 | bench-w | Measure-Command (PowerShell) | wall-clock distribution on Windows | median 104 ms, p95 151 ms; Windows process start-up overhead dominates the difference from bench-a |
| 2025-09-02 | bench-a | py-spy (native + Python frames combined) | check for stack imbalance after a dependency bump | no change of note |
| 2025-10-14 | bench-a | py-spy record, flame graph | confirm the earlier finding still holds after several months of small changes | still true — most of the flame graph is under interpreter start-up, module import, and stdlib parsing of arguments |

A worked example, in case someone wants to reproduce the 2025-10-14 pass: the harness script builds a fresh database file, then times ten sequential invocations under a wrapping sampling profiler with a short sample interval, then merges the resulting profiles into one flame graph with the vendor tool that ships alongside py-spy. The merged graph is kept as `logs/profiling/2025-10-14/cli-merged.svg`.

One recurring note across these sessions: because the command line path is short, jitter from anything else running on the machine at the same time (a background update, a browser tab doing something, whatever) has an outsized effect on the tail. Several early numbers in this table were thrown out and re-run because a background process on bench-w was clearly interfering with the p95 figure. If a number in this table looks suspiciously high, check the raw log folder for that date before trusting it.

## Loopback Service Profiling Sessions

*(Section owner: Devon Ruiz, Core Services)*

The loopback service holds state across many calls, which makes it a better subject for sustained sampling than the command line is. Sessions here generally start the service once, drive it for a fixed window with a load-generating shell loop, and sample throughout.

Load generation is a small shell loop rather than anything fancier:

```
for i in $(seq 1 2000); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}\n' http://127.0.0.1:8642/ >> \
    logs/profiling/2025-10-21/timings.txt
done
```

(The loopback service does have more than one thing you can call against it, but for the purpose of these sessions a single representative call, repeated, is enough to characterize typical latency. Sessions that specifically wanted to compare across the different kinds of calls the service handles are logged separately below.)

| Date | Machine | Tool | Calls issued | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-03-08 | bench-a | py-spy top (live view) | ~500 | first look, mostly to confirm the service starts cleanly under a profiler attached |
| 2025-05-02 | bench-a | py-spy record, 60 s window | 2,000 | default journal mode; most samples land in the standard library's socket handling, a small fraction in the database file access path |
| 2025-05-02 | bench-a | py-spy record, 60 s window | 2,000 | write-ahead mode, same call shape; sampling picture is nearly identical, database-file-related samples shrink slightly |
| 2025-08-11 | bench-w | py-spy record | 1,500 | first Windows-side sampling pass; confirms shape matches bench-a, just shifted upward by overall slower socket handling on this machine |
| 2025-10-21 | bench-a | curl timing loop + concurrent py-spy | 2,000 | used to cross-check the response time numbers reported on the loopback response time page |
| 2025-11-01 | bench-a | py-spy record, 120 s window, mixed call shapes | ~5,000 | longest sustained sampling pass logged so far; used to look for anything that only shows up under longer sustained load |

The 2025-11-01 session is worth a note of its own. It ran for two minutes rather than the usual one, specifically to see whether anything drifted over a longer window — memory growth, slowdown, anything. Nothing did. The flame graph for that session (`logs/profiling/2025-11-01/loopback-sustained.svg`) looks essentially the same at the two-minute mark as it does at the thirty-second mark, just with proportionally more samples in each bucket.

## SQLite Journal Mode and Page Cache Observations

*(Section owner: Lena Kowalski, Data Infra)*

Every profiling session records the SQLite settings in effect on the database file at the time, because both journal mode and page cache size visibly move the numbers elsewhere on this page. The settings tried across sessions logged here are:

| Setting | Values tried | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Journal mode | rollback (default), write-ahead | write-ahead consistently shows lower tail latency on the loopback path |
| Page cache size | 2,000 pages (default, roughly 8 MB at the standard 4,096-byte page size), 8,000 pages (roughly 32 MB), 20,000 pages (roughly 80 MB) | gains beyond 8,000 pages were not measurable in these sessions — the database file used in profiling is small enough that most of it fits in an 8,000-page cache already |
| Page size | 4,096 bytes (default) | never varied in these sessions; changing it means rebuilding the file, which none of these sessions attempted |

Settings were applied by opening the database file directly with the sqlite3 command-line shell before the harness started the process being profiled, then confirming the applied values with the shell's own inspection commands rather than trusting that the setting "took":

```
sqlite3 logs/profiling/2025-05-02/session.db
sqlite> .timeout 3000
sqlite> .dbinfo
```

The `.dbinfo` output was checked by hand against what was expected before the harness was allowed to proceed — this caught one early mistake in April 2025 where a session intended to run under write-ahead mode was actually still on the default rollback mode because the setting had been applied to a different file than the one the harness ended up using. That session's numbers were discarded rather than corrected.

A recurring observation: on bench-w, the gap between rollback mode and write-ahead mode is smaller than on bench-a. The working guess is that Windows's own file system caching narrows the advantage that write-ahead mode gets from avoiding certain kinds of file locking overhead, but nobody has profiled deeply enough to say that with confidence — it's a guess written down here so the next person doesn't have to start from zero.

Page cache size above roughly 20,000 pages was never tried in these sessions and is flagged as an open question — the database file used for profiling tops out around 4,000 pages of content, so a cache larger than the file itself was assumed to be pointless, though nobody has actually confirmed that assumption against a larger generated file.

## Response Time Measurements

*(Section owner: Devon Ruiz, Core Services)*

Response times reported here are measured over the loopback interface using the curl timing loop shown above, unless otherwise noted. All figures are wall-clock, single caller, no concurrent load unless the row says otherwise.

| Date | Journal mode | Cache pages | p50 | p95 | p99 | Sample size |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-05-02 | rollback | 2,000 | 5.1 ms | 13.2 ms | 27.9 ms | 2,000 |
| 2025-05-02 | write-ahead | 2,000 | 4.4 ms | 11.0 ms | 22.1 ms | 2,000 |
| 2025-08-11 | write-ahead | 2,000 | 7.6 ms | 18.4 ms | 34.0 ms | 1,500 (bench-w) |
| 2025-09-30 | write-ahead | 8,000 | 4.2 ms | 10.6 ms | 21.4 ms | 2,000 |
| 2025-10-21 | write-ahead | 8,000 | 4.2 ms | 11.8 ms | 24.3 ms | 2,000 |

The 2025-09-30 and 2025-10-21 rows use the same settings and are close but not identical — this is the ordinary run-to-run noise you get on a shared workstation and not a sign that anything changed between the two dates.

Two things worth flagging for anyone reading this table quickly:

- The bench-w row (2025-08-11) is not directly comparable to the bench-a rows above and below it. Windows loopback handling in general shows higher overhead than Linux loopback handling in these sessions, independent of anything the package does.
- The 2025-10-21 row was cross-checked against a concurrent py-spy session (see the loopback profiling table above) specifically to make sure the extra profiling overhead of running curl and py-spy at the same time wasn't inflating the p99 figure. It appeared to add roughly one millisecond to the tail, which is within the noise already visible between the two write-ahead rows above.

For a more complete treatment of loopback timings, including different call shapes, see the loopback response time page. As of that page's last update it reported a p95 figure in the same range as the numbers above, though it was last revised several weeks before the most recent session logged here, so a small amount of drift between the two is expected.

## Memory Use Observations

*(Section owner: Priya Nair, Systems Reliability)*

Memory figures below are resident set size, sampled at intervals during a loopback session using the operating system's own process inspection (`ps` on bench-a, Process Explorer 17.05 on bench-w) alongside the standard library's own memory tracking, which was enabled for a handful of sessions to see where memory was actually being used rather than just how much.

| Date | Machine | Journal mode | Cache pages | RSS at start | RSS after 2,000 calls | Growth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-05-02 | bench-a | rollback | 2,000 | 16.8 MB | 19.2 MB | 2.4 MB |
| 2025-05-02 | bench-a | write-ahead | 2,000 | 17.1 MB | 20.5 MB | 3.4 MB |
| 2025-08-11 | bench-w | write-ahead | 2,000 | 22.0 MB | 28.6 MB | 6.6 MB |
| 2025-09-30 | bench-a | write-ahead | 8,000 | 17.3 MB | 34.1 MB | 16.8 MB |
| 2025-11-01 | bench-a | write-ahead | 8,000 | 17.5 MB | 33.9 MB | 16.4 MB (over ~5,000 calls, 2 minute window) |

The larger growth figure on 2025-09-30 and 2025-11-01 is expected and not treated as a sign of unbounded growth — an 8,000-page cache means SQLite is allowed to hold up to roughly 32 MB of page data in memory, and the growth observed lines up with the cache filling up as more of the database file is touched during the session, then staying roughly flat afterward. The 2025-11-01 session specifically ran twice as long as the 2025-09-30 one and ended up with a slightly *lower* RSS figure, which is more evidence that the growth plateaus rather than continuing — if it were still climbing at the two-minute mark you'd expect it to be higher, not about the same.

The Windows figures (bench-w, 2025-08-11) run several megabytes higher throughout, which the team currently attributes to baseline overhead in how the Windows build of the interpreter maps shared libraries rather than anything specific to the package. This has not been investigated further.

A note for anyone repeating these sessions: `ps` reports RSS in kilobytes and Process Explorer reports it in the units its column is set to display, which defaults to bytes on a fresh install. The 2025-08-11 figures above were converted by hand from a byte reading and are trusted to two significant figures at most.

## Startup Time Observations

*(Section owner: Owen Fischer, Developer Experience)*

Startup timing sessions distinguish cold start (first launch after the host hasn't run the process recently) from warm start (a launch shortly after a prior one, with relevant pages of the interpreter and shared libraries still resident from the operating system's point of view). All figures below are wall-clock from process launch to the point the harness detects the process is ready to receive a call.

| Date | Machine | Start kind | Median | p95 | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-01-15 | bench-a | cold | 210 ms | 260 ms | first host reboot of the year, used deliberately to get a clean cold reading |
| 2025-01-15 | bench-a | warm | 48 ms | 61 ms | measured immediately after the cold pass above, ten repeats |
| 2025-06-30 | bench-a | cold | 178 ms | 224 ms | after an interpreter patch bump; faster than January, likely unrelated to the package itself |
| 2025-06-30 | bench-a | warm | 44 ms | 58 ms | consistent with January |
| 2025-08-11 | bench-w | cold | 340 ms | 410 ms | first Windows cold-start reading logged |
| 2025-08-11 | bench-w | warm | 95 ms | 118 ms | roughly double the bench-a warm figure |

Cold-start readings are hard to get cleanly on a machine that isn't rebooted for each one — several attempts on bench-a earlier in 2025 were discarded because the operating system's own file cache had clearly kept enough of the interpreter warm from an unrelated process to make the "cold" reading indistinguishable from a warm one. The two cold-start rows above were both taken within a few minutes of a full host reboot specifically to avoid that problem.

A more detailed comparison between cold and warm behavior, including a breakdown of where the time actually goes during a cold start, lives on the cold start versus warm start page. That page's figures were last checked in the middle of 2025 and should be read alongside the rows above rather than instead of them, since a few months separate the two write-ups.

## Files and Host Paths Referenced

- `auditlog/` — the package directory; the thing being profiled in every session on this page.
- `docs/performance-notes/` — this page's own folder, holding this log and its sibling pages.
- `scripts/run_profile_session.sh` — the shell harness used on bench-a (Linux) to start the command line or loopback path under a profiling tool and tear it down afterward.
- `scripts/run_profile_session.ps1` — the PowerShell equivalent, used on bench-w.
- `scripts/gen_load.sh` — the small curl loop used to drive repeated calls against a running loopback service.
- `logs/profiling/` — the directory holding raw output from every session in this log, one date-stamped folder per session.
- a fresh database file created inside each date-stamped session folder — never the same file reused across sessions, so cache warmth and page counts start from a known point each time.

## Tools and Libraries

| Tool / library | Version | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11.6 (bench-a), 3.12.1 (bench-w) | interpreter running the package during every session |
| SQLite (bundled with Python) | 3.42.0 (under 3.11.6), 3.43.2 (under 3.12.1) | the database engine backing the file being profiled |
| py-spy | 0.3.14 | sampling profiler used for flame graphs and live views |
| hyperfine | 1.18.0 | repeated wall-clock timing passes for the command line path |
| curl | 8.4.0 | driving individual calls against the loopback service and timing them |
| sqlite3 command-line shell | bundled with the Python build in use | applying and confirming journal mode and page cache settings on the database file before a session |
| Process Explorer | 17.05 | Windows-side process memory inspection |
| ps (procps) | 3.3.17 | Linux-side process memory inspection |
| standard library memory tracking | (part of the Python standard library) | occasional in-process memory sampling during longer loopback sessions |
| Measure-Command (PowerShell) | built into PowerShell 7.4 | wall-clock timing on bench-w where hyperfine was not used |

5	:Title: Profiling Tools
6	:Version: v1.0.3
7	:Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
8	:Last Updated: 2024-04-27
9	
10	.. contents:: Contents
11	   :depth: 2
12	
13	Overview
14	========
15	
16	This page documents the tools and procedures used to profile the package for performance analysis. Profiling work on the package involves measuring CPU time, memory allocation, database I/O, and startup latency using standard library and system utilities. This page lists which profiling tools we use, the flags we typically pass to each one, and setup procedures for common profiling scenarios.
17	
18	The focus is on practical, repeatable profiling workflows that the team uses during development and when investigating performance regressions. All the tools described here run on Windows without additional dependencies beyond the Python standard library.
19	
20	Using these tools correctly requires understanding a few key concepts around wall-clock time, CPU time, database page faults, and memory pressure. See the Terminology section for definitions.
21	
22	CPU Time Profiling
23	===================
24	
25	*Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)*
26	
27	We profile CPU time using Python's built-in ``cProfile`` module, which measures where the program spends CPU cycles. Because the package is small and lean, CPU profiling usually reveals I/O wait time and SQLite query overhead rather than algorithmic hot spots.
28	
29	Standard Usage
30	--------------
31	
32	To run a profiling session, we wrap execution with the profiler and specify an output file:
33	
34	::
35	
36	  python -m cProfile -o profile.stats ./auditlog-exec-command
37	
38	Use ``pstats`` to examine the output file:
39	
40	::
41	
42	  python -m pstats profile.stats
43	  > sort cumulative
44	  > stats 20
45	
46	This shows the 20 functions using the most cumulative time, including time in functions they call. The ``sort`` command reorders the report; common sort keys are:
47	
48	- ``cumulative``: total time in the function and all functions it calls
49	- ``time``: time spent in the function itself, not in callees
50	- ``calls``: number of times the function was called
51	
52	For the package, we typically run profiling sessions that exercise the loopback HTTP service, because the command line is too fast to profile usefully (under 50 ms most of the time). The loopback service runs longer, allowing the profiler to collect meaningful samples.
53	
54	Reading cProfile Output
55	-----------------------
56	
57	The first column is function call count. The second and third columns are the total time and per-call time. A high per-call time indicates a function is expensive; a high call count with low per-call time usually means a function is called repeatedly but isn't the bottleneck.
58	
59	When examining output, watch for:
60	
61	- SQLite functions that show high cumulative time
62	- Lock acquisition in the standard library's ``threading`` module (indicates contention)
63	- Memory allocation calls in the ``gc`` module (indicates heavy allocation pressure)
64	
65	If a function name is truncated, use the full function name in the report by filtering:
66	
67	::
68	
69	  python -m pstats profile.stats
70	  > callers some_function_name
71	
72	Sampling and Flame Graphs
73	==========================
74	
75	*Owner: Systems Reliability (Priya Nair)*
76	
77	For detailed CPU time breakdown, we use the ``py-spy`` tool, which samples the Python stack at regular intervals and can generate flame graph visualizations. This is useful when the package's service is running in steady state and we want to see which functions use the most time without the overhead of instrumentation.
78	
79	Installation and Basic Use
80	---------------------------
81	
82	Install ``py-spy`` outside the project environment:
83	
84	::
85	
86	  pip install py-spy
87	
88	Start the service in one terminal:
89	
90	::
91	
92	  python ./auditlog-service &
93	  SERVICE_PID=$!
94	
95	In another terminal, attach the profiler:
96	
97	::
98	
99	  py-spy record -o flame.svg --pid $SERVICE_PID -- sleep 10
100	
101	This captures 10 seconds of stack samples and writes a flame graph to ``flame.svg``. Each bar in the graph represents a function; the width shows how much time that function uses. Wider bars are hotter (more time spent there).
102	
103	Interpreting flame graphs requires understanding that:
104	
105	- Tall stacks mean deep call chains; this is often not a problem.
106	- Wide stacks at the same level mean those functions each spend time.
107	- The color has no meaning (it is random by default); ignore it.
108	
109	For the package, flame graphs usually show SQLite library time (narrow), loopback socket I/O (narrow), and JSON serialization (varies depending on payload size).
110	
111	Memory Profiling
112	================
113	
114	*Owner: Core Services (Devon Ruiz)*
115	
116	Memory profiling identifies which parts of the code allocate the most memory and whether the package holds onto memory longer than necessary. The package uses only the standard library, so memory usage is usually stable and low, but we track it during development to catch regressions early.
117	
118	Tools and Methods
119	------------------
120	
121	We use three approaches:
122	
123	1. **``tracemalloc``**: Standard library module that tracks memory allocations by source line.
124	2. **``memory_profiler``**: Third-party tool that shows memory use line-by-line in a function.
125	3. **OS-level tools**: ``tasklist`` and ``Get-Process`` on Windows to check resident set size (RSS).
126	
127	For most work, ``tracemalloc`` is sufficient. It requires no dependencies and works on Windows.
128	
129	tracemalloc Session Example
130	----------------------------
131	
132	To profile memory allocation in the service, create a monitoring script that runs the service and periodically captures the heap:
133	
134	::
135	
136	  python -c "
137	  Import the tracemalloc module
138	  tracemalloc.start()
139	  # code here that exercises the service
140	  Capture the current heap state using tracemalloc
141	  Retrieve statistics organized by source line number
142	  for stat in top_stats[:10]:
143	      print(stat)
144	  "
145	
146	The output shows allocation by file and line number. Watch for:
147	
148	- Repeated allocations in the same loop (possible missing cache or buffer reuse)
149	- Large allocations in module import (only runs once, usually acceptable)
150	- Allocations that grow over time without shrinking (possible unbounded allocation)
151	
152	Measuring Resident Memory
153	---------------------------
154	
155	On Windows, use ``Get-Process`` to monitor memory:
156	
157	::
158	
159	  Get-Process -Name python | Select-Object ProcessName, WorkingSet, PrivateMemorySize
160	
161	The ``WorkingSet`` column shows resident set size (RSS), the amount of physical memory the process holds. Track this before and after profiling runs.
162	
163	A typical baseline for the service is 15–20 MB after startup, growing to 25–35 MB under moderate load (50–100 loopback requests per second).
164	
165	Response Time Measurements on Loopback
166	=======================================
167	
168	*Owner: Core Services (Devon Ruiz)*
169	
170	Loopback response times measure end-to-end latency for the HTTP service running on ``localhost``. We measure from when a request is sent until the full response is received.
171	
172	Setup and Execution
173	-------------------
174	
175	Start the service on the default loopback interface:
176	
177	::
178	
179	  python ./auditlog-service --listen localhost:8080 &
180	  SERVICE_PID=$!
181	
182	Use ``curl`` to send requests and measure latency:
183	
184	::
185	
186	  curl -w "Time: %{time_total}s\n" http://localhost:8080/health
187	
188	The ``-w`` flag prints request metadata. ``%{time_total}`` is wall-clock elapsed time in seconds.
189	
190	For repeated measurements, write a loop:
191	
192	::
193	
194	  for i in {1..100}; do
195	      curl -s -w "%{time_total}\n" http://localhost:8080/health >> times.txt
196	  done
197	  
198	  # Compute statistics
199	  sort -n times.txt | awk '{sum+=$1; count++} END {print "avg: " sum/count, "min: " $1, "max: " $NF}'
200	
201	Expected Response Times
202	------------------------
203	
204	Response time varies by request type:
205	
206	- Health checks: 1–5 ms
207	- Simple queries: 5–50 ms
208	- Complex queries with sorting or filtering: 50–500 ms
209	- Requests with large result sets: 200–2000 ms
210	
211	If response times exceed these ranges, check:
212	
213	- SQLite journal mode and page cache settings (see SQLite Configuration below)
214	- System load (run ``Get-Process`` to check CPU usage of other processes)
215	- Database file fragmentation (rebuilt the database file periodically)
216	
217	Cold vs. Warm Measurements
218	--------------------------
219	
220	Cold latency is measured immediately after starting the service; the OS has not yet cached the database file. Warm latency is measured after a minute of normal operation; the OS file cache is populated.
221	
222	Cold response times are typically 2–3× warm response times. Always measure both in production-like scenarios.
223	
224	SQLite Configuration and Tuning
225	================================
226	
227	*Owner: Data Infra (Lena Kowalski)*
228	
229	The package stores records in a local SQLite database file. SQLite's performance depends heavily on settings such as journal mode, page cache size, and synchronization mode. We use ``sqlite3`` (the command-line tool) to inspect and tune these settings.
230	
231	Measuring Current Settings
232	---------------------------
233	
234	Connect to the database file and query the current settings:
235	
236	::
237	
238	  sqlite3 path/to/database.db
239	  > PRAGMA journal_mode;
240	  > PRAGMA cache_size;
241	  > PRAGMA synchronous;
242	
243	A typical output might be:
244	
245	::
246	
247	  Temporary journal mode
248	  -2000
249	  FULL
250	
251	These settings are described below.
252	
253	Journal Mode
254	~~~~~~~~~~~~
255	
256	The journal mode controls how SQLite writes changes to disk. Common modes:
257	
258	- Temporary journal mode: Default. Creates a temporary journal file during writes; removes it when done. Safe but slow for small writes.
259	- ``wal``: Write-ahead logging. Writes to a log file instead of rewriting the main file. Much faster for many small writes; requires two files (database and log).
260	- ``off``: No journal; dangerous, used only in memory databases or development scenarios.
261	
262	For the package, we recommend **``wal`` mode**. Enable it:
263	
264	::
265	
266	  sqlite3 path/to/database.db "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;"
267	
268	After enabling, the database file is accompanied by a second file ending in ``-wal`` that holds the write-ahead log.
269	
270	Page Cache Size
271	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
272	
273	The page cache holds recently accessed database pages in memory. Larger cache sizes reduce disk I/O.
274	
275	::
276	
277	  sqlite3 path/to/database.db "PRAGMA cache_size=-4000;"
278	
279	The negative sign specifies size in kilobytes. This example allocates 4 MB of cache. A reasonable starting point for the package is 2–4 MB (``-2000`` to ``-4000``).
280	
281	Monitor cache performance by running a workload and checking cache hit rate:
282	
283	::
284	
285	  sqlite3 path/to/database.db
286	  > PRAGMA query_only=ON;
287	  > PRAGMA optimize;
288	  Run a query to force a page to load from the database file
289	  > PRAGMA stats;
290	
291	The ``stats`` pragma shows cache size and hit rate (not all SQLite builds include this pragma; check whether it works before relying on it).
292	
293	Startup Time
294	============
295	
296	*Owner: Developer Experience (Owen Fischer)*
297	
298	Startup time measures how long the package takes to start from process creation to the service being ready to accept requests. We track startup time because even small increases (10–20 ms per startup) accumulate in deployment pipelines and container orchestration.
299	
300	Measurement Procedure
301	---------------------
302	
303	Use the `time` command (available in both PowerShell and Bash):
304	
305	::
306	
307	  Measure-Command { python ./auditlog-service --dry-run }
308	
309	The ``--dry-run`` flag starts the service and exits after initialization, allowing us to measure startup time without keeping a long-running process.
310	
311	Output resembles:
312	
313	::
314	
315	  Days              : 0
316	  Hours             : 0
317	  Minutes           : 0
318	  Seconds           : 0
319	  Milliseconds      : 87
320	  TotalMilliseconds : 87.4
321	
322	A typical baseline is 50–100 ms. Increases above 150 ms warrant investigation.
323	
324	Common sources of startup overhead:
325	
326	- Large module imports (check by running ``python -X importtime -c "import sys; print('ok')"`` to profile the standard library itself)
327	- Initialization of the SQLite connection pool (normally 10–20 ms)
328	- Reading configuration files from disk
329	
330	Profiling imports can reveal if a new dependency is slow:
331	
332	::
333	
334	  python -X importtime ./auditlog-service 2>&1 | grep cumulative
335	
336	This shows cumulative import time and is helpful when tracking down slow imports.
337	
338	Combining Multiple Profiling Approaches
339	========================================
340	
341	*Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)*
342	
343	Real profiling work usually combines multiple tools to get a complete picture. For example, if response times are slow, a typical workflow is:
344	
345	1. Measure baseline response times using curl (as above).
346	2. Run cProfile on a representative workload to identify which functions use the most time.
347	3. Check SQLite settings and measure cache hit rate.
348	4. Measure memory use to ensure the process is not swapping or hitting system limits.
349	5. If needed, use py-spy for a flame graph to see the breakdown within hot functions.
350	
351	Example: Investigating Slow Queries
352	------------------------------------
353	
354	Suppose we observe that certain queries take 200 ms when they should take 50 ms.
355	
356	**Step 1: Confirm the regression with loopback measurements**
357	
358	::
359	
360	  curl -w "%{time_total}\n" http://localhost:8080/query?type=slow
361	
362	**Step 2: Profile the service**
363	
364	::
365	
366	  python -m cProfile -o profile.stats ./auditlog-service &
367	  # Send the slow query several times
368	  curl http://localhost:8080/query?type=slow
369	  curl http://localhost:8080/query?type=slow
370	  kill %1  # stop the service
371	
372	**Step 3: Examine the profile**
373	
374	::
375	
376	  python -m pstats profile.stats
377	  > sort cumulative
378	  > stats 20
379	
380	Look for SQLite functions with high cumulative time or repeated calls to the same function.
381	
382	**Step 4: Check SQLite configuration**
383	
384	::
385

397	  # run the service and send the slow query

407	
408	**Cumulative time**: In cProfile output, the total time spent in a function and all functions it calls. High cumulative time indicates either the function itself is slow or functions it calls are slow.
409	
410	**CPU time**: Time spent executing CPU instructions, measured by the profiler. Different from wall-clock time (elapsed time on a clock), which includes I/O wait and context switches.

=================
Profiling Tools
=================

:Title: Profiling Tools
:Version: v1.0.3
:Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
:Last Updated: 2024-04-27

.. contents:: Contents
   :depth: 2

Overview
========

This page documents the tools and procedures used to profile the package for performance analysis. Profiling work on the package involves measuring CPU time, memory allocation, database I/O, and startup latency using standard library and system utilities. This page lists which profiling tools we use, the flags we typically pass to each one, and setup procedures for common profiling scenarios.

The focus is on practical, repeatable profiling workflows that the team uses during development and when investigating performance regressions. All the tools described here run on Windows without additional dependencies beyond the Python standard library.

Using these tools correctly requires understanding a few key concepts around wall-clock time, CPU time, database page faults, and memory pressure. See the Terminology section for definitions.

CPU Time Profiling
===================

*Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)*

We profile CPU time using Python's built-in ``cProfile`` module, which measures where the program spends CPU cycles. Because the package is small and lean, CPU profiling usually reveals I/O wait time and SQLite query overhead rather than algorithmic hot spots.

Standard Usage
--------------

To run a profiling session, we wrap execution with the profiler and specify an output file:

::

  python -m cProfile -o profile.stats ./auditlog-exec-command

Use ``pstats`` to examine the output file:

::

  python -m pstats profile.stats
  > sort cumulative
  > stats 20

This shows the 20 functions using the most cumulative time, including time in functions they call. The ``sort`` command reorders the report; common sort keys are:

- ``cumulative``: total time in the function and all functions it calls
- ``time``: time spent in the function itself, not in callees
- ``calls``: number of times the function was called

For the package, we typically run profiling sessions that exercise the loopback HTTP service, because the command line is too fast to profile usefully (under 50 ms most of the time). The loopback service runs longer, allowing the profiler to collect meaningful samples.

Reading cProfile Output
-----------------------

The first column is function call count. The second and third columns are the total time and per-call time. A high per-call time indicates a function is expensive; a high call count with low per-call time usually means a function is called repeatedly but isn't the bottleneck.

When examining output, watch for:

- SQLite functions that show high cumulative time
- Lock acquisition in the standard library's ``threading`` module (indicates contention)
- Memory allocation calls in the ``gc`` module (indicates heavy allocation pressure)

If a function name is truncated, use the full function name in the report by filtering:

::

  python -m pstats profile.stats
  > callers some_function_name

Sampling and Flame Graphs
==========================

*Owner: Systems Reliability (Priya Nair)*

For detailed CPU time breakdown, we use the ``py-spy`` tool, which samples the Python stack at regular intervals and can generate flame graph visualizations. This is useful when the package's service is running in steady state and we want to see which functions use the most time without the overhead of instrumentation.

Installation and Basic Use
---------------------------

Install ``py-spy`` outside the project environment:

::

  pip install py-spy

Start the service in one terminal:

::

  python ./auditlog-service &
  SERVICE_PID=$!

In another terminal, attach the profiler:

::

  py-spy record -o flame.svg --pid $SERVICE_PID -- sleep 10

This captures 10 seconds of stack samples and writes a flame graph to ``flame.svg``. Each bar in the graph represents a function; the width shows how much time that function uses. Wider bars are hotter (more time spent there).

Interpreting flame graphs requires understanding that:

- Tall stacks mean deep call chains; this is often not a problem.
- Wide stacks at the same level mean those functions each spend time.
- The color has no meaning (it is random by default); ignore it.

For the package, flame graphs usually show SQLite library time (narrow), loopback socket I/O (narrow), and JSON serialization (varies depending on payload size).

Memory Profiling
================

*Owner: Core Services (Devon Ruiz)*

Memory profiling identifies which parts of the code allocate the most memory and whether the package holds onto memory longer than necessary. The package uses only the standard library, so memory usage is usually stable and low, but we track it during development to catch regressions early.

Tools and Methods
------------------

We use three approaches:

1. **``tracemalloc``**: Standard library module that tracks memory allocations by source line.
2. **``memory_profiler``**: Third-party tool that shows memory use line-by-line in a function.
3. **OS-level tools**: ``tasklist`` and ``Get-Process`` on Windows to check resident set size (RSS).

For most work, ``tracemalloc`` is sufficient. It requires no dependencies and works on Windows.

tracemalloc Session Example
----------------------------

To profile memory allocation in the service, create a monitoring script that runs the service and periodically captures the heap:

::

  python -c "
  Import the tracemalloc module
  tracemalloc.start()
  # code here that exercises the service
  Capture the current heap state using tracemalloc
  Retrieve statistics organized by source line number
  for stat in top_stats[:10]:
      print(stat)
  "

The output shows allocation by file and line number. Watch for:

- Repeated allocations in the same loop (possible missing cache or buffer reuse)
- Large allocations in module import (only runs once, usually acceptable)
- Allocations that grow over time without shrinking (possible unbounded allocation)

Measuring Resident Memory
---------------------------

On Windows, use ``Get-Process`` to monitor memory:

::

  Get-Process -Name python | Select-Object ProcessName, WorkingSet, PrivateMemorySize

The ``WorkingSet`` column shows resident set size (RSS), the amount of physical memory the process holds. Track this before and after profiling runs.

A typical baseline for the service is 15–20 MB after startup, growing to 25–35 MB under moderate load (50–100 loopback requests per second).

Response Time Measurements on Loopback
=======================================

*Owner: Core Services (Devon Ruiz)*

Loopback response times measure end-to-end latency for the HTTP service running on ``localhost``. We measure from when a request is sent until the full response is received.

Setup and Execution
-------------------

Start the service on the default loopback interface:

::

  python ./auditlog-service --listen localhost:8080 &
  SERVICE_PID=$!

Use ``curl`` to send requests and measure latency:

::

  curl -w "Time: %{time_total}s\n" http://localhost:8080/health

The ``-w`` flag prints request metadata. ``%{time_total}`` is wall-clock elapsed time in seconds.

For repeated measurements, write a loop:

::

  for i in {1..100}; do
      curl -s -w "%{time_total}\n" http://localhost:8080/health >> times.txt
  done
  
  # Compute statistics
  sort -n times.txt | awk '{sum+=$1; count++} END {print "avg: " sum/count, "min: " $1, "max: " $NF}'

Expected Response Times
------------------------

Response time varies by request type:

- Health checks: 1–5 ms
- Simple queries: 5–50 ms
- Complex queries with sorting or filtering: 50–500 ms
- Requests with large result sets: 200–2000 ms

If response times exceed these ranges, check:

- SQLite journal mode and page cache settings (see SQLite Configuration below)
- System load (run ``Get-Process`` to check CPU usage of other processes)
- Database file fragmentation (rebuilt the database file periodically)

Cold vs. Warm Measurements
--------------------------

Cold latency is measured immediately after starting the service; the OS has not yet cached the database file. Warm latency is measured after a minute of normal operation; the OS file cache is populated.

Cold response times are typically 2–3× warm response times. Always measure both in production-like scenarios.

SQLite Configuration and Tuning
================================

*Owner: Data Infra (Lena Kowalski)*

The package stores records in a local SQLite database file. SQLite's performance depends heavily on settings such as journal mode, page cache size, and synchronization mode. We use ``sqlite3`` (the command-line tool) to inspect and tune these settings.

Measuring Current Settings
---------------------------

Connect to the database file and query the current settings:

::

  sqlite3 path/to/database.db
  > PRAGMA journal_mode;
  > PRAGMA cache_size;
  > PRAGMA synchronous;

A typical output might be:

::

  Temporary journal mode
  -2000
  FULL

These settings are described below.

Journal Mode
~~~~~~~~~~~~

The journal mode controls how SQLite writes changes to disk. Common modes:

- Temporary journal mode: Default. Creates a temporary journal file during writes; removes it when done. Safe but slow for small writes.
- ``wal``: Write-ahead logging. Writes to a log file instead of rewriting the main file. Much faster for many small writes; requires two files (database and log).
- ``off``: No journal; dangerous, used only in memory databases or development scenarios.

For the package, we recommend **``wal`` mode**. Enable it:

::

  sqlite3 path/to/database.db "PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;"

After enabling, the database file is accompanied by a second file ending in ``-wal`` that holds the write-ahead log.

Page Cache Size
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The page cache holds recently accessed database pages in memory. Larger cache sizes reduce disk I/O.

::

  sqlite3 path/to/database.db "PRAGMA cache_size=-4000;"

The negative sign specifies size in kilobytes. This example allocates 4 MB of cache. A reasonable starting point for the package is 2–4 MB (``-2000`` to ``-4000``).

Monitor cache performance by running a workload and checking cache hit rate:

::

  sqlite3 path/to/database.db
  > PRAGMA query_only=ON;
  > PRAGMA optimize;
  Run a query to force a page to load from the database file
  > PRAGMA stats;

The ``stats`` pragma shows cache size and hit rate (not all SQLite builds include this pragma; check whether it works before relying on it).

Startup Time
============

*Owner: Developer Experience (Owen Fischer)*

Startup time measures how long the package takes to start from process creation to the service being ready to accept requests. We track startup time because even small increases (10–20 ms per startup) accumulate in deployment pipelines and container orchestration.

Measurement Procedure
---------------------

Use the `time` command (available in both PowerShell and Bash):

::

  Measure-Command { python ./auditlog-service --dry-run }

The ``--dry-run`` flag starts the service and exits after initialization, allowing us to measure startup time without keeping a long-running process.

Output resembles:

::

  Days              : 0
  Hours             : 0
  Minutes           : 0
  Seconds           : 0
  Milliseconds      : 87
  TotalMilliseconds : 87.4

A typical baseline is 50–100 ms. Increases above 150 ms warrant investigation.

Common sources of startup overhead:

- Large module imports (check by running ``python -X importtime -c "import sys; print('ok')"`` to profile the standard library itself)
- Initialization of the SQLite connection pool (normally 10–20 ms)
- Reading configuration files from disk

Profiling imports can reveal if a new dependency is slow:

::

  python -X importtime ./auditlog-service 2>&1 | grep cumulative

This shows cumulative import time and is helpful when tracking down slow imports.

Combining Multiple Profiling Approaches
========================================

*Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)*

Real profiling work usually combines multiple tools to get a complete picture. For example, if response times are slow, a typical workflow is:

1. Measure baseline response times using curl (as above).
2. Run cProfile on a representative workload to identify which functions use the most time.
3. Check SQLite settings and measure cache hit rate.
4. Measure memory use to ensure the process is not swapping or hitting system limits.
5. If needed, use py-spy for a flame graph to see the breakdown within hot functions.

Example: Investigating Slow Queries
------------------------------------

Suppose we observe that certain queries take 200 ms when they should take 50 ms.

**Step 1: Confirm the regression with loopback measurements**

::

  curl -w "%{time_total}\n" http://localhost:8080/query?type=slow

**Step 2: Profile the service**

::

  python -m cProfile -o profile.stats ./auditlog-service &
  # Send the slow query several times
  curl http://localhost:8080/query?type=slow
  curl http://localhost:8080/query?type=slow
  kill %1  # stop the service

**Step 3: Examine the profile**

::

  python -m pstats profile.stats
  > sort cumulative
  > stats 20

Look for SQLite functions with high cumulative time or repeated calls to the same function.

**Step 4: Check SQLite configuration**

::

  sqlite3 path/to/database.db "PRAGMA journal_mode; PRAGMA cache_size; PRAGMA synchronous;"

If the journal mode is the default setting and the query performs many writes, try switching to write-ahead logging and remeasure.

**Step 5: Profile memory**

::

  python -c "
  Import the tracemalloc module
  tracemalloc.start()
  # run the service and send the slow query
  Capture the current heap state using tracemalloc
  Iterate through the top line-level statistics
      print(stat)
  "

If memory use is high, allocations might be blocking on garbage collection.

Terminology
===========

**Cumulative time**: In cProfile output, the total time spent in a function and all functions it calls. High cumulative time indicates either the function itself is slow or functions it calls are slow.

**CPU time**: Time spent executing CPU instructions, measured by the profiler. Different from wall-clock time (elapsed time on a clock), which includes I/O wait and context switches.

**Database page**: A fixed-size block of the SQLite database file (typically 4096 bytes). The page cache holds recently accessed pages in memory.

**Flame graph**: A visualization of CPU samples stacked by call depth. The horizontal axis represents time (or sample count); the vertical axis shows the call stack. Wider bars indicate more time in that function.

**Journal file**: A temporary file SQLite uses to record changes before committing them to the main database file. Used only in default journal mode; removed after the write completes.

**Unbounded allocation**: Memory allocated but never freed, causing total memory use to grow over time. Detected by running the process under load and watching memory growth with tools like ``tracemalloc`` or ``Get-Process``.

**Resident set size (RSS)**: The amount of physical memory (RAM) currently used by a process. Measured by tools like ``Get-Process`` on Windows and ``ps`` on Linux.

**Wall-clock time**: Elapsed time measured by a clock on the wall, including time spent waiting for I/O, context switches, and other processes. Different from CPU time.

**Write-ahead logging (WAL)**: A mode of operation for SQLite in which writes are recorded in a log file before being applied to the main database file. Faster than default mode for many small writes.

Repository Files and Paths
===========================

The following files and directories are referenced in profiling work:

- **docs/performance-notes/profiling-tools.rst**: This file.
- **docs/performance-notes/baseline-measurements.yaml**: Baseline performance measurements for the package, captured at version 1.0.0. Contains response time, memory, and startup time measurements for comparison.
- **scripts/profile-cpu.sh**: Bash script wrapper around cProfile and pstats; runs a workload and prints the top 20 functions by cumulative time.
- **scripts/measure-latency.ps1**: PowerShell script that sends 100 requests to the loopback service and computes min/max/mean latency statistics.
- **docs/performance-notes/profiling-sessions.md**: Log of profiling sessions run by the team; includes dates, tools used, findings, and follow-up actions.
- **path/to/database.db**: The SQLite database file written by the package during normal operation; used as input for sqlite3 profiling and journal mode tuning.
- **docs/performance-notes/memory-use-notes.md**: Detailed notes on memory profiling results and expected memory use under load.

Tools and Libraries
===================

The following tools and libraries are used for profiling:

   =============== ================== ==========================================
   Tool            Version            Purpose
   =============== ================== ==========================================
   cProfile        Python 3.10+       CPU profiling (built-in)
   pstats          Python 3.10+       Analyze cProfile output (built-in)
   tracemalloc     Python 3.10+       Memory allocation profiling (built-in)
   py-spy          0.3.14             Stack sampling and flame graphs
   sqlite3         3.40+              Database inspection and tuning
   curl            7.87.0             HTTP requests and latency measurement
