1	# Changelog Writing Conventions
2	
3	**Version:** 1.1
4	**Owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)
5	**Last updated:** 2024-08-19
6	**Summary:** Describes the formatting and section conventions used when writing entries in the package's changelog.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## Purpose and Coverage
11	
12	**Section owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)
13	
14	This page is the working reference for anyone adding a line to the auditlog changelog — the person cutting a release, a contributor fixing a small wording problem in the command line help text, or someone updating the console log format. It covers:
15	
16	- the file the changelog lives in and how it is organized,
17	- the fixed set of category headings we use and what belongs under each one,
18	- how an individual entry should be worded and capitalized,
19	- how entries should reference version numbers,
20	- worked examples for the five kinds of change auditlog's past releases have actually shipped (documentation, packaging, command help text, console log format, and speed), and
21	- how changelog work fits into the release checklist and review steps.
22	
23	It does not cover the numbering scheme itself (see *Version Numbering for the Package*) or the mechanics of building a source distribution file (see *Packaging the Source Distribution*). Those pages are linked at the bottom.
24	
25	The conventions here apply to every entry added to the changelog going forward. Older entries written before this page existed were not rewritten to match; you will see some drift if you scroll far enough back in `docs/CHANGELOG.md`.
26	
27	## Where the Changelog Lives
28	
29	The changelog is a single Markdown file, kept at `docs/CHANGELOG.md`, one folder up from this page. It is not split by year or by release the way some projects do it — auditlog is small enough that one file has worked fine so far. If it ever gets unwieldy we'll revisit, but as of this writing it's a few hundred lines.
30	
31	A few related files live alongside it:
32	
33	- `docs/release-notes/` — this folder, holding the conventions, the checklist, the version numbering rules, and the published notes for past releases.
34	- `docs/release-notes/changelog-snippet-format.txt` — a short plain-text spec for the entry line format, meant to be quoted directly rather than paraphrased. This page's examples are meant to match it; if the two ever disagree, treat the snippet format file as the source of truth for punctuation and the category line, and this page as the source of truth for wording style and worked examples.
35	- `scripts/check-changelog-format.sh` — a small shell script run near the end of the checklist that flags obviously malformed entries (missing category heading, missing version heading, stray tabs). It does not check wording quality — that's a human job.
36	
37	## Changelog File Structure
38	
39	`docs/CHANGELOG.md` is organized newest-first, with one heading per released version and, above all of those, a single `Unreleased` block for work that hasn't shipped yet.
40	
41	The skeleton looks like this:
42	
43	```markdown
44	# Changelog
45	
46	## Unreleased
47	
48	### Added
49	- ...
50	
51	### Changed
52	- ...
53	
54	### Fixed
55	- ...
56	
57	## v1.2.0 - 2025-02-18
58	
59	### Changed
60	- ...
61	
62	### Fixed
63	- ...
64	
65	## v1.1.0 - 2024-09-05
66	
67	### Added
68	- ...
69	```
70	
71	A few rules that keep this consistent:
72	
73	1. The `Unreleased` block sits at the top, always, even when it's empty. An empty block is written as `## Unreleased` followed by nothing but a blank line — don't remove the heading between releases, just clear the entries under it once they've moved into a version heading.
74	2. Version headings use the exact tag that will be used when the release is tagged in git — `v1.2.0`, not `1.2.0` or `Version 1.2.0`. See *Version Numbering for the Package* for how that tag is chosen.
75	3. The date next to the version heading is the date the release was tagged, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form, not the date the changelog entry was written (those are sometimes a day or two apart).
76	4. Category subheadings appear only when they have at least one entry under them. Don't print an empty `### Removed` just to keep some imagined symmetry.
77	5. Entries are bullet points, one line each where possible. If an entry genuinely needs a second line, indent the continuation two spaces under the bullet.
78	
79	## Category Conventions
80	
81	**Section owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)
82	
83	We use a fixed set of category subheadings under each version (or under `Unreleased`). Not every release uses every category — most releases only touch two or three of them.
84	
85	| Category heading | What goes under it |
86	|---|---|
87	| `Added` | New command line options, new console output, anything a user of the package didn't have before. |
88	| `Changed` | Behavior that already existed but now works differently — including changes to command help text wording, console log format, and speed, when those changes aren't simply fixes. |
89	| `Fixed` | Fixes for something that was wrong: a broken help text description, a console log line that didn't line up, a slow path that behaved incorrectly rather than just slowly. |
90	| `Removed` | Options, output lines, or behavior taken away entirely. Rare for auditlog so far. |
91	| `Documentation` | Changes confined to the docs/ folder or README.md — no code changes at all. |
92	| `Packaging` | Changes to how the source distribution file is built or what it contains, without a change to how the package behaves once installed. |
93	
94	A single release can, and often does, mix categories — the v1.1.0 release, for example, had both a `Changed` entry (console log format) and a `Packaging` entry (source distribution contents) side by side. What it should not mix is category *content*: a wording fix to help text goes under `Fixed`, not `Documentation`, even though at first glance "wording" sounds like a documentation change. `Documentation` is reserved specifically for the docs/ folder and README.md — help text lives in the package itself and gets its own line under `Added`, `Changed`, or `Fixed` depending on what happened to it.
95	
96	## Entry Format and Style Guide
97	
98	**Section owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)
99	
100	Each entry is one bullet, written as a complete sentence fragment starting with a past-tense verb, ending with a period. A few worked-through rules:
101	
102	- Start with what changed, not with "we" or "this release." Write "Widened the time column in console output" rather than "We widened the time column."
103	- Keep it to one sentence. If you need "and," consider whether it's really two entries.
104	- Don't restate the category in the sentence — under `Fixed`, write "Corrected the wrapping of long option descriptions," not "Fixed a bug where option descriptions wrapped wrong."
105	- Reference version numbers with the full tag (`v1.2.0`), never a bare number, and only when the entry is genuinely about a comparison across versions — most entries don't need one at all, since the version heading above them already says which release they belong to.
106	- Capitalize the first word of the sentence; don't capitalize the rest unless it's a proper noun. This one has slipped in the past — a few 2024 entries in `docs/CHANGELOG.md` are Title Cased throughout, left as-is rather than rewritten.
107	- Wrap lines at a reasonable width for a text editor's default view — we don't enforce a hard column count, but if a line runs past what fits comfortably in a normal editor window, it usually means the sentence is doing too much.
108	
109	A minimal correctly formatted entry, quoted from `changelog-snippet-format.txt`:
110	
111	```
112	- Reduced startup time by deferring optional setup work until it is first needed.
113	```
114	
115	Note the leading `- `, the period at the end, and the lack of a category word inside the sentence.
116	
117	## Version Number References
118	
119	**Section owner:** Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)
120	
121	Version numbers used in changelog entries and in version headings follow the scheme in *Version Numbering for the Package* (currently at v1.2 of that page). The short version, for the purposes of writing changelog entries:
122	
123	- auditlog uses a three-part number, `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`.
124	- The `Unreleased` block does not carry a version number — don't guess ahead at what the next tag will be, since that call happens later in the checklist, not while entries are being written.
125	- When an entry needs to reference an earlier release for context ("this restores the wording used before v1.1.0"), use the full tag and don't abbreviate it to just the minor number.
126	
127	One point worth calling out because it trips people up: the version heading in the changelog is added at release time, as one of the last checklist steps, not when the individual entries are written. Entries accumulate under `Unreleased` for however long the next release takes to come together — sometimes weeks — and only get a version heading and date once the release is actually tagged.
128	
129	## Worked Examples by Change Type
130	
131	The last several auditlog releases have each been fairly narrow — a release touching only documentation, or only packaging, or only the command line help text, and so on. This is deliberate; small releases are easier to write clean changelog entries for. Below is one worked example per kind of change, matched to the sibling page that goes into it in more depth.
132	
133	### Documentation-only changes
134	
135	**Section owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)
136	
137	These entries go under `Documentation`, never under `Changed`, even when the docs page being fixed describes behavior.
138	
139	```
140	### Documentation
141	- Fixed a broken cross-link between the version numbering page and the
142	  release checklist.
143	- Corrected heading capitalization across the release-notes/ pages to match
144	  the house style.
145	```
146	
147	See *Release Notes: v1.0.0* for a released example of a version made up entirely of entries like these.
148	
149	### Packaging-only changes
150	
151	**Section owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
152	
153	Packaging entries describe what changed in the source distribution file itself, not what changed once the package is installed and running — those two things are usually different and sometimes an entry needs both a `Packaging` line and a separate `Changed` line.
154	
155	```
156	### Packaging
157	- The source distribution now includes the docs/ folder, so a distribution
158	  file carries the same release notes as a full checkout.
159	- Removed a stray build folder that had been getting included in the
160	  distribution file by mistake.
161	```
162	
163	For how the distribution file is actually built, see *Packaging the Source Distribution* and, for the environment it's built in, *Build Environment Notes*.
164	
165	### Command help text changes
166	
167	**Section owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Banks)
168	
169	Help text entries are almost always `Fixed` (wording was wrong or confusing) or `Changed` (wording was fine but is being made clearer or more consistent). They should describe the effect on someone reading the help text, not the words themselves verbatim.
170	
171	```
172	### Fixed
173	- Corrected wrapping of long option descriptions in the command line help
174	  text so they no longer overflow at the default terminal width.
175	
176	### Changed
177	- Reworded several option descriptions in the command line help text for
178	  consistency with one another.
179	```
180	
181	A running list of these, release by release, lives in *Command Help Text Changes Across Releases* — that page is the one to check before writing a new entry, so wording stays consistent with what's already documented there.
182	
183	### Console log format changes
184	
185	**Section owner:** Core Runtime (Sam Okafor)
186	
187	These describe changes to what the console prints while the service or command line tool is running — column widths, ordering, added or removed fields in the printed line. They belong under `Changed` when the format shifts on purpose, and under `Fixed` when a previous format change didn't work as intended.
188	
189	```
190	### Changed
191	- Console log lines now include a fixed-width time column so output lines
192	  up when piped through common line-oriented tools.
193	
194	### Fixed
195	- Corrected a console log line that dropped its trailing field when the
196	  line ran long.
197	```
198	
199	*Console Log Format Changes Across Releases* keeps a fuller record of these across versions; a changelog entry should be a short summary of what's written there in more detail.
200	
201	### Speed changes
202	
203	**Section owner:** Core Runtime (Sam Okafor)
204	
205	Speed entries describe a change in how long something takes, in plain terms a reader can picture — "reduced," "shortened," "no longer waits on" — without giving exact timing figures, since those depend heavily on hardware and aren't something we commit to as a number.
206	
207	```
208	### Changed

# Changelog Writing Conventions

**Version:** 1.1
**Owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)
**Last updated:** 2024-08-19
**Summary:** Describes the formatting and section conventions used when writing entries in the package's changelog.

---

## Purpose and Coverage

**Section owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)

This page is the working reference for anyone adding a line to the auditlog changelog — the person cutting a release, a contributor fixing a small wording problem in the command line help text, or someone updating the console log format. It covers:

- the file the changelog lives in and how it is organized,
- the fixed set of category headings we use and what belongs under each one,
- how an individual entry should be worded and capitalized,
- how entries should reference version numbers,
- worked examples for the five kinds of change auditlog's past releases have actually shipped (documentation, packaging, command help text, console log format, and speed), and
- how changelog work fits into the release checklist and review steps.

It does not cover the numbering scheme itself (see *Version Numbering for the Package*) or the mechanics of building a source distribution file (see *Packaging the Source Distribution*). Those pages are linked at the bottom.

The conventions here apply to every entry added to the changelog going forward. Older entries written before this page existed were not rewritten to match; you will see some drift if you scroll far enough back in `docs/CHANGELOG.md`.

## Where the Changelog Lives

The changelog is a single Markdown file, kept at `docs/CHANGELOG.md`, one folder up from this page. It is not split by year or by release the way some projects do it — auditlog is small enough that one file has worked fine so far. If it ever gets unwieldy we'll revisit, but as of this writing it's a few hundred lines.

A few related files live alongside it:

- `docs/release-notes/` — this folder, holding the conventions, the checklist, the version numbering rules, and the published notes for past releases.
- `docs/release-notes/changelog-snippet-format.txt` — a short plain-text spec for the entry line format, meant to be quoted directly rather than paraphrased. This page's examples are meant to match it; if the two ever disagree, treat the snippet format file as the source of truth for punctuation and the category line, and this page as the source of truth for wording style and worked examples.
- `scripts/check-changelog-format.sh` — a small shell script run near the end of the checklist that flags obviously malformed entries (missing category heading, missing version heading, stray tabs). It does not check wording quality — that's a human job.

## Changelog File Structure

`docs/CHANGELOG.md` is organized newest-first, with one heading per released version and, above all of those, a single `Unreleased` block for work that hasn't shipped yet.

The skeleton looks like this:

```markdown
# Changelog

## Unreleased

### Added
- ...

### Changed
- ...

### Fixed
- ...

## v1.2.0 - 2025-02-18

### Changed
- ...

### Fixed
- ...

## v1.1.0 - 2024-09-05

### Added
- ...
```

A few rules that keep this consistent:

1. The `Unreleased` block sits at the top, always, even when it's empty. An empty block is written as `## Unreleased` followed by nothing but a blank line — don't remove the heading between releases, just clear the entries under it once they've moved into a version heading.
2. Version headings use the exact tag that will be used when the release is tagged in git — `v1.2.0`, not `1.2.0` or `Version 1.2.0`. See *Version Numbering for the Package* for how that tag is chosen.
3. The date next to the version heading is the date the release was tagged, in `YYYY-MM-DD` form, not the date the changelog entry was written (those are sometimes a day or two apart).
4. Category subheadings appear only when they have at least one entry under them. Don't print an empty `### Removed` just to keep some imagined symmetry.
5. Entries are bullet points, one line each where possible. If an entry genuinely needs a second line, indent the continuation two spaces under the bullet.

## Category Conventions

**Section owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)

We use a fixed set of category subheadings under each version (or under `Unreleased`). Not every release uses every category — most releases only touch two or three of them.

| Category heading | What goes under it |
|---|---|
| `Added` | New command line options, new console output, anything a user of the package didn't have before. |
| `Changed` | Behavior that already existed but now works differently — including changes to command help text wording, console log format, and speed, when those changes aren't simply fixes. |
| `Fixed` | Fixes for something that was wrong: a broken help text description, a console log line that didn't line up, a slow path that behaved incorrectly rather than just slowly. |
| `Removed` | Options, output lines, or behavior taken away entirely. Rare for auditlog so far. |
| `Documentation` | Changes confined to the docs/ folder or README.md — no code changes at all. |
| `Packaging` | Changes to how the source distribution file is built or what it contains, without a change to how the package behaves once installed. |

A single release can, and often does, mix categories — the v1.1.0 release, for example, had both a `Changed` entry (console log format) and a `Packaging` entry (source distribution contents) side by side. What it should not mix is category *content*: a wording fix to help text goes under `Fixed`, not `Documentation`, even though at first glance "wording" sounds like a documentation change. `Documentation` is reserved specifically for the docs/ folder and README.md — help text lives in the package itself and gets its own line under `Added`, `Changed`, or `Fixed` depending on what happened to it.

## Entry Format and Style Guide

**Section owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)

Each entry is one bullet, written as a complete sentence fragment starting with a past-tense verb, ending with a period. A few worked-through rules:

- Start with what changed, not with "we" or "this release." Write "Widened the time column in console output" rather than "We widened the time column."
- Keep it to one sentence. If you need "and," consider whether it's really two entries.
- Don't restate the category in the sentence — under `Fixed`, write "Corrected the wrapping of long option descriptions," not "Fixed a bug where option descriptions wrapped wrong."
- Reference version numbers with the full tag (`v1.2.0`), never a bare number, and only when the entry is genuinely about a comparison across versions — most entries don't need one at all, since the version heading above them already says which release they belong to.
- Capitalize the first word of the sentence; don't capitalize the rest unless it's a proper noun. This one has slipped in the past — a few 2024 entries in `docs/CHANGELOG.md` are Title Cased throughout, left as-is rather than rewritten.
- Wrap lines at a reasonable width for a text editor's default view — we don't enforce a hard column count, but if a line runs past what fits comfortably in a normal editor window, it usually means the sentence is doing too much.

A minimal correctly formatted entry, quoted from `changelog-snippet-format.txt`:

```
- Reduced startup time by deferring optional setup work until it is first needed.
```

Note the leading `- `, the period at the end, and the lack of a category word inside the sentence.

## Version Number References

**Section owner:** Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)

Version numbers used in changelog entries and in version headings follow the scheme in *Version Numbering for the Package* (currently at v1.2 of that page). The short version, for the purposes of writing changelog entries:

- auditlog uses a three-part number, `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`.
- The `Unreleased` block does not carry a version number — don't guess ahead at what the next tag will be, since that call happens later in the checklist, not while entries are being written.
- When an entry needs to reference an earlier release for context ("this restores the wording used before v1.1.0"), use the full tag and don't abbreviate it to just the minor number.

One point worth calling out because it trips people up: the version heading in the changelog is added at release time, as one of the last checklist steps, not when the individual entries are written. Entries accumulate under `Unreleased` for however long the next release takes to come together — sometimes weeks — and only get a version heading and date once the release is actually tagged.

## Worked Examples by Change Type

The last several auditlog releases have each been fairly narrow — a release touching only documentation, or only packaging, or only the command line help text, and so on. This is deliberate; small releases are easier to write clean changelog entries for. Below is one worked example per kind of change, matched to the sibling page that goes into it in more depth.

### Documentation-only changes

**Section owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)

These entries go under `Documentation`, never under `Changed`, even when the docs page being fixed describes behavior.

```
### Documentation
- Fixed a broken cross-link between the version numbering page and the
  release checklist.
- Corrected heading capitalization across the release-notes/ pages to match
  the house style.
```

See *Release Notes: v1.0.0* for a released example of a version made up entirely of entries like these.

### Packaging-only changes

**Section owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)

Packaging entries describe what changed in the source distribution file itself, not what changed once the package is installed and running — those two things are usually different and sometimes an entry needs both a `Packaging` line and a separate `Changed` line.

```
### Packaging
- The source distribution now includes the docs/ folder, so a distribution
  file carries the same release notes as a full checkout.
- Removed a stray build folder that had been getting included in the
  distribution file by mistake.
```

For how the distribution file is actually built, see *Packaging the Source Distribution* and, for the environment it's built in, *Build Environment Notes*.

### Command help text changes

**Section owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Banks)

Help text entries are almost always `Fixed` (wording was wrong or confusing) or `Changed` (wording was fine but is being made clearer or more consistent). They should describe the effect on someone reading the help text, not the words themselves verbatim.

```
### Fixed
- Corrected wrapping of long option descriptions in the command line help
  text so they no longer overflow at the default terminal width.

### Changed
- Reworded several option descriptions in the command line help text for
  consistency with one another.
```

A running list of these, release by release, lives in *Command Help Text Changes Across Releases* — that page is the one to check before writing a new entry, so wording stays consistent with what's already documented there.

### Console log format changes

**Section owner:** Core Runtime (Sam Okafor)

These describe changes to what the console prints while the service or command line tool is running — column widths, ordering, added or removed fields in the printed line. They belong under `Changed` when the format shifts on purpose, and under `Fixed` when a previous format change didn't work as intended.

```
### Changed
- Console log lines now include a fixed-width time column so output lines
  up when piped through common line-oriented tools.

### Fixed
- Corrected a console log line that dropped its trailing field when the
  line ran long.
```

*Console Log Format Changes Across Releases* keeps a fuller record of these across versions; a changelog entry should be a short summary of what's written there in more detail.

### Speed changes

**Section owner:** Core Runtime (Sam Okafor)

Speed entries describe a change in how long something takes, in plain terms a reader can picture — "reduced," "shortened," "no longer waits on" — without giving exact timing figures, since those depend heavily on hardware and aren't something we commit to as a number.

```
### Changed
- Reduced the time needed to open the database file on startup by
  deferring optional setup work until it is first needed.

### Fixed
- The command line tool no longer pauses briefly on exit while closing the
  database file; it now closes it immediately.
```

*Speed Notes Across Releases* holds the fuller, per-release notes; keep the changelog entry itself short and let that page carry any additional context.

## Tie-in to the Release Checklist

**Section owner:** Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)

Updating the changelog is one line item in *Release Checklist* (v2.0), and there's a matching line in *Release Checklist Template (YAML)* that gets checked off as part of preparing a release. The order that matters here:

1. Entries accumulate under `Unreleased` as work merges — this page's conventions apply from the moment an entry is written, not just at release time.
2. When the checklist reaches its changelog step, the `Unreleased` heading is renamed to the version tag and given a date, and a fresh empty `Unreleased` heading is added above it.
3. `scripts/check-changelog-format.sh` is run at this point to catch formatting slips before anything is tagged.
4. Once the release is tagged, the newly headed version block in `docs/CHANGELOG.md` becomes the basis for that release's page under `docs/release-notes/release-notes-vX.Y.Z.md` — the published notes summarize the changelog block in prose, they don't just copy it verbatim.

One thing that's easy to get backwards: the checklist step is what adds the version heading, not the changelog convention itself. If you're writing an entry mid-cycle, it always goes under `Unreleased`, even the day before a release is expected to go out.

## Review and Merge Process

**Section owner:** Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)

Changelog entries are added in the same change that introduces the thing they describe — not as a separate follow-up. This keeps the entry accurate about what actually shipped, rather than being written from memory later.

A quick loop for anyone writing one:

- Draft the entry using the category and wording rules above.
- Check `docs/release-notes/command-help-text-changes.md`, `console-log-format-changes.md`, or `speed-notes.md` for existing wording on the same area, if the change touches one of those areas, so the phrasing stays consistent.
- Run `scripts/check-changelog-format.sh` locally before sending the change out for a look — it catches the mechanical problems (wrong heading level, missing bullet dash) so a reviewer doesn't have to.
- Get a second set of eyes on wording the same way any other doc change gets reviewed — there's no separate sign-off step just for the changelog.

Editors sometimes want to expand an entry into two or three sentences to explain *why* something changed. That belongs in the published release notes page, not in the changelog itself — keep the changelog terse and put the fuller explanation in `docs/release-notes/release-notes-vX.Y.Z.md` when that page gets written.

## Tools and Libraries

|---|---|---|
| git | 2.43.0 | Tracking changes to `docs/CHANGELOG.md` alongside the code they describe. |
| Python (interpreter) | 3.11.9 | Running the package itself, which uses only the standard library — no third-party install needed to write or check changelog entries. |
| PowerShell | 7.4.2 | Running `scripts/check-changelog-format.sh` and general repository upkeep on Windows machines. |
| markdownlint-cli | 0.41.0 | Catching stray Markdown formatting problems across the release-notes/ pages, changelog included. |
| sqlite3 command-line shell | 3.45.1 | Looking at the layout of the database file when writing a speed-related entry, without changing anything in it. |
| GNU tar | 1.35 | Checking the contents of a built source distribution file when writing a packaging entry. |

1	Title: Changelog Snippet Format
2	Version: 1.0
3	Owner: Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)
4	Last updated: 2024-06-18
5	
6	## Overview
7	
8	The changelog snippet format is the plain-text markup that contributors and maintainers paste into the main changelog when preparing a release of the auditlog package. This document defines the exact structure, field names, tags, and conventions for these snippets so that both human readers and the documentation build system can parse and process them consistently.
9	
10	All changes going into a release must be represented as a snippet, even if that change spans multiple commits or involves coordination across the team. The snippet becomes the canonical source of what changed in a given release from a user-facing perspective.
11	
12	Snippets are lightweight: they require no special tooling or syntax beyond plain text and square brackets. A contributor can create a snippet in any text editor and place it in the shared folder without any build steps.
13	
14	## Snippet Structure and Format
15	
16	Each snippet occupies one or more lines in the plain-text format. The minimal structure is:
17	
18	- One line declaring the **type** (using square brackets like `[doc]`, `[packaging]`, etc.)
19	- One line stating the **summary** (a short, imperative-mood description)
20	- An optional **body** section for additional detail (indented with spaces)
21	- An optional **issue reference** (using the `refs:` prefix)
22	
23	### Type Tags
24	
25	The type tag appears at the start of the snippet and must be one of the following:
26	
27	- `[doc]` — documentation or README changes
28	- `[packaging]` — package metadata, distribution configuration, or dependency changes
29	- `[cmd-help]` — command-line help text or usage message modifications
30	- `[console-format]` — changes to the console output format or log line structure
31	- `[speed]` — performance improvements or optimizations
32	
33	Do **not** create type tags for anything related to new features, bug fixes in core behavior, system stability, quality improvements, or modules. Those belong in a separate supplementary release-notes document (see the broader release-notes pages). If you are unsure whether your change belongs in a snippet, consult the owner of your change's category or refer to the changelog-conventions.md document.
34	
35	### Type Tag Details (Owner: Release Engineering, Priya Chandran)
36	
37	**[doc]** includes:
38	- Changes to the README.md in the repository root
39	- Modifications to any Markdown, reStructuredText, or plain-text files in the docs/ folder
40	- Improvements or clarifications to existing documentation
41	- Addition of new documentation files within the docs/ folder
42	- Updates to inline code comments that are meant to be read by end users (not internal developer notes)
43	- Changes to the structure or layout of existing documentation
44	
45	**[packaging]** covers:
46	- Updates to the package's setup configuration
47	- Changes to declared dependencies or their version ranges
48	- Adjustments to package metadata such as author, version string, or homepage
49	- Build or distribution script modifications in the scripts/ folder
50	- Creation or removal of configuration files at the repository root
51	- Changes to the build process or release tooling that affect how the package is distributed
52	
53	**[cmd-help]** applies to:
54	- Rewording of the help text that appears when users run the package's command-line interface
55	- Modifications to usage messages, option descriptions, or error messages
56	- Clarifications of argument syntax or behavior in the command output
57	- Addition or removal of command-line flags and their descriptions
58	- Changes to any text the user sees when they request help (such as `--help` or `-h` output)
59	
60	**[console-format]** applies when:
61	- The loopback HTTP service's output format changes (for example, timestamp precision, field order, or coloring)
62	- The package's standard output or standard error format is altered
63	- Log line structure or field names visible to users change
64	- Whitespace, delimiters, or line breaks in the output are modified
65	- New fields are added to the console output or existing fields are removed
66	
67	**[speed]** describes:
68	- Optimizations that reduce memory footprint or execution time,
69	- Caching or algorithmic improvements
70	- Elimination of redundant operations visible to end users (not internal refactoring)
71	- Measurable performance gains in common usage patterns
72	- Reductions in startup time, query time, or response time
73	
74	### Summary Line
75	
76	The summary line must be a short, present-tense, imperative description of what changed. It should fit on a single line, typically 50–70 characters. The imperative mood means you are giving a command or instruction:
77	
78	Correct examples:
79	```
80	Increase SQLite query timeout from 5s to 10s
81	```
82	
83	```
84	Add --json output mode to command interface
85	```
86	
87	```
88	Reorder console output fields for readability
89	```
90	
91	```
92	Document the --database argument in help text
93	```
94	
95	```
96	Cache prepared statements in HTTP service
97	```
98	
99	Incorrect examples (do not use these):
100	- "Added --json output mode" (past tense)
101	- "New --json output mode feature" (noun-based, not imperative)
102	- "Query timeout increased to 10s" (passive voice)
103	
104	Do not include the type tag on the summary line itself; it goes on the preceding line.
105	
106	### Optional Body and References
107	
108	If a change requires more explanation, add a blank line after the summary and then indented paragraphs (using at least two spaces):
109	
110	```
111	  This change was prompted by user feedback that the previous
112	  timeout was too short for large datasets. The new default
113	  accommodates up to 500k records without timing out.
114	```
115	
116	The body section can span multiple paragraphs if needed. Each paragraph should be separated by a blank line, and all content should be indented.
117	
118	To reference an internal tracking system or GitHub issue, add a line starting with `refs:` at the end of the snippet (after the body, if present, or after the summary if there is no body):
119	
120	```
121	refs: PROJ-3412
122	```
123	
124	or
125	
126	```
127	refs: github.com/example/auditlog/issues/42
128	```
129	
130	You may include multiple references if the snippet covers several related issues:
131	
132	```
133	refs: PROJ-3412, PROJ-3413
134	```
135	
136	## Examples and Worked Examples
137	
138	### Example 1: Documentation change
139	
140	```
141	[doc]
142	Update the README to describe the new --verbose output flag
143	
144	  The command-line help text now includes an example of how to use
145	  --verbose mode when debugging a SQLite database issue.
146	  
147	refs: PROJ-2891
148	```
149	
150	### Example 2: Console output format change (minimal)
151	
152	```
153	[console-format]
154	Print timestamp in microsecond precision instead of millisecond
155	```
156	
157	This snippet is short and complete without a body section.
158	
159	### Example 3: Packaging with impact note
160	
161	```
162	[packaging]
163	Raise minimum Python version to 3.9 in setup configuration
164	
165	  Previous releases supported Python 3.7+, but 3.7 and 3.8 are now
166	  beyond their support window. Developers targeting those versions
167	  should pin the package to v1.1.x or earlier.
168	
169	refs: PROJ-3056
170	```
171	
172	### Example 4: Command help text change
173	
174	```
175	[cmd-help]
176	Clarify the --database argument to indicate it accepts a file path
177	
178	  The help text previously read "database location" which was ambiguous.
179	  It now reads "database file path" with an example showing a full path.
180	```
181	
182	### Example 5: Speed improvement with metric
183	
184	```
185	[speed]
186	Cache compiled SQL statements to avoid re-parsing on each request
187	
188	  The loopback HTTP service now reuses prepared statements, which
189	  reduces CPU overhead by approximately 12 percent in typical usage
190	  patterns.
191	```
192	
193	### Example 6: Multi-area change (two snippets, not one)
194	
195	When a single commit affects multiple categories, create separate snippets. For instance, if you improve the help text AND optimize a command, write two snippets:
196	
197	```
198	[cmd-help]
199	Expand --verbose flag description with examples
200	```
201	
202	```
203	[speed]
204	Skip redundant SQL parsing when loading cached configuration
205	```
206	
207	These are two distinct user-facing changes and deserve two entries.
208	
209	### Example 7: Documentation fix for packaging change
210	
211	```
212	[doc]
213	Add section on Python 3.9+ requirement to the setup guide
214	
215	refs: PROJ-3056
216	```
217	
218	```
219	[packaging]
220	Require Python 3.9 or later in package metadata
221	```
222	
223	Again, the documentation change and the configuration change are separate snippets, even though they are related.
224	
225	## Integration with Version Numbering and Changelog Conventions
226	
227	Snippets fit into the broader release workflow. The version-numbering.md page (version 1.3, updated 2024-05-02) defines how snippet categories influence version bumps. A release with only `[doc]` or `[packaging]` snippets might trigger a patch-level increment, while new `[cmd-help]` or `[console-format]` changes could justify a minor version bump depending on the scale and user impact.
228	
229	The changelog-conventions.md document (version 1.1, last updated 2024-08-19) specifies how snippets are aggregated into a human-readable changelog. Snippets are grouped by type, sorted chronologically within each type, and presented under release headings. The order of type sections in the final changelog follows the order: `[doc]`, `[packaging]`, `[cmd-help]`, `[console-format]`, `[speed]`.
230	
231	When a release is being prepared, the Release Engineering team (led by Priya Chandran) reviews all unreleased snippets, checks them against the release-checklist.md (version 2.0, updated 2025-01-10) to ensure completeness, and copies them into the main changelog grouped by type. The snippets are then moved into the appropriate previous release-notes file (for example, release-notes-v1.2.md) for future reference.
232	
233	The release-checklist-template.yaml (version 1.0, updated 2025-01-12) now provides YAML automation for parts of this workflow. Teams may run a script that reads all snippet files in the changelog-snippets/ folder and generates the initial grouped structure, which a human then reviews and edits.
234	
235	## Submission Workflow
236	
237	1. Write a snippet for each distinct change you are making. If your commit spans multiple categories, create multiple snippets.
238	2. Place all snippets intended for the next release in the `docs/changelog-snippets/` folder using the naming convention `YYYYMMDD-description.txt`. For example: `20240618-console-timestamp-precision.txt`.
239	3. The description part of the filename should be lowercase and use hyphens instead of spaces. It should briefly name the change but does not need to match the snippet summary exactly.
240	4. Commit your snippet file(s) to git. The Release Engineering team tracks these as part of their release branch.
241	5. When releasing a new version, the Release Engineering team will use the release-checklist.md (version 2.0) to aggregate snippets into the main changelog file.
242	6. Snippets are then moved to a legacy folder (usually `docs/changelog-snippets/released/`) or simply removed from the unreleased folder once the version is tagged.
243	7. The corresponding release-notes file for that version (e.g., release-notes-v1.2.md) is updated to include the aggregated snippets and any additional technical details.
244	
245	Note: The naming convention uses date prefixes, but the order of inclusion in the changelog is managed by the Release Checklist Template (version 1.0, updated 2025-01-12), which sorts snippets by type and then by date, not by file system sort order.
246	
247	## Common Mistakes and Tips
248	
249	### Mistake: Over-scoping a snippet
250	
251	Snippets should describe a single, user-facing change. If your commit includes both a documentation fix and a command-line output format change, write two snippets. Combining them into one makes it harder for readers to understand what changed, and it blurs the distinction between unrelated areas. A user reading the changelog might look for the output format change in the `[doc]` section and miss it.
252	
253	### Mistake: Using future or past tense
254	
255	Snippets use imperative mood (present tense, command form). Write "Add --json flag" not "Added --json flag" or "Will add --json flag". The imperative mood makes the snippet feel like a direct statement of what the release does for the user.
256	
257	### Mistake: Creating a type tag that does not exist
258	
259	The five allowed tags are `[doc]`, `[packaging]`, `[cmd-help]`, `[console-format]`, and `[speed]`. Do not invent new tags such as `[feature]`, `[bugfix]`, `[internal]`, or `[refactor]` in snippets intended for submission. Internal-only notes or team discussions may use informal tags, but they will not be included in release documentation. If you are uncertain whether your change fits one of the five categories, ask the Release Engineering team or the owner of the change's area.
260	
261	### Mistake: Forgetting to indent the body
262	
263	The body of a snippet must be indented with at least two spaces. If you use only one space or no indentation, the documentation build system may fail to parse it correctly, and the changelog will be malformed. Always use consistent indentation throughout the body (two or more spaces; tabs work too but are less common in this repository).
264	
265	### Mistake: Referencing internal implementation details
266	
267	Snippet summaries and bodies should refer to what the user experiences, not how it works internally. Write "Increase SQLite query timeout" not "Bump the SQLite timeout constant from 5 to 10 in the database module". Users do not care about module names or constants; they care about behavior.
268	
269	### Tip: Include context in the body when the summary is ambiguous
270	
271	If "Improve help text formatting" could mean multiple things, add a sentence explaining which flags or sections are affected. If you are unsure whether your summary is clear, assume readers are not familiar with the code and add a sentence or two.
272	
273	### Tip: Use refs: for traceability
274	
275	Even informal changes benefit from a reference number. It helps the Release Engineering team backtrack to the original discussion or requirement. If your change is not tracked in a formal system, you can omit the refs line, but including it is encouraged.
276	
277	### Tip: Keep summaries short
278	
279	If your summary is longer than 70 characters, you may need to move some detail into the body section. Short summaries are easier to scan in the final changelog.
280	
281	### Tip: Validate your snippet in a text editor
282	
283	If you are unsure whether your indentation or formatting is correct, copy the snippet and paste it into a plain-text editor. Make sure blank lines are truly blank (no trailing spaces) and body content is consistently indented.
284	
285	## Terminology
286	
287	**Changelog** — The main human-readable document listing all released versions of the package and their changes, grouped by version number and category. Stored in the repository root or in docs/CHANGELOG.md (depending on the release cycle).
288	
289	**Changelog Snippet** — A plain-text block representing a single user-facing change. Contributors write snippets; the Release Engineering team aggregates them into the Changelog.
290	
291	**Console Output** — Text printed by the loopback HTTP service or the command-line interface to the user's terminal (standard output or standard error, excluding file writes to the SQLite database).
292	
293	**Imperative Mood** — A grammatical form used for commands or instructions. In changelog snippets, all summary lines use imperative mood: "Add support for", "Fix the", "Improve performance of", etc.
294	
295	**Package Metadata** — Information about the package itself: name, version, author, homepage, license, and declared dependencies. Stored in the package's configuration file at the repository root.
296	
297	**Release** — A tagged, versioned distribution of the package intended for end users. Releases are numbered according to the version-numbering.md guidelines and documented in release-notes files.
298	
299	**SQLite Database** — The local file used by the package to store records. Referred to generically as "the database file" in user-facing documentation.
300	
301	**Type Tag** — One of the five square-bracket labels (`[doc]`, `[packaging]`, `[cmd-help]`, `[console-format]`, `[speed]`) that categorizes a snippet and signals which kind of change it describes.
302	
303	**User-Facing Change** — Any modification that affects what an end user sees or experiences when using the package, including help text, console output, performance, and documentation. Internal refactoring or code reorganization that does not change user behavior is not user-facing.
304	
305	## Related Files and Paths
306	
307	| File or Path | Purpose |
308	|---|---|
309	| `docs/changelog-snippets/` | Directory where contributors place snippets staged for release. Each file is named `YYYYMMDD-description.txt`. This is the source of truth for unreleased changes. |
310	| `docs/changelog-snippets/released/` | Optional legacy folder for snippets that have already been included in a release. Some teams skip this folder and simply remove snippets once they are merged into the main changelog. |
311	| `docs/CHANGELOG.md` or `docs/changelog.rst` | Main changelog file (the format may vary by branch). Aggregated from snippets by the Release Engineering team. This is the human-facing summary of all releases. |
312	| `README.md` | Package overview at the repository root; changes to this file should have an accompanying `[doc]` snippet. |
313	| `docs/` | General documentation folder; Markdown and reStructuredText files here often correspond to `[doc]` snippets. |
314	| `scripts/` | Build, release, or utility scripts; changes here should have a `[packaging]` snippet if they affect the distribution. |
315	| `.gitignore`, `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `pyproject.toml` | Configuration files at the repository root; modifications require a `[packaging]` snippet if they affect users. |
316	| `auditlog/` | The main package directory; internal changes are not documented via snippets. Only user-facing output changes (like `[console-format]` or `[cmd-help]`) require snippets. |
317	
318	## Tools, Packages, and Dependencies
319	
320	| Tool or Package | Version | Purpose |
321	|---|---|---|
322	| Python | 3.9 or later | Runtime environment for the package and build scripts. The package supports no earlier versions as of v1.2.0. |
323	| sqlite3 | bundled with Python | Database library used by the package (no external dependency). |
324	| setuptools | 45.0 or later | Build and packaging tool for creating source distributions. Version 45.0+ is required for modern `setup.cfg` syntax. |
325	| git | 2.30 or later | Version control; used to tag releases and manage snippet files. |
326	| grep or similar | any recent | Optional; used by some teams to quickly locate snippets of a particular type before aggregating them. |
327	
328	(This page assumes the package uses only the Python standard library; no external runtime dependencies are declared.)
329	
330	## Changelog
331	
332	**2024-06-18 (v1.0)** — Initial release of the Changelog Snippet Format specification. Defined the five type tags (`[doc]`, `[packaging]`, `[cmd-help]`, `[console-format]`, `[speed]`) and the plain-text structure for snippets. Established the submission workflow for the changelog-snippets/ folder and naming conventions. *Owner: Docs Guild (Elena Petrova).*
333	
334	**2024-07-12 (v1.0 patch)** — Clarified that the naming convention for snippet files uses date prefixes (YYYYMMDD) but does not determine sort order in the final changelog. The Release Checklist Template will perform the sorting. Updated the integration section to reference version 2.0 of the Release Checklist. Added a note that moved snippets may be stored in a `released/` subfolder. *Owner: Release Engineering (Priya Chandran).*

336	**2024-08-19 (v1.1)** — Synchronized with changelog-conventions.md version 1.1 release. Added the "Common Mistakes and Tips" section based on feedback from the v1.1.0 release cycle. Corrected the list of allowed type tags (removed the deprecated `[internal]` tag that had been suggested in earlier drafts). Expanded body indentation requirements to clarify that two or more spaces are required. *Owner: Docs Guild (Elena Petrova).*
337	
338	**2024-11-03 (v1.2)** — Updated "Related Files and Paths" to reflect the repository structure documented in packaging-source-distribution.rst version 1.4. Added a note that some build steps may use grep or similar tools to filter snippets during aggregation. Clarified that changes to setup.cfg and pyproject.toml require `[packaging]` snippets. *Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen).*
339	
340	**2025-01-10 (v1.3)** — Realigned with release-checklist.md version 2.0. The Release Checklist Template (version 1.0, released 2025-01-12) now provides YAML automation for snippet aggregation. Removed manual example of changelog file paths; snippets no longer need to reference specific file locations outside the changelog-snippets/ folder. Added cross-reference to version-numbering.md version 1.3. *Owner: Release Engineering (Priya Chandran).*

Added "Example 3" and "Example 6" showing multi-area changes and the two-snippet pattern for coordinated changes. Title: Changelog Snippet Format
Version: 1.0
Owner: Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)
Last updated: 2024-06-18

## Overview

The changelog snippet format is the plain-text markup that contributors and maintainers paste into the main changelog when preparing a release of the auditlog package. This document defines the exact structure, field names, tags, and conventions for these snippets so that both human readers and the documentation build system can parse and process them consistently.

All changes going into a release must be represented as a snippet, even if that change spans multiple commits or involves coordination across the team. The snippet becomes the canonical source of what changed in a given release from a user-facing perspective.

Snippets are lightweight: they require no special tooling or syntax beyond plain text and square brackets. A contributor can create a snippet in any text editor and place it in the shared folder without any build steps.

## Snippet Structure and Format

Each snippet occupies one or more lines in the plain-text format. The minimal structure is:

- One line declaring the **type** (using square brackets like `[doc]`, `[packaging]`, etc.)
- One line stating the **summary** (a short, imperative-mood description)
- An optional **body** section for additional detail (indented with spaces)
- An optional **issue reference** (using the `refs:` prefix)

### Type Tags

The type tag appears at the start of the snippet and must be one of the following:

- `[doc]` — documentation or README changes
- `[packaging]` — package metadata, distribution configuration, or dependency changes
- `[cmd-help]` — command-line help text or usage message modifications
- `[console-format]` — changes to the console output format or log line structure
- `[speed]` — performance improvements or optimizations

Do **not** create type tags for anything related to new features, bug fixes in core behavior, system stability, quality improvements, or modules. Those belong in a separate supplementary release-notes document (see the broader release-notes pages). If you are unsure whether your change belongs in a snippet, consult the owner of your change's category or refer to the changelog-conventions.md document.

### Type Tag Details (Owner: Release Engineering, Priya Chandran)

**[doc]** includes:
- Changes to the README.md in the repository root
- Modifications to any Markdown, reStructuredText, or plain-text files in the docs/ folder
- Improvements or clarifications to existing documentation
- Addition of new documentation files within the docs/ folder
- Updates to inline code comments that are meant to be read by end users (not internal developer notes)
- Changes to the structure or layout of existing documentation

**[packaging]** covers:
- Updates to the package's setup configuration
- Changes to declared dependencies or their version ranges
- Adjustments to package metadata such as author, version string, or homepage
- Build or distribution script modifications in the scripts/ folder
- Creation or removal of configuration files at the repository root
- Changes to the build process or release tooling that affect how the package is distributed

**[cmd-help]** applies to:
- Rewording of the help text that appears when users run the package's command-line interface
- Modifications to usage messages, option descriptions, or error messages
- Clarifications of argument syntax or behavior in the command output
- Addition or removal of command-line flags and their descriptions
- Changes to any text the user sees when they request help (such as `--help` or `-h` output)

**[console-format]** applies when:
- The loopback HTTP service's output format changes (for example, timestamp precision, field order, or coloring)
- The package's standard output or standard error format is altered
- Log line structure or field names visible to users change
- Whitespace, delimiters, or line breaks in the output are modified
- New fields are added to the console output or existing fields are removed

**[speed]** describes:
- Optimizations that reduce memory footprint or execution time,
- Caching or algorithmic improvements
- Elimination of redundant operations visible to end users (not internal refactoring)
- Measurable performance gains in common usage patterns
- Reductions in startup time, query time, or response time

### Summary Line

The summary line must be a short, present-tense, imperative description of what changed. It should fit on a single line, typically 50–70 characters. The imperative mood means you are giving a command or instruction:

Correct examples:
```
Increase SQLite query timeout from 5s to 10s
```

```
Add --json output mode to command interface
```

```
Reorder console output fields for readability
```

```
Document the --database argument in help text
```

```
Cache prepared statements in HTTP service
```

Incorrect examples (do not use these):
- "Added --json output mode" (past tense)
- "New --json output mode feature" (noun-based, not imperative)
- "Query timeout increased to 10s" (passive voice)

Do not include the type tag on the summary line itself; it goes on the preceding line.

### Optional Body and References

If a change requires more explanation, add a blank line after the summary and then indented paragraphs (using at least two spaces):

```
  This change was prompted by user feedback that the previous
  timeout was too short for large datasets. The new default
  accommodates up to 500k records without timing out.
```

The body section can span multiple paragraphs if needed. Each paragraph should be separated by a blank line, and all content should be indented.

To reference an internal tracking system or GitHub issue, add a line starting with `refs:` at the end of the snippet (after the body, if present, or after the summary if there is no body):

```
refs: PROJ-3412
```

or

```
refs: github.com/example/auditlog/issues/42
```

You may include multiple references if the snippet covers several related issues:

```
refs: PROJ-3412, PROJ-3413
```

## Examples and Worked Examples

### Example 1: Documentation change

```
[doc]
Update the README to describe the new --verbose output flag

  The command-line help text now includes an example of how to use
  --verbose mode when debugging a SQLite database issue.
  
refs: PROJ-2891
```

### Example 2: Console output format change (minimal)

```
[console-format]
Print timestamp in microsecond precision instead of millisecond
```

This snippet is short and complete without a body section.

### Example 3: Packaging with impact note

```
[packaging]
Raise minimum Python version to 3.9 in setup configuration

  Previous releases supported Python 3.7+, but 3.7 and 3.8 are now
  beyond their support window. Developers targeting those versions
  should pin the package to v1.1.x or earlier.

refs: PROJ-3056
```

### Example 4: Command help text change

```
[cmd-help]
Clarify the --database argument to indicate it accepts a file path

  The help text previously read "database location" which was ambiguous.
  It now reads "database file path" with an example showing a full path.
```

### Example 5: Speed improvement with metric

```
[speed]
Cache compiled SQL statements to avoid re-parsing on each request

  The loopback HTTP service now reuses prepared statements, which
  reduces CPU overhead by approximately 12 percent in typical usage
  patterns.
```

### Example 6: Multi-area change (two snippets, not one)

When a single commit affects multiple categories, create separate snippets. For instance, if you improve the help text AND optimize a command, write two snippets:

```
[cmd-help]
Expand --verbose flag description with examples
```

```
[speed]
Skip redundant SQL parsing when loading cached configuration
```

These are two distinct user-facing changes and deserve two entries.

### Example 7: Documentation fix for packaging change

```
[doc]
Add section on Python 3.9+ requirement to the setup guide

refs: PROJ-3056
```

```
[packaging]
Require Python 3.9 or later in package metadata
```

Again, the documentation change and the configuration change are separate snippets, even though they are related.

## Integration with Version Numbering and Changelog Conventions

Snippets fit into the broader release workflow. The version-numbering.md page (version 1.3, updated 2024-05-02) defines how snippet categories influence version bumps. A release with only `[doc]` or `[packaging]` snippets might trigger a patch-level increment, while new `[cmd-help]` or `[console-format]` changes could justify a minor version bump depending on the scale and user impact.

The changelog-conventions.md document (version 1.1, last updated 2024-08-19) specifies how snippets are aggregated into a human-readable changelog. Snippets are grouped by type, sorted chronologically within each type, and presented under release headings. The order of type sections in the final changelog follows the order: `[doc]`, `[packaging]`, `[cmd-help]`, `[console-format]`, `[speed]`.

When a release is being prepared, the Release Engineering team (led by Priya Chandran) reviews all unreleased snippets, checks them against the release-checklist.md (version 2.0, updated 2025-01-10) to ensure completeness, and copies them into the main changelog grouped by type. The snippets are then moved into the appropriate previous release-notes file (for example, release-notes-v1.2.md) for future reference.

The release-checklist-template.yaml (version 1.0, updated 2025-01-12) now provides YAML automation for parts of this workflow. Teams may run a script that reads all snippet files in the changelog-snippets/ folder and generates the initial grouped structure, which a human then reviews and edits.

## Submission Workflow

1. Write a snippet for each distinct change you are making. If your commit spans multiple categories, create multiple snippets.
2. Place all snippets intended for the next release in the `docs/changelog-snippets/` folder using the naming convention `YYYYMMDD-description.txt`. For example: `20240618-console-timestamp-precision.txt`.
3. The description part of the filename should be lowercase and use hyphens instead of spaces. It should briefly name the change but does not need to match the snippet summary exactly.
4. Commit your snippet file(s) to git. The Release Engineering team tracks these as part of their release branch.
5. When releasing a new version, the Release Engineering team will use the release-checklist.md (version 2.0) to aggregate snippets into the main changelog file.
6. Snippets are then moved to a legacy folder (usually `docs/changelog-snippets/released/`) or simply removed from the unreleased folder once the version is tagged.
7. The corresponding release-notes file for that version (e.g., release-notes-v1.2.md) is updated to include the aggregated snippets and any additional technical details.

Note: The naming convention uses date prefixes, but the order of inclusion in the changelog is managed by the Release Checklist Template (version 1.0, updated 2025-01-12), which sorts snippets by type and then by date, not by file system sort order.

## Common Mistakes and Tips

### Mistake: Over-scoping a snippet

Snippets should describe a single, user-facing change. If your commit includes both a documentation fix and a command-line output format change, write two snippets. Combining them into one makes it harder for readers to understand what changed, and it blurs the distinction between unrelated areas. A user reading the changelog might look for the output format change in the `[doc]` section and miss it.

### Mistake: Using future or past tense

Snippets use imperative mood (present tense, command form). Write "Add --json flag" not "Added --json flag" or "Will add --json flag". The imperative mood makes the snippet feel like a direct statement of what the release does for the user.

### Mistake: Creating a type tag that does not exist

The five allowed tags are `[doc]`, `[packaging]`, `[cmd-help]`, `[console-format]`, and `[speed]`. Do not invent new tags such as `[feature]`, `[bugfix]`, `[internal]`, or `[refactor]` in snippets intended for submission. Internal-only notes or team discussions may use informal tags, but they will not be included in release documentation. If you are uncertain whether your change fits one of the five categories, ask the Release Engineering team or the owner of the change's area.

### Mistake: Forgetting to indent the body

The body of a snippet must be indented with at least two spaces. If you use only one space or no indentation, the documentation build system may fail to parse it correctly, and the changelog will be malformed. Always use consistent indentation throughout the body (two or more spaces; tabs work too but are less common in this repository).

### Mistake: Referencing internal implementation details

Snippet summaries and bodies should refer to what the user experiences, not how it works internally. Write "Increase SQLite query timeout" not "Bump the SQLite timeout constant from 5 to 10 in the database module". Users do not care about module names or constants; they care about behavior.

### Tip: Include context in the body when the summary is ambiguous

If "Improve help text formatting" could mean multiple things, add a sentence explaining which flags or sections are affected. If you are unsure whether your summary is clear, assume readers are not familiar with the code and add a sentence or two.

### Tip: Use refs: for traceability

Even informal changes benefit from a reference number. It helps the Release Engineering team backtrack to the original discussion or requirement. If your change is not tracked in a formal system, you can omit the refs line, but including it is encouraged.

### Tip: Keep summaries short

If your summary is longer than 70 characters, you may need to move some detail into the body section. Short summaries are easier to scan in the final changelog.

### Tip: Validate your snippet in a text editor

If you are unsure whether your indentation or formatting is correct, copy the snippet and paste it into a plain-text editor. Make sure blank lines are truly blank (no trailing spaces) and body content is consistently indented.

## Terminology

**Changelog** — The main human-readable document listing all released versions of the package and their changes, grouped by version number and category. Stored in the repository root or in docs/CHANGELOG.md (depending on the release cycle).

**Changelog Snippet** — A plain-text block representing a single user-facing change. Contributors write snippets; the Release Engineering team aggregates them into the Changelog.

**Console Output** — Text printed by the loopback HTTP service or the command-line interface to the user's terminal (standard output or standard error, excluding file writes to the SQLite database).

**Imperative Mood** — A grammatical form used for commands or instructions. In changelog snippets, all summary lines use imperative mood: "Add support for", "Fix the", "Improve performance of", etc.

**Package Metadata** — Information about the package itself: name, version, author, homepage, license, and declared dependencies. Stored in the package's configuration file at the repository root.

**Release** — A tagged, versioned distribution of the package intended for end users. Releases are numbered according to the version-numbering.md guidelines and documented in release-notes files.

**SQLite Database** — The local file used by the package to store records. Referred to generically as "the database file" in user-facing documentation.

**Type Tag** — One of the five square-bracket labels (`[doc]`, `[packaging]`, `[cmd-help]`, `[console-format]`, `[speed]`) that categorizes a snippet and signals which kind of change it describes.

**User-Facing Change** — Any modification that affects what an end user sees or experiences when using the package, including help text, console output, performance, and documentation. Internal refactoring or code reorganization that does not change user behavior is not user-facing.

## Related Files and Paths

| File or Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docs/changelog-snippets/` | Directory where contributors place snippets staged for release. Each file is named `YYYYMMDD-description.txt`. This is the source of truth for unreleased changes. |
| `docs/changelog-snippets/released/` | Optional legacy folder for snippets that have already been included in a release. Some teams skip this folder and simply remove snippets once they are merged into the main changelog. |
| `docs/CHANGELOG.md` or `docs/changelog.rst` | Main changelog file (the format may vary by branch). Aggregated from snippets by the Release Engineering team. This is the human-facing summary of all releases. |
| `README.md` | Package overview at the repository root; changes to this file should have an accompanying `[doc]` snippet. |
| `docs/` | General documentation folder; Markdown and reStructuredText files here often correspond to `[doc]` snippets. |
| `scripts/` | Build, release, or utility scripts; changes here should have a `[packaging]` snippet if they affect the distribution. |
| `.gitignore`, `setup.py`, `setup.cfg`, `pyproject.toml` | Configuration files at the repository root; modifications require a `[packaging]` snippet if they affect users. |
| `auditlog/` | The main package directory; internal changes are not documented via snippets. Only user-facing output changes (like `[console-format]` or `[cmd-help]`) require snippets. |

## Tools, Packages, and Dependencies

| Tool or Package | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.9 or later | Runtime environment for the package and build scripts. The package supports no earlier versions as of v1.2.0. |
| sqlite3 | bundled with Python | Database library used by the package (no external dependency). |
| setuptools | 45.0 or later | Build and packaging tool for creating source distributions. Version 45.0+ is required for modern `setup.cfg` syntax. |
| git | 2.30 or later | Version control; used to tag releases and manage snippet files. |
| grep or similar | any recent | Optional; used by some teams to quickly locate snippets of a particular type before aggregating them. |

(This page assumes the package uses only the Python standard library; no external runtime dependencies are declared.)
