# Release Checklist

**Version:** 2.0
**Owner:** Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)
**Last updated:** 2025-01-10

## Purpose and Coverage

This page walks through everything Release Engineering and the reviewing teams do between deciding "the next auditlog version is ready" and having that version tagged, packaged, and published. It ties together the version numbering rules, the changelog conventions, the packaging steps for the source distribution, and the smaller per-theme reviews — documentation, packaging, command help text, console log format, and speed — that auditlog releases have settled into since v1.0.0.

Use this page as the master checklist. The linked sibling pages go into more depth on their own topics; this page is where those topics meet in the order a maintainer actually works through them on release day. If you're looking for the fill-in-the-blanks version to paste into a release thread, that's release-checklist-template.yaml — this page is the explanation behind that template, not a replacement for it.

auditlog is small on purpose: a command line interface, a loopback HTTP service, and a local SQLite database file, all built on the standard library with no outside dependencies to track. That smallness is part of why the release process below can stay this short — there's no dependency-bump review, no build matrix across operating systems, and no compiled extension to worry about. Most of what follows exists to catch wording drift between the command line, the console output, and the docs, rather than anything more elaborate.

## Terminology

- **Source distribution (sdist)** — the tarball built from the working tree that contains the package's source files, README.md, and packaging metadata; the only distribution format auditlog currently ships.
- **Wheel** — a pre-built distribution format; auditlog does not currently publish a wheel, since the package has no compiled extension and needs no extra build step for callers.
- **Semantic versioning** — the MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbering convention described in full in version-numbering.md; this page assumes familiarity with it.
- **Unreleased section** — the top block of CHANGELOG.md where entries land as they're written, before a version number and date are assigned at tag time.
- **Tag** — a git tag of the form `vX.Y.Z` applied to the commit that becomes a release.
- **Console log format** — the shape and wording of the lines the package writes to the console while it runs; distinct from the records kept in the database file.
- **Command help text** — the text printed for each command line option and subcommand when a caller asks for help.
- **Database file** — the local SQLite file where the package keeps its records; the release process doesn't touch its contents, only confirms the package still opens and closes the file cleanly.
- **Loopback service** — the small HTTP service the package can run, bound to a loopback port only, used for local access to the same records the command line reads.
- **Checksum** — the SHA-256 value recorded for the sdist tarball once it's built, used to confirm the file that gets published matches the file that was reviewed.
- **Dry run** — building the sdist and installing it into a throwaway virtual environment without publishing it anywhere, to confirm the package still imports and the command line still starts.
- **Narrow release** — a release that only touches one of the five reviewed themes; most auditlog releases since v1.0.0 have been narrow on purpose, to keep sign-off simple.

## Version Numbering — Owner: Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)

auditlog follows semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. The full rules, including what counts as a breaking change for a package this small, live in version-numbering.md — see that page for the worked examples. The short version repeated here for convenience:

- PATCH releases (x.y.**Z**) cover fixes to command help text, console log format wording, or speed, and documentation-only changes. Nothing in the command line surface changes shape.
- MINOR releases (x.**Y**.z) add a new command, a new command line option, or a new field in the console log lines, in a way that doesn't break anything a caller was already relying on.
- MAJOR releases (**X**.y.z) change or remove something a caller was depending on — an existing command line option's meaning, the loopback service's startup behavior, or the on-disk location of the database file.

Most auditlog releases so far have stayed narrow — a single theme, one owning team, a short sign-off. Whether that narrow release is a PATCH or a MINOR sometimes comes down to a judgment call rather than a strict rule; v1.1.0 (packaging only) shipped as a MINOR mostly out of caution, even though a strict reading of the rules above would probably call it a PATCH. When in doubt, Release Engineering rounds up rather than down.

## Changelog Conventions — Owner: Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)

Full conventions, including the exact heading levels and bullet prefixes, are in changelog-conventions.md, with a plain-text reference for line formatting in changelog-snippet-format.txt. Release Engineering doesn't own the conventions, but every release depends on them being followed correctly, so the short version is repeated here:

1. Every change that a caller might observe gets one line in the Unreleased section of CHANGELOG.md at the repository root, added in the same commit (or a nearby one) as the change itself — not written after the fact at release time.
2. Each line starts with one of five tags: `Docs:`, `Packaging:`, `Help:`, `Log:`, or `Speed:`. These line up with the five themes reviewed separately below. A change that doesn't fit one of those five tags is unusual enough that Release Engineering should ask the author about it before the release goes out.
3. Lines are written in the past tense, one sentence, no trailing period — for example, `Log: dropped the trailing space after the timestamp on startup lines`.
4. At tag time, the Unreleased heading is renamed to the version and date, and a new empty Unreleased heading is added above it.

A worked example of the rename, going from one release to the next:

```
## Unreleased

## 1.2.0 - 2025-02-20
- Log: dropped the trailing space after the timestamp on startup lines
- Speed: cut the loopback service's startup time roughly in half
```

becomes, once a documentation change lands after the tag:

```
## Unreleased
- Docs: clarified the paragraph on the database file's default folder

## 1.2.0 - 2025-02-20
- Log: dropped the trailing space after the timestamp on startup lines
- Speed: cut the loopback service's startup time roughly in half
```

Docs Guild has flagged, more than once, that the tag prefixes get typed inconsistently under deadline pressure — `docs:` lowercase, or `Documentation:` spelled out. None of that breaks anything mechanically since nothing parses the changelog automatically, but it makes the file harder to scan, so it's worth a second look during the documentation review step below.

## Owners by Section

| Section | Owner |
|---|---|
| Version numbering | Release Engineering (Priya Chandran) |
| Changelog conventions | Docs Guild (Elena Petrova) |
| Documentation review | Docs Guild (Elena Petrova) |
| Command help text review | Developer Experience (Theo Banks) |
| Console log format review | Core Runtime (Sam Okafor) |
| Speed review | Core Runtime (Sam Okafor) |
| Packaging review | Platform Tools (Mara Olsen) |
| Tagging and publishing | Release Engineering (Priya Chandran) |

## Pre-Release Checklist — Owner: Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)

This is the sequence Release Engineering works through, roughly in order, once someone proposes that the current state of the main branch is ready to become a release. Steps are grouped by theme so the right team can sign off on its own piece without waiting on the others.

### 1. Confirm the Unreleased section is complete

- Read through every commit since the last tag (`git log v1.2.0..HEAD --oneline`) and confirm each one that touches caller-visible behavior has a matching line in the Unreleased section.
- Check that every line uses one of the five tags described above.
- Fix any wording that reads like an internal note rather than something a caller would care about — "cleaned up the code around startup" is not a changelog line; "cut the loopback service's startup time roughly in half" is.

### 2. Documentation review — Owner: Docs Guild (Elena Petrova)

- Confirm README.md still matches the current command line surface.
- Confirm any changed wording in the docs/ folder is consistent with the changelog entries tagged `Docs:`.
- Spell out version numbers and dates consistently — this has been a recurring source of small mismatches between this page and the individual release-notes pages, and it's an easy thing to catch with a careful read.

### 3. Command help text review — Owner: Developer Experience (Theo Banks)

- Print the help text for every command and subcommand and read it start to finish, not just the parts that changed.
- Confirm wording matches what's written in command-help-text-changes.md for the current version's entry.
- Watch for column misalignment when help text wraps in a narrower terminal window — this has caused more narrow releases than any other single cause; command-help-text-changes.md has the specific past examples.

### 4. Console log format review — Owner: Core Runtime (Sam Okafor)

- Start the command line and the loopback service and read the console lines they print during normal startup and shutdown.
- Confirm the format matches the current entry in console-log-format-changes.md.
- Confirm timestamps, spacing, and line endings are consistent across both the command line and the loopback service — these two have drifted apart from each other in the past without anyone catching it until a caller flagged it, which is what prompted v1.2.0.

### 5. Speed review — Owner: Core Runtime (Sam Okafor)

- Run the package through its normal startup and shutdown a handful of times and compare the rough timing by eye against the notes for the previous version in speed-notes.md.
- If a change in this release was tagged `Speed:` in the changelog, confirm the improvement (or the acceptable trade-off) is described accurately there and in speed-notes.md.
- Speed reviews for auditlog are informal — there's no dedicated tooling for this, just a maintainer with a stopwatch and the previous version's notes open side by side. This has worked fine so far given how narrow most speed-related releases have been.

### 6. Packaging review — Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)

- Confirm packaging-source-distribution.rst matches the current pyproject.toml and MANIFEST.in — see the full walkthrough below.
- Confirm build-environment-notes.rst still reflects whatever machine or container image Platform Tools uses to build the sdist.

### 7. Sign-off

Each of the four owning teams above (Docs Guild, Developer Experience, Core Runtime, Platform Tools) gives a short thumbs-up in the release thread once their section is clean. Release Engineering doesn't tag anything until all four have checked in, even for a narrow release that only touches one theme — a documentation-only release still gets a nod from the other three confirming they see nothing of theirs in the diff. This has occasionally felt like overkill for a one-line change, but it's caught a couple of mislabeled changelog entries that would otherwise have shipped under the wrong tag.

## Frequently Missed Steps

A short, informal list of the mistakes that show up most often, kept here because the formal checklist above doesn't always stop them:

- Forgetting to rename the Unreleased heading before tagging, so the tag ends up pointing at a commit where the changelog still says "Unreleased" at the top.
- Building the sdist from a working tree that has uncommitted changes sitting in it — the tarball then doesn't match what's in git, and the checksum recorded in the release thread stops meaning anything useful.
- Skipping the dry-run install because "nothing packaging-related changed this time" — this has bitten Platform Tools at least once, since a documentation-only release can still accidentally add a stray file to the tarball if MANIFEST.in is out of date.
- Announcing the release before the tag is actually pushed, which leaves a short window where the announcement links to a tag that doesn't exist yet on the shared repository.

## Packaging the Source Distribution — Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)

auditlog ships as a single sdist; there is no wheel and no compiled extension to worry about. The full walkthrough, including the exact pyproject.toml fields Platform Tools maintains, lives in packaging-source-distribution.rst. What follows is the shape of it as Release Engineering sees it from the outside.

From a clean working tree, with the version already bumped in pyproject.toml and the changelog heading already renamed:

```
python -m build --sdist
```

This produces a single file under `dist/`, named something like `auditlog-1.2.0.tar.gz`. Platform Tools then:

1. Extracts the tarball into a throwaway folder and confirms the file listing matches what MANIFEST.in describes — no docs/ files that shouldn't be there, no stray files left over from an editor's autosave.
2. Installs the tarball into a fresh virtual environment and confirms the package imports and the command line starts:

```
python -m venv dryrun
dryrun\Scripts\pip install dist\auditlog-1.2.0.tar.gz
```

3. Confirms the database file still opens with its expected default settings by pointing the installed command line at a throwaway file and checking one setting from the sqlite3 command line directly:

```
sqlite3 dryrun.db "PRAGMA journal_mode;"
```

4. Records the SHA-256 checksum of the tarball in the release thread:

```
Get-FileHash dist\auditlog-1.2.0.tar.gz -Algorithm SHA256
```

5. Confirms build-environment-notes.rst still matches the machine that produced the tarball — Python version, operating system, and the exact `build` and `setuptools` versions pinned in the release engineering environment file.

Platform Tools has, twice now, caught a release where the tarball included a leftover file that had been removed from git but was still sitting in the working tree's build cache. Step 1 above exists specifically because of that, and it's the one step Platform Tools has asked never to be shortened, even for a documentation-only release.

## Build Environment Notes

Platform Tools keeps a short record of exactly which machine, operating system, and interpreter version produced each published tarball in build-environment-notes.rst. Release Engineering doesn't maintain that page but checks it during the packaging review step above — a tarball built on an unexpected machine is worth a question before it ships, even if nothing looks wrong on the surface.

## Tagging and Publishing — Owner: Release Engineering (Priya Chandran)

Once sign-off is in from all four owning teams:

```
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "auditlog 1.2.0"
git push origin v1.2.0
```

Then, from the same clean checkout used to build the reviewed tarball:

```
python -m twine upload dist/auditlog-1.2.0.tar.gz
```

Release Engineering posts a short release announcement in the team's wiki channel, linking the renamed changelog heading and, for releases that touch one of the five reviewed themes, the matching thematic page (command-help-text-changes.md, console-log-format-changes.md, or speed-notes.md). Narrow releases — documentation-only or packaging-only — get a one-line announcement; anything wider gets a short paragraph walking through what changed and why.

## Post-Release Steps

- Clear out `dist/` so the next release starts from an empty folder rather than accidentally reusing an old tarball.
- Update release-checklist-template.yaml if any step above changed during this release cycle — the template is meant to stay in sync with this page, and it's easy for the two to drift if the template isn't touched at the same time.
- Confirm README.md in the docs/release-notes/ folder still lists every page correctly, including any new thematic entries added for this release.

## Past Release Summaries

Since v1.0.0, most auditlog releases have stayed narrow on purpose — each one covers a single theme, which keeps the review above short and keeps each of the four owning teams from having to sign off on work outside their area. The table below tracks which theme each past release covered; the full write-up for each is either a dedicated release-notes page (for the three wider releases) or an entry in the matching thematic page (for the narrower ones).

| Version | Date | Theme | Owner | Notes page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1.0.0 | 2024-04-01 | Documentation only | Developer Experience (Theo Banks) | release-notes-v1.0.md |
| v1.1.0 | 2024-09-05 | Packaging only | Platform Tools (Mara Olsen) | release-notes-v1.1.md |
| v1.2.0 | 2025-02-20 | Console log format only | Core Runtime (Sam Okafor) | release-notes-v1.2.md |
| v1.2.1 | 2025-05-18 | Command help text only | Developer Experience (Theo Banks) | command-help-text-changes.md |
| v1.3.0 | 2025-11-02 | Speed only | Core Runtime (Sam Okafor) | speed-notes.md |

Below is a short narrative for each, kept intentionally brief — the dedicated pages have the full record of changes.

### v1.0.0 — documentation only (2024-04-01)

The first tagged release after the package's internal wiki presence was cleaned up. Nothing in the command line, the console log lines, or the loopback service changed at all; the entire diff was inside docs/ and README.md. Release Engineering almost skipped a version bump entirely for this one, on the grounds that nothing caller-visible had changed, but settled on a PATCH release so the tag would give the docs a fixed point to reference going forward. See release-notes-v1.0.md for the full write-up.

### v1.1.0 — packaging only (2024-09-05)

Platform Tools reworked the pyproject.toml fields and tightened MANIFEST.in after the leftover-file problem mentioned above under Packaging the Source Distribution. The installed package was identical to v1.0.0 in every caller-visible way; only the tarball's contents and the build instructions changed. Tagged as a MINOR release out of caution, even though version-numbering.md would probably call this a PATCH in hindsight. See release-notes-v1.1.md.

### v1.2.0 — console log format only (2025-02-20)

Core Runtime changed the timestamp format on the console lines the package prints during startup and shutdown, and made the command line and the loopback service print that format the same way — they had drifted apart, as mentioned under Console Log Format Review above. No command line options changed, no help text changed, and no database file behavior changed. See release-notes-v1.2.md and console-log-format-changes.md for the specific before-and-after wording.

### v1.2.1 — command help text only (2025-05-18)

Developer Experience fixed a column-alignment problem in the help text for one of the package's commands, and cleaned up wording that had gone stale after v1.2.0's log format change — a couple of help strings still described the old timestamp format. No dedicated release-notes page exists for this one; the change is recorded in command-help-text-changes.md.

### v1.3.0 — speed only (2025-11-02)

Core Runtime shaved a measurable amount off the loopback service's startup time by changing how early the service opens the database file relative to when it starts listening for callers. Nothing about the command line, the console log wording, or the packaging changed. Recorded in speed-notes.md rather than a dedicated release-notes page.

1	# Speed Notes Across Releases
2	
3	**Version:** 1.0
4	**Owner:** Core Runtime (Sam Okafor)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-11-02
6	
7	## Summary
8	
9	This page collects the small speed improvements made to the `activitylog` package and to the database file across past releases. None of these were large rewrites — they're the kind of thing you see when you're staring at a cold start on a Monday morning and think "that took longer than it should." This page exists so the next person who sees that something feels slow has somewhere to check before opening a new investigation from scratch.
10	
11	What this page covers is deliberately narrow: startup time, first-write latency, how the database file behaves as it grows, and the console output overhead. It does not cover packaging speed (see `packaging-source-distribution.rst`) or how fast the checklist itself can be completed (nobody has asked).
12	
13	## Terminology
14	
15	- **Cold start** — the time from invoking the package on the command line to the point where it is ready to accept work. Distinct from a "warm" run where the interpreter and file handles are already primed by a prior process in the same shell session.
16	- **First-write latency** — the delay observed on the very first record written to the database file after the file is opened, as opposed to the steady-state latency of subsequent writes.
17	- **Loopback service** — the HTTP service that only accepts connections from the local host; referred to elsewhere as "the service."
18	- **Journal mode** — the SQLite setting controlling how the database file manages its temporary journal during writes; the two modes referenced on this page are the original rollback-journal mode and `WAL`.
19	- **Synchronous setting** — the SQLite pragma controlling how aggressively the database file is flushed to disk after a write; values referenced here are `FULL` and `NORMAL`.
20	- **Console log format** — the layout of lines printed to standard output/error during a run; see `console-log-format-changes.md` for the full account of format changes, several of which had speed side effects.
21	- **Steady state** — the point in a long-running service process where startup costs have been paid and per-record costs dominate.
22	- **Vacuum threshold** — an informal term used on this page for the point at which the database file's internal free space becomes large enough that a maintenance pass is worth doing; not a formal setting name, just how the team talks about it.
23	- **Import surface** — the set of standard library modules loaded at process start; a larger import surface generally means a slower cold start.
24	- **Flush interval** — how often buffered console output is written out during a run; tightened or loosened in a couple of releases as a side effect of format changes.
25	
26	## Version Numbering (see `version-numbering.md` for full details)
27	
28	Speed-related changes have never on their own justified a minor version bump under the scheme in `version-numbering.md`. Every entry on this page rides along with a release that had other, user-facing content — new help text, a changelog fix, a packaging adjustment. If you're the one making a speed change and it's the *only* change in the release, treat it as a patch-level bump and say so plainly in the changelog rather than dressing it up as a feature.
29	
30	One wrinkle worth flagging: `version-numbering.md` (v1.3, Priya Chandran, 2024-05-02) describes the three-part scheme as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with patch reserved for "fixes that don't change behavior visible to a user of the command line." Several of the entries below arguably do change visible behavior (faster startup is visible), and the team has been inconsistent about whether that counts. In practice, if a user could tell the difference by using a stopwatch but not by reading any output, it's gone in as a patch.
31	
32	## Changelog Conventions Applied to Speed Entries
33	
34	Per `changelog-conventions.md` (v1.1, Elena Petrova, 2024-08-19), speed-related entries in `CHANGELOG.md` should:
35	
36	- Use the heading "Changed" rather than "Fixed" unless the prior behavior was a regression from an earlier release.
37	- Avoid unqualified adjectives like "faster" without a number attached, even an approximate one ("cold start improved by roughly 15%" rather than "startup is now faster").
38	- Cross-reference the release notes page for the version where the detail lives, rather than repeating the measurement inline.
39	
40	A worked example of a correctly formatted entry, following `changelog-snippet-format.txt` (v1.0, Elena Petrova, 2024-06-18):
41	
42	```
43	## [1.2.0] - 2025-02-14
44	### Changed
45	- Reduced first-write latency on the database file by adjusting the
46	  synchronous setting from FULL to NORMAL when the WAL journal mode
47	  is active. See release-notes-v1.2.md for measurements.
48	```
49	
50	Note the past-tense verb and the absence of a bare "faster" — this is the house style, not a suggestion.
51	
52	## Release Checklist Items for Speed (Section owner: Priya Chandran, Release Engineering)
53	
54	`release-checklist.md` (v2.0) does not currently have a dedicated speed section, and the team has talked about adding one for two release cycles running without doing it. In the meantime, the informal checklist that gets used is:
55	
56	1. Time a cold start on the release branch using a plain shell timer, three runs, discard the first (disk cache warm-up).
57	2. Compare against the number recorded in the previous version's release notes page under "Speed."
58	3. If the delta is worse than 10%, open a note in the release thread before tagging — do not block the release, just flag it.
59	4. If the delta is better than 10%, write it up properly rather than letting it disappear; several good improvements in 1.1.0 almost went unrecorded this way.
60	5. Check the size of a sample database file after a fixed sequence of writes (see the worked example below) and compare growth rate against the prior release.
61	
62	A shell snippet used to time a cold start, run from the repository root:
63	
64	
65	This is the same pattern used to produce the numbers quoted in the per-version sections below. It is not a formal measurement study; it is a "did we make it worse" tripwire, run on a single developer laptop, not a lab.
66	
67	## Packaging and Speed (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)
68	
69	`packaging-source-distribution.rst` (v1.4, 2024-11-03) covers how the source distribution is built; it is not primarily concerned with speed, but two packaging choices have had measurable speed effects and are recorded here rather than there, since this page is where people look for that kind of thing:
70	
71	- The choice to keep the package as a single flat directory under `activitylog/` (no nested subpackages) keeps import time low because the interpreter does not have to walk multiple package `__init__` files. This was a deliberate constraint reaffirmed during the 1.1.0 packaging review, described in `build-environment-notes.rst` (v1.0, Mara Olsen, 2025-03-21) as "one of the few places where flat really did beat nested."
72	- The source distribution has never bundled compiled bytecode. Cold start on a completely fresh install therefore pays a one-time compile cost on first invocation, then benefits from the interpreter's own bytecode caching on subsequent runs. This is expected behavior, not a defect, and should not be reported against during release verification.
73	
74	## Console Log Format and Speed (Section owner: Sam Okafor, Core Runtime)
75	
76	`console-log-format-changes.md` (v1.1, Sam Okafor, 2025-09-14) tracks format changes line by line. A few of those changes were partly motivated by speed rather than readability, and it's worth naming them here so the motivation isn't lost:
77	
78	- The switch away from per-line flushing (every line forced a flush of standard output) to a buffered mode with a fixed flush interval was primarily a speed change wearing a formatting hat. It reduced the overhead of high-volume console output during long runs, at the cost of slightly delayed visibility of the last few lines if a run was interrupted. This trade-off was accepted and has not been revisited.
79	- Timestamp formatting was simplified from a longer ISO-8601 style string with microsecond precision to second precision. This was primarily a readability change but had the side effect of avoiding a small amount of string formatting work per line, which matters when output volume is high.
80	
81	## Command Help Text and Speed (Section owner: Theo Banks, Developer Experience)
82	
83	Help text itself has no speed cost worth measuring — it's a few printed lines. But `command-help-text-changes.md` (v1.2, Theo Banks, 2025-06-30) is the place to check before assuming any slowdown is speed-related rather than help-text related: a couple of complaints filed against "the command feels slower" over the years turned out to be someone timing a `--help` invocation against a longer help string and not realizing the string had grown, not against any actual processing delay. Worth ruling out early in any investigation.
84	
85	## Speed Notes by Version
86	
87	### v1.0.0 — 2024-04-01 (see `release-notes-v1.0.md`, Theo Banks)
88	
89	No dedicated speed work in this release; it's the baseline. Cold start on the reference laptop (a mid-range machine used consistently for these measurements since 2024) was approximately 140 ms using the timing snippet above, averaged over the two kept runs. First-write latency on a fresh database file was approximately 8 ms with the original rollback-journal mode and default synchronous setting (`FULL`). These numbers are recorded here as the baseline against which later releases are compared; they were not called out as a "Speed" section in the original release notes page, since the convention of doing so hadn't been established yet.
90	
91	### v1.1.0 — 2024-09-05 (see `release-notes-v1.1.md`, Mara Olsen)
92	
93	The first release with a dedicated "Speed" entry in its own release notes page. Two changes:
94	
95	- The database file's journal mode was switched from the original rollback-journal mode to `WAL` by default for new database files. This reduced first-write latency from roughly 8 ms to roughly 3 ms on the reference laptop, because WAL mode avoids the overhead of creating and removing a rollback journal file on every write. Existing database files created under the old default were not migrated automatically — this was a deliberate choice, not an oversight, and it is mentioned again here because it occasionally surprises people who compare speed numbers between an old file and a newly created one and assume something regressed.
96	- Cold start dropped slightly, from roughly 140 ms to roughly 128 ms, attributed to a reduction in the import surface — two standard library modules that were imported but not used at process start in v1.0.0 were removed from the top-level import list and moved to be imported only when the code path that needed them was reached.
97	
98	The release notes page for this version states the cold-start figure as "approximately 125 ms," which is close enough to the 128 ms recorded here that it's probably just measurement noise between the two people who ran the timing, but the two numbers don't quite match if you go looking.
99	
100	### v1.2.0 — 2025-02-20 (see `release-notes-v1.2.md`, Sam Okafor)
101	
102	This is the release referenced in the changelog worked example above.
103	
104	- Synchronous setting for the database file was changed from `FULL` to `NORMAL` for database files opened in `WAL` journal mode (the default set of settings since v1.1.0; files still using the original rollback-journal mode, if any remain, keep `FULL` synchronous, since `NORMAL` is not considered safe without WAL). This reduced first-write latency further, from roughly 3 ms to roughly 1.5 ms on the reference laptop. This is the single largest speed win recorded on this page relative to its own baseline, on a percentage basis.
105	- A change to how the database file's connection is opened avoided re-checking the journal mode setting on every single write; it is now checked once per connection lifetime. This mattered more for the loopback service, which holds a connection open across many requests, than for a single command-line invocation which opens and closes a connection once anyway. Measured effect on the service, under a sustained sequence of writes over a five-minute run: average per-write time dropped from approximately 0.6 ms to approximately 0.35 ms in steady state.
106	- Cold start was not meaningfully affected by either change above and remained close to the v1.1.0 figure, at roughly 126 ms.
107	
108	### v1.2.1 — 2025-04-08 (not documented in its own release notes page; folded into this one)
109	
110	A small patch release that does not have its own file in this folder — it predates the convention of giving every patch its own page, and by the time that convention was adopted nobody went back to backfill it. Content: a single line reverting part of the buffered console output change described under "Console Log Format and Speed" above, because a downstream reader piping the console output into another process was seeing output arrive in bursts large enough to look like the process had hung. The flush interval was tightened from every 200 lines to every 50 lines as a compromise. This is a speed/usability trade-off, not a pure speed win, and is recorded here because there is nowhere else it currently lives.
111	
112	### v1.3.0 — 2025-08-01 (release notes page for this version not present in this folder as of this writing; see the main `CHANGELOG.md` in the repository root for the entry)
113	
114	- Database file growth: a maintenance step was added to the release checklist (informally, not yet reflected in `release-checklist.md` itself) recommending a manual vacuum of the database file once its free space, as reported by the file's own size relative to its live content, crosses what the team calls the vacuum threshold — informally, once the file is more than roughly double the size a fresh file with equivalent content would be. This is not automated and is not run by the package itself; it is a manual step a person can take with the `sqlite3` command-line tool if the file has grown unexpectedly large, for example:
115	
116	```
117	sqlite3 auditlog.db "VACUUM;"
118	```
119	
120	  This is a general SQLite maintenance operation, not specific to this package, and it can take considerable time on a large file — worth doing between runs, not during a busy stretch.
121	- Cold start held steady at roughly 124 ms, within noise of the v1.2.0 figure.
122	
123	### v1.4.0 — 2026-03-10 (in progress; speed section drafted ahead of the release notes page itself)
124	
125	Work in progress as of this writing. Early measurements on the reference laptop show first-write latency essentially unchanged from v1.2.0 (still roughly 1.5 ms), but a change under evaluation would group the timestamp formatting work mentioned under "Console Log Format and Speed" so that it happens once per run setup rather than once per line, which should shave a small amount off high-volume console output scenarios. No final numbers yet; this section will be revised once the release notes page for v1.4.0 exists and the checklist run in the section above has been completed against the release branch.
126	
127	## Reading the Numbers on This Page
128	
129	A caution, since these numbers get quoted in meetings sometimes without this context attached: every figure above comes from a single reference laptop, timed with a plain shell loop, three runs with the first discarded. This is a consistency check between releases, not a rigorous measurement setup — different hardware, different disk (spinning vs. solid-state), or a busy machine will all produce different absolute numbers. The relative direction (did it get better or worse release over release) is the useful signal, not the absolute millisecond count.
130	
131	## Repository Files Referenced by This Page
132	
133	| Path | Purpose |
134	|---|---|
135	| `auditlog/` | The package directory itself; source of the import surface and the database file handling referenced throughout. |
136	| `README.md` (repository root) | Root readme; not specific to speed but the first place a new contributor lands. |
137	| `CHANGELOG.md` (repository root) | Where every dated entry referenced above, including the v1.3.0 entry not otherwise documented in this folder, actually lives. |
138	| `docs/release-notes/README.md` | Folder overview page for this section of the documentation; see Related Pages. |
139	| `docs/release-notes/version-numbering.md` | Defines the MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH scheme referenced under "Version Numbering" above. |
140	| `docs/release-notes/changelog-conventions.md` | House style for changelog entries, applied to the worked example above. |
141	| `docs/release-notes/changelog-snippet-format.txt` | Exact formatting template the worked example follows. |
142	| `docs/release-notes/release-checklist.md` | The formal checklist; does not yet have a dedicated speed section as of this writing. |
143	| `docs/release-notes/release-checklist-template.yaml` | YAML template used when filling out a checklist for a given release. |
144	| `docs/release-notes/packaging-source-distribution.rst` | Packaging process; referenced under "Packaging and Speed" for the flat-directory and bytecode notes. |
145	| `docs/release-notes/build-environment-notes.rst` | Background on the flat-vs-nested packaging choice quoted above. |
146	| `docs/release-notes/command-help-text-changes.md` | Tracks help text changes; referenced to rule out help-text growth as a false speed complaint. |
147	| `docs/release-notes/console-log-format-changes.md` | Full account of console output format changes, several with speed motivations noted on this page. |
148	| `docs/release-notes/release-notes-v1.0.md` | Baseline release notes; no dedicated speed section. |
149	| `docs/release-notes/release-notes-v1.1.md` | First release notes page with a "Speed" section. |
150	| `docs/release-notes/release-notes-v1.2.md` | Release notes for the release with the largest recorded speed win on this page. |
151	| `scripts/` | Holds the informal timing snippet referenced above, kept as a loose shell script rather than a maintained tool. |
152	
153	## Tools and Libraries Referenced
154	
155	| Tool / Library | Version | Used for |
156	|---|---|---|
157	| Python (CPython) | 3.11.x on the reference laptop; package supports 3.9+ | Interpreter running the package; import surface and cold-start timing are interpreter-dependent. |

- **Import surface** — the set of standard library modules loaded at process start; a larger import surface generally means a slower cold start.
- **Flush interval** — how often buffered console output is written out during a run; tightened or loosened in a couple of releases as a side effect of format changes.

## Version Numbering (see `version-numbering.md` for full details)

Speed-related changes have never on their own justified a minor version bump under the scheme in `version-numbering.md`. Every entry on this page rides along with a release that had other, user-facing content — new help text, a changelog fix, a packaging adjustment. If you're the one making a speed change and it's the *only* change in the release, treat it as a patch-level bump and say so plainly in the changelog rather than dressing it up as a feature.

One wrinkle worth flagging: `version-numbering.md` (v1.3, Priya Chandran, 2024-05-02) describes the three-part scheme as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH with patch reserved for "fixes that don't change behavior visible to a user of the command line." Several of the entries below arguably do change visible behavior (faster startup is visible), and the team has been inconsistent about whether that counts. In practice, if a user could tell the difference by using a stopwatch but not by reading any output, it's gone in as a patch.

## Changelog Conventions Applied to Speed Entries

Per `changelog-conventions.md` (v1.1, Elena Petrova, 2024-08-19), speed-related entries in `CHANGELOG.md` should:

- Use the heading "Changed" rather than "Fixed" unless the prior behavior was a regression from an earlier release.
- Avoid unqualified adjectives like "faster" without a number attached, even an approximate one ("cold start improved by roughly 15%" rather than "startup is now faster").
- Cross-reference the release notes page for the version where the detail lives, rather than repeating the measurement inline.

A worked example of a correctly formatted entry, following `changelog-snippet-format.txt` (v1.0, Elena Petrova, 2024-06-18):

```
## [1.2.0] - 2025-02-14
### Changed
- Reduced first-write latency on the database file by adjusting the
  synchronous setting from FULL to NORMAL when the WAL journal mode
  is active. See release-notes-v1.2.md for measurements.
```

Note the past-tense verb and the absence of a bare "faster" — this is the house style, not a suggestion.

## Release Checklist Items for Speed (Section owner: Priya Chandran, Release Engineering)

`release-checklist.md` (v2.0) does not currently have a dedicated speed section, and the team has talked about adding one for two release cycles running without doing it. In the meantime, the informal checklist that gets used is:

1. Time a cold start on the release branch using a plain shell timer, three runs, discard the first (disk cache warm-up).
2. Compare against the number recorded in the previous version's release notes page under "Speed."
3. If the delta is worse than 10%, open a note in the release thread before tagging — do not block the release, just flag it.
4. If the delta is better than 10%, write it up properly rather than letting it disappear; several good improvements in 1.1.0 almost went unrecorded this way.
5. Check the size of a sample database file after a fixed sequence of writes (see the worked example below) and compare growth rate against the prior release.

A shell snippet used to time a cold start, run from the repository root:


This is the same pattern used to produce the numbers quoted in the per-version sections below. It is not a formal measurement study; it is a "did we make it worse" tripwire, run on a single developer laptop, not a lab.

## Packaging and Speed (Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)

`packaging-source-distribution.rst` (v1.4, 2024-11-03) covers how the source distribution is built; it is not primarily concerned with speed, but two packaging choices have had measurable speed effects and are recorded here rather than there, since this page is where people look for that kind of thing:

- The choice to keep the package as a single flat directory under `activitylog/` (no nested subpackages) keeps import time low because the interpreter does not have to walk multiple package `__init__` files. This was a deliberate constraint reaffirmed during the 1.1.0 packaging review, described in `build-environment-notes.rst` (v1.0, Mara Olsen, 2025-03-21) as "one of the few places where flat really did beat nested."
- The source distribution has never bundled compiled bytecode. Cold start on a completely fresh install therefore pays a one-time compile cost on first invocation, then benefits from the interpreter's own bytecode caching on subsequent runs. This is expected behavior, not a defect, and should not be reported against during release verification.

## Console Log Format and Speed (Section owner: Sam Okafor, Core Runtime)

`console-log-format-changes.md` (v1.1, Sam Okafor, 2025-09-14) tracks format changes line by line. A few of those changes were partly motivated by speed rather than readability, and it's worth naming them here so the motivation isn't lost:

- The switch away from per-line flushing (every line forced a flush of standard output) to a buffered mode with a fixed flush interval was primarily a speed change wearing a formatting hat. It reduced the overhead of high-volume console output during long runs, at the cost of slightly delayed visibility of the last few lines if a run was interrupted. This trade-off was accepted and has not been revisited.
- Timestamp formatting was simplified from a longer ISO-8601 style string with microsecond precision to second precision. This was primarily a readability change but had the side effect of avoiding a small amount of string formatting work per line, which matters when output volume is high.

## Command Help Text and Speed (Section owner: Theo Banks, Developer Experience)

Help text itself has no speed cost worth measuring — it's a few printed lines. But `command-help-text-changes.md` (v1.2, Theo Banks, 2025-06-30) is the place to check before assuming any slowdown is speed-related rather than help-text related: a couple of complaints filed against "the command feels slower" over the years turned out to be someone timing a `--help` invocation against a longer help string and not realizing the string had grown, not against any actual processing delay. Worth ruling out early in any investigation.

## Speed Notes by Version

### v1.0.0 — 2024-04-01 (see `release-notes-v1.0.md`, Theo Banks)

No dedicated speed work in this release; it's the baseline. Cold start on the reference laptop (a mid-range machine used consistently for these measurements since 2024) was approximately 140 ms using the timing snippet above, averaged over the two kept runs. First-write latency on a fresh database file was approximately 8 ms with the original rollback-journal mode and default synchronous setting (`FULL`). These numbers are recorded here as the baseline against which later releases are compared; they were not called out as a "Speed" section in the original release notes page, since the convention of doing so hadn't been established yet.

### v1.1.0 — 2024-09-05 (see `release-notes-v1.1.md`, Mara Olsen)

The first release with a dedicated "Speed" entry in its own release notes page. Two changes:

- The database file's journal mode was switched from the original rollback-journal mode to `WAL` by default for new database files. This reduced first-write latency from roughly 8 ms to roughly 3 ms on the reference laptop, because WAL mode avoids the overhead of creating and removing a rollback journal file on every write. Existing database files created under the old default were not migrated automatically — this was a deliberate choice, not an oversight, and it is mentioned again here because it occasionally surprises people who compare speed numbers between an old file and a newly created one and assume something regressed.
- Cold start dropped slightly, from roughly 140 ms to roughly 128 ms, attributed to a reduction in the import surface — two standard library modules that were imported but not used at process start in v1.0.0 were removed from the top-level import list and moved to be imported only when the code path that needed them was reached.

The release notes page for this version states the cold-start figure as "approximately 125 ms," which is close enough to the 128 ms recorded here that it's probably just measurement noise between the two people who ran the timing, but the two numbers don't quite match if you go looking.

### v1.2.0 — 2025-02-20 (see `release-notes-v1.2.md`, Sam Okafor)

This is the release referenced in the changelog worked example above.

- Synchronous setting for the database file was changed from `FULL` to `NORMAL` for database files opened in `WAL` journal mode (the default set of settings since v1.1.0; files still using the original rollback-journal mode, if any remain, keep `FULL` synchronous, since `NORMAL` is not considered safe without WAL). This reduced first-write latency further, from roughly 3 ms to roughly 1.5 ms on the reference laptop. This is the single largest speed win recorded on this page relative to its own baseline, on a percentage basis.
- A change to how the database file's connection is opened avoided re-checking the journal mode setting on every single write; it is now checked once per connection lifetime. This mattered more for the loopback service, which holds a connection open across many requests, than for a single command-line invocation which opens and closes a connection once anyway. Measured effect on the service, under a sustained sequence of writes over a five-minute run: average per-write time dropped from approximately 0.6 ms to approximately 0.35 ms in steady state.
- Cold start was not meaningfully affected by either change above and remained close to the v1.1.0 figure, at roughly 126 ms.

### v1.2.1 — 2025-04-08 (not documented in its own release notes page; folded into this one)

A small patch release that does not have its own file in this folder — it predates the convention of giving every patch its own page, and by the time that convention was adopted nobody went back to backfill it. Content: a single line reverting part of the buffered console output change described under "Console Log Format and Speed" above, because a downstream reader piping the console output into another process was seeing output arrive in bursts large enough to look like the process had hung. The flush interval was tightened from every 200 lines to every 50 lines as a compromise. This is a speed/usability trade-off, not a pure speed win, and is recorded here because there is nowhere else it currently lives.

### v1.3.0 — 2025-08-01 (release notes page for this version not present in this folder as of this writing; see the main `CHANGELOG.md` in the repository root for the entry)

- Database file growth: a maintenance step was added to the release checklist (informally, not yet reflected in `release-checklist.md` itself) recommending a manual vacuum of the database file once its free space, as reported by the file's own size relative to its live content, crosses what the team calls the vacuum threshold — informally, once the file is more than roughly double the size a fresh file with equivalent content would be. This is not automated and is not run by the package itself; it is a manual step a person can take with the `sqlite3` command-line tool if the file has grown unexpectedly large, for example:

```
sqlite3 auditlog.db "VACUUM;"
```

  This is a general SQLite maintenance operation, not specific to this package, and it can take considerable time on a large file — worth doing between runs, not during a busy stretch.
- Cold start held steady at roughly 124 ms, within noise of the v1.2.0 figure.

### v1.4.0 — 2026-03-10 (in progress; speed section drafted ahead of the release notes page itself)

Work in progress as of this writing. Early measurements on the reference laptop show first-write latency essentially unchanged from v1.2.0 (still roughly 1.5 ms), but a change under evaluation would group the timestamp formatting work mentioned under "Console Log Format and Speed" so that it happens once per run setup rather than once per line, which should shave a small amount off high-volume console output scenarios. No final numbers yet; this section will be revised once the release notes page for v1.4.0 exists and the checklist run in the section above has been completed against the release branch.

## Reading the Numbers on This Page

A caution, since these numbers get quoted in meetings sometimes without this context attached: every figure above comes from a single reference laptop, timed with a plain shell loop, three runs with the first discarded. This is a consistency check between releases, not a rigorous measurement setup — different hardware, different disk (spinning vs. solid-state), or a busy machine will all produce different absolute numbers. The relative direction (did it get better or worse release over release) is the useful signal, not the absolute millisecond count.

1	# Release Notes: v1.0.0
2	
3	**Version:** v1.0.0  
4	**Owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Banks)  
5	**Last Updated:** 2024-04-01
6	
7	## Overview
8	
9	This document covers the release process for auditlog, a lightweight Python package that combines command-line tooling with a loopback HTTP service and maintains records in a local SQLite database. The v1.0.0 release represents the first documented and officially packaged version of the service, establishing stable documentation standards, packaging conventions, and standardized command-line interfaces.
10	
11	This page serves as the authoritative guide for packaging and releasing service versions. It consolidates release procedures, versioning strategies, and prior release notes spanning the v1.0 series. For ongoing releases and maintenance, update this page alongside each version milestone.
12	
13	## Version Numbering Strategy
14	
15	The auditlog package follows semantic versioning as documented in the **Version Numbering for the Package** guide (version 1.3). Releases use the format `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`:
16	
17	- **MAJOR** increments on breaking changes to the command-line interface, HTTP service, or database file format
18	- **MINOR** increments on backward-compatible feature additions
19	- **PATCH** increments on bug fixes, documentation updates, and performance improvements
20	
21	The v1.0.0 release establishes the baseline for this versioning scheme. All releases are tagged in the repository using the format `v1.0.0`, `v1.0.1`, etc., with matching entries in the changelog. The major version remains 1 for releases during the current product cycle unless the database schema or HTTP service interface undergoes breaking changes.
22	
23	For pre-release versions during development, use suffixes like `v1.1.0-alpha` or `v1.2.0-beta`. These should be noted separately in changelog entries and are not intended for wide distribution beyond the development team.
24	
25	## Changelog Conventions
26	
27	Changelog entries follow the conventions defined in **Changelog Writing Conventions** (version 1.1), maintained by the Docs Guild. Every release must include a changelog entry describing:
28	
29	- Documentation changes or improvements to user guides
30	- Packaging adjustments or tool version updates
31	- Modifications to command help text or output format
32	- Console log format changes and migration notes
33	- Performance improvements or speed optimizations
34	
35	The changelog uses a consistent format with dated entries organized by version number. Entries should be concise but specific enough to inform users of substantive changes. For formatting guidelines, refer to **Changelog Snippet Format** (version 1.0).
36	
37	A sample entry for v1.0.0 appears as:
38	
39	```
40	## v1.0.0 (2024-04-01)
41	
42	- Initial public release with complete documentation suite
43	- Standardized command help text output across all interfaces
44	- Introduced structured plain-text logging format for console output
45	- Packaged as source distribution using setuptools
46	- Performance baseline established: service startup under 150ms
47	```
48	
49	When creating new releases, ensure every substantive change affecting documentation, packaging, command output, or speed is documented. Minor documentation rewording should still be noted if it changes user-facing messages or help output.
50	
51	## Release Checklist and Procedures
52	
53	The detailed release checklist is maintained in **Release Checklist** (version 2.0), updated most recently on 2025-01-10 by Release Engineering. The checklist provides step-by-step guidance for release coordinators managing a version release.
54	
55	A release coordinator should follow this sequence:
56	
57	1. **Create release branch** from the main branch using the format `release/v1.0.1`
58	2. **Update changelog** entries in the docs folder with all changes since the previous version
59	3. **Update version strings** in setup.cfg and pyproject.toml metadata files
60	4. **Verify packaging** completes successfully without warnings (see Packaging the Source Distribution section below)
61	5. **Create annotated Git tag** with the release version and summary message
62	6. **Push tag** to the central repository
63	7. **Update release notes** on the wiki with the new version and date
64	
65	A YAML template for tracking release progress is available at **Release Checklist Template (YAML)** (version 1.0). Use this template to document which steps have been completed and by whom, especially for releases managed by multiple coordinators or across different teams.
66	
67	The v1.0.0 release checklist was completed on 2024-04-01 by Theo Banks with coordination from Platform Tools. The standardized checklist process was formalized afterward to ensure consistency for subsequent releases.
68	
69	## Packaging the Source Distribution
70	
71	The auditlog package is distributed as a source distribution in tar.gz format rather than as a wheel or binary. Detailed technical instructions for preparing the source distribution are in **Packaging the Source Distribution** (version 1.4), maintained by Platform Tools (Mara Olsen).
72	
73	To build the source distribution locally in your development environment:
74	
75	```bash
76	cd /path/to/auditlog/repo
77	python -m pip install --upgrade build
78	python -m build --sdist
79	```
80	
81	This command produces a `.tar.gz` file in the `dist/` folder, named following the pattern `auditlog-1.0.0.tar.gz` for version 1.0.0.
82	
83	Before releasing, verify the package contents to ensure documentation, configuration, and scripts are included:
84	
85	```bash
86	tar -tzf dist/auditlog-1.0.0.tar.gz | head -30
87	```
88	
89	The package should include:
90	
91	- The main package source directory with implementation files
92	- Documentation files from the `docs/` folder
93	- README.md at the repository root
94	- Configuration files including setup.cfg and pyproject.toml
95	- Scripts directory (if populated)
96	- CHANGELOG.md for version tracking
97	
98	The v1.0.0 release was packaged using setuptools 62.4.0 on Windows 10 Pro. Build environment details including Python version, setuptools configuration, and system requirements are documented in **Build Environment Notes** (version 1.0).
99	
100	## Prior Release Notes
101	
102	### v1.0.0 (2024-04-01)
103	
104	**Owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Banks)  
105	**Status:** Initial Release  
106	**Coordinator:** Theo Banks
107	
108	This version marks the first official release of the auditlog package with comprehensive documentation, standardized tooling, and established release procedures.
109	
110	#### Documentation Improvements
111	
112	The v1.0.0 release includes complete documentation covering:
113	
114	- Installation instructions and system requirements
115	- Command-line interface usage guide with example invocations
116	- HTTP service configuration and operational notes
117	- Database file overview describing location and structure
118	- Getting started guide for new users
119	
120	All documentation was authored in Markdown format and placed in the `docs/` folder organized by topic. A top-level README.md file was added to the repository root to serve as an entry point and guide new users toward the documentation. The documentation was reviewed by the Docs Guild and Platform Tools teams before release.
121	
122	#### Packaging and Distribution
123	
124	The package is distributed as a source distribution in tar.gz format, which users install using standard Python tools. Installation relies on setuptools to resolve metadata and configure the package. Notably, auditlog uses only the Python standard library and declares no external dependencies, simplifying the installation process.
125	
126	The setup.cfg file defines package metadata including name, version (set to 1.0.0), author information, description, and classifier tags. The pyproject.toml file specifies the build backend configuration and minimum build system requirements. These files were generated using setuptools conventions and reviewed for correctness.
127	
128	#### Command Help Text
129	
130	The command-line interface provides consistent, standardized help text across all available subcommands. The primary help output includes:
131	
132	- Brief description of auditlog's purpose and functionality
133	- List of available subcommands with short descriptions
134	- General usage options and flags
135	
136	Individual subcommands display their own help text with:
137	
138	- Argument descriptions and type information
139	- Usage examples where applicable
140	- Default values for optional arguments
141	
142	Help text was finalized during the v1.0.0 development cycle. The text output was carefully reviewed to ensure clarity and consistency across all commands.
143	
144	Example command help output:
145	```
146	usage: auditlog [options] [command]
147	
148	Record management service with loopback HTTP interface
149	
150	commands:
151	  start      Start the service
152	  status     Check service status
153	  query      Query stored records
154	
155	Use 'auditlog [command] --help' for command-specific options
156	```
157	
158	#### Console Log Format
159	
160	Output to the console uses a structured plain-text format designed for human readability and machine parsing. Log messages include:
161	
162	- Timestamp in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS with UTC timezone)
163	- Log level designation (INFO, WARN, ERROR)
164	- Descriptive message text
165	
166	Example console output:
167	```
168	2024-04-01T14:32:00 INFO Service started on port 8080
169	2024-04-01T14:32:05 INFO Received request from loopback interface
170	2024-04-01T14:32:06 INFO Request completed successfully
171	2024-04-01T14:32:15 WARN Database file size approaching 50MB
172	2024-04-01T14:33:01 ERROR Connection timeout on loopback service
173	```
174	
175	The ISO 8601 timestamp format enables easy parsing and sorting by external tools. The fixed-width format facilitates log aggregation and analysis pipelines. This format was chosen to balance human readability with machine consistency.
176	
177	#### Performance
178	
179	Initial performance measurements for v1.0.0 established baseline metrics under typical operating conditions:
180	
181	- Service startup completes in under 150 milliseconds on standard hardware
182	- HTTP request handling averages 5–10 milliseconds per request (loopback)
183	- Database file operations complete in under 1 millisecond for typical lookups
184	- Memory footprint stabilizes at approximately 25–30 MB during steady operation
185	
186	These baselines were measured on a Windows 10 Pro system with an Intel Core i7 processor (8th generation), 16 GB RAM, and SSD storage for the SQLite database file. Performance may vary based on system hardware, database size, and request complexity.
187	
188	Performance metrics were documented to enable tracking of optimization opportunities in future releases. Any changes to startup time, request latency, or memory usage should be compared against these v1.0.0 baselines.
189	
190	## Terminology and Glossary
191	
192	**Semantic Versioning:** A versioning scheme using three numeric components (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) where each component signals the type of change made to the software, enabling predictable compatibility assessment.
193	
194	**Source Distribution:** A packaged form of source code that includes the original Python implementation files, documentation, metadata, and configuration. When distributed as a tar.gz file, also referred to as a "source tarball."
195	
196	**Annotated Tag:** A Git tag object that stores additional metadata such as the tagger name, creation date, and message content. Used to mark official release points in the repository with context.
197	
198	**Release Coordinator:** The team member responsible for executing the release checklist steps and ensuring all items are completed before publishing a new version.
199	
200	**Changelog:** A chronological list of changes included in each release, typically organized by version number and date, describing what changed and why.
201	
202	**Package Metadata:** Configuration information stored in files such as setup.cfg and pyproject.toml that describes the package name, version, author, dependencies, and distribution details.
203	
204	**Console Output:** Plain-text messages printed to standard output or standard error during command execution, typically captured in logs or displayed in a terminal window.
205	
206	**Database File:** The local SQLite file where the service persists records and operational data. The location is configurable at installation time.
207	
208	**Loopback Service:** The HTTP service component that listens for connections only from the local machine (127.0.0.1), preventing external network access.
209	
210	**Setuptools:** A Python package providing tools for building, packaging, and distributing Python projects, including dependency resolution and installation utilities.

# Release Notes: v1.0.0

**Version:** v1.0.0  
**Owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Banks)  
**Last Updated:** 2024-04-01

## Overview

This document covers the release process for auditlog, a lightweight Python package that combines command-line tooling with a loopback HTTP service and maintains records in a local SQLite database. The v1.0.0 release represents the first documented and officially packaged version of the service, establishing stable documentation standards, packaging conventions, and standardized command-line interfaces.

This page serves as the authoritative guide for packaging and releasing service versions. It consolidates release procedures, versioning strategies, and prior release notes spanning the v1.0 series. For ongoing releases and maintenance, update this page alongside each version milestone.

## Version Numbering Strategy

The auditlog package follows semantic versioning as documented in the **Version Numbering for the Package** guide (version 1.3). Releases use the format `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`:

- **MAJOR** increments on breaking changes to the command-line interface, HTTP service, or database file format
- **MINOR** increments on backward-compatible feature additions
- **PATCH** increments on bug fixes, documentation updates, and performance improvements

The v1.0.0 release establishes the baseline for this versioning scheme. All releases are tagged in the repository using the format `v1.0.0`, `v1.0.1`, etc., with matching entries in the changelog. The major version remains 1 for releases during the current product cycle unless the database schema or HTTP service interface undergoes breaking changes.

For pre-release versions during development, use suffixes like `v1.1.0-alpha` or `v1.2.0-beta`. These should be noted separately in changelog entries and are not intended for wide distribution beyond the development team.

## Changelog Conventions

Changelog entries follow the conventions defined in **Changelog Writing Conventions** (version 1.1), maintained by the Docs Guild. Every release must include a changelog entry describing:

- Documentation changes or improvements to user guides
- Packaging adjustments or tool version updates
- Modifications to command help text or output format
- Console log format changes and migration notes
- Performance improvements or speed optimizations

The changelog uses a consistent format with dated entries organized by version number. Entries should be concise but specific enough to inform users of substantive changes. For formatting guidelines, refer to **Changelog Snippet Format** (version 1.0).

A sample entry for v1.0.0 appears as:

```
## v1.0.0 (2024-04-01)

- Initial public release with complete documentation suite
- Standardized command help text output across all interfaces
- Introduced structured plain-text logging format for console output
- Packaged as source distribution using setuptools
- Performance baseline established: service startup under 150ms
```

When creating new releases, ensure every substantive change affecting documentation, packaging, command output, or speed is documented. Minor documentation rewording should still be noted if it changes user-facing messages or help output.

## Release Checklist and Procedures

The detailed release checklist is maintained in **Release Checklist** (version 2.0), updated most recently on 2025-01-10 by Release Engineering. The checklist provides step-by-step guidance for release coordinators managing a version release.

A release coordinator should follow this sequence:

1. **Create release branch** from the main branch using the format `release/v1.0.1`
2. **Update changelog** entries in the docs folder with all changes since the previous version
3. **Update version strings** in setup.cfg and pyproject.toml metadata files
4. **Verify packaging** completes successfully without warnings (see Packaging the Source Distribution section below)
5. **Create annotated Git tag** with the release version and summary message
6. **Push tag** to the central repository
7. **Update release notes** on the wiki with the new version and date

A YAML template for tracking release progress is available at **Release Checklist Template (YAML)** (version 1.0). Use this template to document which steps have been completed and by whom, especially for releases managed by multiple coordinators or across different teams.

The v1.0.0 release checklist was completed on 2024-04-01 by Theo Banks with coordination from Platform Tools. The standardized checklist process was formalized afterward to ensure consistency for subsequent releases.

## Packaging the Source Distribution

The auditlog package is distributed as a source distribution in tar.gz format rather than as a wheel or binary. Detailed technical instructions for preparing the source distribution are in **Packaging the Source Distribution** (version 1.4), maintained by Platform Tools (Mara Olsen).

To build the source distribution locally in your development environment:

```bash
cd /path/to/auditlog/repo
python -m pip install --upgrade build
python -m build --sdist
```

This command produces a `.tar.gz` file in the `dist/` folder, named following the pattern `auditlog-1.0.0.tar.gz` for version 1.0.0.

Before releasing, verify the package contents to ensure documentation, configuration, and scripts are included:

```bash
tar -tzf dist/auditlog-1.0.0.tar.gz | head -30
```

The package should include:

- The main package source directory with implementation files
- Documentation files from the `docs/` folder
- README.md at the repository root
- Configuration files including setup.cfg and pyproject.toml
- Scripts directory (if populated)
- CHANGELOG.md for version tracking

The v1.0.0 release was packaged using setuptools 62.4.0 on Windows 10 Pro. Build environment details including Python version, setuptools configuration, and system requirements are documented in **Build Environment Notes** (version 1.0).

## Prior Release Notes

### v1.0.0 (2024-04-01)

**Owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Banks)  
**Status:** Initial Release  
**Coordinator:** Theo Banks

This version marks the first official release of the auditlog package with comprehensive documentation, standardized tooling, and established release procedures.

#### Documentation Improvements

The v1.0.0 release includes complete documentation covering:

- Installation instructions and system requirements
- Command-line interface usage guide with example invocations
- HTTP service configuration and operational notes
- Database file overview describing location and structure
- Getting started guide for new users

All documentation was authored in Markdown format and placed in the `docs/` folder organized by topic. A top-level README.md file was added to the repository root to serve as an entry point and guide new users toward the documentation. The documentation was reviewed by the Docs Guild and Platform Tools teams before release.

#### Packaging and Distribution

The package is distributed as a source distribution in tar.gz format, which users install using standard Python tools. Installation relies on setuptools to resolve metadata and configure the package. Notably, auditlog uses only the Python standard library and declares no external dependencies, simplifying the installation process.

The setup.cfg file defines package metadata including name, version (set to 1.0.0), author information, description, and classifier tags. The pyproject.toml file specifies the build backend configuration and minimum build system requirements. These files were generated using setuptools conventions and reviewed for correctness.

#### Command Help Text

The command-line interface provides consistent, standardized help text across all available subcommands. The primary help output includes:

- Brief description of auditlog's purpose and functionality
- List of available subcommands with short descriptions
- General usage options and flags

Individual subcommands display their own help text with:

- Argument descriptions and type information
- Usage examples where applicable
- Default values for optional arguments

Help text was finalized during the v1.0.0 development cycle. The text output was carefully reviewed to ensure clarity and consistency across all commands.

Example command help output:
```
usage: auditlog [options] [command]

Record management service with loopback HTTP interface

commands:
  start      Start the service
  status     Check service status
  query      Query stored records

Use 'auditlog [command] --help' for command-specific options
```

#### Console Log Format

Output to the console uses a structured plain-text format designed for human readability and machine parsing. Log messages include:

- Timestamp in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS with UTC timezone)
- Log level designation (INFO, WARN, ERROR)
- Descriptive message text

Example console output:
```
2024-04-01T14:32:00 INFO Service started on port 8080
2024-04-01T14:32:05 INFO Received request from loopback interface
2024-04-01T14:32:06 INFO Request completed successfully
2024-04-01T14:32:15 WARN Database file size approaching 50MB
2024-04-01T14:33:01 ERROR Connection timeout on loopback service
```

The ISO 8601 timestamp format enables easy parsing and sorting by external tools. The fixed-width format facilitates log aggregation and analysis pipelines. This format was chosen to balance human readability with machine consistency.

#### Performance

Initial performance measurements for v1.0.0 established baseline metrics under typical operating conditions:

- Service startup completes in under 150 milliseconds on standard hardware
- HTTP request handling averages 5–10 milliseconds per request (loopback)
- Database file operations complete in under 1 millisecond for typical lookups
- Memory footprint stabilizes at approximately 25–30 MB during steady operation

These baselines were measured on a Windows 10 Pro system with an Intel Core i7 processor (8th generation), 16 GB RAM, and SSD storage for the SQLite database file. Performance may vary based on system hardware, database size, and request complexity.

Performance metrics were documented to enable tracking of optimization opportunities in future releases. Any changes to startup time, request latency, or memory usage should be compared against these v1.0.0 baselines.

## Terminology and Glossary

**Semantic Versioning:** A versioning scheme using three numeric components (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) where each component signals the type of change made to the software, enabling predictable compatibility assessment.

**Source Distribution:** A packaged form of source code that includes the original Python implementation files, documentation, metadata, and configuration. When distributed as a tar.gz file, also referred to as a "source tarball."

**Annotated Tag:** A Git tag object that stores additional metadata such as the tagger name, creation date, and message content. Used to mark official release points in the repository with context.

**Release Coordinator:** The team member responsible for executing the release checklist steps and ensuring all items are completed before publishing a new version.

**Changelog:** A chronological list of changes included in each release, typically organized by version number and date, describing what changed and why.

**Package Metadata:** Configuration information stored in files such as setup.cfg and pyproject.toml that describes the package name, version, author, dependencies, and distribution details.

**Console Output:** Plain-text messages printed to standard output or standard error during command execution, typically captured in logs or displayed in a terminal window.

**Database File:** The local SQLite file where the service persists records and operational data. The location is configurable at installation time.

**Loopback Service:** The HTTP service component that listens for connections only from the local machine (127.0.0.1), preventing external network access.

**Setuptools:** A Python package providing tools for building, packaging, and distributing Python projects, including dependency resolution and installation utilities.

## Repository Files and Paths

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `auditlog/` | Main package source directory containing the Python implementation |
| `docs/` | User-facing documentation in Markdown format organized by topic |
| `scripts/` | Utility scripts for development and operational tasks |
| `README.md` | Repository root documentation serving as entry point for new users |
| `setup.cfg` | Setuptools configuration defining package metadata and build options |
| `pyproject.toml` | Build system requirements and additional project configuration |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | Complete changelog documenting changes across all releases |
| `release-notes/` | Folder containing detailed release notes for each major version |

## Tools and Libraries

| Tool / Library | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.10+ | Runtime environment and interpreter |
| setuptools | 62.4.0 | Package building and distribution framework |
| pip | 23.0+ | Package installation and dependency management tool |
| git | 2.40+ | Version control and tag management |
| SQLite | 3.41.0 | Database engine (bundled with Python standard library) |
| tar | GNU tar 1.34 | File bundling and unbundling tool |

## Changelog

| Date | Version | Owner | Changes |
|------|---------|-------|---------|
| 2024-04-01 | v1.0.0 | Theo Banks | Initial release with documentation, standardized packaging, command help text, console log format, and baseline performance metrics |
| 2024-05-02 | v1.0.1 | Release Engineering (Priya Chandran) | Updated version numbering documentation and clarified semantic versioning advancement rules |
| 2024-06-18 | v1.0.2 | Docs Guild (Elena Petrova) | Added changelog snippet format documentation and standardized entry layout guidelines |
| 2024-08-19 | v1.0.3 | Docs Guild (Elena Petrova) | Refined changelog conventions guide for improved clarity; no package code changes |
| 2024-11-03 | v1.0.4 | Platform Tools (Mara Olsen) | Improved packaging source distribution documentation and build environment notes |
| 2025-01-10 | v1.0.5 | Release Engineering (Priya Chandran) | Released updated release checklist template and refined release coordination procedures |

## Related Pages

The release process documentation suite includes:

- **Release Notes Folder Overview** (README.md, version 1.0, owner Docs Guild) — Introduction to release notes and overview of related documentation
- **Version Numbering for the Package** (version-numbering.md, version 1.3, owner Release Engineering) — Detailed semantic versioning rules and advancement criteria
- **Changelog Writing Conventions** (changelog-conventions.md, version 1.1, owner Docs Guild) — Standards for changelog formatting and content requirements

- **Build Environment Notes** (build-environment-notes.rst, version 1.0, owner Platform Tools) — Environment setup and tool versions for consistent builds
