1	================================================================================
2	BRANCHING AND PULL REQUESTS
3	================================================================================
4	Version:        2.4
5	Owner:          Release Engineering (Owen Fitzgerald)
6	Last updated:   2026-01-22
7	
8	Summary: Describes the branching model and pull request flow contributors
9	follow when proposing changes to the auditlog repository, from creating a
10	topic branch through merge and branch cleanup.
11	
12	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
13	1. OVERVIEW
14	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
15	auditlog is a small package, but the repository has accumulated enough
16	record of accidental direct pushes to main that Release Engineering formalized
17	this page in mid-2024. Every change to auditlog/ or README.md, no matter how
18	small, goes through a branch and a pull request. There is no exception for
19	"one-line fixes" — the smallest changes are usually the ones that get pushed
20	straight to main by accident, and this page exists to stop that.
21	
22	This page assumes you have already completed workstation setup and have a
23	working checkout of the repository. If you have not, stop here and go through
24	Workstation Setup first; nothing below will make sense without a configured
25	git identity and a cloned copy of the repository.
26	
27	Before opening your first pull request, confirm your local git identity
28	matches the identifier you use for your GitHub account:
29	
30	    git config user.name "B. Gigurtsis"
31	    git config user.contact "bgigurtsis@gmail.com"
32	
33	Commits made under a mismatched identity are still accepted by GitHub, but
34	they show up under "unverified" contributors in the pull request UI and
35	reviewers will ask you to fix it before they look at anything else.
36	
37	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
38	2. BRANCHING MODEL
39	    (Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald, Release Engineering)
40	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
41	auditlog uses a single long-lived branch, main, plus short-lived topic
42	branches. There is no develop branch and there has not been one since the
43	repository was reorganized in 2024 — if you see references to develop in an
44	old pull request, ignore them, that workflow was retired.
45	
46	Release branches are the one exception to "short-lived." When Release
47	Engineering cuts a release, a branch named release/<version> is created from
48	main and kept around only long enough to receive any last adjustments before
49	the tag is cut. Once the tag exists, the release branch is removed; it is not
50	a permanent home for a version's fixes.
51	
52	In practice this gives the repository three kinds of branches:
53	
54	  1. main — always deployable, always green, never pushed to directly.
55	  2. topic branches — one contributor's work on one change, opened from main
56	     and merged back into main.
57	  3. release/<version> — short-lived, cut from main, removed after tagging.
58	
59	There is no branch for the database file's structure specifically. Changes
60	to how the package's local store is structured go through a normal topic
61	branch, but they get an extra reviewer, as described in section 8.
62	
63	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
64	3. BRANCH NAMING CONVENTIONS
65	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
66	Branch names are lowercase, hyphen-separated, and prefixed by kind of work.
67	The prefix is what the build system and the branch-name check script key off
68	of, so getting it wrong will fail the first check on your pull request before
69	anything else runs.
70	
71	| Prefix       | Used for                                             | Example                          |
72	|--------------|-------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
73	| feature/     | new behavior in the command line or the service        | feature/loopback-timeout-flag     |
74	| fix/         | a fix to existing behavior                              | fix/db-file-locking-on-windows    |
75	| docs/        | documentation-only changes, including this page         | docs/branching-page-cleanup       |
76	| chore/       | dependency bumps, formatting-only changes, cleanup       | chore/bump-stdlib-min-version     |
77	| release/     | release branches cut by Release Engineering              | release/2.4                       |
78	
79	A few conventions that are not in the table but that reviewers will flag:
80	
81	* Do not include your name or initials in a branch name. It used to be
82	  common (jsmith-fix-db-lock) and some old closed pull requests still show
83	  it, but it is no longer the convention and reviewers will ask you to
84	  rename the branch.
85	* Keep branch names under about 40 characters. The check script does not
86	  enforce a hard limit, but long branch names make the pull request list
87	  unreadable.
88	* Issue numbers are optional in the branch name but encouraged for
89	  fix/ branches, e.g. fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118, where 118 is the
90	  GitHub issue number.
91	
92	The naming check runs locally if you have the repository's git hooks
93	installed (see scripts/check-branch-name.sh) and again as the first step of
94	the build system's checks on the pull request itself.
95	
96	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
97	4. CREATING A BRANCH
98	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
99	Start every branch from an up-to-date main:
100	
101	    git checkout main
102	    git pull origin main
103	    git checkout -b fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118
104	
105	Push the branch to origin as soon as you have your first commit, even if the
106	change is not finished. This gives you a place to open a draft pull request
107	(see section 7) and gives the build system something to run checks against
108	early, rather than surprising you with a failing check right before you are
109	ready to ask for review.
110	
111	    git push -u origin fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118
112	
113	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
114	5. KEEPING A BRANCH UP TO DATE
115	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
116	main moves faster than most individual branches, especially during a release
117	window. Rebase your branch onto main regularly rather than merging main into
118	it — the repository's convention is a linear log on main, and merge commits
119	from main into a topic branch make that log harder to read once the branch
120	is squashed in.
121	
122	    git fetch origin
123	    git rebase origin/main
124	    git push --force-with-lease
125	
126	Always use --force-with-lease rather than a plain --force. A plain force
127	push can silently overwrite a teammate's commits if they pushed to your
128	branch (which happens more than you'd expect on shared branches for larger
129	changes) — --force-with-lease refuses the push if the remote branch has
130	moved since you last fetched it.
131	
132	If your branch has been open for more than about two weeks, rebase it before
133	asking for review even if you were not asked to. Reviewers routinely reject
134	requests to review a branch that is more than a few dozen commits behind
135	main, because the diff shown in GitHub becomes unreliable once the branch
136	has drifted.
137	
138	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
139	6. COMMIT PRACTICES ON A BRANCH
140	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
141	Full commit message conventions live in Commit Message Style; this section
142	covers only what is specific to working on a branch bound for a pull
143	request.
144	
145	* Commit as often as you like on your own branch. There is no expectation
146	  that every commit on a topic branch is individually well-formed — that
147	  is what squash-on-merge is for (section 10).
148	* Do not amend or rebase commits that a reviewer has already commented on
149	  by line number unless you have told them you are about to; it breaks the
150	  line-level comment context in GitHub's diff view.
151	* If a reviewer asks for a change, add it as a new commit rather than
152	  rewriting an earlier one. Reword or squash once review is finished, not
153	  during it.
154	* The final squashed commit message, the one that lands on main, follows
155	  the format in Commit Message Style version 1.2. That page is the
156	  reference; do not invent your own format for the squashed message even
157	  if your intermediate commits used something else.
158	
159	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
160	7. OPENING A PULL REQUEST
161	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
162	Open the pull request as soon as your branch has a coherent first draft of
163	the change, even if it is not finished — mark it as a draft pull request in
164	GitHub rather than waiting. This lets the build system start running checks
165	and gives interested reviewers visibility earlier.
166	
167	    gh pr create --draft --base main --head fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118 \
168	      --title "fix: correct db file locking on Windows" \
169	      --body-file .github/pull_request_template.md
170	
171	GitHub pre-fills the description from .github/pull_request_template.md. Fill
172	in every section of the template; an empty "What changed" section is the
173	single most common reason a pull request sits open without review for days.
174	
175	The template's sections, and what belongs in each:
176	
177	  1. What changed — one or two sentences, plain language, no jargon from
178	     the change itself.
179	  2. Why — the issue number or the reason this change exists.
180	  3. How to check it — the manual steps a reviewer can follow to confirm
181	     the change works, since the repository does not have an automated way
182	     to demonstrate command-line or service behavior in a pull request
183	     description.
184	  4. Anything the reviewer should look at closely — call out risky parts
185	     of the diff yourself; do not make the reviewer find them.
186	
187	When you are ready for review, mark the pull request "Ready for review"
188	(this converts it out of draft) and add a reviewer per section 8.
189	
190	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
191	8. CODE REVIEW AND SIGN-OFF
192	    (Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald, Release Engineering)
193	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
194	The full etiquette for giving and receiving review comments — how to phrase
195	suggestions, how quickly to respond, what counts as a blocking comment — is
196	covered in Code Review Conventions, version 3.1. This section covers only
197	the branching- and merge-specific mechanics.
198	
199	* Every pull request needs at least one sign-off before it can merge.
200	  Changes that touch the database file's structure, or the service's
201	  startup behavior, need a second sign-off, and that second reviewer must
202	  come from Core Services.
203	* Reviewers alternate by week rather than by a fixed list — check the
204	  current reviewer for the week in the pinned message in the team's chat
205	  channel before assigning a review yourself if you are not sure who is
206	  up.
207	* A reviewer's sign-off is tied to the commit they reviewed. If you push
208	  new commits after a sign-off — other than a rebase that changes no
209	  lines — GitHub dismisses the sign-off automatically and you need a fresh
210	  one. This trips people up constantly; plan for it rather than being
211	  surprised by it.
212	* Reviewers are expected to respond to a pull request within one business
213	  day of being added, and within one business day of any comment reply.
214	  This is a norm, not an enforced rule — nothing in GitHub blocks a merge
215	  because a reviewer was slow, but a maintainer will nudge them in the
216	  chat channel after two business days.
217	
218	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
219	9. CONTINUOUS INTEGRATION CHECKS BEFORE MERGE
220	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
221	The build system runs a fixed set of checks on every push to a pull
222	request's branch, defined in .github/workflows/. All of them must finish
223	green before the merge button becomes usable.
224	
225	| Check                | What it confirms                                            |
226	|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
227	| branch-name           | branch matches the prefix table in section 3                 |
228	| lint-and-format       | the package passes the checks described in Linting and Formatting |
229	| build                 | the package installs cleanly with only the standard library  |
230	| doc-links             | internal links between docs/ pages resolve                   |
231	
232	If a check fails, push a new commit rather than waiting — the checks re-run
233	automatically on every push. There is no manual "re-run" button most
234	contributors have clearance to use; if a check looks stuck (rather than
235	failed) for more than about ten minutes, ask in the chat channel rather than
236	pushing an empty commit to force it.
237	
238	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
239	10. MERGE STRATEGIES
240	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
241	The repository allows exactly one merge strategy from the GitHub UI: squash
242	and merge. Merge commits and rebase-merges are both disabled at the
243	repository level.
244	
245	| Strategy       | Allowed on this repository | Notes                                    |
246	|-----------------|------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
247	| Squash and merge | Yes — the only option        | Produces one commit on main per pull request |
248	| Merge commit     | No                            | Disabled to keep main's log linear          |
249	| Rebase and merge | No                            | Disabled; squash covers the same goal       |
250	
251	Because every pull request becomes exactly one commit on main, the commit
252	message you write (or edit) in GitHub's squash dialog at merge time is the
253	one that matters — see Commit Message Style for the format. GitHub
254	pre-fills the squash message from the pull request title and the individual
255	commit messages; edit it down to a proper commit message rather than
256	accepting the pre-filled list of your intermediate commits.
257	
258	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
259	11. HANDLING LONG-RUNNING BRANCHES
260	    (Section owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services)
261	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
262	Most auditlog changes are small enough to open, review, and merge within a
263	few days. Occasionally a change to the database file's structure or to the
264	service's startup behavior needs to stay open longer — sometimes a couple of
265	weeks — while Core Services works through it with the author.
266	
267	For anything expected to stay open more than a week:
268	
269	* Split the work into more than one pull request if you can. A first pull
270	  request that adds new behavior behind an unused code path, followed by a
271	  second that turns it on, is almost always easier to review than one large
272	  change.
273	* If splitting is genuinely not possible, say so in the pull request
274	  description and get sign-off from a Core Services reviewer on the
275	  overall approach before investing more time — this saves everyone from
276	  a large diff being rejected for a structural reason after the fact.
277	* Rebase weekly at minimum (see section 5). Long-running branches that
278	  drift from main are the most common source of a merge that looks clean
279	  in the pull request but breaks something else once it lands.
280	* Draft pull requests are the right tool for a long-running branch. Keep it
281	  in draft state until it is genuinely ready, rather than marking it
282	  "Ready for review" and asking reviewers to hold off commenting.
283	
284	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
285	12. CLEANING UP AFTER MERGE
286	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
287	Once a pull request is merged, GitHub offers to remove the remote branch —
288	accept that offer; there is no reason to keep a merged branch around on
289	origin.
290	
291	Locally, remove your branch and switch back to a current main:
292	
293	    git checkout main
294	    git pull origin main
295	    git branch -d fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118
296	
297	If a branch was rebased in a way that makes git refuse the -d (it will
298	complain the branch is "not fully merged" because the commit hashes
299	differ from what is on main after a squash), use -D instead — this is
300	expected after a squash merge and is not a sign anything went wrong:
301	
302	    git branch -D fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118
303	
304	Contributors who accumulate more than a handful of stale local branches
305	tend to lose track of which ones still matter. scripts/clean-merged-branches.sh
306	removes any local branch whose remote counterpart no longer exists; run it
307	from the repository root every so often.
308	
309	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
310	13. TROUBLESHOOTING COMMON PULL REQUEST ISSUES
311	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
312	- "My branch-name check is failing but the name looks right."
313	  Check for a trailing slash or an extra hyphen; the check is stricter
314	  about the prefix format than the table in section 3 makes it look. It
315	  wants exactly one of the five prefixes followed by a hyphen, not a
316	  slash-then-hyphen.
317	
318	- "GitHub says my branch has conflicts but I don't see any locally."
319	  You are probably comparing against a stale local copy of main. Fetch and
320	  rebase (section 5) before trusting your local diff.
321	
322	- "My sign-off disappeared after I pushed."
323	  Expected behavior described in section 8 — any push other than a
324	  no-line-change rebase clears prior sign-offs.
325	
326	- "The merge button is gray even though checks are green and I have a
327	  sign-off."
328	  Confirm the pull request is not still marked as a draft; a draft pull
329	  request cannot be merged no matter how green its checks are.
330	
331	- "Squash and merge produced a commit message full of my intermediate
332	  commit messages."
333	  Edit the message in the squash dialog before confirming; GitHub does not
334	  edit it for you.
335	
336	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
337	14. TERMINOLOGY
338	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
339	Topic branch — a short-lived branch created from main to hold one
340	contributor's work on one change; merged and removed once that change
341	lands.
342	
343	Long-lived branch — a branch that is not expected to be removed shortly
344	after creation. main is the only true long-lived branch in this repository.
345	
346	Draft pull request — a pull request marked in GitHub so it cannot be
347	merged and does not require a full review yet, while still running the
348	build system's checks and remaining visible to the team.
349	
350	Fast-forward — a merge where the target branch's pointer simply moves
351	forward to the tip of the source branch, with no new commit created. Not
352	used on this repository since squash and merge always creates a new commit.
353	
354	Squash and merge — the repository's only allowed merge strategy;
355	condenses every commit on a pull request's branch into a single commit on
356	main.
357	
358	Rebase — replaying a branch's commits on top of a new base, typically an
359	updated main, to keep the branch current without a merge commit.
360	
361	Force-with-lease — a form of git push --force that refuses to overwrite
362	the remote branch if it has moved since you last fetched it; the required
363	form of force-pushing on this repository.
364	
365	Protected branch — a branch, main in this repository, configured so that
366	direct pushes are blocked and a pull request must pass the build system's
367	checks and receive a sign-off before it can merge.
368	
369	Stale branch — a branch that has not had a commit pushed to it in an
370	extended period and whose remote counterpart has likely already been
371	removed after its pull request merged.
372	
373	Squash message — the single commit message written or edited at merge
374	time that becomes the permanent record of a pull request's change on main;
375	follows the format in Commit Message Style.
376	
377	Reviewer rota — informal term for the week-by-week arrangement of
378	which team member is the default reviewer for new pull requests; tracked
379	in the team's chat channel, not in this repository.

================================================================================
BRANCHING AND PULL REQUESTS
================================================================================
Version:        2.4
Owner:          Release Engineering (Owen Fitzgerald)
Last updated:   2026-01-22

Summary: Describes the branching model and pull request flow contributors
follow when proposing changes to the auditlog repository, from creating a
topic branch through merge and branch cleanup.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. OVERVIEW
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
auditlog is a small package, but the repository has accumulated enough
record of accidental direct pushes to main that Release Engineering formalized
this page in mid-2024. Every change to auditlog/ or README.md, no matter how
small, goes through a branch and a pull request. There is no exception for
"one-line fixes" — the smallest changes are usually the ones that get pushed
straight to main by accident, and this page exists to stop that.

This page assumes you have already completed workstation setup and have a
working checkout of the repository. If you have not, stop here and go through
Workstation Setup first; nothing below will make sense without a configured
git identity and a cloned copy of the repository.

Before opening your first pull request, confirm your local git identity
matches the identifier you use for your GitHub account:

    git config user.name "B. Gigurtsis"
    git config user.contact "bgigurtsis@gmail.com"

Commits made under a mismatched identity are still accepted by GitHub, but
they show up under "unverified" contributors in the pull request UI and
reviewers will ask you to fix it before they look at anything else.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. BRANCHING MODEL
    (Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald, Release Engineering)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
auditlog uses a single long-lived branch, main, plus short-lived topic
branches. There is no develop branch and there has not been one since the
repository was reorganized in 2024 — if you see references to develop in an
old pull request, ignore them, that workflow was retired.

Release branches are the one exception to "short-lived." When Release
Engineering cuts a release, a branch named release/<version> is created from
main and kept around only long enough to receive any last adjustments before
the tag is cut. Once the tag exists, the release branch is removed; it is not
a permanent home for a version's fixes.

In practice this gives the repository three kinds of branches:

  1. main — always deployable, always green, never pushed to directly.
  2. topic branches — one contributor's work on one change, opened from main
     and merged back into main.
  3. release/<version> — short-lived, cut from main, removed after tagging.

There is no branch for the database file's structure specifically. Changes
to how the package's local store is structured go through a normal topic
branch, but they get an extra reviewer, as described in section 8.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. BRANCH NAMING CONVENTIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Branch names are lowercase, hyphen-separated, and prefixed by kind of work.
The prefix is what the build system and the branch-name check script key off
of, so getting it wrong will fail the first check on your pull request before
anything else runs.

| Prefix       | Used for                                             | Example                          |
|--------------|-------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| feature/     | new behavior in the command line or the service        | feature/loopback-timeout-flag     |
| fix/         | a fix to existing behavior                              | fix/db-file-locking-on-windows    |
| docs/        | documentation-only changes, including this page         | docs/branching-page-cleanup       |
| chore/       | dependency bumps, formatting-only changes, cleanup       | chore/bump-stdlib-min-version     |
| release/     | release branches cut by Release Engineering              | release/2.4                       |

A few conventions that are not in the table but that reviewers will flag:

* Do not include your name or initials in a branch name. It used to be
  common (jsmith-fix-db-lock) and some old closed pull requests still show
  it, but it is no longer the convention and reviewers will ask you to
  rename the branch.
* Keep branch names under about 40 characters. The check script does not
  enforce a hard limit, but long branch names make the pull request list
  unreadable.
* Issue numbers are optional in the branch name but encouraged for
  fix/ branches, e.g. fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118, where 118 is the
  GitHub issue number.

The naming check runs locally if you have the repository's git hooks
installed (see scripts/check-branch-name.sh) and again as the first step of
the build system's checks on the pull request itself.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. CREATING A BRANCH
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Start every branch from an up-to-date main:

    git checkout main
    git pull origin main
    git checkout -b fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118

Push the branch to origin as soon as you have your first commit, even if the
change is not finished. This gives you a place to open a draft pull request
(see section 7) and gives the build system something to run checks against
early, rather than surprising you with a failing check right before you are
ready to ask for review.

    git push -u origin fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. KEEPING A BRANCH UP TO DATE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
main moves faster than most individual branches, especially during a release
window. Rebase your branch onto main regularly rather than merging main into
it — the repository's convention is a linear log on main, and merge commits
from main into a topic branch make that log harder to read once the branch
is squashed in.

    git fetch origin
    git rebase origin/main
    git push --force-with-lease

Always use --force-with-lease rather than a plain --force. A plain force
push can silently overwrite a teammate's commits if they pushed to your
branch (which happens more than you'd expect on shared branches for larger
changes) — --force-with-lease refuses the push if the remote branch has
moved since you last fetched it.

If your branch has been open for more than about two weeks, rebase it before
asking for review even if you were not asked to. Reviewers routinely reject
requests to review a branch that is more than a few dozen commits behind
main, because the diff shown in GitHub becomes unreliable once the branch
has drifted.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. COMMIT PRACTICES ON A BRANCH
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Full commit message conventions live in Commit Message Style; this section
covers only what is specific to working on a branch bound for a pull
request.

* Commit as often as you like on your own branch. There is no expectation
  that every commit on a topic branch is individually well-formed — that
  is what squash-on-merge is for (section 10).
* Do not amend or rebase commits that a reviewer has already commented on
  by line number unless you have told them you are about to; it breaks the
  line-level comment context in GitHub's diff view.
* If a reviewer asks for a change, add it as a new commit rather than
  rewriting an earlier one. Reword or squash once review is finished, not
  during it.
* The final squashed commit message, the one that lands on main, follows
  the format in Commit Message Style version 1.2. That page is the
  reference; do not invent your own format for the squashed message even
  if your intermediate commits used something else.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. OPENING A PULL REQUEST
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Open the pull request as soon as your branch has a coherent first draft of
the change, even if it is not finished — mark it as a draft pull request in
GitHub rather than waiting. This lets the build system start running checks
and gives interested reviewers visibility earlier.

    gh pr create --draft --base main --head fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118 \
      --title "fix: correct db file locking on Windows" \
      --body-file .github/pull_request_template.md

GitHub pre-fills the description from .github/pull_request_template.md. Fill
in every section of the template; an empty "What changed" section is the
single most common reason a pull request sits open without review for days.

The template's sections, and what belongs in each:

  1. What changed — one or two sentences, plain language, no jargon from
     the change itself.
  2. Why — the issue number or the reason this change exists.
  3. How to check it — the manual steps a reviewer can follow to confirm
     the change works, since the repository does not have an automated way
     to demonstrate command-line or service behavior in a pull request
     description.
  4. Anything the reviewer should look at closely — call out risky parts
     of the diff yourself; do not make the reviewer find them.

When you are ready for review, mark the pull request "Ready for review"
(this converts it out of draft) and add a reviewer per section 8.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8. CODE REVIEW AND SIGN-OFF
    (Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald, Release Engineering)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The full etiquette for giving and receiving review comments — how to phrase
suggestions, how quickly to respond, what counts as a blocking comment — is
covered in Code Review Conventions, version 3.1. This section covers only
the branching- and merge-specific mechanics.

* Every pull request needs at least one sign-off before it can merge.
  Changes that touch the database file's structure, or the service's
  startup behavior, need a second sign-off, and that second reviewer must
  come from Core Services.
* Reviewers alternate by week rather than by a fixed list — check the
  current reviewer for the week in the pinned message in the team's chat
  channel before assigning a review yourself if you are not sure who is
  up.
* A reviewer's sign-off is tied to the commit they reviewed. If you push
  new commits after a sign-off — other than a rebase that changes no
  lines — GitHub dismisses the sign-off automatically and you need a fresh
  one. This trips people up constantly; plan for it rather than being
  surprised by it.
* Reviewers are expected to respond to a pull request within one business
  day of being added, and within one business day of any comment reply.
  This is a norm, not an enforced rule — nothing in GitHub blocks a merge
  because a reviewer was slow, but a maintainer will nudge them in the
  chat channel after two business days.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
9. CONTINUOUS INTEGRATION CHECKS BEFORE MERGE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The build system runs a fixed set of checks on every push to a pull
request's branch, defined in .github/workflows/. All of them must finish
green before the merge button becomes usable.

| Check                | What it confirms                                            |
|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| branch-name           | branch matches the prefix table in section 3                 |
| lint-and-format       | the package passes the checks described in Linting and Formatting |
| build                 | the package installs cleanly with only the standard library  |
| doc-links             | internal links between docs/ pages resolve                   |

If a check fails, push a new commit rather than waiting — the checks re-run
automatically on every push. There is no manual "re-run" button most
contributors have clearance to use; if a check looks stuck (rather than
failed) for more than about ten minutes, ask in the chat channel rather than
pushing an empty commit to force it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
10. MERGE STRATEGIES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The repository allows exactly one merge strategy from the GitHub UI: squash
and merge. Merge commits and rebase-merges are both disabled at the
repository level.

| Strategy       | Allowed on this repository | Notes                                    |
|-----------------|------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Squash and merge | Yes — the only option        | Produces one commit on main per pull request |
| Merge commit     | No                            | Disabled to keep main's log linear          |
| Rebase and merge | No                            | Disabled; squash covers the same goal       |

Because every pull request becomes exactly one commit on main, the commit
message you write (or edit) in GitHub's squash dialog at merge time is the
one that matters — see Commit Message Style for the format. GitHub
pre-fills the squash message from the pull request title and the individual
commit messages; edit it down to a proper commit message rather than
accepting the pre-filled list of your intermediate commits.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
11. HANDLING LONG-RUNNING BRANCHES
    (Section owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Most auditlog changes are small enough to open, review, and merge within a
few days. Occasionally a change to the database file's structure or to the
service's startup behavior needs to stay open longer — sometimes a couple of
weeks — while Core Services works through it with the author.

For anything expected to stay open more than a week:

* Split the work into more than one pull request if you can. A first pull
  request that adds new behavior behind an unused code path, followed by a
  second that turns it on, is almost always easier to review than one large
  change.
* If splitting is genuinely not possible, say so in the pull request
  description and get sign-off from a Core Services reviewer on the
  overall approach before investing more time — this saves everyone from
  a large diff being rejected for a structural reason after the fact.
* Rebase weekly at minimum (see section 5). Long-running branches that
  drift from main are the most common source of a merge that looks clean
  in the pull request but breaks something else once it lands.
* Draft pull requests are the right tool for a long-running branch. Keep it
  in draft state until it is genuinely ready, rather than marking it
  "Ready for review" and asking reviewers to hold off commenting.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
12. CLEANING UP AFTER MERGE
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Once a pull request is merged, GitHub offers to remove the remote branch —
accept that offer; there is no reason to keep a merged branch around on
origin.

Locally, remove your branch and switch back to a current main:

    git checkout main
    git pull origin main
    git branch -d fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118

If a branch was rebased in a way that makes git refuse the -d (it will
complain the branch is "not fully merged" because the commit hashes
differ from what is on main after a squash), use -D instead — this is
expected after a squash merge and is not a sign anything went wrong:

    git branch -D fix/db-file-locking-on-windows-118

Contributors who accumulate more than a handful of stale local branches
tend to lose track of which ones still matter. scripts/clean-merged-branches.sh
removes any local branch whose remote counterpart no longer exists; run it
from the repository root every so often.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
13. TROUBLESHOOTING COMMON PULL REQUEST ISSUES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
- "My branch-name check is failing but the name looks right."
  Check for a trailing slash or an extra hyphen; the check is stricter
  about the prefix format than the table in section 3 makes it look. It
  wants exactly one of the five prefixes followed by a hyphen, not a
  slash-then-hyphen.

- "GitHub says my branch has conflicts but I don't see any locally."
  You are probably comparing against a stale local copy of main. Fetch and
  rebase (section 5) before trusting your local diff.

- "My sign-off disappeared after I pushed."
  Expected behavior described in section 8 — any push other than a
  no-line-change rebase clears prior sign-offs.

- "The merge button is gray even though checks are green and I have a
  sign-off."
  Confirm the pull request is not still marked as a draft; a draft pull
  request cannot be merged no matter how green its checks are.

- "Squash and merge produced a commit message full of my intermediate
  commit messages."
  Edit the message in the squash dialog before confirming; GitHub does not
  edit it for you.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
14. TERMINOLOGY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Topic branch — a short-lived branch created from main to hold one
contributor's work on one change; merged and removed once that change
lands.

Long-lived branch — a branch that is not expected to be removed shortly
after creation. main is the only true long-lived branch in this repository.

Draft pull request — a pull request marked in GitHub so it cannot be
merged and does not require a full review yet, while still running the
build system's checks and remaining visible to the team.

Fast-forward — a merge where the target branch's pointer simply moves
forward to the tip of the source branch, with no new commit created. Not
used on this repository since squash and merge always creates a new commit.

Squash and merge — the repository's only allowed merge strategy;
condenses every commit on a pull request's branch into a single commit on
main.

Rebase — replaying a branch's commits on top of a new base, typically an
updated main, to keep the branch current without a merge commit.

Force-with-lease — a form of git push --force that refuses to overwrite
the remote branch if it has moved since you last fetched it; the required
form of force-pushing on this repository.

Protected branch — a branch, main in this repository, configured so that
direct pushes are blocked and a pull request must pass the build system's
checks and receive a sign-off before it can merge.

Stale branch — a branch that has not had a commit pushed to it in an
extended period and whose remote counterpart has likely already been
removed after its pull request merged.

Squash message — the single commit message written or edited at merge
time that becomes the permanent record of a pull request's change on main;
follows the format in Commit Message Style.

Reviewer rota — informal term for the week-by-week arrangement of
which team member is the default reviewer for new pull requests; tracked
in the team's chat channel, not in this repository.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
15. REPOSITORY FILES AND PATHS REFERENCED
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
| Path                                              | Purpose                                                       |
|-----------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| auditlog/                                           | The package directory; every change described here eventually touches something under here or README.md |
| README.md                                           | Repository root readme; links into docs/developer-handbook/ for new contributors |
| docs/developer-handbook/branching-and-pull-requests.txt | This page |
| docs/developer-handbook/commit-message-style.md     | Format for individual and squashed commit messages |

| docs/CHANGELOG.md                                   | Running log of user-facing changes, updated by pull requests that add or change behavior |
| scripts/check-branch-name.sh                        | Local hook that validates a branch name against the table in section 3 before push |
| scripts/clean-merged-branches.sh                    | Utility that removes local branches whose remote counterpart no longer exists |
| .github/pull_request_template.md                    | Template GitHub pre-fills when a pull request is opened |
| .github/workflows/                                  | Build system configuration defining the checks in section 9 |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1	Changelog Conventions
2	=======================
3	
4	:Version: v1.0.4
5	:Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
6	:Last updated: 2025-07-19
7	
8	Purpose
9	-------
10	
11	This page describes how a contributor records a change to the auditlog
12	package in the repository's changelog file once that change has landed
13	on the main branch. auditlog ships as a small standard-library-only
14	package with a command line and a loopback HTTP service, and its users
15	generally learn what changed between one tag and the next by reading
16	the changelog rather than by reading the diff. Because of that, the
17	changelog is treated as a first-class artifact of a change, not an
18	afterthought added the day of a cut. If a change alters anything a
19	user of the package or the service would observe, it gets an entry.
20	If it does not, it usually does not.
21	
22	The conventions below apply to every branch that targets ``main`` in
23	the auditlog repository. They were adopted after several quarters of
24	inconsistent entries made it hard to tell, from the file alone, which
25	line belonged to which release. Platform Tools now treats the file's
26	shape as something worth defending the same way the team defends
27	formatting or commit subject lines.
28	
29	Where changelog entries live
30	-----------------------------
31	
32	The canonical file is ``CHANGELOG.rst`` at the repository root, next
33	to ``README.md`` and the ``auditlog/`` package directory. There is no
34	second changelog anywhere inside ``auditlog/`` itself, and there
35	should never be one — a contributor who is tempted to leave a short
36	note inside the package directory should instead add a line to the
37	root file.
38	
39	The file is organized top to bottom, newest first, like this:
40	
41	.. code-block:: text
42	
43	   Unreleased
44	   ----------
45	
46	   Added
47	   ~~~~~
48	   - ...
49	
50	   Changed
51	   ~~~~~~~
52	   - ...
53	
54	   v1.4.0 - 2025-06-30
55	   --------------------
56	
57	   Added
58	   ~~~~~
59	   - ...
60	
61	   v1.3.2 - 2025-05-11
62	   --------------------
63	   ...
64	
65	The top-most heading is always the literal word ``Unreleased``. Every
66	change that has merged but has not yet gone out under a tag lives
67	under that heading. When a release is cut, the release engineer on
68	duty renames ``Unreleased`` to the new tag and date, and opens a fresh,
69	empty ``Unreleased`` heading above it. Contributors should never write
70	directly under a tagged heading — only the person cutting the release
71	does that, and only by way of the rename described above.
72	
73	When to add an entry
74	---------------------
75	
76	Add a changelog entry when a pull request does any of the following:
77	
78	- Changes the behavior of the command line in a way a person invoking
79	  it would be observed.
80	- Changes what the loopback service returns or how it behaves for a
81	  caller that already integrates with it.
82	- Changes the shape of records kept in the database file, or how an
83	  existing record is read back.
84	- Fixes a defect that a user could have hit and worked around.
85	- Removes something that was previously available.
86	- Changes a default that a user has not explicitly set.
87	
88	Do not add an entry for:
89	
90	- Internal refactors that do not change observable behavior.
91	- Comment-only or documentation-only edits inside ``auditlog/``.
92	- Formatting-only changes produced by the team's linting tools.
93	- Changes confined to files under ``docs/`` (those are covered by
94	  their own review conventions, not this one).
95	
96	When in doubt, add the entry. A short, slightly unnecessary line is
97	cheaper to carry than a change nobody can find later.
98	
99	Entry format
100	------------
101	
102	Each entry is a single bullet, one sentence, written in the past
103	tense, under one of five category labels:
104	
105	.. list-table::
106	   :header-rows: 1
107	
108	   * - Label
109	     - Used for
110	   * - Added
111	     - New commands, new flags, new fields in a returned record.
112	   * - Changed
113	     - Any change to existing, already-shipped behavior or defaults.
114	   * - Fixed
115	     - A defect that produced wrong or missing output.
116	   * - Removed
117	     - A command, flag, or field taken out of the package.
118	   * - Deprecated
119	     - Something still working today that will be taken out later.
120	
121	A category label only appears in a release's section if there is at
122	least one entry under it — an empty ``Removed`` heading with nothing
123	beneath it is left out of that release entirely rather than kept as a
124	sample stand-in text.
125	
126	Each bullet follows this shape:
127	
128	.. code-block:: text
129	
130	   - <What changed>, <optionally: why or under what condition>.
131	
132	Examples that meet the bar:
133	
134	.. code-block:: text
135	
136	   - Added a flag to the command line for choosing where the database
137	     file is created.
138	   - Fixed a case where the loopback service returned an empty list
139	     instead of the most recent record when the database file was
140	     freshly created.
141	   - Changed the default location of the database file from the
142	     current working directory to a directory under the user's home
143	     directory.
144	
145	Examples that do not meet the bar, and why:
146	
147	.. code-block:: text
148	
149	   - Fixed a bug.                        (no detail — a reader can't
150	                                           tell what was affected)
151	   - Refactored the record-reading code. (not observable to a user)
152	   - Various small improvements.         (not a single, checkable
153	                                           statement)
154	
155	An entry should be understandable by someone who has never read the
156	pull request that produced it. If writing the sentence requires
157	naming an internal helper or a private detail, that is usually a sign
158	the change does not need an entry at all.
159	
160	Worked examples
161	----------------
162	
163	**Example 1 — a small, user-visible fix.**
164	
165	A contributor observes that the command line prints a path using
166	backslashes on one operating system and forward slashes on another,
167	and unifies the output. The pull request adds this line under
168	``Unreleased`` / ``Fixed``:
169	
170	.. code-block:: text
171	
172	   Fixed
173	   ~~~~~
174	   - Fixed the command line printing the database file's path with
175	     mixed separators depending on the operating system.
176	
177	**Example 2 — a change with a default shift.**
178	
179	A change makes the loopback service listen on a different local port
180	by default, to avoid clashing with a port commonly used by other
181	local tools. This is both a behavior change and worth calling out on
182	its own, so it gets two lines rather than one combined line:
183	
184	.. code-block:: text
185	
186	   Changed
187	   ~~~~~~~
188	   - Changed the loopback service's default port from 8765 to 8811.
189	   - Changed the command line's `--port` flag to fall back to the new
190	     default described above.
191	
192	**Example 3 — a multi-commit branch, one entry.**
193	
194	A branch has six commits: three that add a feature, two that fix
195	things the first three broke, and one that tidies formatting. The
196	changelog gets exactly one entry, describing the feature as it exists
197	once the branch is done, not the path taken to get there:
198	
199	.. code-block:: text
200	
201	   Added
202	   ~~~~~
203	   - Added a command for listing records in the database file within
204	     a given date range.
205	
206	**Example 4 — coordinating with a sibling change.**
207	
208	Two open branches both touch ``CHANGELOG.rst`` under ``Unreleased``.
209	The second branch to merge is responsible for resolving the conflict
210	by keeping both bullets, in whatever relative order reads cleanest,
211	rather than dropping either one. See the git snippet below.
212	
213	Handling changelog merge conflicts
214	-------------------------------------
215	
216	Because every open branch adds lines to the same ``Unreleased``
217	heading, conflicts on ``CHANGELOG.rst`` are common and expected — they
218	are not treated as a sign something went wrong. The standard way to
219	resolve one from the shell:
220	
221	.. code-block:: shell
222	
223	   git fetch origin
224	   git rebase origin/main
225	   # resolve CHANGELOG.rst by hand, keeping both sets of bullets
226	   git add CHANGELOG.rst
227	   git rebase --continue
228	
229	The rule of thumb: never resolve a ``CHANGELOG.rst`` conflict by
230	picking one side and discarding the other. If both sides added an
231	entry, both entries survive the merge, even if that means the same
232	category label appears with bullets from two different branches
233	sitting next to each other.
234	
235	Release cut procedure
236	-----------------------
237	
238	Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools
239	
240	When a release is ready to go out, whoever is on point for the cut
241	performs the following, in order:
242	
243	1. Confirm ``Unreleased`` has at least one entry. A release with no
244	   entries under ``Unreleased`` almost always means something that
245	   should have had a changelog line did not get one, and is worth a
246	   second look before proceeding.
247	2. Decide the new tag by walking the entries: any ``Removed`` or a
248	   backward-incompatible ``Changed`` line means a jump in the leading
249	   number; new ``Added`` entries with nothing backward-incompatible
250	   mean a jump in the middle number; ``Fixed``-only releases move the
251	   trailing number.
252	3. Rename the ``Unreleased`` heading to the new tag and the date of
253	   the cut, in the form ``vX.Y.Z - YYYY-MM-DD``.
254	4. Add a fresh, empty ``Unreleased`` heading above the renamed one, so
255	   the next contributor has somewhere to write.
256	5. Confirm the version marker carried by the package directory matches
257	   the new tag before it is created.
258	6. Commit the changelog rename on its own, with a subject line such as
259	   ``chore: cut v1.4.0``.
260	7. Create the tag and push it:
261	
262	.. code-block:: shell
263	
264	   git commit -am "chore: cut v1.4.0"
265	   git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "v1.4.0"
266	   git push origin main --tags
267	
268	The person doing the cut does not write new entries at this step —
269	by the time a cut happens, every entry under ``Unreleased`` should
270	already have been added by the branch that introduced the change it
271	describes.
272	
273	Review checklist for changelog entries
274	------------------------------------------
275	
276	Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald, Release Engineering
277	
278	A reviewer looking at a pull request that touches package behavior
279	checks the following before finalizing:
280	
281	- [ ] Is there a ``CHANGELOG.rst`` line at all, if one is warranted?
282	- [ ] Is it under ``Unreleased``, and not under an already-tagged
283	  heading?
284	- [ ] Is it under the right category label?
285	- [ ] Does it read on its own, without needing the pull request open
286	  in another tab to make sense of it?
287	- [ ] Is it one sentence, past tense, ending in a period?
288	- [ ] If the change touched more than one category — for instance a
289	  fix that also changed a default — are there two separate bullets
290	  rather than one bullet trying to cover both?
291	- [ ] Does the wording avoid naming internal names that mean nothing
292	  to someone reading the file later?
293	
294	This checklist is a subset of the broader review conventions the
295	team follows; see the sibling page for everything else a reviewer is
296	expected to look at.
297	
298	Common mistakes
299	-----------------
300	
301	The following show up often enough to call out on their own:
302	
303	* Writing the entry in present tense ("Adds a flag...") instead of
304	  past tense ("Added a flag..."). The file reads as a single voice
305	  looking back at what already happened, so a present-tense line
306	  stands out awkwardly next to the rest.
307	* Combining two unrelated changes into one bullet because they landed
308	  in the same pull request. Split them.
309	* Describing what the code does internally rather than what a user
310	  of the package or the service would observe.
311	* Forgetting to move the entry when a branch is rebased across a
312	  release cut — if a branch was opened before a cut and lands after
313	  it, double check the entry is still sitting under the current
314	  ``Unreleased`` heading and not under the now-tagged one it started
315	  under.
316	* Adding a changelog line for a change that only affects the internal
317	  layout of the ``auditlog/`` directory, with nothing a user would
318	  observed.
319	* Using a category label that does not exist. There are exactly five:
320	  Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed, Deprecated. There is no sixth.
321	
322	Tools and packages used for changelog checks
323	------------------------------------------------
324	
325	Section owner: Ines Bakker, Tooling Guild
326	
327	.. list-table::
328	   :header-rows: 1
329	
330	   * - Tool
331	     - Version
332	     - Used for
333	   * - git
334	     - 2.43.0
335	     - branch, tag, and cut workflow described above
336	   * - Python
337	     - 3.11.9
338	     - runs the local changelog-shape checker script
339	   * - rstcheck
340	     - 6.2.4
341	     - validates that CHANGELOG.rst is well-formed RST
342	   * - codespell
343	     - 2.2.6
344	     - flags common misspellings inside new entries
345	   * - pre-commit
346	     - 3.7.1
347	     - runs the two checks above automatically before a commit
348	   * - GitHub CLI (gh)
349	     - 2.50.0
350	     - used by the release owner to create the tag's release note
351	
352	The shape checker and the spelling checker both run as part of the
353	same pre-commit hook set the team already uses for other checks; see
354	the coding style page (version 3.4, last touched by Platform Tools)
355	for how that hook set is installed on a new workstation.
356	
357	Terminology
358	-------------
359	
360	**Category label**
361	  One of the five fixed headings — Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed,
362	  Deprecated — that groups entries within a release's section of the
363	  changelog.
364	
365	**Changelog entry**
366	  A single bullet line describing one user-observable change, filed
367	  under a category label within either ``Unreleased`` or a tagged
368	  release heading.
369	
370	**Cut**
371	  The act of renaming ``Unreleased`` to a concrete tag and date, then
372	  creating the corresponding git tag. Performed by whoever is on
373	  point for a given release, not by the author of any individual
374	  change.
375	
376	**Tag**
377	  A git tag of the form ``vX.Y.Z`` marking the exact commit a release
378	  corresponds to. The tag name is what the changelog heading is
379	  renamed to during a cut.
380	
381	**Unreleased heading**
382	  The topmost heading in ``CHANGELOG.rst``, always spelled exactly
383	  ``Unreleased``, under which every merged-but-not-yet-tagged entry is
384	  filed.
385	
386	**Version marker**
387	  The single line inside the ``auditlog/`` package directory that
388	  states the package's current number. It must match the tag created
389	  during a cut before that tag is pushed.
390	
391	**Backward-incompatible change**
392	  A ``Changed`` or ``Removed`` entry describing something that would
393	  break a caller already relying on the prior behavior of the command
394	  line, the loopback service, or the shape of a record kept in the
395	  database file. Determines whether a cut moves the leading or middle
396	  number.
397	
398	**Shape checker**
399	  The local script, run through pre-commit, that confirms
400	  ``CHANGELOG.rst`` still parses as RST and that its top heading is
401	  literally ``Unreleased``.
402	
403	**Single-entry rule**
404	  The convention that a multi-commit branch produces exactly one
405	  changelog line per user-observable change it introduces, regardless
406	  of how many commits were needed to get there.
407	
408	Referenced files and paths
409	------------------------------
410	
411	.. list-table::
412	   :header-rows: 1
413	
414	   * - Path
415	     - Function
416	   * - ``CHANGELOG.rst``
417	     - The single, canonical changelog file at the repository root.
418	   * - ``README.md``
419	     - Repository root readme; links out to this page and the rest of
420	       the handbook under ``docs/developer-handbook/``.
421	   * - ``auditlog/``
422	     - The package directory; carries the version marker that must
423	       agree with the tag created during a cut.
424	   * - ``docs/developer-handbook/changelog-conventions.rst``
425	     - This page.
426	   * - ``docs/developer-handbook/code-review-conventions.md``
427	     - Covers the rest of what a reviewer checks beyond the changelog
428	       checklist reproduced above.
429	   * - ``docs/developer-handbook/commit-message-style.md``
430	     - Covers subject-line and body wording for the commit that
431	       renames ``Unreleased`` during a cut.
432	   * - ``docs/developer-handbook/branching-and-pull-requests.txt``
433	     - Covers how a branch is opened and landed; referenced above for
434	       the rebase-across-a-cut case.
435	   * - ``.pre-commit-config.yaml``
436	     - Wires up rstcheck and codespell so they run automatically
437	       against ``CHANGELOG.rst`` before a commit is accepted locally.
438	
439	Change log
440	------------
441	
442	- **2024-06-10 — v1.0.0** — First version of this page, published
443	  alongside the auditlog v1.0.0 tag. Introduced the five category
444	  labels and the ``Unreleased`` heading convention.
445	- **2024-09-02 — v1.0.1** — Added the worked examples section after
446	  a run of pull requests came in with vague, single-word entries like
447	  "Fixed a bug."
448	- **2024-12-15 — v1.0.2** — Added the merge-conflict handling section
449	  following a release where two branches silently overwrote each
450	  other's ``Unreleased`` entries.
451	- **2025-03-01 — v1.0.3** — Split the release cut steps out of the
452	  general procedure section into their own heading, ahead of the
453	  auditlog v1.3.0 release, and named a section owner for the first
454	  time.
455	- **2025-05-22 — v1.0.3** — Corrected the category label table after
456	  a contributor pointed out ``Deprecated`` was missing from it
457	  entirely for the better part of two quarters.
458	- **2025-07-19 — v1.0.4** — Added the tools table and the review
459	  checklist, matching changes made to the review conventions page
460	  around the same time; published ahead of the auditlog v1.4.0 cut.
461	
462	Related pages
463	---------------
464	
465	- Developer Handbook Overview

Changelog Conventions
=======================

:Version: v1.0.4
:Owner: Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
:Last updated: 2025-07-19

Purpose
-------

This page describes how a contributor records a change to the auditlog
package in the repository's changelog file once that change has landed
on the main branch. auditlog ships as a small standard-library-only
package with a command line and a loopback HTTP service, and its users
generally learn what changed between one tag and the next by reading
the changelog rather than by reading the diff. Because of that, the
changelog is treated as a first-class artifact of a change, not an
afterthought added the day of a cut. If a change alters anything a
user of the package or the service would observe, it gets an entry.
If it does not, it usually does not.

The conventions below apply to every branch that targets ``main`` in
the auditlog repository. They were adopted after several quarters of
inconsistent entries made it hard to tell, from the file alone, which
line belonged to which release. Platform Tools now treats the file's
shape as something worth defending the same way the team defends
formatting or commit subject lines.

Where changelog entries live
-----------------------------

The canonical file is ``CHANGELOG.rst`` at the repository root, next
to ``README.md`` and the ``auditlog/`` package directory. There is no
second changelog anywhere inside ``auditlog/`` itself, and there
should never be one — a contributor who is tempted to leave a short
note inside the package directory should instead add a line to the
root file.

The file is organized top to bottom, newest first, like this:

.. code-block:: text

   Unreleased
   ----------

   Added
   ~~~~~
   - ...

   Changed
   ~~~~~~~
   - ...

   v1.4.0 - 2025-06-30
   --------------------

   Added
   ~~~~~
   - ...

   v1.3.2 - 2025-05-11
   --------------------
   ...

The top-most heading is always the literal word ``Unreleased``. Every
change that has merged but has not yet gone out under a tag lives
under that heading. When a release is cut, the release engineer on
duty renames ``Unreleased`` to the new tag and date, and opens a fresh,
empty ``Unreleased`` heading above it. Contributors should never write
directly under a tagged heading — only the person cutting the release
does that, and only by way of the rename described above.

When to add an entry
---------------------

Add a changelog entry when a pull request does any of the following:

- Changes the behavior of the command line in a way a person invoking
  it would be observed.
- Changes what the loopback service returns or how it behaves for a
  caller that already integrates with it.
- Changes the shape of records kept in the database file, or how an
  existing record is read back.
- Fixes a defect that a user could have hit and worked around.
- Removes something that was previously available.
- Changes a default that a user has not explicitly set.

Do not add an entry for:

- Internal refactors that do not change observable behavior.
- Comment-only or documentation-only edits inside ``auditlog/``.
- Formatting-only changes produced by the team's linting tools.
- Changes confined to files under ``docs/`` (those are covered by
  their own review conventions, not this one).

When in doubt, add the entry. A short, slightly unnecessary line is
cheaper to carry than a change nobody can find later.

Entry format
------------

Each entry is a single bullet, one sentence, written in the past
tense, under one of five category labels:

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1

   * - Label
     - Used for
   * - Added
     - New commands, new flags, new fields in a returned record.
   * - Changed
     - Any change to existing, already-shipped behavior or defaults.
   * - Fixed
     - A defect that produced wrong or missing output.
   * - Removed
     - A command, flag, or field taken out of the package.
   * - Deprecated
     - Something still working today that will be taken out later.

A category label only appears in a release's section if there is at
least one entry under it — an empty ``Removed`` heading with nothing
beneath it is left out of that release entirely rather than kept as a
sample stand-in text.

Each bullet follows this shape:

.. code-block:: text

   - <What changed>, <optionally: why or under what condition>.

Examples that meet the bar:

.. code-block:: text

   - Added a flag to the command line for choosing where the database
     file is created.
   - Fixed a case where the loopback service returned an empty list
     instead of the most recent record when the database file was
     freshly created.
   - Changed the default location of the database file from the
     current working directory to a directory under the user's home
     directory.

Examples that do not meet the bar, and why:

.. code-block:: text

   - Fixed a bug.                        (no detail — a reader can't
                                           tell what was affected)
   - Refactored the record-reading code. (not observable to a user)
   - Various small improvements.         (not a single, checkable
                                           statement)

An entry should be understandable by someone who has never read the
pull request that produced it. If writing the sentence requires
naming an internal helper or a private detail, that is usually a sign
the change does not need an entry at all.

Worked examples
----------------

**Example 1 — a small, user-visible fix.**

A contributor observes that the command line prints a path using
backslashes on one operating system and forward slashes on another,
and unifies the output. The pull request adds this line under
``Unreleased`` / ``Fixed``:

.. code-block:: text

   Fixed
   ~~~~~
   - Fixed the command line printing the database file's path with
     mixed separators depending on the operating system.

**Example 2 — a change with a default shift.**

A change makes the loopback service listen on a different local port
by default, to avoid clashing with a port commonly used by other
local tools. This is both a behavior change and worth calling out on
its own, so it gets two lines rather than one combined line:

.. code-block:: text

   Changed
   ~~~~~~~
   - Changed the loopback service's default port from 8765 to 8811.
   - Changed the command line's `--port` flag to fall back to the new
     default described above.

**Example 3 — a multi-commit branch, one entry.**

A branch has six commits: three that add a feature, two that fix
things the first three broke, and one that tidies formatting. The
changelog gets exactly one entry, describing the feature as it exists
once the branch is done, not the path taken to get there:

.. code-block:: text

   Added
   ~~~~~
   - Added a command for listing records in the database file within
     a given date range.

**Example 4 — coordinating with a sibling change.**

Two open branches both touch ``CHANGELOG.rst`` under ``Unreleased``.
The second branch to merge is responsible for resolving the conflict
by keeping both bullets, in whatever relative order reads cleanest,
rather than dropping either one. See the git snippet below.

Handling changelog merge conflicts
-------------------------------------

Because every open branch adds lines to the same ``Unreleased``
heading, conflicts on ``CHANGELOG.rst`` are common and expected — they
are not treated as a sign something went wrong. The standard way to
resolve one from the shell:

.. code-block:: shell

   git fetch origin
   git rebase origin/main
   # resolve CHANGELOG.rst by hand, keeping both sets of bullets
   git add CHANGELOG.rst
   git rebase --continue

The rule of thumb: never resolve a ``CHANGELOG.rst`` conflict by
picking one side and discarding the other. If both sides added an
entry, both entries survive the merge, even if that means the same
category label appears with bullets from two different branches
sitting next to each other.

Release cut procedure
-----------------------

Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools

When a release is ready to go out, whoever is on point for the cut
performs the following, in order:

1. Confirm ``Unreleased`` has at least one entry. A release with no
   entries under ``Unreleased`` almost always means something that
   should have had a changelog line did not get one, and is worth a
   second look before proceeding.
2. Decide the new tag by walking the entries: any ``Removed`` or a
   backward-incompatible ``Changed`` line means a jump in the leading
   number; new ``Added`` entries with nothing backward-incompatible
   mean a jump in the middle number; ``Fixed``-only releases move the
   trailing number.
3. Rename the ``Unreleased`` heading to the new tag and the date of
   the cut, in the form ``vX.Y.Z - YYYY-MM-DD``.
4. Add a fresh, empty ``Unreleased`` heading above the renamed one, so
   the next contributor has somewhere to write.
5. Confirm the version marker carried by the package directory matches
   the new tag before it is created.
6. Commit the changelog rename on its own, with a subject line such as
   ``chore: cut v1.4.0``.
7. Create the tag and push it:

.. code-block:: shell

   git commit -am "chore: cut v1.4.0"
   git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "v1.4.0"
   git push origin main --tags

The person doing the cut does not write new entries at this step —
by the time a cut happens, every entry under ``Unreleased`` should
already have been added by the branch that introduced the change it
describes.

Review checklist for changelog entries
------------------------------------------

Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald, Release Engineering

A reviewer looking at a pull request that touches package behavior
checks the following before finalizing:

- [ ] Is there a ``CHANGELOG.rst`` line at all, if one is warranted?
- [ ] Is it under ``Unreleased``, and not under an already-tagged
  heading?
- [ ] Is it under the right category label?
- [ ] Does it read on its own, without needing the pull request open
  in another tab to make sense of it?
- [ ] Is it one sentence, past tense, ending in a period?
- [ ] If the change touched more than one category — for instance a
  fix that also changed a default — are there two separate bullets
  rather than one bullet trying to cover both?
- [ ] Does the wording avoid naming internal names that mean nothing
  to someone reading the file later?

This checklist is a subset of the broader review conventions the
team follows; see the sibling page for everything else a reviewer is
expected to look at.

Common mistakes
-----------------

The following show up often enough to call out on their own:

* Writing the entry in present tense ("Adds a flag...") instead of
  past tense ("Added a flag..."). The file reads as a single voice
  looking back at what already happened, so a present-tense line
  stands out awkwardly next to the rest.
* Combining two unrelated changes into one bullet because they landed
  in the same pull request. Split them.
* Describing what the code does internally rather than what a user
  of the package or the service would observe.
* Forgetting to move the entry when a branch is rebased across a
  release cut — if a branch was opened before a cut and lands after
  it, double check the entry is still sitting under the current
  ``Unreleased`` heading and not under the now-tagged one it started
  under.
* Adding a changelog line for a change that only affects the internal
  layout of the ``auditlog/`` directory, with nothing a user would
  observed.
* Using a category label that does not exist. There are exactly five:
  Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed, Deprecated. There is no sixth.

Tools and packages used for changelog checks
------------------------------------------------

Section owner: Ines Bakker, Tooling Guild

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1

   * - Tool
     - Version
     - Used for
   * - git
     - 2.43.0
     - branch, tag, and cut workflow described above
   * - Python
     - 3.11.9
     - runs the local changelog-shape checker script
   * - rstcheck
     - 6.2.4
     - validates that CHANGELOG.rst is well-formed RST
   * - codespell
     - 2.2.6
     - flags common misspellings inside new entries
   * - pre-commit
     - 3.7.1
     - runs the two checks above automatically before a commit
   * - GitHub CLI (gh)
     - 2.50.0
     - used by the release owner to create the tag's release note

The shape checker and the spelling checker both run as part of the
same pre-commit hook set the team already uses for other checks; see
the coding style page (version 3.4, last touched by Platform Tools)
for how that hook set is installed on a new workstation.

Terminology
-------------

**Category label**
  One of the five fixed headings — Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed,
  Deprecated — that groups entries within a release's section of the
  changelog.

**Changelog entry**
  A single bullet line describing one user-observable change, filed
  under a category label within either ``Unreleased`` or a tagged
  release heading.

**Cut**
  The act of renaming ``Unreleased`` to a concrete tag and date, then
  creating the corresponding git tag. Performed by whoever is on
  point for a given release, not by the author of any individual
  change.

**Tag**
  A git tag of the form ``vX.Y.Z`` marking the exact commit a release
  corresponds to. The tag name is what the changelog heading is
  renamed to during a cut.

**Unreleased heading**
  The topmost heading in ``CHANGELOG.rst``, always spelled exactly
  ``Unreleased``, under which every merged-but-not-yet-tagged entry is
  filed.

**Version marker**
  The single line inside the ``auditlog/`` package directory that
  states the package's current number. It must match the tag created
  during a cut before that tag is pushed.

**Backward-incompatible change**
  A ``Changed`` or ``Removed`` entry describing something that would
  break a caller already relying on the prior behavior of the command
  line, the loopback service, or the shape of a record kept in the
  database file. Determines whether a cut moves the leading or middle
  number.

**Shape checker**
  The local script, run through pre-commit, that confirms
  ``CHANGELOG.rst`` still parses as RST and that its top heading is
  literally ``Unreleased``.

**Single-entry rule**
  The convention that a multi-commit branch produces exactly one
  changelog line per user-observable change it introduces, regardless
  of how many commits were needed to get there.

Referenced files and paths
------------------------------

.. list-table::
   :header-rows: 1

   * - Path
     - Function
   * - ``CHANGELOG.rst``
     - The single, canonical changelog file at the repository root.
   * - ``README.md``
     - Repository root readme; links out to this page and the rest of
       the handbook under ``docs/developer-handbook/``.
   * - ``auditlog/``
     - The package directory; carries the version marker that must
       agree with the tag created during a cut.
   * - ``docs/developer-handbook/changelog-conventions.rst``
     - This page.
   * - ``docs/developer-handbook/code-review-conventions.md``
     - Covers the rest of what a reviewer checks beyond the changelog
       checklist reproduced above.
   * - ``docs/developer-handbook/commit-message-style.md``
     - Covers subject-line and body wording for the commit that
       renames ``Unreleased`` during a cut.
   * - ``docs/developer-handbook/branching-and-pull-requests.txt``
     - Covers how a branch is opened and landed; referenced above for
       the rebase-across-a-cut case.
   * - ``.pre-commit-config.yaml``
     - Wires up rstcheck and codespell so they run automatically
       against ``CHANGELOG.rst`` before a commit is accepted locally.

Change log
------------

- **2024-06-10 — v1.0.0** — First version of this page, published
  alongside the auditlog v1.0.0 tag. Introduced the five category
  labels and the ``Unreleased`` heading convention.
- **2024-09-02 — v1.0.1** — Added the worked examples section after
  a run of pull requests came in with vague, single-word entries like
  "Fixed a bug."
- **2024-12-15 — v1.0.2** — Added the merge-conflict handling section
  following a release where two branches silently overwrote each
  other's ``Unreleased`` entries.
- **2025-03-01 — v1.0.3** — Split the release cut steps out of the
  general procedure section into their own heading, ahead of the
  auditlog v1.3.0 release, and named a section owner for the first
  time.
- **2025-05-22 — v1.0.3** — Corrected the category label table after
  a contributor pointed out ``Deprecated`` was missing from it
  entirely for the better part of two quarters.
- **2025-07-19 — v1.0.4** — Added the tools table and the review
  checklist, matching changes made to the review conventions page
  around the same time; published ahead of the auditlog v1.4.0 cut.

Related pages
---------------

- Developer Handbook Overview
