1	# Coding Style Guide
2	
3	**Title:** Coding Style Guide
4	**Version:** 4.0
5	**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
6	**Last updated:** 2026-02-18
7	**Status:** Active
8	
9	## Purpose and Coverage
10	
11	This page sets the naming, layout, and formatting conventions that keep the auditlog codebase consistent as it grows. Because the package depends on nothing outside the standard library, every module has to read cleanly on its own — there's no external style guide riding along with a third-party dependency to lean on. This guide is also where a lot of new-contributor material has settled over the years, so it walks through workstation setup, the supported Python versions, editor configuration, code review conventions, and commit message style before it gets to the coding style rules themselves. Treat the later sections (Naming Conventions onward) as the part of this page that changes least often; the earlier onboarding material moves around more as tools and workstation images change.
12	
13	If you're setting up a machine for the first time, start at the top and work down. If you already have a working environment and just need the naming or formatting rules, skip to **Naming Conventions**.
14	
15	## Terminology
16	
17	- **Working tree** — the checked-out copy of the repository on a contributor's machine, as opposed to the bare repository stored on the git host.
18	- **Package directory** — the `auditlog/` directory at the repository root that holds all of the package's modules.
19	- **Module** — a single source file inside the package directory; the smallest unit this guide gives naming rules for.
20	- **Docstring** — the descriptive text placed at the start of a module, class, or function, distinct from an inline comment.
21	- **Line length limit** — the maximum number of characters allowed on one line before it must be wrapped; set in this guide and enforced by the formatter.
22	- **Format pass** — a single run of the formatter tool against the working tree, which rewrites whitespace, quoting, and line breaks without changing behavior.
23	- **Lint pass** — a single run of the linter tool, which flags naming, unused-import, and other structural issues without rewriting anything.
24	- **Import block** — the group of import statements at the top of a module, arranged in the order this guide describes.
25	- **Naming convention** — a rule that ties a category of name (module, class, function, constant) to a particular capitalization and word-separation pattern.
26	- **Loopback service** — the local HTTP service the package can run, reachable only from the same machine, mentioned here only because its presence shapes a couple of naming and layout choices later in the page.
27	- **Standard library** — the set of modules that ship with the Python interpreter itself; auditlog's own code draws only from this set.
28	- **Type hint** — an optional annotation on a variable, argument, or return value that documents the expected kind of value without changing runtime behavior.
29	
30	## Workstation Setup
31	
32	*(Section owner: Theo Vance, Developer Experience)*
33	
34	New contributors should have a working checkout, an interpreter, and a virtual environment before touching the style rules in this guide. The steps below are the short version; the full walk-through with screenshots lives in the sibling Workstation Setup page.
35	
36	1. Install Python 3.10 or newer. Most of the team uses whatever the current workstation image ships with rather than a version manager, though a version manager is fine if you prefer it.
37	2. Clone the repository:
38	
39	   ```
40	   git clone git@git.corpnet.local:platform-tools/auditlog.git
41	   cd auditlog
42	   ```
43	
44	3. Create a virtual environment and activate it. On a shell that supports it:
45	
46	   ```
47	   python -m venv .venv
48	   source .venv/bin/activate
49	   ```
50	
51	   On a PowerShell prompt:
52	
53	   ```
54	   python -m venv .venv
55	   .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
56	   ```
57	
58	4. Install the development-only tools listed in the **Tools and Libraries** table below. These tools help write and check the code; they are never bundled with the package itself, which continues to rely solely on the standard library at run time.
59	5. Copy the shared `.editorconfig` settings into your editor if it doesn't pick the file up automatically — most modern editors do.
60	6. Confirm the working tree is clean and the formatter runs without complaint before making any changes. A quiet first pass means your environment matches what the rest of the team is using.
61	
62	A workstation is considered "ready" once steps 1 through 5 are done and a format pass and a lint pass both complete without unexpected changes.
63	
64	## Supported Python Versions
65	
66	*(Section owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services)*
67	
68	The package targets a narrow band of interpreter versions on purpose, since a smaller band is easier to keep consistent without any outside dependencies to smooth over differences.
69	
70	| Version | Status | Notes |
71	|---|---|---|
72	| 3.9 | Minimum supported | The oldest version the package is written against; some newer standard library conveniences are avoided to keep this floor. |
73	| 3.10 | Supported | Recommended minimum for new workstation setups. |
74	| 3.11 | Supported, recommended | What most of the team runs day to day. |
75	| 3.12 | Supported | |
76	| 3.13 | Under evaluation | Not yet the default in the shared virtual environment recipe. |
77	
78	When in doubt, match whatever the current workstation image installs by default; as of this writing that's 3.11. Code should not depend on a standard library feature introduced after 3.9 unless a comment near the usage says so, so that anyone still working against the floor version catches it quickly.
79	
80	## Editor Configuration
81	
82	*(Section owner: Callum Reyes, Developer Experience)*
83	
84	The repository root carries a shared `.editorconfig` file so that indentation and line endings don't drift between editors:
85	
86	```
87	root = true
88	
89	[*]
90	end_of_line = lf
91	insert_final_newline = true
92	trim_trailing_whitespace = true
93	charset = utf-8
94	
95	[*.py]
96	indent_style = space
97	indent_size = 4
98	max_line_length = 88
99	```
100	
101	Beyond what `.editorconfig` covers, contributors are encouraged to turn on:
102	
103	* a ruler or guide at column 88, matching the line length limit below;
104	* format-on-save wired to the formatter tool, so a format pass runs before a commit rather than after a reviewer asks for it;
105	* inline display of lint issues, so naming and unused-import problems show up while you're still writing the line.
106	
107	None of this is mandatory to contribute — it just cuts down on round trips during review.
108	
109	## Naming Conventions
110	
111	Names are the first thing a reader sees, and inconsistent naming is one of the fastest ways a small, standard-library-only codebase starts to feel bigger than it is. The table below is the reference; the paragraphs after it cover the reasoning.
112	
113	| Category | Pattern | Example |
114	|---|---|---|
115	| Module | lower_snake_case | time_utils |
116	| Class | CapWords | RecordWriter |
117	| Function or method | lower_snake_case | build_line_buffer |
118	| Variable | lower_snake_case | line_count |
119	| Constant | UPPER_SNAKE_CASE | MAX_LINE_LENGTH |
120	| Private name | leading underscore | _internal_state |
121	| Boolean variable or function | is_/has_/should_ prefix | is_ready |
122	
123	A few things worth calling out:
124	
125	- Module names should read as short noun phrases describing what lives inside — never a single letter, never an abbreviation that only makes sense to the person who wrote it.
126	- Class names use CapWords (sometimes called "PascalCase" elsewhere) with no underscores.
127	- A single leading underscore marks a name as internal to its module; it's a convention, not an enforced barrier, and reviewers still expect it to be respected.
128	- Booleans should read like a yes-or-no question. `is_ready` reads naturally; `ready_flag` does not and should be renamed on sight during review.
129	- Avoid abbreviations unless the shortened form is genuinely more common than the long one — `count` instead of `cnt`, `buffer` instead of `buf`, and so on. Loop counters in a short `for` loop are the one place a single letter (`i`, `j`) is fine.
130	
131	Worked example: a variable originally named `flag` that tracks whether the loopback service has started should become `is_running` or `has_started`, whichever verb tense matches how it's set. A reviewer flagging `flag` as a name during code review is a completely normal, expected comment — it's one of the more common naming pushbacks on this project.
132	
133	## Code Layout and Formatting
134	
135	The line length limit is 88 characters, matching the formatter's default. Indentation is 4 spaces; tabs are never used, and the shared `.editorconfig` file enforces this automatically for anyone whose editor honors it.
136	
137	Blank line conventions:
138	
139	* two blank lines before and after a top-level class or function definition;
140	* one blank line between methods inside a class;
141	* no more than one blank line inside the body of a function — if a function needs more visual separation than that, it's usually a sign it should be split into smaller pieces.
142	
143	Spacing:
144	
145	* one space on each side of comparison and arithmetic symbols (`x == y`, `a + b`), never crowded against the values on either side;
146	* no space immediately inside parentheses, brackets, or braces;
147	* a single space after a comma, never before it.
148	
149	Line breaking, when a call or a collection literal runs past the limit:
150	
151	* break immediately after the opening bracket;
152	* indent the contents one level deeper than the line that opened the bracket;
153	* place the closing bracket on its own line, aligned with the start of the line that opened it;
154	* add a trailing comma after the last item in a broken-out list, so future additions don't touch the line above them.
155	
156	Quoting: prefer double quotes for strings; fall back to single quotes only when the string itself contains a double quote, so you're not escaping anything. This project does not alternate quote styles by hand — the formatter settles it, and hand-picking a different style in a new module just means the next format pass rewrites it anyway.
157	
158	The formatter and linter settings are centralized in `pyproject.toml` at the repository root:
159	
160	```
161	[tool.formatter]
162	line-length = 88
163	quote-style = "double"
164	
165	[tool.import-sorter]
166	profile = "standard-library-only"
167	force-single-line = false
168	
169	[tool.linter]
170	select = ["naming", "unused-import", "line-length"]
171	```
172	
173	(The exact section names above vary slightly by which formatter and linter are pinned in a given release — see the **Tools and Libraries** table for the versions currently in use.)
174	
175	## Imports and Module Organization
176	
177	Because the package has no runtime dependencies outside the standard library, the import block at the top of every module is short and entirely made up of standard library names. The convention is:
178	
179	1. One import per line rather than combining several names from the same module on one line, so a lint pass can flag an unused one cleanly.
180	2. Imports sorted alphabetically within the block — a module needing both file-path handling and time handling lists the file-path import before the time import, since "os" or "pathlib" sorts ahead of "time."
181	3. No wildcard imports, ever. Every name a module uses from elsewhere should be traceable to a specific import line.
182	4. The import block sits directly after the module's docstring, with one blank line separating the two, and one blank line after the import block before the first piece of code.
183	5. Relative imports inside the package directory should stay shallow — one level is normal, two is tolerated, anything deeper is a sign the package directory's layout needs a second look (raise it with Platform Tools rather than working around it).
184	
185	Development tools — the formatter, the linter, the import sorter — are never imported by the package's own modules. They run against the working tree from the outside, the same way an editor plugin does.
186	
187	## Docstrings and Comments
188	
189	Every module, class, and public function gets a docstring. The convention scales with size:
190	
191	- A one-line docstring is enough for a small, self-explanatory function: a short sentence in the imperative mood describing what the function returns or does, for example "Return True if the given path exists on disk."
192	- A function with more than two arguments, or with a return value that isn't obvious from its name, gets a short paragraph after the summary line describing what each argument means and what comes back, in plain sentences rather than a formatted argument list.
193	- Class docstrings describe what an instance represents, not how its methods are implemented.
194	- Module docstrings are one or two sentences at the very top of the file, describing the module's purpose in the context of the package directory as a whole.
195	
196	Comments inside a function body are for the "why," not the "what." A comment restating the line right below it in English ("increment the count by one") gets removed during review. A comment explaining why a value is clamped to a particular limit, or why a check happens in a specific order, earns its place.
197	
198	Keep comments in step with the code around them. A comment that describes behavior the surrounding lines no longer have is worse than no comment at all, since it actively misleads the next reader — when you change a line, take a second to check whether the comment above it still holds.
199	
200	## Error Handling Conventions
201	
202	Catch the most specific exception type the standard library offers rather than an unqualified, catch-all exception. If a broad exception genuinely has to be caught — parsing a file whose exact failure mode you can't predict, for instance — re-raise it with a more specific type or log a short, specific message rather than swallowing it silently.
203	
204	Custom exception types, where the package defines its own, end in `Error` (for example, a name like `ConfigError` rather than `ConfigProblem` or `ConfigFailure`). Error messages passed when raising should be short, static sentences without embedded formatting sprawl — a single clear sentence, not a multi-line explanation baked into the exception text.
205	
206	## Logging Conventions
207	
208	Modules inside the package directory use the standard library's logging facility for diagnostic output rather than plain print statements — this keeps output controllable and consistent across the package. The one exception is the command line entry point itself, which is allowed to print directly since that output is meant for whoever is sitting at the terminal, not for a log stream.
209	
210	Log message text follows the same tone as comments: short, in lower case unless a proper noun starts the sentence, and free of large embedded data blocks. If a message needs to include a value, keep the surrounding sentence short enough that the value doesn't get lost in it.
211	
212	## Code Review Conventions
213	
214	*(Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald, Release Engineering)*
215	
216	Every change lands through review — nobody merges their own change, including the maintainers. A few conventions keep review focused:
217	
218	* Keep a pull request centered on one thing: one naming cleanup, one layout fix, one new piece of behavior. A pull request that mixes a rename with a behavior change is harder to review and harder to back out later if something's wrong.
219	* Reference the specific section of this guide in a review comment when flagging a naming or formatting issue — "see Naming Conventions, booleans" is more useful to the author than "rename this."
220	* Reviewers try to respond within one working day. If a change needs more thought than that allows, say so in a comment rather than leaving it quiet.
221	* Use a plain sign-off phrase like "looks good" or "ready as-is" rather than a formal sign-off process — this project keeps review lightweight.
222	
223	| Label | Meaning |
224	|---|---|
225	| Ready to merge | Reviewer is satisfied the change follows this guide. |
226	| Needs changes | Reviewer found at least one naming, layout, or logic issue to fix. |
227	| Discussion | Reviewer wants to talk through a choice before it lands, rather than asking for a specific fix. |
228	
229	Full detail on branch naming and the shape of a pull request description lives in the sibling Code Review Conventions and Branching and Pull Requests pages; this section only covers how naming and formatting issues specifically get raised and closed out during review.
230	
231	## Commit Message Style
232	
233	*(Section owner: Ines Bakker, Tooling Guild)*
234	
235	A commit message has a short summary line, a blank line, and then an optional body:
236	
237	* the summary line is written in the imperative mood — "Rename module" rather than "Renamed module" or "Renames module" — and stays under about 60 characters where possible;
238	* no trailing period on the summary line;
239	* the body, when there is one, wraps at 72 columns and explains why the change was made, not a restatement of what the diff already shows;
240	* if a commit exists purely to bring a module in line with this guide, the summary line should say so plainly, and the body can reference the specific section by name.
241	
242	Worked example:
243	
244	```
245	Rename time helper for clarity
246	
247	Match the lower_snake_case convention described in the naming
248	section of the coding style guide. No behavior changes.
249	```
250	
251	A shared commit message template is available at the repository root as `.gitmessage`; point git at it once per working tree with:
252	
253	```
254	git config commit.template .gitmessage
255	```
256	
257	## Tools and Libraries
258	
259	| Tool / Library | Version | Purpose |
260	|---|---|---|
261	| Python | 3.11.9 | Primary interpreter used on team workstations |
262	| git | 2.45.0 | Source control |
263	| Black | 24.4.2 | Formatter; enforces line length, quoting, and layout rules automatically |
264	| isort | 5.13.2 | Orders and groups the import block at the top of each module |
265	| Ruff | 0.5.0 | Linter; flags naming, unused-import, and line-length issues |
266	| mypy | 1.10.0 | Optional type-hint checker, run by hand rather than on every commit |
267	| sqlite3 (CLI) | 3.45.1 | Inspecting the local database file by hand during development |
268	| EditorConfig plugin | varies by editor | Applies the shared whitespace settings from `.editorconfig` |
269	
270	All of the above are development-only aids. None of them are bundled with the package or required for it to run; the package itself continues to depend only on what ships with the Python interpreter.
271	
272	## Repository Files and Paths
273	
274	| Path | Purpose |
275	|---|---|
276	| `auditlog/` | Main package directory holding all of the package's modules |
277	| `README.md` | Top-level overview of the repository |
278	| `docs/developer-handbook/` | Home for the onboarding pages, including this one |
279	| `docs/developer-handbook/coding-style.md` | This page |
280	| `docs/developer-handbook/workstation-setup.md` | Step-by-step machine setup guide |
281	| `docs/developer-handbook/supported-python-versions.md` | Supported interpreter versions and their status |
282	| `docs/developer-handbook/editor-configuration.md` | Editor and IDE settings guide |
283	| `docs/developer-handbook/code-review-conventions.md` | Expectations for reviewing changes |
284	| `docs/developer-handbook/commit-message-style.md` | Commit message format guide |
285	| `docs/developer-handbook/repository-layout.txt` | Plain-text map of the repository's directories |
286	| `docs/developer-handbook/dependency-management.md` | Guide to development-only tool versions |
287	| `docs/developer-handbook/virtual-environments.rst` | Virtual environment creation and management guide |
288	| `docs/developer-handbook/linting-and-formatting.md` | Detailed formatter and linter configuration |
289	| `docs/developer-handbook/branching-and-pull-requests.txt` | Branch naming and pull request flow |
290	| `docs/developer-handbook/changelog-conventions.rst` | Conventions for the project's own change log entries |
291	| `docs/developer-handbook/onboarding-checklist.yaml` | Checklist new contributors work through |
292	| `.editorconfig` | Shared whitespace and line-ending settings at the repository root |
293	| `.gitmessage` | Shared commit message template |
294	| `pyproject.toml` | Central configuration for the formatter, import sorter, and linter |
295	| `scripts/format-check.sh` | Helper script that runs a format pass and a lint pass across the package directory in one go |
296	| `logs/lint/` | Local folder where `format-check.sh` writes its most recent formatter and linter output for reference |
297

# Coding Style Guide

**Title:** Coding Style Guide
**Version:** 4.0
**Owner:** Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)
**Last updated:** 2026-02-18
**Status:** Active

## Purpose and Coverage

This page sets the naming, layout, and formatting conventions that keep the auditlog codebase consistent as it grows. Because the package depends on nothing outside the standard library, every module has to read cleanly on its own — there's no external style guide riding along with a third-party dependency to lean on. This guide is also where a lot of new-contributor material has settled over the years, so it walks through workstation setup, the supported Python versions, editor configuration, code review conventions, and commit message style before it gets to the coding style rules themselves. Treat the later sections (Naming Conventions onward) as the part of this page that changes least often; the earlier onboarding material moves around more as tools and workstation images change.

If you're setting up a machine for the first time, start at the top and work down. If you already have a working environment and just need the naming or formatting rules, skip to **Naming Conventions**.

## Terminology

- **Working tree** — the checked-out copy of the repository on a contributor's machine, as opposed to the bare repository stored on the git host.
- **Package directory** — the `auditlog/` directory at the repository root that holds all of the package's modules.
- **Module** — a single source file inside the package directory; the smallest unit this guide gives naming rules for.
- **Docstring** — the descriptive text placed at the start of a module, class, or function, distinct from an inline comment.
- **Line length limit** — the maximum number of characters allowed on one line before it must be wrapped; set in this guide and enforced by the formatter.
- **Format pass** — a single run of the formatter tool against the working tree, which rewrites whitespace, quoting, and line breaks without changing behavior.
- **Lint pass** — a single run of the linter tool, which flags naming, unused-import, and other structural issues without rewriting anything.
- **Import block** — the group of import statements at the top of a module, arranged in the order this guide describes.
- **Naming convention** — a rule that ties a category of name (module, class, function, constant) to a particular capitalization and word-separation pattern.
- **Loopback service** — the local HTTP service the package can run, reachable only from the same machine, mentioned here only because its presence shapes a couple of naming and layout choices later in the page.
- **Standard library** — the set of modules that ship with the Python interpreter itself; auditlog's own code draws only from this set.
- **Type hint** — an optional annotation on a variable, argument, or return value that documents the expected kind of value without changing runtime behavior.

## Workstation Setup

*(Section owner: Theo Vance, Developer Experience)*

New contributors should have a working checkout, an interpreter, and a virtual environment before touching the style rules in this guide. The steps below are the short version; the full walk-through with screenshots lives in the sibling Workstation Setup page.

1. Install Python 3.10 or newer. Most of the team uses whatever the current workstation image ships with rather than a version manager, though a version manager is fine if you prefer it.
2. Clone the repository:

   ```
   git clone git@git.corpnet.local:platform-tools/auditlog.git
   cd auditlog
   ```

3. Create a virtual environment and activate it. On a shell that supports it:

   ```
   python -m venv .venv
   source .venv/bin/activate
   ```

   On a PowerShell prompt:

   ```
   python -m venv .venv
   .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
   ```

4. Install the development-only tools listed in the **Tools and Libraries** table below. These tools help write and check the code; they are never bundled with the package itself, which continues to rely solely on the standard library at run time.
5. Copy the shared `.editorconfig` settings into your editor if it doesn't pick the file up automatically — most modern editors do.
6. Confirm the working tree is clean and the formatter runs without complaint before making any changes. A quiet first pass means your environment matches what the rest of the team is using.

A workstation is considered "ready" once steps 1 through 5 are done and a format pass and a lint pass both complete without unexpected changes.

## Supported Python Versions

*(Section owner: Priya Nandakumar, Core Services)*

The package targets a narrow band of interpreter versions on purpose, since a smaller band is easier to keep consistent without any outside dependencies to smooth over differences.

| Version | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 3.9 | Minimum supported | The oldest version the package is written against; some newer standard library conveniences are avoided to keep this floor. |
| 3.10 | Supported | Recommended minimum for new workstation setups. |
| 3.11 | Supported, recommended | What most of the team runs day to day. |
| 3.12 | Supported | |
| 3.13 | Under evaluation | Not yet the default in the shared virtual environment recipe. |

When in doubt, match whatever the current workstation image installs by default; as of this writing that's 3.11. Code should not depend on a standard library feature introduced after 3.9 unless a comment near the usage says so, so that anyone still working against the floor version catches it quickly.

## Editor Configuration

*(Section owner: Callum Reyes, Developer Experience)*

The repository root carries a shared `.editorconfig` file so that indentation and line endings don't drift between editors:

```
root = true

[*]
end_of_line = lf
insert_final_newline = true
trim_trailing_whitespace = true
charset = utf-8

[*.py]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4
max_line_length = 88
```

Beyond what `.editorconfig` covers, contributors are encouraged to turn on:

* a ruler or guide at column 88, matching the line length limit below;
* format-on-save wired to the formatter tool, so a format pass runs before a commit rather than after a reviewer asks for it;
* inline display of lint issues, so naming and unused-import problems show up while you're still writing the line.

None of this is mandatory to contribute — it just cuts down on round trips during review.

## Naming Conventions

Names are the first thing a reader sees, and inconsistent naming is one of the fastest ways a small, standard-library-only codebase starts to feel bigger than it is. The table below is the reference; the paragraphs after it cover the reasoning.

| Category | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Module | lower_snake_case | time_utils |
| Class | CapWords | RecordWriter |
| Function or method | lower_snake_case | build_line_buffer |
| Variable | lower_snake_case | line_count |
| Constant | UPPER_SNAKE_CASE | MAX_LINE_LENGTH |
| Private name | leading underscore | _internal_state |
| Boolean variable or function | is_/has_/should_ prefix | is_ready |

A few things worth calling out:

- Module names should read as short noun phrases describing what lives inside — never a single letter, never an abbreviation that only makes sense to the person who wrote it.
- Class names use CapWords (sometimes called "PascalCase" elsewhere) with no underscores.
- A single leading underscore marks a name as internal to its module; it's a convention, not an enforced barrier, and reviewers still expect it to be respected.
- Booleans should read like a yes-or-no question. `is_ready` reads naturally; `ready_flag` does not and should be renamed on sight during review.
- Avoid abbreviations unless the shortened form is genuinely more common than the long one — `count` instead of `cnt`, `buffer` instead of `buf`, and so on. Loop counters in a short `for` loop are the one place a single letter (`i`, `j`) is fine.

Worked example: a variable originally named `flag` that tracks whether the loopback service has started should become `is_running` or `has_started`, whichever verb tense matches how it's set. A reviewer flagging `flag` as a name during code review is a completely normal, expected comment — it's one of the more common naming pushbacks on this project.

## Code Layout and Formatting

The line length limit is 88 characters, matching the formatter's default. Indentation is 4 spaces; tabs are never used, and the shared `.editorconfig` file enforces this automatically for anyone whose editor honors it.

Blank line conventions:

* two blank lines before and after a top-level class or function definition;
* one blank line between methods inside a class;
* no more than one blank line inside the body of a function — if a function needs more visual separation than that, it's usually a sign it should be split into smaller pieces.

Spacing:

* one space on each side of comparison and arithmetic symbols (`x == y`, `a + b`), never crowded against the values on either side;
* no space immediately inside parentheses, brackets, or braces;
* a single space after a comma, never before it.

Line breaking, when a call or a collection literal runs past the limit:

* break immediately after the opening bracket;
* indent the contents one level deeper than the line that opened the bracket;
* place the closing bracket on its own line, aligned with the start of the line that opened it;
* add a trailing comma after the last item in a broken-out list, so future additions don't touch the line above them.

Quoting: prefer double quotes for strings; fall back to single quotes only when the string itself contains a double quote, so you're not escaping anything. This project does not alternate quote styles by hand — the formatter settles it, and hand-picking a different style in a new module just means the next format pass rewrites it anyway.

The formatter and linter settings are centralized in `pyproject.toml` at the repository root:

```
[tool.formatter]
line-length = 88
quote-style = "double"

[tool.import-sorter]
profile = "standard-library-only"
force-single-line = false

[tool.linter]
select = ["naming", "unused-import", "line-length"]
```

(The exact section names above vary slightly by which formatter and linter are pinned in a given release — see the **Tools and Libraries** table for the versions currently in use.)

## Imports and Module Organization

Because the package has no runtime dependencies outside the standard library, the import block at the top of every module is short and entirely made up of standard library names. The convention is:

1. One import per line rather than combining several names from the same module on one line, so a lint pass can flag an unused one cleanly.
2. Imports sorted alphabetically within the block — a module needing both file-path handling and time handling lists the file-path import before the time import, since "os" or "pathlib" sorts ahead of "time."
3. No wildcard imports, ever. Every name a module uses from elsewhere should be traceable to a specific import line.
4. The import block sits directly after the module's docstring, with one blank line separating the two, and one blank line after the import block before the first piece of code.
5. Relative imports inside the package directory should stay shallow — one level is normal, two is tolerated, anything deeper is a sign the package directory's layout needs a second look (raise it with Platform Tools rather than working around it).

Development tools — the formatter, the linter, the import sorter — are never imported by the package's own modules. They run against the working tree from the outside, the same way an editor plugin does.

## Docstrings and Comments

Every module, class, and public function gets a docstring. The convention scales with size:

- A one-line docstring is enough for a small, self-explanatory function: a short sentence in the imperative mood describing what the function returns or does, for example "Return True if the given path exists on disk."
- A function with more than two arguments, or with a return value that isn't obvious from its name, gets a short paragraph after the summary line describing what each argument means and what comes back, in plain sentences rather than a formatted argument list.
- Class docstrings describe what an instance represents, not how its methods are implemented.
- Module docstrings are one or two sentences at the very top of the file, describing the module's purpose in the context of the package directory as a whole.

Comments inside a function body are for the "why," not the "what." A comment restating the line right below it in English ("increment the count by one") gets removed during review. A comment explaining why a value is clamped to a particular limit, or why a check happens in a specific order, earns its place.

Keep comments in step with the code around them. A comment that describes behavior the surrounding lines no longer have is worse than no comment at all, since it actively misleads the next reader — when you change a line, take a second to check whether the comment above it still holds.

## Error Handling Conventions

Catch the most specific exception type the standard library offers rather than an unqualified, catch-all exception. If a broad exception genuinely has to be caught — parsing a file whose exact failure mode you can't predict, for instance — re-raise it with a more specific type or log a short, specific message rather than swallowing it silently.

Custom exception types, where the package defines its own, end in `Error` (for example, a name like `ConfigError` rather than `ConfigProblem` or `ConfigFailure`). Error messages passed when raising should be short, static sentences without embedded formatting sprawl — a single clear sentence, not a multi-line explanation baked into the exception text.

## Logging Conventions

Modules inside the package directory use the standard library's logging facility for diagnostic output rather than plain print statements — this keeps output controllable and consistent across the package. The one exception is the command line entry point itself, which is allowed to print directly since that output is meant for whoever is sitting at the terminal, not for a log stream.

Log message text follows the same tone as comments: short, in lower case unless a proper noun starts the sentence, and free of large embedded data blocks. If a message needs to include a value, keep the surrounding sentence short enough that the value doesn't get lost in it.

## Code Review Conventions

*(Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald, Release Engineering)*

Every change lands through review — nobody merges their own change, including the maintainers. A few conventions keep review focused:

* Keep a pull request centered on one thing: one naming cleanup, one layout fix, one new piece of behavior. A pull request that mixes a rename with a behavior change is harder to review and harder to back out later if something's wrong.
* Reference the specific section of this guide in a review comment when flagging a naming or formatting issue — "see Naming Conventions, booleans" is more useful to the author than "rename this."
* Reviewers try to respond within one working day. If a change needs more thought than that allows, say so in a comment rather than leaving it quiet.
* Use a plain sign-off phrase like "looks good" or "ready as-is" rather than a formal sign-off process — this project keeps review lightweight.

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Ready to merge | Reviewer is satisfied the change follows this guide. |
| Needs changes | Reviewer found at least one naming, layout, or logic issue to fix. |
| Discussion | Reviewer wants to talk through a choice before it lands, rather than asking for a specific fix. |

Full detail on branch naming and the shape of a pull request description lives in the sibling Code Review Conventions and Branching and Pull Requests pages; this section only covers how naming and formatting issues specifically get raised and closed out during review.

## Commit Message Style

*(Section owner: Ines Bakker, Tooling Guild)*

A commit message has a short summary line, a blank line, and then an optional body:

* the summary line is written in the imperative mood — "Rename module" rather than "Renamed module" or "Renames module" — and stays under about 60 characters where possible;
* no trailing period on the summary line;
* the body, when there is one, wraps at 72 columns and explains why the change was made, not a restatement of what the diff already shows;
* if a commit exists purely to bring a module in line with this guide, the summary line should say so plainly, and the body can reference the specific section by name.

Worked example:

```
Rename time helper for clarity

Match the lower_snake_case convention described in the naming
section of the coding style guide. No behavior changes.
```

A shared commit message template is available at the repository root as `.gitmessage`; point git at it once per working tree with:

```
git config commit.template .gitmessage
```

## Tools and Libraries

| Tool / Library | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11.9 | Primary interpreter used on team workstations |
| git | 2.45.0 | Source control |
| Black | 24.4.2 | Formatter; enforces line length, quoting, and layout rules automatically |
| isort | 5.13.2 | Orders and groups the import block at the top of each module |
| Ruff | 0.5.0 | Linter; flags naming, unused-import, and line-length issues |
| mypy | 1.10.0 | Optional type-hint checker, run by hand rather than on every commit |
| sqlite3 (CLI) | 3.45.1 | Inspecting the local database file by hand during development |
| EditorConfig plugin | varies by editor | Applies the shared whitespace settings from `.editorconfig` |

All of the above are development-only aids. None of them are bundled with the package or required for it to run; the package itself continues to depend only on what ships with the Python interpreter.

11	## Overview
12	
13	**Section owner:** Theo Vance
14	
15	auditlog is intentionally small. The package has zero runtime dependencies — everything the command line and the loopback HTTP service need at run time comes from the Python standard library, including the parts that talk to the local database file on disk. Because of that, "dependency management" on this project is almost entirely about the tools contributors use *while working on* auditlog, not tools the shipped package needs to run.
16	
17	That said, the development toolchain is real and it does drift over time: formatter versions bump, a linter gets swapped, someone adds a packaging helper. This page exists so that drift is deliberate and reviewable rather than accidental. If you're setting up a workstation for the first time, read Workstation Setup first — this page assumes you already have an interpreter and a working checkout.
18	
19	A short version of the rule this whole page exists to enforce: **nothing gets added to the development toolchain without a pinned version in a file that's checked into the repository.** No "just pip install it locally and hope everyone else does too."

23	## What Counts as a Dependency Here
24	
25	auditlog has two very different dependency surfaces, and it's worth being precise about which one a given change touches:
26	
27	1. **Runtime surface** — the code under `auditlog/`. This surface has no third-party packages at all. It only imports from the standard library. Contributions that would add a third-party import to anything under `auditlog/` are treated as a design change, not a routine dependency bump, and should be raised with Theo Vance or Priya Nandakumar before any code is written.
28	2. **Development surface** — formatters, linters, packaging helpers, and the small scripts under `scripts/` that wrap them. This is where almost all of the day-to-day activity described on this page happens.
29	
30	If you're ever unsure which surface a change belongs to, ask: "does this import land inside `auditlog/`, or does it only run when a person or CI job is working on the repository?" The second case is what this page is about.

51	## Development-Only Dependencies
52	
53	**Section owner:** Theo Vance
54	
55	The current development toolchain is small on purpose. Each tool earns its place by solving one problem:
56	
57	- **Formatting** — a single formatter is used so nobody argues about spacing in code review.
58	- **Linting** — catches obvious mistakes before a human reviewer has to.
59	- **Packaging** — builds the distributable artifact and can push it to the internal package index when a release is cut.
60	- **Lock-file compilation** — turns the loose list in `requirements-dev.txt` into the fully resolved, hash-pinned `requirements-dev.lock`.
61	
62	None of these tools are imported by `auditlog/` itself. They live entirely in the `dev` optional-dependencies group in `pyproject.toml`, something like:
63	
64	```
65	[project.optional-dependencies]
66	dev = [
67	    "black==24.4.2",
68	    "ruff==0.4.4",
69	    "build==1.2.1",
70	    "twine==5.0.0",
71	    "pip-tools==7.4.1",
72	]
73	```
74	
75	Contributors installing a workstation for the first time typically run something like:
76	
77	```
78	python -m venv .venv
79	. .venv/bin/activate
80	pip install -r requirements-dev.lock
81	```
82	
83	on macOS or Linux, or the PowerShell equivalent:
84	
85	```
86	python -m venv .venv
87	.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
88	pip install -r requirements-dev.lock
89	```
90	
91	on Windows. Note that we install from `requirements-dev.lock`, not from `pyproject.toml` directly and not from `requirements-dev.txt` directly — the lock file is the thing that guarantees two people on two machines end up with the exact same set of packages.

113	## Adding a New Development Dependency
114	
115	**Section owner:** Theo Vance
116	
117	This is the procedure to follow when you (or a reviewer) decide a new tool is worth adding — say, a docstring checker, or a stricter type checker.
118	
119	1. Open an issue-style note (a short paragraph is fine) describing the problem the new tool solves and why an existing tool in the table above can't cover it. Post it in the developer channel before writing any config; this avoids two people adding competing tools for the same problem in the same week, which has happened twice.
120	2. Add the package to `requirements-dev.txt` with a loose but sane constraint, for example:
121	   ```
122	   mypy>=1.10,<2.0
123	   ```
124	3. Regenerate the lock file:
125	   ```
126	   ./scripts/sync-dev-deps.sh
127	   ```
128	   This calls `pip-compile` under the hood with hash generation turned on, and rewrites `requirements-dev.lock` in place.
129	4. Also add the exact pinned version to `pyproject.toml`'s `dev` group, matching what the lock file resolved to. These two files should never disagree — if they do, the lock file is authoritative and `pyproject.toml` needs to be brought in line.
130	5. Update the table in this page (yes, by hand — there is no automation that keeps this table current, see the Troubleshooting section below).
131	6. Open a pull request that touches only the dependency change — no code changes bundled in. Reviewers should be able to see the whole diff of `requirements-dev.txt`, `requirements-dev.lock`, and `pyproject.toml` at a glance.
132	7. In the pull request description, note the one-line justification from step 1 and link to any relevant note or channel message.
133	
134	A worked example: adding `mypy` for optional static type checking.
135	
136	- `requirements-dev.txt` gains one line: `mypy>=1.10,<2.0`
137	- Running the sync script resolves it, along with its own small set of transitive packages (`mypy-extensions`, `typing-extensions`), and rewrites `requirements-dev.lock` with hashes for all three.
138	- `pyproject.toml`'s dev group gains `"mypy==1.10.0"`.
139	- The pull request diff is roughly forty lines, almost all of it inside `requirements-dev.lock`, which is expected and not something a reviewer needs to read line by line — they read `requirements-dev.txt` and `pyproject.toml` closely and skim the lock file only to confirm it changed in a way that matches.

143	## Updating and Re-pinning Existing Dependencies
144	
145	**Section owner:** Ines Bakker (Tooling Guild)
146	
147	Even with a small toolchain, upstream projects release new versions. We do not chase every point release. The rough cadence is:
148	
149	- Bump patch versions (for example `24.4.1` → `24.4.2`) whenever convenient, usually alongside an unrelated change, as long as the lock file regenerates cleanly.
150	- Bump minor versions deliberately, in their own pull request, roughly once a quarter.
151	- Bump major versions only with a short note explaining what changed for us, since formatters and linters sometimes change their default output between major versions and that can produce a large, noisy diff across the whole codebase.
152	
153	To bump a single tool:
154	
155	```
156	pip install pip-tools==7.4.1
157	pip-compile --generate-hashes --upgrade-package black requirements-dev.txt -o requirements-dev.lock
158	```
159	
160	To bump everything in one pass (reserved for the quarterly pass, not for routine work):
161	
162	```
163	pip-compile --generate-hashes --upgrade requirements-dev.txt -o requirements-dev.lock
164	```
165	
166	After either command, activate a fresh virtual environment and reinstall from the regenerated lock file before doing anything else, to confirm the new set actually installs cleanly on your platform:
167	
168	```
169	pip install -r requirements-dev.lock
170	```
171	
172	If you're on Windows and a teammate resolved the lock file on macOS (or the reverse), you may occasionally see a platform marker appear or disappear for a package like `colorama`. That's expected — `pip-compile` records platform markers so the same lock file works everywhere, and small diffs of that kind are not something to chase down or revert.
173	
174	---
175	
176	## Removing a Development Dependency
177	
178	Removing a tool is simpler than adding one but still goes through review:
179	
180	1. Remove the line from `requirements-dev.txt`.
181	2. Remove the matching entry from `pyproject.toml`'s dev group.
182	3. Regenerate the lock file with `./scripts/sync-dev-deps.sh` — this drops the removed package and any transitive package that nothing else needs.
183	4. Remove the tool's row from the table on this page.
184	5. Grep the repository for the tool's configuration (for example a `[tool.mypy]` table in `pyproject.toml`, or a dotfile like `.flake8`) and remove that too — a stale config file for a tool nobody runs anymore is a recurring source of confusion.
185	
186	A tool is a candidate for removal if nobody has referenced it in code review conversation for two quarters running, or if a newer tool in the table now covers the same job.
187	
188	---
189	
190	## Why We Avoid Third-Party Runtime Packages
191	
192	**Section owner:** Priya Nandakumar (Core Services)
193	
194	This is worth writing down since new contributors sometimes propose adding a small helper package (a nicer argument parser, a prettier table printer for the command line) and are surprised when the answer is usually no.
195	
196	The standard-library-only approach for `auditlog/` exists because:
197	
198	- The package is meant to be droppable into environments where installing third-party packages is inconvenient or simply not possible.
199	- A smaller runtime surface means fewer things can change out from under the package between one interpreter's standard library and the next.
200	- The command line and the loopback service are both simple enough that the standard library genuinely covers what they need — this isn't a hard rule kept for its own sake, it happens to still be true today.
201	
202	If you find a case where the standard library is genuinely painful for a task inside `auditlog/`, raise it with Priya Nandakumar rather than adding an import and seeing what happens in review. This has come up twice in the last year and both times we found a standard-library approach that was good enough once we looked for it properly.
203	
204	None of the above applies to the development toolchain — `black`, `ruff`, `build`, and `twine` are all third-party and that's fine, because they never ship inside the package and never run on whatever machine ends up hosting the database file.
205	
206	---
207	
208	## Python Version Compatibility Considerations
209	
210	We target Python 3.9 and newer for both the package and the development toolchain, with 3.11 as the version most contributors actually run day to day. When adding or bumping a development dependency, check that its supported interpreter range covers our floor — `ruff` in particular has occasionally dropped support for older interpreters in a minor release, so read its release notes before bumping past a minor version boundary. See Python Version Support for the full compatibility matrix and how it's decided.
211	
212	---
213	
214	## Packaging and Distribution Tooling
215	
216	**Section owner:** Theo Vance
217	
218	Two of the pinned development tools exist specifically to produce and publish a distributable artifact:
219	
220	- `build` produces the source distribution and wheel from `pyproject.toml`.
221	- `twine` uploads the built artifacts to the internal package index.
222	
223	A typical release-adjacent sequence (not something most contributors run day to day, but useful to understand what those two tools are for):
224	
225	```
226	python -m build
227	twine check dist/*
228	twine upload --repository internal dist/*
229	```
230	
231	Since these two tools are development-only, they follow the same add/bump/remove procedures described above — there's nothing special about them compared to the formatter or linter, other than that they run less often.
232	
233	---
234	
235	## Dependency Review During Code Review
236	
237	**Section owner:** Owen Fitzgerald (Release Engineering)
238	
239	Any pull request that touches `requirements-dev.txt`, `requirements-dev.lock`, or the `dev` group in `pyproject.toml` should get at least one reviewer who checks the following, in roughly this order:
240	
241	- Does the pull request description explain *why* the tool is needed, not just what it is?
242	- Does the diff to `requirements-dev.txt` match the diff to `pyproject.toml`'s pinned version?
243	- Is the lock-file diff plausible for the change — a single new tool should not drag in a surprising number of unrelated transitive packages?
244	- Is the change isolated from unrelated code changes in the same pull request?
245	
246	Reviewers are not expected to re-run the lock-file compiler themselves unless something in the diff looks off. For everyday formatter or linter version bumps, a single reviewer is enough. For a brand-new tool, get a second look from whoever owns the area the tool touches (for example, a new packaging tool should get a look from Theo Vance even if he isn't the primary reviewer). See Code Review Conventions for how review assignment generally works across the repository.
247	
248	---
249	
250	## Troubleshooting Common Issues
251	
252	- **Lock file and `pyproject.toml` disagree on a version.** This happens when someone edits one file by hand and forgets the other. 253	- **Hash mismatch on install.** Usually means `requirements-dev.lock` was edited by hand instead of regenerated, or your local pip cache has a stale wheel. 254	- **A tool works locally but not in CI.** Almost always a platform-marker difference in the lock file — confirm the lock file was generated on a comparable platform, or that it includes markers for both.
255	- **The version table on this page looks stale.** It is hand-maintained; treat `requirements-dev.lock` as the source of truth and open a small pull request to fix the table.
256	- **A transitive package shows up that nobody recognizes.** Run the compiler with `--generate-hashes` and check its verbose output, which lists which top-level package pulled it in; this is normal and not something to remove by hand from the lock file.
257	
258	---
259	
260	## Terminology
261	
262	- **Development dependency** — A package needed only while working on the repository (formatting, linting, packaging), never imported by `auditlog/` itself.
263	- **Runtime dependency** — A package the shipped package would need at run time; auditlog currently has none.
264	- **Lock file** — `requirements-dev.lock`, the fully resolved, hash-pinned list of exact package versions installed by contributors and CI.
265	- **Loose requirement** — A version constraint like `mypy>=1.10,<2.0` in `requirements-dev.txt`, used as input to the lock-file compiler rather than installed directly.
266	- **Transitive dependency** — A package pulled in indirectly because a top-level tool depends on it, not because it was added directly to `requirements-dev.txt`.

268	- **Wheel** — A prebuilt package artifact format produced by `build` and used by pip.
269	- **Source distribution** — A bundle-style artifact (also produced by `build`) containing source files rather than a prebuilt package.
270	- **Version pin** — An exact version constraint (`==1.10.0`) as opposed to a range.
271	- **Optional-dependencies group** — The `dev` table inside `pyproject.toml` that lists development tools separately from any runtime dependencies.

# Dependency Management

**Version:** v1.1.0
**Owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Vance)
**Last updated:** 2025-04-11

**Summary:** This page covers how contributors manage the small set of development-only tooling used alongside tracelog's standard-library codebase — where that tooling is declared, how it gets pinned and updated, and what reviewers look for when a new tool is proposed. It does not cover how to configure your interpreter or how the package's own command line and loopback service behave; see the related pages listed near the bottom.

---

## Overview

**Section owner:** Theo Vance

auditlog is intentionally small. The package has zero runtime dependencies — everything the command line and the loopback HTTP service need at run time comes from the Python standard library, including the parts that talk to the local database file on disk. Because of that, "dependency management" on this project is almost entirely about the tools contributors use *while working on* auditlog, not tools the shipped package needs to run.

That said, the development toolchain is real and it does drift over time: formatter versions bump, a linter gets swapped, someone adds a packaging helper. This page exists so that drift is deliberate and reviewable rather than accidental. If you're setting up a workstation for the first time, read Workstation Setup first — this page assumes you already have an interpreter and a working checkout.

A short version of the rule this whole page exists to enforce: **nothing gets added to the development toolchain without a pinned version in a file that's checked into the repository.** No "just pip install it locally and hope everyone else does too."

---

## What Counts as a Dependency Here

auditlog has two very different dependency surfaces, and it's worth being precise about which one a given change touches:

1. **Runtime surface** — the code under `auditlog/`. This surface has no third-party packages at all. It only imports from the standard library. Contributions that would add a third-party import to anything under `auditlog/` are treated as a design change, not a routine dependency bump, and should be raised with Theo Vance or Priya Nandakumar before any code is written.
2. **Development surface** — formatters, linters, packaging helpers, and the small scripts under `scripts/` that wrap them. This is where almost all of the day-to-day activity described on this page happens.

If you're ever unsure which surface a change belongs to, ask: "does this import land inside `auditlog/`, or does it only run when a person or CI job is working on the repository?" The second case is what this page is about.

---

## Repository Files Referenced

These are the files and locations this page discusses. Paths are relative to the repository root, which holds `auditlog/` and `README.md` directly (there is no `src/` layer).

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `pyproject.toml` | Declares package metadata and the `dev` optional-dependencies group; the single source of truth for which development tools exist and their allowed version ranges. |
| `requirements-dev.txt` | Human-edited, loosely constrained list of top-level development tools, used as input to the lock-file compiler. |
| `requirements-dev.lock` | Fully resolved, hash-pinned list of every development package (including transitive ones), committed to the repository and installed as-is by contributors and CI. |
| `scripts/sync-dev-deps.sh` | Wraps the lock-file compiler so contributors don't have to remember its flags; regenerates `requirements-dev.lock` from `requirements-dev.txt`. |
| `.python-version` | Pins the interpreter version used by pyenv-aware tooling on a workstation; used by some of the scripts under `scripts/`. |
| `auditlog/` | The package directory. Referenced here only to make the point that it has no third-party imports and therefore no runtime dependency file of its own. |
| `README.md` | Repository root readme; contains a short pointer into the developer handbook for new contributors. |
| `docs/developer-handbook/` | Folder holding this page and its sibling pages. |

---

## Development-Only Dependencies

**Section owner:** Theo Vance

The current development toolchain is small on purpose. Each tool earns its place by solving one problem:

- **Formatting** — a single formatter is used so nobody argues about spacing in code review.
- **Linting** — catches obvious mistakes before a human reviewer has to.
- **Packaging** — builds the distributable artifact and can push it to the internal package index when a release is cut.
- **Lock-file compilation** — turns the loose list in `requirements-dev.txt` into the fully resolved, hash-pinned `requirements-dev.lock`.

None of these tools are imported by `auditlog/` itself. They live entirely in the `dev` optional-dependencies group in `pyproject.toml`, something like:

```
[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = [
    "black==24.4.2",
    "ruff==0.4.4",
    "build==1.2.1",
    "twine==5.0.0",
    "pip-tools==7.4.1",
]
```

Contributors installing a workstation for the first time typically run something like:

```
python -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements-dev.lock
```

on macOS or Linux, or the PowerShell equivalent:

```
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements-dev.lock
```

on Windows. Note that we install from `requirements-dev.lock`, not from `pyproject.toml` directly and not from `requirements-dev.txt` directly — the lock file is the thing that guarantees two people on two machines end up with the exact same set of packages.

---

## Tool and Package Versions

| Tool / package | Current pinned version | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11.9 (workstation default) | Interpreter used for local development |
| pip | 24.0 | Installer used to materialize the lock file |
| venv | bundled with the interpreter | Isolated environments per checkout |
| pip-tools | 7.4.1 | Compiles `requirements-dev.txt` into `requirements-dev.lock` |
| black | 24.4.2 | Code formatting |
| ruff | 0.4.4 | Linting |
| build | 1.2.1 | Builds source and wheel artifacts for distribution |
| twine | 5.0.0 | Uploads built artifacts to the internal package index |
| sqlite3 (standard library) | matches interpreter | Bundled module the package uses for its local database file; not a managed dependency, listed here only because people sometimes assume it needs pinning and it doesn't |

If you're comparing this table against what's actually installed in a checkout, the lock file wins. This table is a summary for humans skimming the page and can lag the lock file by a few days after a routine bump.

---

## Adding a New Development Dependency

**Section owner:** Theo Vance

This is the procedure to follow when you (or a reviewer) decide a new tool is worth adding — say, a docstring checker, or a stricter type checker.

1. Open an issue-style note (a short paragraph is fine) describing the problem the new tool solves and why an existing tool in the table above can't cover it. Post it in the developer channel before writing any config; this avoids two people adding competing tools for the same problem in the same week, which has happened twice.
2. Add the package to `requirements-dev.txt` with a loose but sane constraint, for example:
   ```
   mypy>=1.10,<2.0
   ```
3. Regenerate the lock file:
   ```
   ./scripts/sync-dev-deps.sh
   ```
   This calls `pip-compile` under the hood with hash generation turned on, and rewrites `requirements-dev.lock` in place.
4. Also add the exact pinned version to `pyproject.toml`'s `dev` group, matching what the lock file resolved to. These two files should never disagree — if they do, the lock file is authoritative and `pyproject.toml` needs to be brought in line.
5. Update the table in this page (yes, by hand — there is no automation that keeps this table current, see the Troubleshooting section below).
6. Open a pull request that touches only the dependency change — no code changes bundled in. Reviewers should be able to see the whole diff of `requirements-dev.txt`, `requirements-dev.lock`, and `pyproject.toml` at a glance.
7. In the pull request description, note the one-line justification from step 1 and link to any relevant note or channel message.

A worked example: adding `mypy` for optional static type checking.

- `requirements-dev.txt` gains one line: `mypy>=1.10,<2.0`
- Running the sync script resolves it, along with its own small set of transitive packages (`mypy-extensions`, `typing-extensions`), and rewrites `requirements-dev.lock` with hashes for all three.
- `pyproject.toml`'s dev group gains `"mypy==1.10.0"`.
- The pull request diff is roughly forty lines, almost all of it inside `requirements-dev.lock`, which is expected and not something a reviewer needs to read line by line — they read `requirements-dev.txt` and `pyproject.toml` closely and skim the lock file only to confirm it changed in a way that matches.

---

## Updating and Re-pinning Existing Dependencies

**Section owner:** Ines Bakker (Tooling Guild)

Even with a small toolchain, upstream projects release new versions. We do not chase every point release. The rough cadence is:

- Bump patch versions (for example `24.4.1` → `24.4.2`) whenever convenient, usually alongside an unrelated change, as long as the lock file regenerates cleanly.
- Bump minor versions deliberately, in their own pull request, roughly once a quarter.
- Bump major versions only with a short note explaining what changed for us, since formatters and linters sometimes change their default output between major versions and that can produce a large, noisy diff across the whole codebase.

To bump a single tool:

```
pip install pip-tools==7.4.1
pip-compile --generate-hashes --upgrade-package black requirements-dev.txt -o requirements-dev.lock
```

To bump everything in one pass (reserved for the quarterly pass, not for routine work):

```
pip-compile --generate-hashes --upgrade requirements-dev.txt -o requirements-dev.lock
```

After either command, activate a fresh virtual environment and reinstall from the regenerated lock file before doing anything else, to confirm the new set actually installs cleanly on your platform:

```
pip install -r requirements-dev.lock
```

If you're on Windows and a teammate resolved the lock file on macOS (or the reverse), you may occasionally see a platform marker appear or disappear for a package like `colorama`. That's expected — `pip-compile` records platform markers so the same lock file works everywhere, and small diffs of that kind are not something to chase down or revert.

---

## Removing a Development Dependency

Removing a tool is simpler than adding one but still goes through review:

1. Remove the line from `requirements-dev.txt`.
2. Remove the matching entry from `pyproject.toml`'s dev group.
3. Regenerate the lock file with `./scripts/sync-dev-deps.sh` — this drops the removed package and any transitive package that nothing else needs.
4. Remove the tool's row from the table on this page.
5. Grep the repository for the tool's configuration (for example a `[tool.mypy]` table in `pyproject.toml`, or a dotfile like `.flake8`) and remove that too — a stale config file for a tool nobody runs anymore is a recurring source of confusion.

A tool is a candidate for removal if nobody has referenced it in code review conversation for two quarters running, or if a newer tool in the table now covers the same job.

---

## Why We Avoid Third-Party Runtime Packages

**Section owner:** Priya Nandakumar (Core Services)

This is worth writing down since new contributors sometimes propose adding a small helper package (a nicer argument parser, a prettier table printer for the command line) and are surprised when the answer is usually no.

- The package is meant to be droppable into environments where installing third-party packages is inconvenient or simply not possible.
- A smaller runtime surface means fewer things can change out from under the package between one interpreter's standard library and the next.
- The command line and the loopback service are both simple enough that the standard library genuinely covers what they need — this isn't a hard rule kept for its own sake, it happens to still be true today.

If you find a case where the standard library is genuinely painful for a task inside `auditlog/`, raise it with Priya Nandakumar rather than adding an import and seeing what happens in review. This has come up twice in the last year and both times we found a standard-library approach that was good enough once we looked for it properly.

None of the above applies to the development toolchain — `black`, `ruff`, `build`, and `twine` are all third-party and that's fine, because they never ship inside the package and never run on whatever machine ends up hosting the database file.

---

See Python Version Support for the full compatibility matrix and how it's decided.

---

## Packaging and Distribution Tooling

**Section owner:** Theo Vance

Two of the pinned development tools exist specifically to produce and publish a distributable artifact:

- `build` produces the source distribution and wheel from `pyproject.toml`.
- `twine` uploads the built artifacts to the internal package index.

A typical release-adjacent sequence (not something most contributors run day to day, but useful to understand what those two tools are for):

```
python -m build
twine check dist/*
twine upload --repository internal dist/*
```

Since these two tools are development-only, they follow the same add/bump/remove procedures described above — there's nothing special about them compared to the formatter or linter, other than that they run less often.

---

## Dependency Review During Code Review

**Section owner:** Owen Fitzgerald (Release Engineering)

Any pull request that touches `requirements-dev.txt`, `requirements-dev.lock`, or the `dev` group in `pyproject.toml` should get at least one reviewer who checks the following, in roughly this order:

- Does the pull request description explain *why* the tool is needed, not just what it is?
- Does the diff to `requirements-dev.txt` match the diff to `pyproject.toml`'s pinned version?

- Is the change isolated from unrelated code changes in the same pull request?

Reviewers are not expected to re-run the lock-file compiler themselves unless something in the diff looks off. For everyday formatter or linter version bumps, a single reviewer is enough. For a brand-new tool, get a second look from whoever owns the area the tool touches (for example, a new packaging tool should get a look from Theo Vance even if he isn't the primary reviewer). See Code Review Conventions for how review assignment generally works across the repository.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

- **Lock file and `pyproject.toml` disagree on a version.** This happens when someone edits one file by hand and forgets the other. Regenerate the lock file from `requirements-dev.txt`, then update `pyproject.toml` to match what actually resolved — don't hand-edit the lock file's version numbers.
- **Hash mismatch on install.** Usually means `requirements-dev.lock` was edited by hand instead of regenerated, or your local pip cache has a stale wheel. - **The version table on this page looks stale.** It is hand-maintained; treat `requirements-dev.lock` as the source of truth and open a small pull request to fix the table.
- **A transitive package shows up that nobody recognizes.** Run the compiler with `--generate-hashes` and check its verbose output, which lists which top-level package pulled it in; this is normal and not something to remove by hand from the lock file.

---

## Terminology

- **Development dependency** — A package needed only while working on the repository (formatting, linting, packaging), never imported by `auditlog/` itself.
- **Runtime dependency** — A package the shipped package would need at run time; auditlog currently has none.
- **Lock file** — `requirements-dev.lock`, the fully resolved, hash-pinned list of exact package versions installed by contributors and CI.

3	**Version:** v1.6.2
4	**Owner:** Developer Experience (Callum Reyes)
