7	## Overview
8	
9	This page documents the linting and formatting tools that contributors run against the package before opening a pull request. The package itself uses only the Python standard library, but the tools that check its style are ordinary third-party developer tools installed into a local virtual environment — they are never shipped with the package and never run as part of the service or the command line.
10	
11	The short version: format the working tree, run the linter, run the type checker, and let the pre-commit hook manager catch anything you forgot. The rest of this page explains how those pieces fit together, where their configuration lives, and what reviewers expect to see (and not see) in a diff.
12	
13	This page assumes you have already followed [Workstation Setup](workstation-setup.md) and have a working virtual environment as described in the sibling `virtual-environments.rst` page. If your interpreter isn't on the supported list, stop here and go fix that first — see [Supported Python Versions](supported-python-versions.md).
14	
15	## Terminology
16	
17	- **Linter** — a static tool that reads source files without running them and reports style problems, unused names, and likely mistakes.
18	- **Formatter** — a tool that rewrites source files into a single canonical layout so that diffs stay small and arguments about spacing stop happening.
19	- **Static type checker** — a tool that reads type annotations and flags places where the declared types don't line up, without executing the code.
20	- **Import ordering** — the convention that import statements are grouped and sorted in a fixed sequence (standard library, then third-party, then local) so that two contributors touching the same file don't produce conflicting diffs.
21	- **Line length limit** — the maximum number of characters allowed on a single line before the formatter wraps it; this repository standardizes on 100 characters (see the note under Coding Style Highlights).
22	- **Pre-commit hook** — a small program registered with git that runs automatically before a commit is created, and can block the commit if a check fails.
23	- **Idempotent formatting** — the property that running the formatter twice in a row produces no further changes; if a second run still edits files, something in the configuration is inconsistent.
24	- **Diff noise** — unrelated whitespace or reordering changes that show up in a pull request because the formatter or linter version used locally doesn't match the one pinned for the project.
25	- **Config file discovery** — the process most of these tools use to walk up from the current directory looking for a settings file (usually `pyproject.toml`) before falling back to built-in defaults.
26	- **Suppression comment** — an inline marker that tells the linter or type checker to skip a specific line or block, used sparingly and always with a short explanation.
27	- **Exit status** — the numeric result a command-line tool returns to the shell; zero means "no problems found," anything else means the check failed and the pre-commit hook (or the pull request gate) will refuse to proceed.
28	
29	## Toolchain and Versions
30	
31	*(Section owner: Callum Reyes, Developer Experience)*
32	
33	| Tool | Version | Purpose |
34	|---|---|---|
35	| flake8 | 7.1.1 | Style and correctness linter (wraps pyflakes and pycodestyle) |
36	| black | 24.8.0 | Code formatter; the single source of truth for layout |
37	| isort | 5.13.2 | Import ordering, configured to match black's line length |
38	| mypy | 1.11.2 | Static type checking |
39	| pre-commit | 3.8.0 | Hook manager that runs the checks above before each commit |
40	| pyproject-fmt | 2.2.4 | Keeps `pyproject.toml` itself in a consistent layout |
41	| editorconfig-checker | 2.7.2 | Confirms editor whitespace settings match `.editorconfig` |
42	
43	Install this set into your project virtual environment; do not install it globally, and do not install it alongside the package's own runtime dependencies (there are none — the package is standard-library only, which is exactly why these tools are the *only* third-party software you'll be adding to your environment for this repository).
44	
45	```powershell
46	python -m venv .venv
47	.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
48	pip install flake8==7.1.1 black==24.8.0 isort==5.13.2 mypy==1.11.2 pre-commit==3.8.0 pyproject-fmt==2.2.4 editorconfig-checker==2.7.2
49	```
50	
51	On macOS or Linux the activation step is `source .venv/bin/activate` instead; everything else on this page is identical across platforms unless a section says otherwise.
52	
53	## Workstation Prerequisites
54	
55	*(Section owner: Theo Vance, Developer Experience)*
56	
57	Before running any of the tools above:
58	
59	1. Clone the repository and confirm the top-level layout matches `repository-layout.txt` — you should see the package directory and `README.md` at the root, with no `src/` folder.
60	2. Create and activate a virtual environment as described in `virtual-environments.rst`.
61	3. Confirm your interpreter version against [Supported Python Versions](supported-python-versions.md). The linter and formatter versions pinned in the table above are validated against interpreter 3.11 and 3.12; older interpreters may still run the tools but are not part of the validated set.
62	4. Install the toolchain using the pip command shown above, or by running the wrapper script described later in this page.
63	
64	Do not rely on a tool that happens to already be installed on your machine from another project — version drift here is the single most common cause of "works on my machine, fails in the pull request" surprises. If `black --version` doesn't match the table above, reinstall inside the virtual environment before you do anything else.
65	
66	## Editor Configuration for Linting and Formatting
67	
68	The full editor setup, including recommended extensions and keybindings, lives in [Editor Configuration](editor-configuration.md). This section covers only the settings that affect linting and formatting behavior:
69	
70	- Enable **format on save**, targeting the formatter listed in the toolchain table. Do not enable a second, editor-bundled formatter at the same time — several editors ship one by default, and having two active formatters fighting over the same file produces flapping diffs.
71	- Point your editor's linter integration at the same virtual environment you activated in the previous section, not at a global interpreter. Most editors auto-detect `.venv` at the repository root; if yours doesn't, set the interpreter path manually.
72	- Enable inline diagnostics for the type checker so that annotation problems show up as you type rather than only at commit time.
73	- Install an `.editorconfig` reader if your editor doesn't support it natively (most current editors do out of the box).
74	
75	A minimal `.editorconfig` for this repository:
76	
77	```ini
78	root = true
79	
80	[*]
81	charset = utf-8
82	end_of_line = lf
83	insert_final_newline = true
84	trim_trailing_whitespace = true
85	
86	[*.py]
87	indent_style = space
88	indent_size = 4
89	max_line_length = 100
90	
91	[*.{toml,ini,cfg,yaml,yml}]
92	indent_style = space
93	indent_size = 2
94	```
95	
96	If your editor reports a mismatch here, trust `.editorconfig` over any editor default.
97	
98	## Configuration Files
99	
100	*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*
101	
102	Formatter and linter settings live in `pyproject.toml` wherever possible, with a couple of exceptions where the tool doesn't yet support that file.
103	
104	```toml
105	[tool.black]
106	line-length = 100
107	target-version = ["py311", "py312"]
108	
109	[tool.isort]
110	profile = "black"
111	line_length = 100
112	known_first_party = ["package"]
113	
114	[tool.mypy]
115	python_version = "3.11"
116	warn_unused_ignores = true
117	warn_redundant_casts = true
118	disallow_untyped_defs = false
119	```
120	
121	`flake8` does not yet read `pyproject.toml` cleanly in the version pinned above, so its settings live in a small standalone file at the repository root:
122	
123	```ini
124	[flake8]
125	max-line-length = 100
126	extend-ignore = E203, W503
127	exclude = .venv,build,dist
128	```
129	
130	The two codes excluded there (`E203`, `W503`) exist specifically because black's formatting style disagrees with the default linter rules on whitespace before a colon and line breaks before a binary math symbol — this is a well-known, intentional exclusion pair and not an oversight.
131	
132	`mypy` reads its section from `pyproject.toml` above, but some contributors still keep a separate `mypy.ini` for local overrides that they don't want to commit; if you do this, make sure it's covered by your personal git excludes and not the shared `.gitignore`, so you don't accidentally hide it from teammates who need the shared settings.
133	
134	## Running Checks Locally
135	
136	Run these in order — each one assumes the previous one has already put the tree into a known state.
137	
138	1. **Format first.**
139	   ```powershell
140	   black auditlog
141	   isort auditlog
142	   ```
143	2. **Then lint.**
144	   ```powershell
145	   flake8 auditlog
146	   ```
147	3. **Then type-check.**
148	   ```powershell
149	   mypy auditlog
150	   ```
151	4. Confirm the formatter is idempotent by running it a second time with `--check` — it should report no changes:
152	   ```powershell
153	   black --check auditlog
154	   isort --check-only auditlog
155	   ```
156	
157	If step 4 reports changes, something in your configuration disagrees with the shared one — usually a stale local override or a version mismatch against the toolchain table.
158	
159	For convenience, two wrapper scripts in `scripts/` chain all of this together:
160	
161	- `scripts/lint.ps1` — Windows PowerShell wrapper, runs format-check, lint, and type-check in sequence and stops at the first non-zero exit status.
162	- `scripts/lint.sh` — the POSIX equivalent for macOS and Linux.
163	
164	```powershell
165	.\scripts\lint.ps1
166	```
167	
168	Neither script touches git, and neither one runs the package's own command line or the loopback service — they only import the checking tools and point them at the package directory and its top-level README.
169	
170	## Pre-commit Hooks
171	
172	*(Section owner: Ines Bakker, Tooling Guild)*
173	
174	Install the hook manager once per clone:
175	
176	```powershell
177	pre-commit install
178	```
179	
180	The hook definitions live in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`:
181	
182	```yaml
183	repos:
184	  - repo: https://github.com/psf/black
185	    rev: 24.8.0
186	    hooks:
187	      - id: black
188	  - repo: https://github.com/PyCQA/isort
189	    rev: 5.13.2
190	    hooks:
191	      - id: isort
192	  - repo: https://github.com/PyCQA/flake8
193	    rev: 7.1.1
194	    hooks:
195	      - id: flake8
196	  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/mirrors-mypy
197	    rev: v1.11.2
198	    hooks:
199	      - id: mypy
200	```
201	
202	Once installed, every `git commit` runs the four hooks above against the files you've staged. A hook that rewrites a file (black, isort) will stage its own changes and stop the commit so you can review what changed before committing again — this is expected, not a failure.
203	
204	If you need to bypass the hooks for a single commit — for example, a work-in-progress commit on a personal branch that you plan to squash later — use:
205	
206	```powershell
207	git commit --no-verify -m "wip: draft only, formatting not run yet"
208	```
209	
210	Never do this on a commit you intend to open a pull request from. Reviewers will ask you to re-run the checks and amend the commit.
211	
212	To update all hook versions at once when the toolchain table above changes:
213	
214	```powershell
215	pre-commit autoupdate
216	```
217	
218	Run this deliberately, as its own commit, so the version bump is easy to spot in the log rather than buried inside an unrelated change.
219	
220	## Continuous Integration
221	
222	The same checks run again on the shared build server before a pull request can be merged, using a thin wrapper (`scripts/lint.sh`, the same script described above) rather than a separate CI-only configuration. This is intentional: if it passes locally, it passes on the server, and if it fails on the server but not locally, the first thing to check is a version mismatch between your local toolchain and the pinned versions in the table above.
223	
224	The build server does not accept `--no-verify` commits as a substitute for a clean run — every commit on the branch is checked, not just the final one, so squash or amend work-in-progress commits before requesting review.
225	
226	## Coding Style Highlights Enforced by Lint
227	
228	The full style guide lives in [Coding Style Guide](coding-style.md); this section covers only the parts that the linter and formatter actually enforce automatically, as opposed to conventions that rely on a human reviewer catching them.
229	
230	- Line length is capped at 100 characters, matching the limit set out in the Coding Style Guide (v3.4).
231	- Double quotes are preferred for string literals; the formatter rewrites single-quoted strings automatically unless the string itself contains a double quote.
232	- Trailing commas are added automatically to multi-line collections and call arguments, which keeps future diffs to a single added line instead of a rewritten one.
233	- Import statements are grouped standard-library first, then third-party, then local, with a blank line between each group — isort enforces the grouping, but naming individual imports sensibly is still on you.
234	- Function and variable names use lowercase with underscores; the linter does not enforce naming style directly, but a companion check in the same run flags names that don't match the expected pattern.
235	- Docstrings are not validated by any tool in this toolchain — their presence and quality is a code review concern, not a lint one.
236	
237	If the formatter and the written style guide ever disagree on a specific point, the formatter wins for anything mechanical (spacing, quoting, wrapping), and the written guide wins for anything the formatter can't decide (naming, structure, when to add a comment).
238	
239	## Commit Message Conventions for Formatting Changes
240	
241	The full commit message conventions live in [Commit Message Style](commit-message-style.md). For changes produced purely by running the formatter or the import sorter, keep the commit isolated from any behavioral change:
242	
243	```
244	style: apply black and isort to package directory
245	
246	No behavioral change. Formatter version bumped to 24.8.0 per the
247	autumn dependency update; this commit only reflows existing lines.
248	```
249	
250	Do not combine a formatting-only commit with a substantive change in the same commit — reviewers cannot tell which lines matter and which lines simply moved. If your editor's format-on-save silently reformatted a file you didn't mean to touch, split that change into its own commit before pushing.
251	
252	## Code Review Conventions for Lint Findings
253	
254	*(Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald, Release Engineering)*
255	
256	The full review process is described in [Code Review Conventions](code-review-conventions.md). Specific to linting and formatting:
257	
258	- A pull request with a failing lint, format, or type-check run will not be reviewed until the run is clean. Reviewers are asked to close the request rather than comment on it line by line.
259	- Reviewers should not ask contributors to manually reformat something the formatter already handles correctly — if the formatted output looks odd, that's a formatter configuration question, not a reviewer style preference.
260	- Suppression comments (`# noqa`-style markers, or their type-checker equivalent) require a short justification in the same line or the line above, and reviewers should push back on any suppression that doesn't explain itself.
261	- A reviewer who wants a naming or structural change that the linter doesn't catch should say so explicitly in the review — silence on a lint-clean pull request is not the same as silence on style overall.
262	
263	## Troubleshooting
264	
265	| Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix |
266	|---|---|---|
267	| Formatter reformats the same file every run | Local tool version doesn't match the pinned version | Reinstall from the toolchain table, inside the virtual environment |
268	| Linter and formatter disagree on the same line | Missing `extend-ignore` entry for a black-specific style choice | Confirm `E203`/`W503` are still excluded in the flake8 config |
269	| Pre-commit hook does nothing on commit | Hook manager was never installed for this clone | Run `pre-commit install` again |
270	| Type checker reports errors only on the build server | Different interpreter version between local and server | Check the version against [Supported Python Versions](supported-python-versions.md) |
271	| Import order changes every time isort runs | `profile = "black"` missing from the isort config | Add it under `[tool.isort]` in `pyproject.toml` |
272	| Editor doesn't pick up `.editorconfig` | Editor lacks native support | Install an editorconfig plugin for your editor |
273	
274	## Files and Paths Referenced by This Page
275	
276	| Path | Purpose |
277	|---|---|
278	| Package directory (repository root) | The source tree that every check in this page runs against |
279	| `README.md` | Repository root readme; links out to the developer handbook |
280	| `pyproject.toml` | Shared config for the formatter, import sorter, and type checker |
281	| `.flake8` | Standalone linter config (line length, excluded codes, excluded paths) |
282	| `.pre-commit-config.yaml` | Hook definitions for the commit-time check pipeline |
283	| `.editorconfig` | Cross-editor whitespace and newline settings |
284	| `scripts/lint.ps1` | Windows wrapper that runs format-check, lint, and type-check in order |
285	| `scripts/lint.sh` | POSIX equivalent of the wrapper above |
286	| `docs/developer-handbook/coding-style.md` | Full written style guide this page's rules are drawn from |
287	| `docs/developer-handbook/editor-configuration.md` | Editor setup this page's editor section points to |
288	
289	## Change Log
290	
291	- **2023-02-10 — v1.0.0** — Page created; documented initial adoption of flake8 and black.
292	- **2023-08-04 — v1.1.0** — Added isort and its dedicated config file.
293	- **2024-01-15 — v1.2.0** — Introduced pre-commit as the hook manager, replacing hand-written git hooks.
294	- **2024-06-21 — v1.3.0** — Added mypy to the toolchain; strict mode left disabled for now.
295	- **2025-02-11 — v1.4.0** — Line length limit changed from 88 to 100 to match the written style guide.
296	- **2025-06-30 — v1.5.0** — Added editorconfig-checker and pyproject-fmt to the toolchain table.
297	- **2025-10-01 — v1.6.2** — Updated pinned tool versions for the autumn dependency update; page ownership moved from Theo Vance to Callum Reyes.
298	- **2025-10-14 — v1.6.3** — Bumped black to 24.8.0 following a formatting-only pass across the entire package directory.
299	
300	## Related Pages
301	
302	- [Developer Handbook Overview](README.md)
303	- [Workstation Setup](workstation-setup.md)
304	- [Supported Python Versions](supported-python-versions.md)

# Linting and Formatting

**Version:** v1.6.2
**Owner:** Developer Experience (Callum Reyes)
**Last updated:** 2025-10-01

## Overview

This page documents the linting and formatting tools that contributors run against the package before opening a pull request. The package itself uses only the Python standard library, but the tools that check its style are ordinary third-party developer tools installed into a local virtual environment — they are never shipped with the package and never run as part of the service or the command line.

The short version: format the working tree, run the linter, run the type checker, and let the pre-commit hook manager catch anything you forgot. The rest of this page explains how those pieces fit together, where their configuration lives, and what reviewers expect to see (and not see) in a diff.

This page assumes you have already followed [Workstation Setup](workstation-setup.md) and have a working virtual environment as described in the sibling `virtual-environments.rst` page. If your interpreter isn't on the supported list, stop here and go fix that first — see [Supported Python Versions](supported-python-versions.md).

## Terminology

- **Linter** — a static tool that reads source files without running them and reports style problems, unused names, and likely mistakes.
- **Formatter** — a tool that rewrites source files into a single canonical layout so that diffs stay small and arguments about spacing stop happening.
- **Static type checker** — a tool that reads type annotations and flags places where the declared types don't line up, without executing the code.
- **Import ordering** — the convention that import statements are grouped and sorted in a fixed sequence (standard library, then third-party, then local) so that two contributors touching the same file don't produce conflicting diffs.
- **Line length limit** — the maximum number of characters allowed on a single line before the formatter wraps it; this repository standardizes on 100 characters (see the note under Coding Style Highlights).
- **Pre-commit hook** — a small program registered with git that runs automatically before a commit is created, and can block the commit if a check fails.
- **Idempotent formatting** — the property that running the formatter twice in a row produces no further changes; if a second run still edits files, something in the configuration is inconsistent.
- **Diff noise** — unrelated whitespace or reordering changes that show up in a pull request because the formatter or linter version used locally doesn't match the one pinned for the project.
- **Config file discovery** — the process most of these tools use to walk up from the current directory looking for a settings file (usually `pyproject.toml`) before falling back to built-in defaults.
- **Suppression comment** — an inline marker that tells the linter or type checker to skip a specific line or block, used sparingly and always with a short explanation.
- **Exit status** — the numeric result a command-line tool returns to the shell; zero means "no problems found," anything else means the check failed and the pre-commit hook (or the pull request gate) will refuse to proceed.

## Toolchain and Versions

*(Section owner: Callum Reyes, Developer Experience)*

| Tool | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| flake8 | 7.1.1 | Style and correctness linter (wraps pyflakes and pycodestyle) |
| black | 24.8.0 | Code formatter; the single source of truth for layout |
| isort | 5.13.2 | Import ordering, configured to match black's line length |
| mypy | 1.11.2 | Static type checking |
| pre-commit | 3.8.0 | Hook manager that runs the checks above before each commit |
| pyproject-fmt | 2.2.4 | Keeps `pyproject.toml` itself in a consistent layout |
| editorconfig-checker | 2.7.2 | Confirms editor whitespace settings match `.editorconfig` |

Install this set into your project virtual environment; do not install it globally, and do not install it alongside the package's own runtime dependencies (there are none — the package is standard-library only, which is exactly why these tools are the *only* third-party software you'll be adding to your environment for this repository).

```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install flake8==7.1.1 black==24.8.0 isort==5.13.2 mypy==1.11.2 pre-commit==3.8.0 pyproject-fmt==2.2.4 editorconfig-checker==2.7.2
```

On macOS or Linux the activation step is `source .venv/bin/activate` instead; everything else on this page is identical across platforms unless a section says otherwise.

## Workstation Prerequisites

*(Section owner: Theo Vance, Developer Experience)*

Before running any of the tools above:

1. Clone the repository and confirm the top-level layout matches `repository-layout.txt` — you should see the package directory and `README.md` at the root, with no `src/` folder.
2. Create and activate a virtual environment as described in `virtual-environments.rst`.
3. Confirm your interpreter version against [Supported Python Versions](supported-python-versions.md). The linter and formatter versions pinned in the table above are validated against interpreter 3.11 and 3.12; older interpreters may still run the tools but are not part of the validated set.
4. Install the toolchain using the pip command shown above, or by running the wrapper script described later in this page.

Do not rely on a tool that happens to already be installed on your machine from another project — version drift here is the single most common cause of "works on my machine, fails in the pull request" surprises. If `black --version` doesn't match the table above, reinstall inside the virtual environment before you do anything else.

## Editor Configuration for Linting and Formatting

The full editor setup, including recommended extensions and keybindings, lives in [Editor Configuration](editor-configuration.md). This section covers only the settings that affect linting and formatting behavior:

- Enable **format on save**, targeting the formatter listed in the toolchain table. Do not enable a second, editor-bundled formatter at the same time — several editors ship one by default, and having two active formatters fighting over the same file produces flapping diffs.
- Point your editor's linter integration at the same virtual environment you activated in the previous section, not at a global interpreter. Most editors auto-detect `.venv` at the repository root; if yours doesn't, set the interpreter path manually.
- Enable inline diagnostics for the type checker so that annotation problems show up as you type rather than only at commit time.
- Install an `.editorconfig` reader if your editor doesn't support it natively (most current editors do out of the box).

A minimal `.editorconfig` for this repository:

```ini
root = true

[*]
charset = utf-8
end_of_line = lf
insert_final_newline = true
trim_trailing_whitespace = true

[*.py]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4
max_line_length = 100

[*.{toml,ini,cfg,yaml,yml}]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 2
```

If your editor reports a mismatch here, trust `.editorconfig` over any editor default.

## Configuration Files

*(Section owner: Mara Olsen, Platform Tools)*

Formatter and linter settings live in `pyproject.toml` wherever possible, with a couple of exceptions where the tool doesn't yet support that file.

```toml
[tool.black]
line-length = 100
target-version = ["py311", "py312"]

[tool.isort]
profile = "black"
line_length = 100
known_first_party = ["package"]

[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.11"
warn_unused_ignores = true
warn_redundant_casts = true
disallow_untyped_defs = false
```

`flake8` does not yet read `pyproject.toml` cleanly in the version pinned above, so its settings live in a small standalone file at the repository root:

```ini
[flake8]
max-line-length = 100
extend-ignore = E203, W503
exclude = .venv,build,dist
```

The two codes excluded there (`E203`, `W503`) exist specifically because black's formatting style disagrees with the default linter rules on whitespace before a colon and line breaks before a binary math symbol — this is a well-known, intentional exclusion pair and not an oversight.

`mypy` reads its section from `pyproject.toml` above, but some contributors still keep a separate `mypy.ini` for local overrides that they don't want to commit; if you do this, make sure it's covered by your personal git excludes and not the shared `.gitignore`, so you don't accidentally hide it from teammates who need the shared settings.

## Running Checks Locally

Run these in order — each one assumes the previous one has already put the tree into a known state.

1. **Format first.**
   ```powershell
   black auditlog
   isort auditlog
   ```
2. **Then lint.**
   ```powershell
   flake8 auditlog
   ```
3. **Then type-check.**
   ```powershell
   mypy auditlog
   ```
4. Confirm the formatter is idempotent by running it a second time with `--check` — it should report no changes:
   ```powershell
   black --check auditlog
   isort --check-only auditlog
   ```

If step 4 reports changes, something in your configuration disagrees with the shared one — usually a stale local override or a version mismatch against the toolchain table.

For convenience, two wrapper scripts in `scripts/` chain all of this together:

- `scripts/lint.ps1` — Windows PowerShell wrapper, runs format-check, lint, and type-check in sequence and stops at the first non-zero exit status.
- `scripts/lint.sh` — the POSIX equivalent for macOS and Linux.

```powershell
.\scripts\lint.ps1
```

Neither script touches git, and neither one runs the package's own command line or the loopback service — they only import the checking tools and point them at the package directory and its top-level README.

## Pre-commit Hooks

*(Section owner: Ines Bakker, Tooling Guild)*

Install the hook manager once per clone:

```powershell
pre-commit install
```

The hook definitions live in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`:

```yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/psf/black
    rev: 24.8.0
    hooks:
      - id: black
  - repo: https://github.com/PyCQA/isort
    rev: 5.13.2
    hooks:
      - id: isort
  - repo: https://github.com/PyCQA/flake8
    rev: 7.1.1
    hooks:
      - id: flake8
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/mirrors-mypy
    rev: v1.11.2
    hooks:
      - id: mypy
```

Once installed, every `git commit` runs the four hooks above against the files you've staged. A hook that rewrites a file (black, isort) will stage its own changes and stop the commit so you can review what changed before committing again — this is expected, not a failure.

If you need to bypass the hooks for a single commit — for example, a work-in-progress commit on a personal branch that you plan to squash later — use:

```powershell
git commit --no-verify -m "wip: draft only, formatting not run yet"
```

Never do this on a commit you intend to open a pull request from. Reviewers will ask you to re-run the checks and amend the commit.

To update all hook versions at once when the toolchain table above changes:

```powershell
pre-commit autoupdate
```

Run this deliberately, as its own commit, so the version bump is easy to spot in the log rather than buried inside an unrelated change.

## Continuous Integration

The same checks run again on the shared build server before a pull request can be merged, using a thin wrapper (`scripts/lint.sh`, the same script described above) rather than a separate CI-only configuration. This is intentional: if it passes locally, it passes on the server, and if it fails on the server but not locally, the first thing to check is a version mismatch between your local toolchain and the pinned versions in the table above.

The build server does not accept `--no-verify` commits as a substitute for a clean run — every commit on the branch is checked, not just the final one, so squash or amend work-in-progress commits before requesting review.

## Coding Style Highlights Enforced by Lint

The full style guide lives in [Coding Style Guide](coding-style.md); this section covers only the parts that the linter and formatter actually enforce automatically, as opposed to conventions that rely on a human reviewer catching them.

- Line length is capped at 100 characters, matching the limit set out in the Coding Style Guide (v3.4).
- Double quotes are preferred for string literals; the formatter rewrites single-quoted strings automatically unless the string itself contains a double quote.
- Trailing commas are added automatically to multi-line collections and call arguments, which keeps future diffs to a single added line instead of a rewritten one.
- Import statements are grouped standard-library first, then third-party, then local, with a blank line between each group — isort enforces the grouping, but naming individual imports sensibly is still on you.
- Function and variable names use lowercase with underscores; the linter does not enforce naming style directly, but a companion check in the same run flags names that don't match the expected pattern.
- Docstrings are not validated by any tool in this toolchain — their presence and quality is a code review concern, not a lint one.

If the formatter and the written style guide ever disagree on a specific point, the formatter wins for anything mechanical (spacing, quoting, wrapping), and the written guide wins for anything the formatter can't decide (naming, structure, when to add a comment).

## Commit Message Conventions for Formatting Changes

The full commit message conventions live in [Commit Message Style](commit-message-style.md). For changes produced purely by running the formatter or the import sorter, keep the commit isolated from any behavioral change:

```
style: apply black and isort to package directory

No behavioral change. Formatter version bumped to 24.8.0 per the
autumn dependency update; this commit only reflows existing lines.
```

Do not combine a formatting-only commit with a substantive change in the same commit — reviewers cannot tell which lines matter and which lines simply moved. If your editor's format-on-save silently reformatted a file you didn't mean to touch, split that change into its own commit before pushing.

## Code Review Conventions for Lint Findings

*(Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald, Release Engineering)*

The full review process is described in [Code Review Conventions](code-review-conventions.md). Specific to linting and formatting:

- A pull request with a failing lint, format, or type-check run will not be reviewed until the run is clean. Reviewers are asked to close the request rather than comment on it line by line.
- Reviewers should not ask contributors to manually reformat something the formatter already handles correctly — if the formatted output looks odd, that's a formatter configuration question, not a reviewer style preference.
- Suppression comments (`# noqa`-style markers, or their type-checker equivalent) require a short justification in the same line or the line above, and reviewers should push back on any suppression that doesn't explain itself.
- A reviewer who wants a naming or structural change that the linter doesn't catch should say so explicitly in the review — silence on a lint-clean pull request is not the same as silence on style overall.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Formatter reformats the same file every run | Local tool version doesn't match the pinned version | Reinstall from the toolchain table, inside the virtual environment |
| Linter and formatter disagree on the same line | Missing `extend-ignore` entry for a black-specific style choice | Confirm `E203`/`W503` are still excluded in the flake8 config |
| Pre-commit hook does nothing on commit | Hook manager was never installed for this clone | Run `pre-commit install` again |
| Type checker reports errors only on the build server | Different interpreter version between local and server | Check the version against [Supported Python Versions](supported-python-versions.md) |
| Import order changes every time isort runs | `profile = "black"` missing from the isort config | Add it under `[tool.isort]` in `pyproject.toml` |
| Editor doesn't pick up `.editorconfig` | Editor lacks native support | Install an editorconfig plugin for your editor |

## Files and Paths Referenced by This Page

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Package directory (repository root) | The source tree that every check in this page runs against |
| `README.md` | Repository root readme; links out to the developer handbook |
| `pyproject.toml` | Shared config for the formatter, import sorter, and type checker |
| `.flake8` | Standalone linter config (line length, excluded codes, excluded paths) |
| `.pre-commit-config.yaml` | Hook definitions for the commit-time check pipeline |
| `.editorconfig` | Cross-editor whitespace and newline settings |
| `scripts/lint.ps1` | Windows wrapper that runs format-check, lint, and type-check in order |
| `scripts/lint.sh` | POSIX equivalent of the wrapper above |
| `docs/developer-handbook/coding-style.md` | Full written style guide this page's rules are drawn from |
| `docs/developer-handbook/editor-configuration.md` | Editor setup this page's editor section points to |

173	  section_owner: "Release Engineering (Owen Fitzgerald)"
174	  summary: >
175	    The short version: keep pull requests small, respond to every
176	    comment thread even if only to disagree with it, and prefer follow-up

178	    against it.

181	      description: >

183	        early feedback welcome" and lets a reviewer catch a wrong
184	        direction before it costs a full day of work.
185	    - stage: "Ready for review"
186	      description: >
187	        Mark it ready only once the formatter, linter, and pre-commit
188	        hooks are clean locally. Reviewers are within their rights to
189	        bounce a pull request straight back if the checklist above
190	        clearly was not followed.

201	        so the diff stays reviewable incrementally.

203	      description: >

title: "Onboarding Checklist"
version: "1.9"
owner: "Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)"
last_updated: "2025-02-28"
summary: >
  A short checklist that new contributors work through during their first
  week on the auditlog repository. It links out to the workstation setup,
  supported Python versions, editor configuration, code review conventions,
  commit message style, and coding style pages, and restates the parts of
  each that matter most on day one. Treat this page as the front door to
  the developer handbook rather than a full replacement for any of the
  linked pages.

overview: >
  auditlog is small and deliberately unglamorous: a command line, a
  loopback HTTP service, and a local database file, all built on the
  standard library with no third-party runtime dependencies. Because the
  package has so few moving parts, most onboarding friction comes from
  environment setup and from getting used to the team's conventions rather
  than from the size of the codebase itself. New contributors are usually
  productive by the middle of their first week if they follow the steps
  below in order and do not skip the editor and linting setup, which tends
  to save a full review round on the first pull request.

first_week_checklist:
  section_owner: "Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)"
  note: >
    This checklist assumes a laptop that already has git and a supported
    Python interpreter installed system-wide. If neither is true, start
    with workstation-setup.md before returning here.
  days:
    - day: "Day 1"
      goal: "Get the repository cloned and the environment reproducible."
      tasks:
        - "Clone the repository and confirm the default branch checks out cleanly."
        - "Create and activate a virtual environment scoped to this project."
        - "Install the package in editable mode inside that environment."
        - "Configure git user name and contact info for commits (local config, not global, on shared machines)."
        - "Open the repository in the team's recommended editor and let it pick up the workspace settings automatically."
    - day: "Day 2"
      goal: "Confirm tooling and linting run cleanly before writing any code."
      tasks:
        - "Run the formatter and linter across the untouched tree and confirm zero findings."
        - "Install the pre-commit hooks and run them once against all files."
        - "Read coding-style.md fully; skim commit-message-style.md."
        - "Pick a small, low-risk first task from the open issue list (something documentation-adjacent is fine)."
    - day: "Day 3"
      goal: "Make a first small change and open a draft pull request."
      tasks:
        - "Create a topic branch named after the issue, not after yourself."
        - "Write the change in small, reviewable commits."
        - "Push the branch and open a draft pull request early, even before the change is finished."
    - day: "Day 4"
      goal: "Take the draft pull request through review."
      tasks:
        - "Mark the pull request ready for review once local checks are clean."
        - "Respond to review comments with follow-up commits rather than force-pushing over them (see code-review-conventions.md)."
        - "Watch how a senior contributor structures their comments, to calibrate tone for your own future reviews."
    - day: "Day 5"
      goal: "Land the first change and set up longer-term habits."
      tasks:
        - "Get the first pull request merged."
        - "Subscribe to the repository's activity so you see conventions changing over time."
        - "Schedule a fifteen-minute sync with your onboarding buddy to ask anything that still feels unclear."

workstation_setup:
  section_owner: "Developer Experience (Theo Vance)"
  summary: >
    Full detail lives in workstation-setup.md; this section is the
    condensed version most people actually follow on day one.
  steps:
    - "Install a supported Python interpreter (see supported_python_versions below) and confirm it is first on PATH inside a fresh shell."
    - "Install git 2.30 or newer."
    - "Clone the repository over SSH, not HTTPS, so day-to-day pushes do not prompt for anything."
    - "Create a virtual environment inside the repository root, named .venv, so editor tooling finds it automatically."
    - "Activate the virtual environment and install the package in editable mode along with the development extras."
    - "Install the pre-commit hooks so formatting and linting run automatically before each commit."
  clone_and_env_snippet: |
    git clone git@internal-git:core-services/auditlog.git
    cd auditlog
    python -m venv .venv
    # PowerShell
    .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
    # bash / zsh
    source .venv/bin/activate
    python -m pip install --upgrade pip
    python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
    pre-commit install
  editor_note: >
    Once the environment is active, open the repository in your editor
    from the same shell session so it inherits the interpreter path
    without any manual configuration. See Editor Configuration v1.9 for
    the recommended workspace settings.
  verification: >
    A correct setup shows a clean formatter run, a clean linter run, and
    a pre-commit hook that completes in under a few seconds on an empty
    diff. If any of those three take significantly longer than expected,
    the virtual environment is probably picking up a system-wide
    interpreter instead of the project one; deactivate, remove .venv,
    and recreate it.

supported_python_versions:
  section_owner: "Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)"
  summary: >
    auditlog uses only the standard library, so the supported version
    window is set by what the team is willing to keep exercising by hand
    rather than by any external dependency constraint.
  table:
    - version: "3.9"
      status: "minimum supported"
      notes: "Oldest interpreter still installed on shared build machines."
    - version: "3.10"
      status: "supported"
      notes: "No known differences from 3.11 behavior for this package."
    - version: "3.11"
      status: "recommended"
      notes: "What most of the team runs locally."
    - version: "3.12"
      status: "supported"
      notes: "Verified on Windows and Linux workstations."
    - version: "3.13"
      status: "experimental"
      notes: "Works locally; not yet the default in workstation-setup.md."
  guidance: >
    New contributors should install 3.11 unless they have a specific
    reason to check against a different interpreter. The minimum supported
    version is 3.10; code that only works on 3.11 or newer without a
    documented reason will come back in review.

editor_configuration:
  section_owner: "Developer Experience (Callum Reyes)"
  recommended_editor: "Visual Studio Code, current stable channel"
  summary: >
    Full settings and extension recommendations live in
    editor-configuration.md. This is the subset that matters for getting
    format-on-save and lint-on-save working correctly on the first day.
  workspace_settings_snippet: |
    {
      "editor.formatOnSave": true,
      "editor.rulers": [88],
      "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
      "files.insertFinalNewline": true,
      "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python"
    }
  windows_interpreter_note: >
    On Windows, set python.defaultInterpreterPath to
    ${workspaceFolder}\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe instead of the
    Unix-style path shown above.
  recommended_extensions:
    - "Python (Microsoft)"
    - "Pylance"
    - "EditorConfig for VS Code"
  editorconfig_snippet: |
    root = true

    [*]
    charset = utf-8
    end_of_line = lf
    insert_final_newline = true
    trim_trailing_whitespace = true
    indent_style = space
    indent_size = 4

    [*.md]
    trim_trailing_whitespace = false
  other_editors: >
    Vim and Emacs users are common enough on the team that
    editor-configuration.md carries equivalent snippets for both; ask in
    the developer chat channel if you use something else entirely and
    want your settings added.

code_review_conventions:
  section_owner: "Release Engineering (Owen Fitzgerald)"
  summary: >
    The short version: keep pull requests small, respond to every
    comment thread even if only to disagree with it, and prefer follow-up
    commits over rewriting the record on a branch that already has comments
    against it.
  stages:
    - stage: "Draft"
      description: >
        Open early. A draft pull request signals "this is in progress,
        early feedback welcome" and lets a reviewer catch a wrong
        direction before it costs a full day of work.
    - stage: "Ready for review"
      description: >
        Mark it ready only once the formatter, linter, and pre-commit
        hooks are clean locally. Reviewers are within their rights to
        bounce a pull request straight back if the checklist above
        clearly was not followed.
    - stage: "Under review"
      description: >
        At least one contributor outside the author's immediate team
        should look at any change that touches the command line or the
        loopback service surface. Documentation-only changes need one
        reviewer from anywhere on the team.
    - stage: "Working through feedback"
      description: >
        Reply to every open comment thread. Push follow-up commits rather
        than amending or force-pushing once a reviewer has left comments,
        so the diff stays reviewable incrementally.
    - stage: "Cleared for merge"
      description: >
        Once every open thread is resolved and checks are green, either
        the author or the reviewer merges, depending on team convention
        for that area of the codebase; ask your onboarding buddy which
        convention applies where you're working.
  comment_style_guidance:
    - "Lead with the concern, not the fix, when the fix isn't obvious: describe the problem before prescribing the solution."
    - "Mark purely stylistic comments as such (\"nit:\") so the author can weigh them differently from substantive ones."
    - "Avoid rewriting someone's sentence in a comment just to show a preference; suggest the change and let them decide."
  size_guidance: >
    A pull request that changes more than roughly 300 lines outside of
    generated or vendored files usually means the change should have
    been split. Reviewers are encouraged to ask for a split rather than
    push through a long review on a single oversized diff.

commit_message_style:
  section_owner: "Tooling Guild (Ines Bakker)"
  summary: >
    The team follows a conventional-commit-flavored style. The prefix
    matters more than most people expect, because tooling further along
    the developer handbook (see changelog-conventions.rst) groups commits
    by prefix when drafting release notes.
  format: "<type>(<area>): <short summary, imperative mood, no trailing period>"
  allowed_types:
    - type: "feat"
      meaning: "a new capability visible to users of the command line or service"
    - type: "fix"
      meaning: "a bug fix with no behavior change beyond removing the bug"
    - type: "docs"
      meaning: "documentation-only changes, including pages like this one"
    - type: "chore"
      meaning: "tooling, formatting configuration, or repository housekeeping"
    - type: "refactor"
      meaning: "internal restructuring with no intended behavior change"
  examples:
    - "feat(cli): add --format option for output selection"
    - "fix(storage): correct a rare off-by-one when reading the database file"
    - "docs(handbook): update onboarding checklist for 1.9"
    - "chore(lint): raise line length limit to 88 columns"
  body_guidance: >
    Use the commit body to explain *why*, not *what* — the diff already
    shows what changed. A short body is fine; an empty body is fine for
    genuinely small commits, but do not pad a body with restated summary
    text just to have one.
  branch_naming: >
    Branch names should read as <issue-number>-<short-slug>, for example
    482-fix-cli-format-flag. commit-message-style.md, last revised in
    early 2025, has a longer list of acceptable prefixes for older
    branches that predate this convention; new branches should stick to
    the short list above.

coding_style:
  section_owner: "Platform Tools (Mara Olsen)"
  summary: >
    coding-style.md (v3.6) is the full reference; the points below are
    the ones that come up most often in review during someone's first
    month.
  conventions:
    - "Line length limit is 88 columns, matching the formatter's default; do not raise it locally."
    - "Type hints are required on all new public functions and methods; existing untyped code is being migrated gradually and does not need to be fixed opportunistically as a side effect of an unrelated change."
    - "Prefer explicit imports over wildcard imports everywhere, including in short scripts under scripts/."
    - "Keep functions short enough to read on one screen; if you need a comment to explain a block in the middle of a function, that block is usually a candidate for its own helper."
    - "Docstrings use one-line summaries for simple functions and a short paragraph plus an Args/Returns-style section for anything with more than two parameters."
    - "Avoid deeply nested conditionals; prefer early returns over an else-heavy structure."
    - "Constants live near the top of the module that uses them, in upper snake case."
  formatting_and_linting: >
    Formatting and linting are enforced automatically through the
    pre-commit hooks installed during workstation setup; see
    linting-and-formatting.md for the exact tool versions and
    configuration files. Do not hand-format code to match the formatter's
    output — run the formatter and let it decide.
  naming_conventions:
    - context: "modules"
      style: "short, lowercase, no underscores unless needed for readability"
    - context: "classes"
      style: "CapWords"
    - context: "functions and variables"
      style: "lower_snake_case"
    - context: "constants"
      style: "UPPER_SNAKE_CASE"

terminology:
  - term: "Virtual environment"
    definition: >
      An isolated Python installation created with the standard venv
      module, used so the package and its development extras do not
      collide with anything installed system-wide.
  - term: "Editable install"
    definition: >
      An installation mode where changes made in the working tree take
      effect immediately without reinstalling the package.
  - term: "Loopback service"
    definition: >
      The HTTP service auditlog runs, reachable only from the local
      machine rather than from the network at large.
  - term: "Database file"
    definition: >
      The single local SQLite file where auditlog keeps its records.
  - term: "Pre-commit hook"
    definition: >
      A short script that runs automatically before a commit completes,
      used here to run the formatter and linter before code reaches the
      repository.
  - term: "Draft pull request"
    definition: >
      A pull request explicitly marked as unfinished, used to invite
      early feedback without signaling that the change is ready to be
      merged.
  - term: "Topic branch"
    definition: >
      A short-lived branch created for a single, focused change and
      removed once it has been merged.
  - term: "Formatter"
    definition: >
      A tool that rewrites source files into a single, consistent
      layout, removing the need for manual spacing or wrapping choices.
  - term: "Linter"
    definition: >
      A tool that checks source files for likely mistakes and style
      violations without changing them.
  - term: "Type hints"
    definition: >
      Optional annotations on function declarations and variables that
      describe expected types, checked by editor tooling rather than at
      run time.

content.content:
1	Repository Layout
2	================
3	
4	Title: Repository Layout
5	Version: 1.5
6	Owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)
7	Last updated: 2024-09-30
8	Summary: Outlines the top-level directories of the repository and explains where command line, service, and shared code live.
9	
10	
11	Overview
12	--------
13	
14	The auditlog repository is organized to separate concerns between the package, its service component, documentation, and development tooling. This page describes the physical layout of the repository root and the purposes of each directory, along with guidelines for onboarding to the project. It assumes you have already cloned the repository and can access it from your workstation.
15	
16	The repository root contains the auditlog/ package directory alongside supporting folders for scripts, documentation, and configuration files. There is no src/ layout; the package lives at the top level.
17	
18	
19	Top-Level Directory Structure
20	------------------------------
21	
22	**auditlog/** — The main package directory. Contains all code that implements the command-line interface and the loopback HTTP service. The package uses only the standard library and has no external dependencies. This directory is what gets installed when you run installation commands during setup.
23	
24	**docs/** — Documentation files for end users and operations staff. Contains guides for installing the service on different platforms, HTTP request examples, and database format specifications. Not intended for developer onboarding; see the developer-handbook/ folder instead.
25	
26	**developer-handbook/** — Internal documentation for team members working on the package. This folder contains this file along with sibling pages covering workstation setup, Python version requirements, editor configuration, code review practices, commit message conventions, and coding standards. Owned by the Core Services team.
27	
28	**scripts/** — Utility scripts used by developers and CI systems. Includes scripts for running the service locally, building distributions, and checking code against project standards. Most scripts are shell scripts written for both Bash and PowerShell environments.
29	
30	**config/** — Configuration file templates and examples. Contains SQLite journal settings used by the package when creating the database file, and example configurations for the service's loopback socket binding. Not all of these files are used during normal development.
31	
32	**Checks/** — Verification suites and helper scenarios. Organized by module within the package. (See the separate evaluation documentation for details.)
33	
34	
35	Workstation Setup — Section Owner: Developer Experience (Theo Vance)
36	-------------------------------------------------------------------
37	
38	Before you begin contributing to auditlog, your workstation must be configured with Python, Git, and a text editor. A full walkthrough is available in the workstation-setup.md page in this folder, updated 2025-06-02.
39	
40	At a minimum, you need:
41	
42	- Git 2.30 or later for cloning and working with the repository.
43	- Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12 installed locally. (See supported-python-versions.md for the authoritative list; as of 2024-11-20 the team supports back to 3.9.)
44	- A text editor or IDE that can be configured for this project. Most of the team uses VS Code, but Vim, Neovim, and PyCharm are also common.
45	- Virtual environment support. The team uses venv, which comes with Python.
46	
47	To clone the repository:
48	
49	    git clone https://github.com/internal-team/auditlog.git
50	    cd auditlog
51	
52	To create and activate a virtual environment on Windows (PowerShell):
53	
54	    python -m venv venv
55	    .\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
56	
57	On Linux or macOS (Bash):
58	
59	    python3 -m venv venv
60	    source venv/bin/activate
61	
62	Once the virtual environment is active, install the package in editable mode:
63	
64	    pip install -e .
65	
66	This makes the package importable and ensures that any changes you make to the code are reflected immediately. You can then run both the command-line interface and the service without reinstalling after each edit.
67	
68	
69	Python Version Support
70	----------------------
71	
72	The team currently supports Python 3.9 through 3.12. See the supported-python-versions.md page (version 1.8, last updated 2024-11-20) for detailed information on version-specific behavior and deprecation timelines. The package relies only on standard library modules, so there are no pip dependencies that might restrict version support.
73	
74	When developing locally, you should verify your changes against at least Python 3.10 and 3.11 before submitting a pull request. The CI system will verify compatibility with all supported versions. If you use an incompatible feature, the linting stage will catch it during code review.
75	
76	
77	Editor Configuration
78	--------------------
79	
80	The team provides configuration files for several common editors to ensure consistent formatting and linting across the repository. See editor-configuration.md (version v2.0.1, last updated 2025-03-09) for complete setup instructions for VS Code, Vim, Neovim, and PyCharm.
81	
82	A .editorconfig file at the repository root specifies indentation, line ending, and character encoding settings that apply universally. Most editors can read this file automatically; install an EditorConfig extension if yours does not.
83	
84	For Python-specific linting and formatting, the repository uses two tools:
85	
86	- **Linter**: Pylint, configured to enforce naming conventions and catch common mistakes.
87	- **Formatter**: Black, configured to use 88 characters per line and maintain consistency across all Python files.
88	
89	Both tools are configured in the pyproject.toml file. Running either tool without arguments will use the repository settings.
90	
91	Before you commit, run the linting and formatting tools to ensure your code meets project standards. The code-review-conventions.md page (version 3.1, owned by Release Engineering, last updated 2025-08-27) requires this as part of the pull request workflow.
92	
93	
94	Code Review Conventions — Section Owner: Release Engineering (Owen Fitzgerald)
95	--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
96	
97	All changes to the package, documentation, or scripts must pass code review before merging. The branching-and-pull-requests.txt page (version 2.4, last updated 2026-01-22) describes the full workflow. This section covers what reviewers look for when evaluating your changes.
98	
99	When you open a pull request, at least two reviewers from the Core Services team must sign off on it. Reviewers will check that:
100	
101	- Your code follows the project's coding style (see coding-style.md, version 4.0).
102	- Commit messages follow the project's conventions (see commit-message-style.md, version v1.2.3).
103	- You have not introduced any new external dependencies.
104	- The linting and formatting tools pass without errors.
105	- Your changes do not break existing functionality in the CLI or service.
106	
107	The CI system runs these checks automatically and reports results as a status on the pull request. If the CI status is red, the pull request will not be reviewed until all checks pass. You can run these checks locally using the commands documented in the scripts/ folder.
108	
109	For significant changes—those that modify the service's behavior, add new command-line options, or restructure the package—a design review with the team lead is required before you submit the pull request. Post a design proposal in the team's documentation system and wait for sign-off before you begin implementation.
110	
111	
112	Commit Message Style
113	--------------------
114	
115	All commits to the repository must follow a specific message format. The commit-message-style.md page (version v1.2.3, owned by Tooling Guild, last updated 2024-05-15) documents the full requirements. Here is a summary:
116	
117	Each commit message has a single-line subject (50 characters or less) followed by a blank line and a detailed body (wrapped at 72 characters). The subject uses the imperative mood—write "Add feature" instead of "Added feature"—and does not end with a period.
118	
119	Example structure:
120	
121	    Fix quoting bug in command-line argument parsing
122	    
123	    The service incorrectly handled quoted arguments when parsing

Repository Layout
================

Title: Repository Layout
Version: 1.5
Owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)
Last updated: 2024-09-30
Summary: Outlines the top-level directories of the repository and explains where command line, service, and shared code live.


Overview
--------

The auditlog repository is organized to separate concerns between the package, its service component, documentation, and development tooling. This page describes the physical layout of the repository root and the purposes of each directory, along with guidelines for onboarding to the project. It assumes you have already cloned the repository and can access it from your workstation.

The repository root contains the auditlog/ package directory alongside supporting folders for scripts, documentation, and configuration files. There is no src/ layout; the package lives at the top level.


Top-Level Directory Structure
------------------------------

**auditlog/** — The main package directory. Contains all code that implements the command-line interface and the loopback HTTP service. The package uses only the standard library and has no external dependencies. This directory is what gets installed when you run installation commands during setup.

**docs/** — Documentation files for end users and operations staff. Contains guides for installing the service on different platforms, HTTP request examples, and database format specifications. Not intended for developer onboarding; see the developer-handbook/ folder instead.

**developer-handbook/** — Internal documentation for team members working on the package. This folder contains this file along with sibling pages covering workstation setup, Python version requirements, editor configuration, code review practices, commit message conventions, and coding standards. Owned by the Core Services team.

**scripts/** — Utility scripts used by developers and CI systems. Includes scripts for running the service locally, building distributions, and checking code against project standards. Most scripts are shell scripts written for both Bash and PowerShell environments.

**config/** — Configuration file templates and examples. Contains SQLite journal settings used by the package when creating the database file, and example configurations for the service's loopback socket binding. Not all of these files are used during normal development.

**Checks/** — Verification suites and helper scenarios. Organized by module within the package. (See the separate evaluation documentation for details.)


Workstation Setup — Section Owner: Developer Experience (Theo Vance)
-------------------------------------------------------------------

Before you begin contributing to auditlog, your workstation must be configured with Python, Git, and a text editor. A full walkthrough is available in the workstation-setup.md page in this folder, updated 2025-06-02.

At a minimum, you need:

- Git 2.30 or later for cloning and working with the repository.
- Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, or 3.12 installed locally. (See supported-python-versions.md for the authoritative list; as of 2024-11-20 the team supports back to 3.9.)
- A text editor or IDE that can be configured for this project. Most of the team uses VS Code, but Vim, Neovim, and PyCharm are also common.
- Virtual environment support. The team uses venv, which comes with Python.

To clone the repository:

    git clone https://github.com/internal-team/auditlog.git
    cd auditlog

To create and activate a virtual environment on Windows (PowerShell):

    python -m venv venv
    .\venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

On Linux or macOS (Bash):

    python3 -m venv venv
    source venv/bin/activate

Once the virtual environment is active, install the package in editable mode:

    pip install -e .

This makes the package importable and ensures that any changes you make to the code are reflected immediately. You can then run both the command-line interface and the service without reinstalling after each edit.


Python Version Support
----------------------

The team currently supports Python 3.9 through 3.12. See the supported-python-versions.md page (version 1.8, last updated 2024-11-20) for detailed information on version-specific behavior and deprecation timelines. The package relies only on standard library modules, so there are no pip dependencies that might restrict version support.

When developing locally, you should verify your changes against at least Python 3.10 and 3.11 before submitting a pull request. The CI system will verify compatibility with all supported versions. If you use an incompatible feature, the linting stage will catch it during code review.


Editor Configuration
--------------------

The team provides configuration files for several common editors to ensure consistent formatting and linting across the repository. See editor-configuration.md (version v2.0.1, last updated 2025-03-09) for complete setup instructions for VS Code, Vim, Neovim, and PyCharm.

A .editorconfig file at the repository root specifies indentation, line ending, and character encoding settings that apply universally. Most editors can read this file automatically; install an EditorConfig extension if yours does not.

For Python-specific linting and formatting, the repository uses two tools:

- **Linter**: Pylint, configured to enforce naming conventions and catch common mistakes.
- **Formatter**: Black, configured to use 88 characters per line and maintain consistency across all Python files.

Both tools are configured in the pyproject.toml file. Running either tool without arguments will use the repository settings.

Before you commit, run the linting and formatting tools to ensure your code meets project standards. The code-review-conventions.md page (version 3.1, owned by Release Engineering, last updated 2025-08-27) requires this as part of the pull request workflow.


Code Review Conventions — Section Owner: Release Engineering (Owen Fitzgerald)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

All changes to the package, documentation, or scripts must pass code review before merging. The branching-and-pull-requests.txt page (version 2.4, last updated 2026-01-22) describes the full workflow. This section covers what reviewers look for when evaluating your changes.

When you open a pull request, at least two reviewers from the Core Services team must sign off on it. Reviewers will check that:

- Your code follows the project's coding style (see coding-style.md, version 4.0).
- Commit messages follow the project's conventions (see commit-message-style.md, version v1.2.3).
- You have not introduced any new external dependencies.
- The linting and formatting tools pass without errors.
- Your changes do not break existing functionality in the CLI or service.

The CI system runs these checks automatically and reports results as a status on the pull request. If the CI status is red, the pull request will not be reviewed until all checks pass. You can run these checks locally using the commands documented in the scripts/ folder.

For significant changes—those that modify the service's behavior, add new command-line options, or restructure the package—a design review with the team lead is required before you submit the pull request. Post a design proposal in the team's documentation system and wait for sign-off before you begin implementation.


Commit Message Style
--------------------

All commits to the repository must follow a specific message format. The commit-message-style.md page (version v1.2.3, owned by Tooling Guild, last updated 2024-05-15) documents the full requirements. Here is a summary:

Each commit message has a single-line subject (50 characters or less) followed by a blank line and a detailed body (wrapped at 72 characters). The subject uses the imperative mood—write "Add feature" instead of "Added feature"—and does not end with a period.

Example structure:

    Fix quoting bug in command-line argument parsing
    
    The service incorrectly handled quoted arguments when parsing
    command-line options. This commit adds proper escaping for both
    single and double quotes, and updates the related documentation
    examples to show correct usage.
    
    Fixes #347

If your commit concerns an issue in the tracking system, include "Fixes #<number>" or "Related to #<number>" in the body.

Commits that are purely routine (such as updating documentation unrelated to a feature or fix) may use "docs:" or "chore:" as a prefix if appropriate. Consult the commit-message-style.md page if in doubt.


Coding Style Guide
------------------

The team maintains a Python coding style guide in coding-style.md (version 4.0, owned by Platform Tools, last updated 2026-02-18). The guide covers naming conventions, docstring formatting, type hints, and code organization. A summary of key points:

- Use snake_case for variable and function names, PascalCase for classes.
- All modules, classes, and public functions must have docstrings in Google style.
- Type hints are required for all public functions and class methods. Private functions may omit them if the type is obvious from context.
- Maximum line length is 88 characters (enforced by Black).
- Imports are organized in three groups: standard library, third-party (none currently), and local. Each group is separated by a blank line.
- Avoid deep nesting; prefer early returns or extracted functions.
- Comments should explain the "why," not the "what." Code should be clear enough that readers understand what it does without additional explanation.

The linting and formatting tools check many of these rules automatically. Some require manual review during code review, such as docstring quality and comment style. Pay close attention to reviewer feedback on these points during your first few pull requests.

1	# Supported Python Versions
2	
3	**Version:** 1.8
4	**Owner:** Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)
5	**Last updated:** 2024-11-20
6	
7	**Summary:** Lists the Python interpreter versions the package currently targets and notes when older versions are dropped from support.
8	
9	This page is part of the `developer-handbook/` set. It is the reference that everyone on the team — from someone setting up a laptop for the first time to a reviewer deciding whether a pull request can merge — should check when a question comes up about "does auditlog still run on 3.9?" or "can I use this newer syntax yet?"
10	
11	## Purpose and Audience
12	
13	auditlog is a small package that relies only on the standard library, and it is meant to run comfortably on whatever interpreter a workstation, a build node, or a lightweight host already has installed. Because we don't pull in third-party runtime dependencies, our interpreter support window is really the single biggest constraint on what syntax and standard-library features contributors are allowed to reach for.
14	
15	This page is aimed at:
16	
17	- New contributors setting up a workstation for the first time.
18	- Reviewers checking whether a change is safe to merge against the oldest interpreter we still support.
19	- Anyone deciding whether it's time to raise the minimum version or add a newer one.
20	
21	If you're looking for general environment setup instead of version-specific guidance, start with Workstation Setup and come back here once you need to pick an actual interpreter number.
22	
23	## Currently Supported Interpreter Versions
24	
25	**Section owner:** Core Services — Priya Nandakumar
26	
27	| Interpreter | Status | Notes |
28	|---|---|---|
29	| Python 3.9 | Supported (minimum) | Oldest interpreter the package must still run on. |
30	| Python 3.10 | Supported | No known constraints. |
31	| Python 3.11 | Supported, recommended | What most of Core Services runs locally. |
32	| Python 3.12 | Supported | Added after the interpreter compatibility workflow was extended. |
33	
34	The package does not currently promise anything for interpreters outside this table. If you're running something newer on your workstation because it shipped with your operating system, that's fine for day-to-day editing, but don't assume it's covered until it appears in the table above.
35	
36	Python 3.9 is the floor. We do not accept changes that require anything introduced after 3.9 unless the change also raises the minimum version documented here — see [Deprecation Schedule and Dropping Older Versions](#deprecation-schedule-and-dropping-older-versions) below for how these are determined and documented.
37	
38	## Support Window Rules
39	
40	A few rules govern how this table changes over time:
41	
42	1. **Minimum version** is the oldest interpreter any contributor is expected to keep the package running on. Nothing in `auditlog/` may use a language feature or standard-library addition that postdates the minimum.

44	3. **Upper bound** is soft. We don't cap how new an interpreter you can develop against, but the compatibility workflow only exercises the versions listed in the table, so anything newer is unverified rather than unsupported.
45	4. A version is only removed from the table in the same change that raises the documented minimum — see the deprecation section.

47	There is no fixed calendar cadence for dropping old interpreters. We generally wait until an interpreter has stopped receiving maintenance updates from upstream, or until keeping it around would block a standard-library feature the team wants to lean on.
48	
49	## Bringing a Workstation Up to a Supported Interpreter
50	
51	**Section owner:** Developer Experience — Theo Vance
52	
53	Most contributors manage interpreters with `pyenv` rather than relying on whatever ships with the operating system. This keeps the version you build against explicit instead of implicit.
54	
55	On macOS or Linux:
56	
57	```
58	brew install pyenv
59	pyenv install 3.11.9
60	pyenv global 3.11.9
61	pyenv versions
62	```
63	
64	`pyenv versions` should show 3.11.9 marked with an asterisk once the global default is set. If you need to keep an older interpreter around for a quick check, install it alongside rather than replacing your default:
65	
66	```
67	pyenv install 3.9.19
68	pyenv local 3.9.19
69	```
70	
71	Running `pyenv local` inside the repository writes a `.python-version` file into your working copy, which overrides the global default for anything you run from that directory. Don't commit that file — it's a personal choice, not a project setting.
72	
73	On Windows, the team standardizes on the official `py` launcher rather than pyenv-win, mostly because pyenv-win has been flaky with our shell configuration in the past. Install Python 3.9 and 3.11 from python.org (check "Add py launcher to PATH" during setup, uncheck "Add python.exe to PATH" so the launcher stays in charge of version selection), then confirm both are visible:
74	
75	```
76	py -0p
77	py -3.11 --version
78	py -3.9 --version
79	```
80	
81	If `py -0p` only shows one interpreter, re-run the 3.9 installer and make sure "py launcher" was selected as a component — this is the single most common workstation setup mistake reported to Core Services.
82	
83	A quick sanity check once an interpreter is installed:
84	
85	
86	This confirms both that the interpreter is on your `PATH` under the name you expect, and that its bundled `sqlite3` module can actually open the SQLite library your operating system ships — the package's on-disk records depend on that module being present and working.

88	## Creating a Pinned Virtual Environment

90	**Section owner:** Tooling Guild — Ines Bakker

92	Once the interpreter itself is installed, create a virtual environment tied to a specific version rather than whatever `python` happens to resolve to that day:
93	
94	```
95	python3.11 -m venv .venv
96	source .venv/bin/activate      # macOS/Linux
97	.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1     # Windows PowerShell
98	python --version
99	```

103	If you regularly switch between the minimum-supported interpreter and the recommended one, it's worth keeping two environments side by side rather than tearing one down each time:

105	- `.venv-3.9/` — minimum-version environment, used before opening a pull request to confirm nothing newer crept in.
106	- `.venv-3.11/` — day-to-day environment.

108	Fuller detail on environment tooling and package pinning lives on Virtual Environments and Dependency Management; this page only covers the version-selection piece.

112	**Section owner:** Developer Experience — Callum Reyes
113	
114	Whatever editor you use, point it at the virtual environment's interpreter explicitly rather than letting it guess. For VS Code, add this to `.vscode/settings.json` (not committed — it's workstation-specific):

116	```
117	{
118	  "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python",

120	}
121	```

123	Setting `python.analysis.pythonVersion` to the minimum supported version, rather than whatever interpreter you happen to be running, is deliberate — it makes the editor flag syntax that wouldn't run on 3.9 while you're still typing, instead of a reviewer catching it later.

130	
131	**Section owner:** Platform Tools — Mara Olsen
132	
133	Because the minimum supported interpreter lags the recommended one, a few language features are off-limits even though they'd work fine on most contributors' machines:
134	
135	- **Structural pattern matching** (`match`/`case`) requires 3.10 and is not usable until the documented minimum reaches 3.10. It currently doesn't.
136	- **Parenthesized context managers** across multiple lines also require 3.10.

138	- **Union types written with `|`** in annotations (`int | None` instead of `Optional[int]`) require 3.10 for runtime evaluation, though they're fine inside string annotations or under `from __future__ import annotations` on 3.9. 150

160	**Section owner:** Tooling Guild — Ines Bakker
161	
162	Changes that touch the supported version list follow the same conventional-style prefixes as the rest of the repository (see Commit Message Style for the full set), but with a consistent `python` label so these commits are easy to find later:

164	```
165	chore(python): add 3.12 to the supported interpreter list

168	```
