171	
172	* The subject line should name the version number, not just say "update supported versions" — someone scanning `git log --oneline` should be able to tell what changed without opening the commit.

177	
178	**Section owner:** Core Services — Priya Nandakumar
179

181	|---|---|---|

194	```

218	## Terminology
219	
220	**Interpreter** — The specific build of Python (for example, CPython 3.11.9) that executes the package's code. "Version" and "interpreter" are used somewhat interchangeably on this page.
221	
222	**CPython** — The reference implementation of Python maintained by the Python Software Foundation. Unless stated otherwise, every version number on this page refers to a Cpython build.
223	
224	**Virtual environment** — An isolated directory containing its own interpreter link and installed packages, created with the standard library's `venv` module (or `virtualenv` for older interpreters).
225	
226	**Minimum supported version** — The oldest interpreter the package is required to keep running on; currently Python 3.9.
227

229

231	
232	**Shim** — A thin wrapper `pyenv` installs on your `PATH` in place of a real interpreter binary, which resolves to the correct version based on `.python-version` or the global default.

234	**Lockfile** — A file recording the exact versions of development tools installed alongside the interpreter, so a workstation setup can be reproduced later. See Dependency Management for how the team's lockfile is structured.
235	
236	**Loopback interface** — The local-only network interface (`127.0.0.1`) the package's HTTP service binds to. Mentioned here only because interpreter version can occasionally affect the standard-library networking module's defaults.

238	**Byte-compiled cache** — The `__pycache__` directories the interpreter writes alongside source files. Switching interpreter versions without clearing this cache has occasionally caused confusing stale-import errors during onboarding.
239	
240	**PEP** — A Python Enhancement Proposal; the numbered documents that describe new language or standard-library features and the version in which they land.

245	|---|---|
246	| `pyproject.toml` | Declares the package's minimum interpreter requirement and build metadata. |

251	| `docs/developer-handbook/` | The folder containing this page and its sibling pages. |

271	- **2022-02-01 — Version 1.2** — Initial recommendation of pyenv for workstation interpreter management; dropped Python 3.6.
272

# Supported Python Versions

**Version:** 1.8
**Owner:** Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)
**Last updated:** 2024-11-20

**Summary:** Lists the Python interpreter versions the package currently targets and notes when older versions are dropped from support.

This page is part of the `developer-handbook/` set. It is the reference that everyone on the team — from someone setting up a laptop for the first time to a reviewer deciding whether a pull request can merge — should check when a question comes up about "does auditlog still run on 3.9?" or "can I use this newer syntax yet?"

## Purpose and Audience

auditlog is a small package that relies only on the standard library, and it is meant to run comfortably on whatever interpreter a workstation, a build node, or a lightweight host already has installed. Because we don't pull in third-party runtime dependencies, our interpreter support window is really the single biggest constraint on what syntax and standard-library features contributors are allowed to reach for.

This page is aimed at:

- New contributors setting up a workstation for the first time.
- Reviewers checking whether a change is safe to merge against the oldest interpreter we still support.
- Anyone deciding whether it's time to raise the minimum version or add a newer one.

If you're looking for general environment setup instead of version-specific guidance, start with Workstation Setup and come back here once you need to pick an actual interpreter number.

## Currently Supported Interpreter Versions

**Section owner:** Core Services — Priya Nandakumar

| Interpreter | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Python 3.9 | Supported (minimum) | Oldest interpreter the package must still run on. |
| Python 3.10 | Supported | No known constraints. |
| Python 3.11 | Supported, recommended | What most of Core Services runs locally. |
| Python 3.12 | Supported | Added after the interpreter compatibility workflow was extended. |

The package does not currently promise anything for interpreters outside this table. If you're running something newer on your workstation because it shipped with your operating system, that's fine for day-to-day editing, but don't assume it's covered until it appears in the table above.

Python 3.9 is the floor. We do not accept changes that require anything introduced after 3.9 unless the change also raises the minimum version documented here — see [Deprecation Schedule and Dropping Older Versions](#deprecation-schedule-and-dropping-older-versions) below for how these are determined and documented.

```

If you don't keep a second environment around, `pyenv shell 3.9.19` followed by a fresh `venv` works just as well for a one-off check. The point is to actually run the interpreter, not just read its version number — some standard-library behavior differs subtly between 3.9 and 3.11 even where the syntax is identical.

## Terminology

**Interpreter** — The specific build of Python (for example, CPython 3.11.9) that executes the package's code. "Version" and "interpreter" are used somewhat interchangeably on this page.

**CPython** — The reference implementation of Python maintained by the Python Software Foundation. Unless stated otherwise, every version number on this page refers to a Cpython build.

**Virtual environment** — An isolated directory containing its own interpreter link and installed packages, created with the standard library's `venv` module (or `virtualenv` for older interpreters).

**Minimum supported version** — The oldest interpreter the package is required to keep running on; currently Python 3.9.

**Recommended version** — The interpreter new contributors are pointed toward for day-to-day work; currently Python 3.11.

**Compatibility workflow** — The automated configuration that exercises the package under each version in the supported table on every pushed branch.

**Shim** — A thin wrapper `pyenv` installs on your `PATH` in place of a real interpreter binary, which resolves to the correct version based on `.python-version` or the global default.

**Lockfile** — A file recording the exact versions of development tools installed alongside the interpreter, so a workstation setup can be reproduced later. See Dependency Management for how the team's lockfile is structured.

**Loopback interface** — The local-only network interface (`127.0.0.1`) the package's HTTP service binds to. Mentioned here only because interpreter version can occasionally affect the standard-library networking module's defaults.

**Byte-compiled cache** — The `__pycache__` directories the interpreter writes alongside source files. Switching interpreter versions without clearing this cache has occasionally caused confusing stale-import errors during onboarding.

**PEP** — A Python Enhancement Proposal; the numbered documents that describe new language or standard-library features and the version in which they land.

## Repository Files and Paths

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `pyproject.toml` | Declares the package's minimum interpreter requirement and build metadata. |
| `auditlog/` | The package directory; its code must remain compatible with every interpreter listed in the supported table above. |
| `requirements/dev.txt` | Pinned versions of the workstation tooling listed in the table below. |
| `scripts/check-python-version.sh` | Shell helper that compares the active interpreter against the documented minimum. |
| `.github/workflows/interpreter-matrix.yml` | Workflow configuration that exercises the package against each supported interpreter on every pushed branch. |
| `docs/developer-handbook/` | The folder containing this page and its sibling pages. |

## Tools and Package Versions

| Tool | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| pyenv | 2.4.10 | Manages multiple installed interpreter versions on a workstation. |
| CPython | 3.9.19, 3.11.9, 3.12.6, 3.13.1 | Reference implementation builds used across the supported table and the compatibility workflow. |
| pip | 24.2 | Installs development tooling into the virtual environment. |
| virtualenv | 20.26.3 | Fallback environment creator for interpreters older than the improvements in the built-in `venv`. |
| build | 1.2.1 | Produces the wheel and source distribution during packaging checks. |

## Change Log

- **2024-11-20 — Version 1.8** — Dropped Python 3.8 from the support window; raised the documented minimum to 3.9.
- **2024-06-03 — Version 1.7** — Added Python 3.12 to the supported list after the interpreter compatibility workflow was extended to cover it.
- **2023-12-11 — Version 1.6** — Documented the byte-compiled cache clearing step for developers switching interpreter versions during onboarding.
- **2023-08-22 — Version 1.5** — Clarified that Windows developers must use the `py` launcher for version selection rather than relying on `PATH` order.
- **2023-03-14 — Version 1.4** — Dropped Python 3.7 from the support window.
- **2022-10-05 — Version 1.3** — Added Python 3.11 to the supported list and set it as the recommended version.
- **2022-02-01 — Version 1.2** — Initial recommendation of pyenv for workstation interpreter management; dropped Python 3.6.

## Related Pages

- Developer Handbook Overview
- Workstation Setup
- Editor Configuration
- Virtual Environments
- Dependency Management
- Coding Style Guide
- Code Review Conventions
- Commit Message Style
- Linting and Formatting
- Repository Layout
- Onboarding Checklist

1	Virtual Environments
2	====================
3	
4	**Version:** 2.2  
5	**Owner:** Tooling Guild (Ines Bakker)  
6	**Last updated:** 2024-12-05  
7	**Summary:** Shows contributors how to create and manage an isolated Python environment for building and running the package locally.
8	
9	.. contents::
10	
11	Introduction
12	============
13	
14	This page covers the setup and management of Python virtual environments for contributors to the auditlog package. A virtual environment provides an isolated Python workspace on your machine, preventing conflicts between the package's dependencies and other Python projects you may be working on.
15	
16	Virtual environments are not optional—every developer on the team uses one, and CI systems enforce this practice. If you are new to the repository, start here before reading the Workstation Setup and Dependency Management pages. This guide assumes you have already installed Python on your system; if you have not, refer to workstation-setup.md for OS-specific installation instructions.
17	
18	Setting Up Your First Virtual Environment
19	==========================================
20	
21	*Owner: Tooling Guild (Ines Bakker)*
22	
23	The quickest way to get started is to use Python's built-in `venv` module. This module is included with all supported Python versions and requires no additional installation.
24	
25	Navigate to the root of the auditlog repository:
26	
27	.. code-block:: bash
28	
29	    cd path/to/auditlog
30	
31	Create the virtual environment using the following command. We recommend naming it `venv` for consistency across the team:
32	
33	.. code-block:: bash
34	
35	    python -m venv venv
36	
37	On Windows, if the above command fails with a path-length error, try:
38	
39	.. code-block:: bash
40	
41	    py -m venv venv
42	
43	The `venv` directory will be created in your repository root. **Do not commit this directory to git.** It is already listed in `.gitignore`. The environment directory typically grows to 50–100 MB depending on the Python version and installed packages; this is normal.
44	
45	What actually happens when you run this command: Python creates a new directory structure containing a copy of the interpreter, scripts for activation, and a `site-packages` directory where packages will be installed. All your work in the repository will use this isolated environment, not your system Python.
46	
47	Activating Your Virtual Environment
48	====================================
49	
50	Once created, activate the virtual environment before starting work.
51	
52	**On macOS and Linux:**
53	
54	.. code-block:: bash
55	
56	    source venv/bin/activate
57	
58	**On Windows (PowerShell):**
59	
60	.. code-block:: bash
61	
62	    venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
63	
64	**On Windows (Command Prompt):**
65	
66	.. code-block:: bash
67	
68	    venv\Scripts\activate.bat
69	
70	After activation, your shell prompt should display `(venv)` or similar, indicating the virtual environment is active. All Python commands you run will now use the isolated interpreter and packages from the virtual environment. Your editor will also respect this environment if configured to do so.
71	
72	To deactivate the environment and return to your system Python, simply type:
73	
74	.. code-block:: bash
75	
76	    deactivate
77	
78	Some developers like to deactivate at the end of the day or when switching projects; others leave it active in a dedicated terminal. There is no penalty for keeping it active.
79	
80	Python Version Selection and Verification
81	=====================================
82	
83	*Owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)*
84	
85	The auditlog package is verified to work on Python 3.8 through 3.12. Do not use Python 2 or versions earlier than 3.8. The Core Services team publishes the definitive list on the supported-python-versions page; if there is any conflict between this page and that one, defer to the supported-python-versions page.
86	
87	When creating a virtual environment, the default Python version on your system will be used. If you need a different version, specify it at creation time:
88	
89	.. code-block:: bash
90	
91	    python3.10 -m venv venv-py310
92	    python3.8 -m venv venv-py38
93	
94	Developers should verify they are checking against at least two supported versions locally before submitting a pull request. The CI pipeline checks all six versions automatically, but local checks are much faster and catch subtle version-specific issues early. On systems with multiple Python installations (common on macOS with Homebrew or on Linux with `pyenv`), use `python --version` to check which interpreter is active before creating your virtual environment.
95	
96	**Note:** The supported-python-versions page mentions that Python 3.13 support is "planned for Q4 2025," but active development of 3.13 support is still in progress. Do not create virtual environments using Python 3.13 for development work at this time. It may be available on the next major release.
97	
98	Installing Dependencies
99	=======================
100	
101	Once your virtual environment is activated, install the package and its development dependencies. The repository includes a `requirements.txt` file and a `requirements-dev.txt` file in the root directory.
102	
103	First, upgrade pip itself to the latest version:
104	
105	.. code-block:: bash
106	
107	    pip install --upgrade pip
108	
109	Then install development dependencies:
110	
111	.. code-block:: bash
112	
113	    pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
114	
115	This single command installs all development tools (linters, formatters, documentation generators) plus the base package dependencies listed in `requirements.txt`, since `requirements-dev.txt` includes a reference to it.
116	
117	Verify installation by checking that the package can be imported:
118	
119	.. code-block:: bash
120	
121	    Run Python on the command line with a one-liner to import the auditlog package and print its version number.
122	
123	If successful, you should see a version number. If you see an import error, check that your virtual environment is activated (the prompt should show `(venv)`) and that the installation completed without errors. Look for any "ERROR" or "FAILED" messages in the pip output.
124	
125	The dependency-management page contains detailed guidance on adding, updating, or removing dependencies. Do not modify requirements files by hand; follow the peer-review process outlined there.
126	
127	Virtual Environment Maintenance and Cleanup
128	============================================
129	
130	Your virtual environment should be treated as a temporary, recreatable artifact. If you find yourself with stale packages, conflicting versions, or other issues, the safest approach is to remove and recreate it.
131	
132	To remove your virtual environment:
133	
134	.. code-block:: bash
135	
136	    rm -rf venv
137	
138	On Windows:
139	
140	.. code-block:: bash
141	
142	    rmdir /s /q venv
143	
144	After removing it, simply recreate it using the steps in the "Setting Up Your First Virtual Environment" section and reinstall dependencies. There is no data loss; all your code changes are tracked in git.
145	
146	Some developers prefer to use this approach regularly—for example, at the start of each sprint or after pulling a major update to the requirements files. Others maintain the same environment for months and rarely remove it. There is no penalty for doing so; a fresh environment is recreated in under a minute on most systems.
147	
148	A minor inconsistency: the dependency-management page recommends removing and recreating weekly, while many of us do it only when needed. Use your judgment based on how often dependencies change.
149	
150	Editor and IDE Integration
151	===========================
152	
153	*Owner: Developer Experience (Callum Reyes)*
154	
155	Most editors and IDEs can be configured to use your virtual environment as the Python interpreter for linting, code completion, intellisense, and integrated terminals.
156	
157	**Visual Studio Code (VSCode):**
158	
159	After creating your virtual environment, VSCode typically detects it automatically when you open the folder. If it does not appear in the interpreter dropdown (click the Python version in the bottom right), open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P) and search for "Python: Select Interpreter." Choose the interpreter from the `venv/bin` (or `venv\Scripts` on Windows) directory.
160	
161	Once selected, the integrated terminal will automatically activate the virtual environment when you open a new terminal window.
162	
163	**PyCharm:**
164	
165	Go to **File → Settings → Project: auditlog → Python Interpreter**. Click the gear icon in the top right of the interpreter dropdown, select **Add**, then choose **Existing Environment** and navigate to the interpreter inside your venv directory. On Windows, this is usually `venv\Scripts\python.exe`. On Unix-like systems, it is `venv/bin/python`.
166	
167	PyCharm will also configure the integrated terminal to use this environment automatically.
168	
169	**Vim / Neovim:**
170	
171	If you are using Vim with a Python language server (such as pylsp or pyright), ensure the server is run with your virtual environment activated, or configure it to use the full path to the interpreter:
172	
173	- Path on Unix-like systems: `/path/to/auditlog/venv/bin/python`
174	- Path on Windows: `C:\path\to\auditlog\venv\Scripts\python.exe`
175	
176	For pylsp specifically, you can pass the interpreter path in your language server configuration. Refer to the editor-configuration page for detailed per-editor setup, including linting and formatting configurations.
177	
178	Code Review, Commit Messages, and Coding Style
179	===============================================
180	
181	When you open a pull request, reviewers will check that:
182	
183	1. Your changes follow the coding style guide (see coding-style.md);
184	2. Your commit messages follow the required format (see commit-message-style.md);
185	3. Your code passes linting and formatting checks in the CI pipeline.
186	
187	All of these checks can be run locally in your virtual environment before pushing to save review cycles. Refer to code-review-conventions.md and linting-and-formatting.md for details on running checks locally.
188	
189	Commit messages must include a descriptive subject line and, for anything beyond trivial changes, a body explaining the reasoning behind the change. The Tooling Guild maintains the commit-message-style.md guide; some teams use conventional commit format, but the auditlog repository uses a simpler style. See commit-message-style.md for examples.
190	
191	Code style is enforced by automated linting tools installed in your development dependencies. Run these tools locally before committing to catch style issues early.
192	
193	Working with Multiple Virtual Environments
194	===========================================
195	
196	*Owner: Tooling Guild (Ines Bakker)*
197	
198	Some developers prefer to maintain separate virtual environments for different Python versions or long-running feature branches. This is supported and useful for checking cross-version compatibility before the CI pipeline runs, or for keeping experimental dependencies separate from your main development environment.
199	
200	To create multiple environments, simply create each in the repository root with a descriptive name:
201	
202	.. code-block:: bash
203	
204	    python3.8 -m venv venv-py38
205	    python3.10 -m venv venv-py310
206	    python3.12 -m venv venv-py312
207	
208	Each environment is independent. Activate whichever one you need, install dependencies into it, and work normally. To switch between them:
209	
210	.. code-block:: bash
211	
212	    deactivate
213	    source venv-py310/bin/activate
214	
215	Or on Windows:
216	
217	.. code-block:: bash
218	
219	    deactivate
220	    venv-py310\Scripts\Activate.ps1
221	
222	To avoid confusion about which environment is active, many developers add comments to their shell startup files, customize their terminal tab title, or use a shell prompt customization that displays the active environment name (most shells show this by default, but you can customize it further).
223	
224	Do not commit any of these directories to the repository; they are all local to your machine.
225	
226	Troubleshooting Virtual Environment Issues
227	===========================================
228	
229	**Problem: "python: command not found" on macOS or Linux**
230	
231	This usually means Python is not in your system PATH, or a Python version is not installed. Try:
232	
233	.. code-block:: bash
234	
235	    python3 -m venv venv
236	
237	If that fails, check that Python 3 is installed by running `python3 --version`. If you see "command not found," install Python using Homebrew (macOS):
238	
239	.. code-block:: bash
240	
241	    brew install python@3.10
242	
243	Or on Linux, use your system package manager. Refer to workstation-setup.md for OS-specific installation instructions.
244	
245	**Problem: Virtual environment activation does not work on Windows**
246	
247	PowerShell may block execution of the activation script due to its default execution restrictions. Run this command once in PowerShell (as your regular user, not with elevated access):
248	
249	.. code-block:: bash
250	
251	    Run a PowerShell command to set the execution restrictions for the current user to allow local and verified remote scripts.
252	
253	Then try activating again. If you continue to see errors, use Command Prompt instead of PowerShell, or use Git Bash if you have it installed.
254	
255	**Problem: Packages installed in the virtual environment are not found**
256	
257	Verify that your virtual environment is activated by checking that `(venv)` or similar appears in your shell prompt. If it does not, activate it again using the activation script for your OS. Then check that you installed the dependencies:
258	
259	.. code-block:: bash
260	
261	    pip list
262	
263	If the expected packages are missing, run `pip install -r requirements-dev.txt` again. If pip reports that the packages are already installed, but your code still cannot find them, your shell or editor may still be using the system Python. Close and reopen your terminal or editor.
264	
265	**Problem: Import errors when running code**
266	
267	Ensure you are using the Python interpreter from the virtual environment, not the system Python. Check which interpreter is in use:
268	
269	.. code-block:: bash
270	
271	    which python
272	
273	On Windows:
274	
275	.. code-block:: bash
276	
277	    where python
278	
279	The path should include `venv`. If it does not (for example, it shows `/usr/bin/python` on Unix or `C:\Python\python.exe` on Windows), your virtual environment is not activated. Activate it again.
280	
281	**Problem: Access denied when activating on macOS or Linux**
282	
283	If you see "Access denied," the activation script is not marked as executable. Fix this with:
284	
285	.. code-block:: bash
286	
287	    chmod +x venv/bin/activate
288	
289	Then try activating again.
290	
291	**Problem: Virtual environment created with the wrong Python version**
292	
293	If you created a venv with Python 3.8 but meant to use 3.10, simply remove and recreate it:
294	
295	.. code-block:: bash
296	
297	    rm -rf venv
298	    python3.10 -m venv venv
299	    pip install --upgrade pip
300	    pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
301	
302	Files and Paths Referenced
303	===========================
304	
305	The following files and directories in the repository are relevant to virtual environment setup and management:
306	
307	+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
308	| Path                              | Purpose                                                    |
309	+===================================+======================================================================+
310	| `venv/`                           | Virtual environment directory (created locally, not          |
311	|                                   | committed). Created with `python -m venv venv`.              |
312	+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
313	| `venv/bin/` (Unix-like systems)   | Contains the Python interpreter, pip, and activation         |
314	|                                   | scripts for Unix-like systems (macOS, Linux).                |
315	+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
316	| `venv/Scripts/` (Windows)         | Contains the Python interpreter, pip, and activation         |
317	|                                   | scripts for Windows.                                         |
318	+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
319	| `.gitignore`                      | Contains `venv/` and other local artifacts, ensuring          |
320	|                                   | virtual environments are not committed to git.               |
321	+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
322	| `requirements.txt`                | Lists the package's core dependencies (those needed to        |
323	|                                   | run auditlog in production).                                 |
324	+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
325	| `requirements-dev.txt`            | Lists development dependencies, including those for          |
326	|                                   | linting, formatting, type checking, and building             |
327	|                                   | documentation. Includes `requirements.txt`.                  |
328	+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
329	| `README.md`                       | Repository overview (quick-start section mentions            |
330	|                                   | virtual environment setup).                                  |
331	+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
332	| `docs/`                           | Documentation source files (built using tools installed      |
333	|                                   | via `requirements-dev.txt`).                                 |
334	+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
335	| `scripts/`                        | Utility scripts for development tasks, typically run with    |
336	|                                   | the virtual environment activated.                           |
337	+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
338	
339	Tools, Packages, and Versions
340	=============================
341	
342	The following table lists key tools and their supported versions for virtual environment management and development:
343	
344	+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
345	| Tool / Package               | Supported Ver.   | Notes                                         |
346	+==============================+==================+===============================================+
347	| Python (venv module)         | 3.8 to 3.12      | Built-in; no separate installation needed.    |
348	+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
349	| pip                          | 21.0+            | Upgrade to latest before installing deps.    |
350	+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
351	| setuptools                   | 59.0+            | Usually installed with pip; needed for build. |
352	+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
353	| wheel                        | 0.37.0+          | Optional but recommended for package builds.  |
354	+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
355	| auditlog (package)           | 1.4.2            | The package itself; installed via             |
356	|                              |                  | `requirements-dev.txt`.                       |
357	+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
358	| virtualenv (alternative)     | 20.0+            | Alternative to venv; not required but common. |
359	+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
360	
361	Terminology and Glossary
362	=========================
363	
364	**Virtual Environment (venv)**
365	An isolated Python installation directory created with `python -m venv` that contains its own Python interpreter, scripts, and site-packages directory. Allows multiple projects to use different package versions without conflicts.
366	
367	**Activation**
368	The process of configuring your shell session to use the Python interpreter and packages from a specific virtual environment. Performed via a shell script (e.g., `source venv/bin/activate` on Unix or `venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` on Windows).
369	
370	**Deactivation**
371	The process of exiting a virtual environment and returning to the system Python interpreter. Performed by typing `deactivate` in an active shell session, or closing the terminal.
372	
373	**pip**
374	The Python package installer. Used to download and install packages from the Python Package Index (PyPI) and from local files. Available as a command after Python is installed and remains available inside virtual environments.
375	
376	**Interpreter**
377	The Python executable that runs Python code. Each virtual environment has its own interpreter located in `bin/` (Unix-like systems) or `Scripts/` (Windows). The interpreter is a copy of the system Python used to create the environment.
378	
379	**Site-packages**
380	The directory inside a virtual environment where installed packages are stored. On Unix-like systems: `venv/lib/python3.X/site-packages/`. On Windows: `venv\Lib\site-packages\`. Isolated to the virtual environment; does not affect the system Python.
381	
382	**Dependency**
383	A package that auditlog or its development tools require to function. Listed in `requirements.txt` (core dependencies) or `requirements-dev.txt` (development-only dependencies).
384	
385	**PATH (environment variable)**
386	A list of directories the shell searches for executable programs. When a virtual environment is activated, its `bin/` or `Scripts/` directory is added to the front of PATH, ensuring its Python is used first when you type commands like `python` or `pip`.
387	
388	**Isolation**
389	The separation of a virtual environment from the system Python and from other projects' virtual environments, preventing package version conflicts and accidental breakage of unrelated code or system tools.
390

Virtual Environments
====================

**Version:** 2.2  
**Owner:** Tooling Guild (Ines Bakker)  
**Last updated:** 2024-12-05  
**Summary:** Shows contributors how to create and manage an isolated Python environment for building and running the package locally.

.. contents::

Introduction
============

This page covers the setup and management of Python virtual environments for contributors to the auditlog package. A virtual environment provides an isolated Python workspace on your machine, preventing conflicts between the package's dependencies and other Python projects you may be working on.

Virtual environments are not optional—every developer on the team uses one, and CI systems enforce this practice. If you are new to the repository, start here before reading the Workstation Setup and Dependency Management pages. This guide assumes you have already installed Python on your system; if you have not, refer to workstation-setup.md for OS-specific installation instructions.

Setting Up Your First Virtual Environment
==========================================

*Owner: Tooling Guild (Ines Bakker)*

The quickest way to get started is to use Python's built-in `venv` module. This module is included with all supported Python versions and requires no additional installation.

Navigate to the root of the auditlog repository:

.. code-block:: bash

    cd path/to/auditlog

Create the virtual environment using the following command. We recommend naming it `venv` for consistency across the team:

.. code-block:: bash

    python -m venv venv

On Windows, if the above command fails with a path-length error, try:

.. code-block:: bash

    py -m venv venv

The `venv` directory will be created in your repository root. **Do not commit this directory to git.** It is already listed in `.gitignore`. The environment directory typically grows to 50–100 MB depending on the Python version and installed packages; this is normal.

What actually happens when you run this command: Python creates a new directory structure containing a copy of the interpreter, scripts for activation, and a `site-packages` directory where packages will be installed. All your work in the repository will use this isolated environment, not your system Python.

Activating Your Virtual Environment
====================================

Once created, activate the virtual environment before starting work.

**On macOS and Linux:**

.. code-block:: bash

    source venv/bin/activate

**On Windows (PowerShell):**

.. code-block:: bash

    venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

**On Windows (Command Prompt):**

.. code-block:: bash

    venv\Scripts\activate.bat

After activation, your shell prompt should display `(venv)` or similar, indicating the virtual environment is active. All Python commands you run will now use the isolated interpreter and packages from the virtual environment. Your editor will also respect this environment if configured to do so.

To deactivate the environment and return to your system Python, simply type:

.. code-block:: bash

    deactivate

Some developers like to deactivate at the end of the day or when switching projects; others leave it active in a dedicated terminal. There is no penalty for keeping it active.

Python Version Selection and Verification
=====================================

*Owner: Core Services (Priya Nandakumar)*

The auditlog package is verified to work on Python 3.8 through 3.12. Do not use Python 2 or versions earlier than 3.8. The Core Services team publishes the definitive list on the supported-python-versions page; if there is any conflict between this page and that one, defer to the supported-python-versions page.

When creating a virtual environment, the default Python version on your system will be used. If you need a different version, specify it at creation time:

.. code-block:: bash

    python3.10 -m venv venv-py310
    python3.8 -m venv venv-py38

Developers should verify they are checking against at least two supported versions locally before submitting a pull request. The CI pipeline checks all six versions automatically, but local checks are much faster and catch subtle version-specific issues early. On systems with multiple Python installations (common on macOS with Homebrew or on Linux with `pyenv`), use `python --version` to check which interpreter is active before creating your virtual environment.

**Note:** The supported-python-versions page mentions that Python 3.13 support is "planned for Q4 2025," but active development of 3.13 support is still in progress. Do not create virtual environments using Python 3.13 for development work at this time. It may be available on the next major release.

Installing Dependencies
=======================

Once your virtual environment is activated, install the package and its development dependencies. The repository includes a `requirements.txt` file and a `requirements-dev.txt` file in the root directory.

First, upgrade pip itself to the latest version:

.. code-block:: bash

    pip install --upgrade pip

Then install development dependencies:

.. code-block:: bash

    pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

This single command installs all development tools (linters, formatters, documentation generators) plus the base package dependencies listed in `requirements.txt`, since `requirements-dev.txt` includes a reference to it.

Verify installation by checking that the package can be imported:

.. code-block:: bash

    Run Python on the command line with a one-liner to import the auditlog package and print its version number.

If successful, you should see a version number. If you see an import error, check that your virtual environment is activated (the prompt should show `(venv)`) and that the installation completed without errors. Look for any "ERROR" or "FAILED" messages in the pip output.

The dependency-management page contains detailed guidance on adding, updating, or removing dependencies. Do not modify requirements files by hand; follow the peer-review process outlined there.

Virtual Environment Maintenance and Cleanup
============================================

Your virtual environment should be treated as a temporary, recreatable artifact. If you find yourself with stale packages, conflicting versions, or other issues, the safest approach is to remove and recreate it.

To remove your virtual environment:

.. code-block:: bash

    rm -rf venv

On Windows:

.. code-block:: bash

    rmdir /s /q venv

After removing it, simply recreate it using the steps in the "Setting Up Your First Virtual Environment" section and reinstall dependencies. There is no data loss; all your code changes are tracked in git.

Some developers prefer to use this approach regularly—for example, at the start of each sprint or after pulling a major update to the requirements files. Others maintain the same environment for months and rarely remove it. There is no penalty for doing so; a fresh environment is recreated in under a minute on most systems.

A minor inconsistency: the dependency-management page recommends removing and recreating weekly, while many of us do it only when needed. Use your judgment based on how often dependencies change.

Editor and IDE Integration
===========================

*Owner: Developer Experience (Callum Reyes)*

Most editors and IDEs can be configured to use your virtual environment as the Python interpreter for linting, code completion, intellisense, and integrated terminals.

**Visual Studio Code (VSCode):**

After creating your virtual environment, VSCode typically detects it automatically when you open the folder. If it does not appear in the interpreter dropdown (click the Python version in the bottom right), open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P) and search for "Python: Select Interpreter." Choose the interpreter from the `venv/bin` (or `venv\Scripts` on Windows) directory.

Once selected, the integrated terminal will automatically activate the virtual environment when you open a new terminal window.

**PyCharm:**

Go to **File → Settings → Project: auditlog → Python Interpreter**. Click the gear icon in the top right of the interpreter dropdown, select **Add**, then choose **Existing Environment** and navigate to the interpreter inside your venv directory. On Windows, this is usually `venv\Scripts\python.exe`. On Unix-like systems, it is `venv/bin/python`.

PyCharm will also configure the integrated terminal to use this environment automatically.

**Vim / Neovim:**

If you are using Vim with a Python language server (such as pylsp or pyright), ensure the server is run with your virtual environment activated, or configure it to use the full path to the interpreter:

- Path on Unix-like systems: `/path/to/auditlog/venv/bin/python`
- Path on Windows: `C:\path\to\auditlog\venv\Scripts\python.exe`

For pylsp specifically, you can pass the interpreter path in your language server configuration. Refer to the editor-configuration page for detailed per-editor setup, including linting and formatting configurations.

Code Review, Commit Messages, and Coding Style
===============================================

When you open a pull request, reviewers will check that:

1. Your changes follow the coding style guide (see coding-style.md);
2. Your commit messages follow the required format (see commit-message-style.md);
3. Your code passes linting and formatting checks in the CI pipeline.

All of these checks can be run locally in your virtual environment before pushing to save review cycles. Refer to code-review-conventions.md and linting-and-formatting.md for details on running checks locally.

Commit messages must include a descriptive subject line and, for anything beyond trivial changes, a body explaining the reasoning behind the change. The Tooling Guild maintains the commit-message-style.md guide; some teams use conventional commit format, but the auditlog repository uses a simpler style. See commit-message-style.md for examples.

Code style is enforced by automated linting tools installed in your development dependencies. Run these tools locally before committing to catch style issues early.

Working with Multiple Virtual Environments
===========================================

*Owner: Tooling Guild (Ines Bakker)*

Some developers prefer to maintain separate virtual environments for different Python versions or long-running feature branches. This is supported and useful for checking cross-version compatibility before the CI pipeline runs, or for keeping experimental dependencies separate from your main development environment.

To create multiple environments, simply create each in the repository root with a descriptive name:

.. code-block:: bash

    python3.8 -m venv venv-py38
    python3.10 -m venv venv-py310
    python3.12 -m venv venv-py312

Each environment is independent. Activate whichever one you need, install dependencies into it, and work normally. To switch between them:

.. code-block:: bash

    deactivate
    source venv-py310/bin/activate

Or on Windows:

.. code-block:: bash

    deactivate
    venv-py310\Scripts\Activate.ps1

To avoid confusion about which environment is active, many developers add comments to their shell startup files, customize their terminal tab title, or use a shell prompt customization that displays the active environment name (most shells show this by default, but you can customize it further).

Do not commit any of these directories to the repository; they are all local to your machine.

Troubleshooting Virtual Environment Issues
===========================================

**Problem: "python: command not found" on macOS or Linux**

This usually means Python is not in your system PATH, or a Python version is not installed. Try:

.. code-block:: bash

    python3 -m venv venv

If that fails, check that Python 3 is installed by running `python3 --version`. If you see "command not found," install Python using Homebrew (macOS):

.. code-block:: bash

    brew install python@3.10

Or on Linux, use your system package manager. Refer to workstation-setup.md for OS-specific installation instructions.

**Problem: Virtual environment activation does not work on Windows**

PowerShell may block execution of the activation script due to its default execution restrictions. Run this command once in PowerShell (as your regular user, not with elevated access):

.. code-block:: bash

    Run a PowerShell command to set the execution restrictions for the current user to allow local and verified remote scripts.

Then try activating again. If you continue to see errors, use Command Prompt instead of PowerShell, or use Git Bash if you have it installed.

**Problem: Packages installed in the virtual environment are not found**

Verify that your virtual environment is activated by checking that `(venv)` or similar appears in your shell prompt. If it does not, activate it again using the activation script for your OS. Then check that you installed the dependencies:

.. code-block:: bash

    pip list

If the expected packages are missing, run `pip install -r requirements-dev.txt` again. If pip reports that the packages are already installed, but your code still cannot find them, your shell or editor may still be using the system Python. Close and reopen your terminal or editor.

**Problem: Import errors when running code**

Ensure you are using the Python interpreter from the virtual environment, not the system Python. Check which interpreter is in use:

.. code-block:: bash

    which python

On Windows:

.. code-block:: bash

    where python

The path should include `venv`. If it does not (for example, it shows `/usr/bin/python` on Unix or `C:\Python\python.exe` on Windows), your virtual environment is not activated. Activate it again.

**Problem: Access denied when activating on macOS or Linux**

If you see "Access denied," the activation script is not marked as executable. Fix this with:

.. code-block:: bash

    chmod +x venv/bin/activate

Then try activating again.

**Problem: Virtual environment created with the wrong Python version**

If you created a venv with Python 3.8 but meant to use 3.10, simply remove and recreate it:

.. code-block:: bash

    rm -rf venv
    python3.10 -m venv venv
    pip install --upgrade pip
    pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

Files and Paths Referenced
===========================

The following files and directories in the repository are relevant to virtual environment setup and management:

+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| Path                              | Purpose                                                    |
+===================================+======================================================================+
| `venv/`                           | Virtual environment directory (created locally, not          |
|                                   | committed). Created with `python -m venv venv`.              |
+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| `venv/bin/` (Unix-like systems)   | Contains the Python interpreter, pip, and activation         |
|                                   | scripts for Unix-like systems (macOS, Linux).                |
+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| `venv/Scripts/` (Windows)         | Contains the Python interpreter, pip, and activation         |
|                                   | scripts for Windows.                                         |
+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| `.gitignore`                      | Contains `venv/` and other local artifacts, ensuring          |
|                                   | virtual environments are not committed to git.               |
+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| `requirements.txt`                | Lists the package's core dependencies (those needed to        |
|                                   | run auditlog in production).                                 |
+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| `requirements-dev.txt`            | Lists development dependencies, including those for          |
|                                   | linting, formatting, type checking, and building             |
|                                   | documentation. Includes `requirements.txt`.                  |
+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| `README.md`                       | Repository overview (quick-start section mentions            |
|                                   | virtual environment setup).                                  |
+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| `docs/`                           | Documentation source files (built using tools installed      |
|                                   | via `requirements-dev.txt`).                                 |
+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| `scripts/`                        | Utility scripts for development tasks, typically run with    |
|                                   | the virtual environment activated.                           |
+-----------------------------------+--------------------------------------------------------------+

Tools, Packages, and Versions
=============================

The following table lists key tools and their supported versions for virtual environment management and development:

+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| Tool / Package               | Supported Ver.   | Notes                                         |
+==============================+==================+===============================================+
| Python (venv module)         | 3.8 to 3.12      | Built-in; no separate installation needed.    |
+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| pip                          | 21.0+            | Upgrade to latest before installing deps.    |
+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| setuptools                   | 59.0+            | Usually installed with pip; needed for build. |
+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| wheel                        | 0.37.0+          | Optional but recommended for package builds.  |
+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| auditlog (package)           | 1.4.2            | The package itself; installed via             |
|                              |                  | `requirements-dev.txt`.                       |
+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+
| virtualenv (alternative)     | 20.0+            | Alternative to venv; not required but common. |
+------------------------------+------------------+-----------------------------------------------+

Terminology and Glossary
=========================

**Virtual Environment (venv)**
An isolated Python installation directory created with `python -m venv` that contains its own Python interpreter, scripts, and site-packages directory. Allows multiple projects to use different package versions without conflicts.

**Activation**
The process of configuring your shell session to use the Python interpreter and packages from a specific virtual environment. Performed via a shell script (e.g., `source venv/bin/activate` on Unix or `venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1` on Windows).

**Deactivation**
The process of exiting a virtual environment and returning to the system Python interpreter. Performed by typing `deactivate` in an active shell session, or closing the terminal.

**pip**
The Python package installer. Used to download and install packages from the Python Package Index (PyPI) and from local files. Available as a command after Python is installed and remains available inside virtual environments.

**Interpreter**
The Python executable that runs Python code. Each virtual environment has its own interpreter located in `bin/` (Unix-like systems) or `Scripts/` (Windows). The interpreter is a copy of the system Python used to create the environment.

**Site-packages**
The directory inside a virtual environment where installed packages are stored. On Unix-like systems: `venv/lib/python3.X/site-packages/`. On Windows: `venv\Lib\site-packages\`. Isolated to the virtual environment; does not affect the system Python.

**Dependency**
A package that auditlog or its development tools require to function. Listed in `requirements.txt` (core dependencies) or `requirements-dev.txt` (development-only dependencies).

**PATH (environment variable)**
A list of directories the shell searches for executable programs. When a virtual environment is activated, its `bin/` or `Scripts/` directory is added to the front of PATH, ensuring its Python is used first when you type commands like `python` or `pip`.

**Isolation**
The separation of a virtual environment from the system Python and from other projects' virtual environments, preventing package version conflicts and accidental breakage of unrelated code or system tools.

Changelog
=========

Updated Python 3.13 support note; moved to "planned for Q4 2025" status. Added troubleshooting section for PowerShell execution restrictions on Windows. Clarified activation for Command Prompt vs. PowerShell.

Synchronized supported Python version range with supported-python-versions.md (added 3.12, dropped 3.7). Noted Core Services as authority on version support.

Added editor and IDE integration guidance for VSCode, PyCharm, and Vim/Neovim. Expanded troubleshooting section to cover import errors and access-related issues.

Reorganized sections for clarity and reading flow. Added named section owners. Fixed broken links to sibling pages (code-review-conventions, linting-and-formatting).

**2024-04-10** (v1.8) — Theo Vance  
Clarified virtual environment naming convention as `venv` (lowercase). Added note on removal and recreation as routine maintenance strategy. Documented multiple environment setup.

**2024-02-28** (v1.7) — Ines Bakker  
Initial version. Covered venv creation, activation on multiple operating systems, dependency installation, and basic troubleshooting scenarios.

Related Pages
=============

1	# Workstation Setup
2	
3	**Version:** v1.4.0
4	**Owner:** Developer Experience (Theo Vance)
5	**Last updated:** 2025-06-02
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Overview
10	
11	This page walks a new contributor through preparing a workstation for local work on the auditlog repository — the package directory, the command line front end, and the small loopback HTTP service that reads and writes the local database file. It covers installing the tools you need, cloning a local checkout, choosing and configuring an editor, and the conventions the team expects for commits and reviews. If you are setting up a machine for the first time, start at the top and work down; if you're re-imaging a machine you've used before, the tool version table and the editor snippets are the parts worth re-checking.
12	
13	New contributors should also work through the onboarding checklist in parallel with this page — the two overlap somewhat but the checklist tracks completion, while this page is the how-to reference.
14	
15	## Terminology
16	
17	- **Local checkout** — the copy of the repository you clone onto your own machine, as opposed to the shared copy on the remote.
18	- **Virtual environment** — an isolated Python installation, created with the standard library `venv` module, that keeps this repository's installed packages separate from anything else on your machine.
19	- **Loopback HTTP service** — the small HTTP service the package can run, bound to the loopback interface (127.0.0.1) rather than any outward-facing interface, so it only answers requests made from the same machine.
20	- **Database file** — the local SQLite file the package reads from and writes to; it lives on disk next to wherever you run the package unless you point it somewhere else.
21	- **Linter** — a tool that reads source files and reports style or correctness issues without changing the files.
22	- **Formatter** — a tool that rewrites source files in place to match an agreed layout, so contributors don't argue about spacing or line breaks.
23	- **Commit header** — the first line of a commit message, kept short, summarizing the change.
24	- **Area tag** — a short parenthetical tag in a commit header naming the part of the package a change touches, for example `(cli)` or `(storage)`.
25	- **Pull request** — a proposed set of commits opened against the main branch and reviewed before it is merged.
26	- **EditorConfig file** — the `.editorconfig` file at the repository root that tells compliant editors which indentation and line-ending rules to apply per file type.
27	- **Package manager** — here, `pip`, used inside a virtual environment to install the package and its local development tools.
28	- **Shell profile** — the startup file for your shell (`.bashrc`, `.zshrc`, or a PowerShell profile script) where environment variables and tool activation commands are typically set.
29	
30	## Workstation Prerequisites
31	
32	*Section owner: Theo Vance*
33	
34	Before cloning the repository, confirm your machine has the following:
35	
36	1. A supported operating system — Windows 10 or 11, macOS 13 or newer, or a current Linux distribution with glibc 2.31 or newer.
37	2. Git 2.30 or newer installed and on your `PATH`.
38	3. A supported Python interpreter (see the version table below) installed and on your `PATH`, or available through a version manager such as `pyenv`.
39	4. At least 500 MB of free disk space for a checkout, a virtual environment, and local development tool caches.
40	5. A plain-text editor or IDE — VS Code is the team's default and is covered in detail further down this page.
41	
42	On Windows, install Git for Windows from the official installer and accept the default line-ending settings unless you have a specific reason to change them. On macOS, either install Git via the Xcode Command Line Tools (`xcode-select --install`) or via Homebrew (`brew install git`). On Linux, use your distribution's package manager — for example, `sudo apt install git` on Debian-based systems.
43	
44	Once Git is installed, set your name and the contact you use for commits so that this information is recorded correctly:
45	
46	```
47	git config --global user.name "Your Name"
48	git config --global user.name "Your Name"
49	git config --global init.defaultBranch main
50	```
51	
52	It is also worth setting a default editor for interactive Git operations such as rebases:
53	
54	```
55	git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
56	```
57	
58	## Supported Python Versions
59	
60	*Section owner: Priya Nandakumar*
61	
62	The package only uses the standard library, which keeps the supported range wide, but the team still tracks a minimum and a recommended version so contributors don't drift too far apart.
63	
64	| Python version | Status                                             |
65	|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
66	| 3.8             | No longer installed on any team machine images       |
67	| 3.9             | Minimum supported version                            |
68	| 3.10            | Supported                                            |
69	| 3.11            | Supported                                            |
70	| 3.12            | Supported, recommended for new checkouts             |
71	| 3.13            | Considered for adoption, not yet a default anywhere  |
72	
73	Install Python from the official installer on [python.org](https://www.python.org/) on Windows and macOS, or through your distribution's package manager on Linux. Contributors who work across several branches or need to switch interpreters often often reach for a version manager instead:
74	
75	```
76	# pyenv example
77	pyenv install 3.12.3
78	pyenv local 3.12.3
79	```
80	
81	Confirm the interpreter you'll use before creating a virtual environment:
82	
83	```
84	python --version
85	```
86	
87	If this reports something older than 3.8, install a newer interpreter before continuing — the package's local development tools assume at least that floor even though the package itself has no such requirement.
88	
89	## Cloning and Preparing a Local Checkout
90	
91	*Section owner: Theo Vance*
92	
93	Clone the repository into a working folder of your choosing:
94	
95	```
96	git clone https://github.com/example-org/auditlog.git
97	cd auditlog
98	```
99	
100	The repository root holds the `auditlog/` package directory and `README.md`, along with `docs/` and `scripts/` folders that hold reference material and helper scripts respectively. There is no `src/` layer — the package directory sits directly at the top level.
101	
102	Create a virtual environment next to your checkout so installed tools stay isolated:
103	
104	```
105	python -m venv .venv
106	```
107	
108	Activate it. On macOS and Linux:
109	
110	```
111	source .venv/bin/activate
112	```
113	
114	On Windows, in PowerShell:
115	
116	```
117	.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
118	```
119	
120	With the environment active, upgrade `pip` and install the package along with the local development tools:
121	
122	```
123	pip install --upgrade pip
124	pip install -e ".[dev]"
125	```
126	
127	The team keeps a small helper script for this in `scripts/setup-workstation.ps1` (Windows) and `scripts/setup-workstation.sh` (macOS/Linux) that runs the same steps in order and prints the interpreter version and installed tool versions at the end, so you can compare against the tool table further down this page. Run whichever matches your platform from a freshly cloned checkout:
128	
129	```
130	./scripts/setup-workstation.sh
131	```
132	
133	Once the environment is prepared, confirm the interpreter inside your virtual environment matches what you expect:
134	
135	```
136	python -c "import sys; print(sys.version)"
137	```
138	
139	If you plan to run the local loopback service during local work, note that it will create the database file in your working directory unless you point it elsewhere — keep that in mind if you're switching between checkouts, since stale database files left in an old checkout can be confusing later.
140	
141	## Editor Configuration
142	
143	*Section owner: Callum Reyes*
144	
145	VS Code is the team's recommended editor, currently on version 1.89 or newer, paired with the Microsoft Python extension and Pylance for type-aware completion. Contributors are free to use another editor, but the conventions below (line length, indentation, import ordering) apply regardless of what you use, and most editors can be made to follow them.
146	
147	Recommended VS Code extensions:
148	
149	- Python (ms-python.python)
150	- Pylance (ms-python.vscode-pylance)
151	- EditorConfig for VS Code (editorconfig.editorconfig)
152	- A linter integration extension matching whichever linter the repository uses locally
153	
154	A minimal `.vscode/settings.json` for this repository looks like:
155	
156	```json
157	{
158	    "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python",
159	    "editor.formatOnSave": true,
160	    "editor.rulers": [88],
161	    "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
162	    "files.insertFinalNewline": true
163	}
164	```
165	
166	On Windows, set `python.defaultInterpreterPath` to `${workspaceFolder}\\.venv\\Scripts\\python.exe` instead.
167	
168	The repository's `.editorconfig` file at the root sets shared indentation and line-ending rules that most editors read automatically once the EditorConfig extension (or built-in support) is installed:
169	
170	```
171	root = true
172	
173	[*]
174	indent_style = space
175	indent_size = 4
176	end_of_line = lf
177	charset = utf-8
178	trim_trailing_whitespace = true
179	insert_final_newline = true
180	
181	[*.md]
182	trim_trailing_whitespace = false
183	```
184	
185	If your editor supports format-on-save, turn it on — the team formats on save rather than as a separate manual step, which keeps diffs small and focused on actual content changes.
186	
187	## Code Review Conventions
188	
189	*Section owner: Owen Fitzgerald*
190	
191	Open pull requests against `main` once a change is ready for other eyes, even if it's still small. Contributors generally aim to keep pull requests under about 400 changed lines where practical — larger changes are welcome but tend to sit open longer simply because they take longer to read carefully.
192	
193	A pull request description should cover, at minimum:
194	
195	1. What changed and why, in a sentence or two.
196	2. Any follow-up work you're intentionally leaving for later.
197	3. Anything a reviewer should look at closely — an unusual code path, a rename that touches many files, and so on.
198	
199	Turnaround expectations:
200	
201	| Pull request size (lines changed) | Expected first response |
202	|------------------------------------|--------------------------|
203	| Under 100                          | Same working day         |
204	| 100–400                            | Within one working day   |
205	| Over 400                           | Within two working days  |
206	
207	The team requires at least one sign-off from someone other than the author before a pull request merges; changes touching the loopback service or the database file layer generally get a second pair of eyes from Priya Nandakumar as owner of that area. Reviewers are expected to leave comments as suggestions where the fix is small and obvious, and as open questions where it isn't — avoid rewriting someone's change in a comment thread when a short question would do.
208	
209	Once a reviewer gives the green light, the writer is responsible for merging (using a squash merge by default) rather than the reviewer doing it on their behalf, since the writer is best placed to judge whether any last-minute comments still need handling first.
210	
211	## Commit Message Style
